Now, since it was my intention to add this fragment to the bundle of Letters, I thought it right to dress it in the same style in which it was written, so that I should not seem to take anything away from it or to interpret its sense differently from what its author intended. And so it has come about that this Collection of Letters comes out in a variegated Romance and French language, just as I have taken up the habit of doing, which I now do with you, Illustrious Sir, adorning it in a similarly patterned dress, laying French over Latin. For since I have been a foreigner in England for nearly fifty years, I am almost equally a foreigner and stranger in my native tongue, and I can now unfold my thoughts only with difficulty in the language in which I was brought up in my first years. units.tr: You have no need of the help or favour of fortune to maintain yourself with honour in the illustrious rank you hold in the world. And although you despise what attaches others most, all the advantages of fortune and birth are nevertheless united in your person, and, what is far more valuable, those of grace and piety as well. This is something found in very few people. You also make profession of a religion in which you satisfy yourself by the light you draw from the word of God, from good sense, and from those convincing reasons with which you furnish others, and which I have enjoyed with extreme pleasure for several years, since I have had the honour of knowing you. During that time, Sir, it has not been very difficult for me to make you notice the error of those who have wished to introduce into the world a National Church of Divine Right, and to set up in it a tribunal equal to that of the Pope, or an independent power.

units.tr: But since I am not moved by these considerations, it should not seem strange that I employ the little strength, study and light that God has given me to uphold well this truth, which is abandoned and which they call a new opinion, on the pretext that it has been hidden for some time, and to which they nevertheless wish to deny the grace of novelty that they grant to the philosophy of Mr Descartes. This is no surprise, since, although it has to combat an empty imagination with no foundation, it is nonetheless supported by pomp, brilliance, vanity, display and worldly interests. It is by such means that it has made itself mistress of minds. It has so well adorned itself with reason that it blinds people, to prevent them from discovering the error. Although the truth that I oppose to it is always the same in all my books, so that I have been accused of saying the same thing a hundred times, there are minds just as there are tastes: what is seasoned one way pleases one person and not another. One must give different reasonings for the same thing to try to satisfy everyone. One must do as Aesop did at the feast he gave for his master's friends, where he served only tongues, yet they still passed for different dishes and were found excellent, because of the variety of sauces. I hope likewise that the different turn I give to my hypotheses will help to establish them better among people of good sense, and that they will even find several important points that I have not touched on elsewhere. units.tr: ADMONITIO.

units.la: ADmonebo Lectorem meum de duobus : De uno quidem, quod in limine Epistolæ ad Reverendum virum Petrum Mussardum, affirmo post Salmasium, Episcopatum fuisse pestem, & radicem omnium malorum, tum invexisse Papam in orbem Christianum ; unde Judicium vieum crimini dabitur in Ecclesiam Anglicanam, quæ Episcopatum retinuit, à quo
units.tr: I will warn my reader about two things. The first is what I affirm at the beginning of the Epistle to the Reverend Mr Pierre Mussard, following Salmasius: that episcopacy was a plague and the root of all evils, and that it introduced the Pope into the Christian world. Hence an adverse judgment on this charge will be passed against the Church of England, which has retained episcopacy, from which

units.la: * quo tamen nullus est ascensus ad Papam, nec ullus metus ab eo Episcopatu ad tyrannidem Papali consimilem. Sed æqui le�concluding
units.tr: from which, however, there is no ascent to the Pope, nor any fear from that episcopacy of a tyranny like the Papal one. But fair-minded

units.la: Admonitio.
units.tr: Admonition.

units.la: id juris sibi vendicat. Neque enim existimo Episcopatum, ut habetur in Anglia de jure humano, esse pestem & radicem omnium malorum: Imo contra puto si quem molitur ascensum, futurum ut non divertat ad Papam, aut in eo, sed in Rege gradum sistat quem Ecclesia Anglicana agnoscit suum Caput: Caeterum sententiam de Episcopatu de Jure Divino habito & retento, crimen esse laesae Majestatis in Anglia, ut me docuit non ita pridem longè Illustrissimus Comes Schafsburiensis in sua Oratione ad Pares regni. Cum enim (inquit) Rex Serenissimus
units.tr: claims that right for itself. For I do not think that episcopacy, as it is held in England by human right, is the pest and root of all evils. On the contrary, I think that if it makes any upward climb, it will not turn aside to the Pope or stop at him, but will halt at the king, whom the English Church acknowledges as its Head. Moreover, that the opinion that episcopacy is held and retained by divine right is a crime of treason in England, as the most illustrious Earl of Shaftesbury taught me not long ago in his speech to the peers of the realm. For, he says, "since the most serene King

units.la: Admonitio.
units.tr: Admonition.

units.la: mus, non solum deleget Episcopis Jurisdictionem in Presbyteros, Ecclesias, Decanum & Capitulum; imo creet sibi Vicarium generalem in Ecclesiasticis de natione laica, ipsi Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi prælatum: quod factum legimus ab Henrico VIII. sed & ubi libet, hosce ab omni servitio exhibendo Episcopis aut Archiepiscopis liberet; peccaret Rex Clementissimus contra jus Divinum; si gratiam faceret cuiquam obsequii in Deum; nam sic posset eximere uxorem è mariti imperio & liberos ab obligatione obsequii, quod Parentibus præstare debent.
units.tr: will not only delegate to the bishops jurisdiction over presbyters, churches, the dean and chapter; indeed he may create for himself a Vicar General in ecclesiastical affairs, a layman set above the Archbishop of Canterbury himself. We read that Henry VIII did this. Moreover, wherever he pleases, he may free these men from all the service owed to bishops or archbishops. The most merciful King would sin against divine law if he granted anyone exemption from obedience to God; for in that way he could take a wife out from under her husband's authority, and children from the obligation of obedience which they owe their parents.

units.la: Admonitio.
units.tr: Admonitio.

units.la: bent. Porro quod affirmavi in Epistola ad Mussardum, non magis in me crimen est quam in magno Theologo Guillielmo Witakero Anglo, cujus sensa & verba, nisi essent tempore priora Salmasianis & meis, viderentur ab eo reposita; Etenim tractatu in Sanderum, ait Episcopatum de Iure Divino assumptum, fuisse remedium ad Schisma, pejus malo, & Papam cum sua Monarchia peperisse. Nec ego sane video, si semel hoc remedium ad schismata, vel tollenda, vel praecavenda admittimus & amplectimur, cur & quomodo est sistendus gradus, donec ad summum Pontificem qui præsit toti Ecclesiæ deveniamus.
units.tr: bent. As for what I affirmed in my letter to Mussardus, the charge lies no more on me than on the great theologian William Whitaker, an Englishman, whose opinions and words would seem to have been borrowed from him, if they were not earlier in time than those of Salmasius and mine. For in his treatise against Sander he says that the episcopate, taken up by divine right, was a remedy for schism, worse than the disease, and gave birth to the Pope with his monarchy. Indeed I certainly do not see, if we once admit and embrace this remedy for removing or preventing schisms, why and how the advance should be halted before we arrive at a supreme Pontiff who presides over the whole Church.

units.la: Alterum est quo submonere lectorem meum debeo, illud est; quod cum Scripta Clarissimi viri Petri Molinæi Canonici Cantuariensis, tum mea, soleant ire in vulgus, ut unius authoris partus; atque inde quæ in uno, aut displicent, aut probantur, alteri imputentur; Ut nolim quicquam detrahi Illi, quem Parentis loco habeo, observo & colo, propter ejus ingentia in me merita, ita velim ab eo distingui, qui me longis spatiis ætatis, longioribus ingenii & eruditionis
units.tr: Another point I must bring to my reader's attention: since the writings of the most distinguished Pierre Du Moulin, canon of Canterbury, as well as my own, tend to circulate among the public as the work of one author, so that what displeases or pleases in one is imputed to the other; just as I would not want anything taken away from him whom I regard in the place of a parent, whom I respect and cherish for his great services to me, so I would want to be distinguished from him by one separated from me by long spans of age, and by much greater talent and learning.

units.la: Admonitio.
units.tr: Admonition.

units.la: ditionis post se relinquit, ne in posterum vir reverendus, alieni peccati, ( si tamen est peccatum) fiat piaculum; vapulando, ut flagrum Ecclesiæ & Divini humanique juris & ordinis eversor, qualem me multi volunt aut prædicant, propter pronunciatum, quod non est fratris, sed meum; verùm à quo plus est periculi Papæ, & toti Romanensi apparatui, quod malè urat Arnaldum Sorbonistam, & ejus judicio sit detestandum; quodque altè imbibi cum veritate Divina concordare, nempe Potestatem Ecclesiastic am & ejus sobolem Excom-
units.tr: ...ditionis leaves behind him, so that in future the reverend man does not become a scapegoat for another's sin (if indeed it is a sin), being beaten as the scourge of the Church and the subverter of divine and human law and order, as many want or proclaim me to be, on account of a statement which is not my brother's but mine. Yet it is more dangerous to the Pope and to the whole Roman apparatus that it harshly burns Arnaldus the Sorbonist and is to be detested by his judgment; and that I have deeply imbibed that it agrees with divine truth, namely that ecclesiastical power and its offspring, Excom-

units.la: Admonitio.
units.tr: Admonitio.

units.la: communicationem, non solúm esse humana figmenta, ut pote à sacra scriptura & ratione abhorrentia, sed & fuisse, esse & futura tamdiu res perniciofissimas Orbi Christiano, quoad Deus liberaverit mentes Regum, Magistratuum & Theologorum istis deliramentis: De quibus ut de totius controversiæ complexu nihil scripsit Frater,sed rem in medio reliquit ; haud dubium tamen in præsenti lite quæ mihi est cum magno & celeberrimo Theologo, non futurùs otiosus spectator, sed calculos positurus, ut id eligat in quo vicerit ratio.
units.tr: that excommunication is not only a human fiction, as being repugnant to Holy Scripture and to reason, but has been, is, and will be most pernicious to the Christian world for as long as God has not delivered the minds of kings, magistrates and theologians from these delusions. Concerning these matters, as concerning the whole complex of the controversy, my brother has written nothing, but has left the question open. Yet there is no doubt that in the present dispute, which I am having with a great and very famous theologian, he will not be an idle spectator, but will cast his own votes, so that he may choose that side in which reason has prevailed.

units.la: Amicissimo Capiti, sed longé Clarissimo & Doctissimo viro D. Petro Mussardo, Pastori Ordinario Ecclesiæ Gallo-Londinensis. S.
units.tr: To my most dear head, but by far most illustrious and learned man, Mr. Peter Mussard, ordinary minister of the Gallo-London church. Greetings.

units.la: PRævideram, vir Præstantissime, non defuturos qui tentarent te flectere ad sequius judicium de sententia mea circa potestatem Ecclesiasticam, hinc odiosè exagitata à pluribus, illinc altissima prædicatione laudata & comprobata à nonnullis. Cujus sententiæ meæ hæc sunt præcipua Capita.
units.tr: I had foreseen, most excellent sir, that there would be no lack of those who would try to turn you to a worse judgment about my opinion on ecclesiastical power, which many have harshly harangued on one side and some have praised and approved with the highest commendation on the other. The principal heads of this opinion of mine are these.

units.la: Usum ipsum, non abusum potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, intulisse Antichristum, hoc est Papam in terras, tum Episcopatum, hoc est, ut ait Salmasius, pestem & radicem omnium malorum, cum in orbem Christianum, tum maximè in Reformatum, atque Protestantes inter se collisisse. Cæterum Potestatem Ecclesiasticam, tam esse deliramentum & figmentum humanum, quam potestas Medica, Chirurgica, fabrilis, &c. Istius autem potestatis chimericæ sobolem excommunicationem, esse merum terriculamentum avium, saltem esse censuram abhorrentem à praxi Ecclesia Judaicæ, nec nixam ulla authoritate sacræ scripturæ, multò minus nomine & authoritate Domini nostri Jesu Christi, aut cujusquam, nisi forsan Calvini, jaculatam & vibratam in caput peccatorum perditorum, quos longa serie recenset, eóque minus, si excommunicatio & traditio satanæ sunt una & eadem res. In quas nostras Δόξας, si non pronior, saltem minus iniquus mihi visus es. Sed cum hacce jucunda opinione me sustentem, futurum ut aliquando nostrer sis, consilium est hâc Epistolâ tibi eximere omnem scrupulum in quo hærere potes.
units.tr: That the use itself, not the abuse, of ecclesiastical power has brought in Antichrist, that is, the Pope, upon the earth, and then the episcopate, which Salmasius calls the plague and root of all evils, and has set Christians against one another, both throughout the Christian world and especially among the Reformed and Protestants. Moreover, ecclesiastical power is as much a human fiction and invention as medical, surgical, smithing power and so on. Excommunication, the offspring of this chimerical power, is pure bugbear for birds; at the least it is a censure foreign to the practice of the Jewish Church, and not founded on any authority of Holy Scripture, much less on the name and authority of our Lord Jesus Christ or of anyone, except perhaps Calvin, hurled and brandished against the heads of the wicked and ruined sinners whom he recounts in a long list; and so much the less so if excommunication and the delivery to Satan are one and the same thing. In these opinions of ours, if you were not more inclined, you seemed at least less unfair to me. But since I hold myself up with this pleasant hope, that you will someday be one of us, I have resolved by this letter to remove from you every scruple on which you may hang back.

units.la: Dicis, cum Ecclesia non sit (sicut reliquæ societates hominum) arbitraria, quæ haberi & omitti possit, sed impeimperata jure Divino, tum necèssaria, sine qua salus obtineri nequit, par esse ut potestatem adhibeat ad sui ordinationem & conservationem, quæ non incommodè dici possit Ecclesiastica & Spiritualis, quia independens est à jurisdictione civili.
units.tr: You say that since the Church is not (as other human societies are) something arbitrary that may be kept or dropped, but is commanded by divine right and is necessary, without which salvation cannot be obtained, it is fitting that it should employ a power for its own ordering and preservation, which may not inappropriately be called ecclesiastical and spiritual, because it is independent of civil jurisdiction.

units.la: Respondeo,id verum esse de Ecclesia, ad quam, nec ordo, nec regimen adhibentur, nisi ut frequentes conveniant homines ad audiendum verbum, & participanda sacramenta. In ejusmodi Ecclesia, Reges & Principes juxta, tam tenentur audientes esse, & se morigeros præstare verbo Pastoris, aut potius Dei, quam quivis de plebe: atque eatenus, objectio mihi non ossicit, qui omnem Ecclesiasticam potestatem elimino, non ab ejusmodi Ecclesia, sed à Consistorio, Synodis, & ejusmodi cœtibus, qui tam sunt politici quam conventus juridici.
units.tr: I answer that this is true of a Church to which neither order nor government is applied, except that people gather frequently to hear the Word and partake of the sacraments. In such a Church, kings and princes are bound, no less than the common people, to be hearers and to show themselves obedient to the word of the minister, or rather of God. So far the objection does not trouble me, since I do away with all ecclesiastical power, not in such a Church, but in the consistory, synods, and gatherings of that kind, which are as much political as juridical assemblies.

units.la: Quocirca hæc objectio non valuit ante adventum J. Christi, nec in Ecclesia sub Veteri Testamento, in qua, Ecclesia, à Republica non fuit distincta, in qua omnes synagogæ, societates, confessus virorum, & synedria erant perinde Ecclesiæ, & de omni causa tractabant, cujus norma credendorum & agendorum esset Decalogus,& cujus custodes, seu Rex,seu Principes populi, in quibus erant Sacerdotes, ad finem subordinatum & ultimum juxta collimabant, nempe pacem in terris, & in conscientia,tum salutem animarum, & gloriam Dei. Qui quidem Decalogus cum complexus esset omnis juris, omnium officiorum, & qui recte & appositè in duas tabulas fuit partitus, inficetè & absurdè quædam ejus officia & mandata dicta fuissent civilia, alia Ecclesiastica, ut nonnullorum cognitio esset fori Ecclesiastici, aliorum fori civilis. Quæ quidem divisio Decalogi, potuit esse de fabrica Romanensi,sed non debuit arripi à Protestantibus.
units.tr: Hence this objection did not hold before the coming of Jesus Christ, nor in the Church under the Old Testament, in which the Church was not distinct from the commonwealth; in which all synagogues, societies, assemblies of men, and sanhedrins were equally churches, and dealt with every matter, whose rule of what was to be believed and done was the Decalogue, and whose guardians, whether king or princes of the people, among whom were the priests, aimed at the subordinate and ultimate end, namely peace on earth, and in conscience, the salvation of souls, and the glory of God. Indeed, since the Decalogue embraced all law and all duties, and was rightly and aptly divided into two tables, it would have been silly and absurd to call some of its duties and commands civil and others ecclesiastical, so that the knowledge of some belonged to the ecclesiastical forum and of others to the civil forum. This division of the Decalogue may have been of Roman make, but it ought not to have been seized upon by Protestants.

units.la: Sed par vis argumenti ad astruendam potestatem œconomicam, tam separatam jure Divino à potestate Ecclesiæ, quam Ecclesia separata est à Republica, cùm tamen potestas Patrisfamilias, quæ nec habetur nec derivatur à potestate seculari & summa, illi fit subordinata, quia Respublica & familia, lia, unum conficiunt corpus.
units.tr: But the same force of argument can be brought to establish an economic power, separated by divine right from the power of the Church, as the Church is separated from the commonwealth; yet the power of the head of the household, which is neither had nor derived from the secular and supreme power, is made subordinate to it, because the commonwealth and the household make up one body.

units.la: Nec valet illa objectio in imperio (ut fuit Romanum) & in regno, uti Galliæ & Angliæ, in quo primùm deliberaretur de disciplina Ecclesiastica statuenda, de reditibus Ecclesiasticis, de Decimis, de Pastorum gradibus & officiis, de fide sancta & Apostolica stabilienda publicè, de præmiis & pœnis decerneretur, per quas hæretici & ἄτακτοι, in ordinem cogerentur, de danda licentia cæteris hominum ordinibus qui in modo disciplinæ seorsim ab aliis abeunt, & separatim amant suum habere cultum & modum regiminis. Hic te rogatum velim, statuas quid hic valeat vestra potestas Ecclesiastica, quis ejus usus, & quænam possunt esse Pastorum partes, præterquam conferre vota, preces, consilia, & declarare suam animi sententiam super optima ratione constituendi fidem & disciplinam? & quid concordet cum jure divino, quid ab eo discordet? Jam si non aliter possit se exerere potestas Ecclesiastica, in hocce sectando bono publico necessario, unde pendet pax in terris, fides illibata commendata pluribus, concordia inter omnes ordines hominum qui parent imperio Regis, velim scire cur eadem potestas Ecclesiastica, potiori jure se exeret in ordinandis rebus privatæ Ecclesiæ paucorum duntaxat hominum, quam Ecclesiæ aut Provincialis, aut Nationalis? Annon Decalogus, symbolum Apostolorum, perinde sunt regula credendorum & agendorum & imperandorum in Ecclesia Nationali, in synodo œcumenica, quam in Ecclesia particulari, aut in synedrio constanti xii. aut xiv. capitibus?
units.tr: Nor does that objection hold in an empire (such as Rome was) or in a kingdom, such as France and England, in which it would first be deliberated how ecclesiastical discipline should be established, how church revenues and tithes should be ordered, what grades and duties of ministers there should be, how the holy and apostolic faith should be publicly established, what rewards and penalties should be decreed by which heretics and disorderly persons might be brought into order, and whether to grant permission to other classes of men who, in the manner of discipline, depart separately from others and prefer to have their own worship and form of government apart. Here I would ask you to determine what your ecclesiastical power is worth here, what its use is, and what the parts of the ministers can be, other than to offer vows, prayers, and counsels, and to declare their own opinion on the best way of settling faith and discipline; and what agrees with divine right, and what disagrees with it. Now, if ecclesiastical power cannot otherwise show itself in pursuing this necessary public good, on which peace on earth depends, faith commended unimpaired to many, and concord among all the orders of men who obey the king's rule, I would like to know why that same ecclesiastical power should exert itself with greater right in ordering the affairs of a private church of only a few men, than of a provincial or national Church. Are not the Decalogue and the Apostles' Creed equally the rule of what is to be believed, done, and enjoined in a national Church, in an ecumenical synod, as in a particular church, or in a standing sanhedrin of twelve or fourteen chapters?

units.la: Concidit ergo, & in irritum cadit objectio, ubi sunt ferendæ leges, decernendæ poenæ, censuræ infligendæ, turbones, hæretici, factioli reprimendi, & in ordinem cogendi, sive in Ecclesia Nationali, sive in privata, ubi & utrobique tantopere decantata potestas Ecclesiastica, erit juxta utilis & inutilis.
units.tr: The objection therefore collapses and comes to nothing, where laws must be carried, penalties decreed, censures inflicted, and troublemakers, heretics, and little factions restrained and brought into order, whether in a national Church or in a private one; and there, in both cases, the ecclesiastical power so loudly sung about will be useful or useless alike.

units.la: Quod ad astruendam potestatem Ecclesiasticam, & jus arcendi à sacris impium, allegautur verba J. Christi, ut margaritæ & sancta non abjiciantur ad pedes porcorum. Nihil puto posse dici futilius, nam quid hoc ad tribuendam papastoribus seorsim potestatem Ecclesiasticam distinctam à civili virtute clavium, & potestatis ligandi & solvendi, cùm hoc mandatum Christi, omnes promiscuè attineat? Nam hocce idem imperatum fuit & obtinuit mandatum sub œconomia legali, sub qua nulla erat distinctio Ecclesiæ à Republica, nec potestatis Ecclesiasticæ à Civili, nec verba Christi potius dicta sunt Pastoribus quam cuivis de plebe, ut jam si authoritatem tribuunt pastoribus arcendi à sacris impium, æquo jure concedant privato cuique eundem Anathemate feriendi. Sed nec Sacerdoti nec Levitæ debebatur jurisdictio virtute sacerdotii, & sacræ functionis, sed quatenus uno eodemque jure potiebatur cum Principibus & Judicibus populi. Quod reverendus vir D. Primirofius conatur in commodum sensum trahere diram illam denunciationem in synaxi ante cænam. In nomine & authoritate J. Christi excommunico Idololatras, hæreticos, &c. eamque clausulam mollire mitiori interpretatione, quasi per eam Pastor Evangelicus solum declararet Idololatras, hæreticos, hominesque quoscumque ad vitia projectæ vitæ, indignos esse qui participes fiant sacrorum symbolorum, non puto quemquam Pastorem salvâ conscientiâ, si credit excommunicationem esse figmentum humanum, & perperam fundari in potestate clavium & ligandi & solvendi, quod credidit Calvinus, non puto, inquam, salvâ conscientiâ quemquam totidem verba Calvini repetere posse, illumque sensum hisce adscribere qui plane alius est ab illo quem Calvinus indidit & intellexit. Namque ea fuit mens Calvini, innodare Anathemate illos quos recenset impios, virtute clavium & potestatis ligandi & solvendi, ut ligare sit excommunicare, solvere autem, absolvere. Tum sensuit Calvinus illam excommunicationem, non solum interris, sed & in cælis vim suam habere, tum per eam impium tradi satanæ, unde non possit expediri & liberari præterquam ab illo pastore, aut cœtu qui fulmen illud excommunicationis intorsit in caput ejus. Sane notum est pueris in leges jurari conceptis verbis secundum sensum legislatoris quem aut dedit, aut dare voluit. Quid? quod etiamnum apud te hærere debet, an dominus Jesus contulerit potestatem Pastoribus arcendi à sacris, etiam impios, si quidem nulla inde labes accrescat bonis viris assidentibus, ut testatur Beza, nec ministri partes sint judicare de dignitate aut indignitate communicantis, quandoquidem exprese & diserte Sanctus Paulus jubeat unumquemque seipsum judicare, & de se pronunciare, excutiendo suam propriam conscientiam: sed nec mandatum non communicandi cum impiis, magis infert potestatem Pastoris in impium, eumque anathemate feriendi, hoc est tradendi satanæ, quam actio medici denegantis facere medicinam aut desperato, aut non egenti ope medici, arguit imperium medici in ægrum: Adde quod perperam in synaxi Calvini, excommunicantur Papistæ, seu Idololatræ, nec satis pie, viri boni & sancti, ut sunt Independentes, à communione Protestantium arcentur, quod seorsim suos conventus habeant.
units.tr: As for establishing ecclesiastical power and the right to keep the impious from the sacred things, the words of Jesus Christ are alleged: "Do not cast pearls and holy things before the feet of swine." I think nothing can be said more trifling, for what does this have to do with granting to ministers alone an ecclesiastical power distinct from the civil, by the virtue of the keys and the power of binding and loosing, since this command of Christ concerns all people indiscriminately? For this same command was also given and held under the legal economy, under which there was no distinction between the Church and the commonwealth, nor between ecclesiastical and civil power, and the words of Christ were not spoken to ministers rather than to any common person; so that if they now grant to ministers the authority to keep the impious from the sacred things, they should by equal right concede to each private person the right to strike them with the same anathema. But neither the priest nor the Levite had jurisdiction by virtue of the priesthood and the sacred office, but only insofar as he shared the same right with the princes and judges of the people. This is what the reverend Mr. Primirofius tries to bend into a more convenient sense, that dreadful denunciation at the Communion service before the supper: "In the name and by the authority of Jesus Christ I excommunicate idolaters, heretics, etc." He softens that clause by a milder interpretation, as if through it the evangelical minister merely declared that idolaters, heretics, and whoever else has been cast into vicious living are unworthy to share in the holy symbols. I do not think any minister, if he believes that excommunication is a human fiction and wrongly grounded on the power of the keys and of binding and loosing, which Calvin believed, can, I say, with a clear conscience repeat Calvin's very words while ascribing to them a sense that is plainly different from the one Calvin put into them and understood. For it was Calvin's intention to bind with anathema, by the virtue of the keys and the power of binding and loosing, those impious persons whom he lists, so that to bind means to excommunicate and to loose means to absolve. He also thought that this excommunication has its force not only on earth but also in heaven, and that through it the impious man is delivered to Satan, from whom he cannot be freed or released except by that minister or assembly which hurled that thunderbolt of excommunication upon his head. Certainly it is well known that boys are sworn to laws in words framed according to the sense of the lawgiver, which he either gave or wished to give. What about this, which should still trouble you: whether the Lord Jesus conferred on ministers the power to keep away from the sacred things even the impious, provided that no harm accrues from it to the good men sitting by, as Beza testifies, and that it is not the minister's part to judge the worth or unworthiness of the communicant, since Saint Paul expressly and plainly bids each man to examine himself and pronounce on himself, searching his own conscience? Yet the command not to communicate with the impious implies no more power of the minister over the impious man, and striking him with anathema, that is, delivering him to Satan, than the act of a physician who refuses to give medicine to one who is hopeless or does not need the physician's help proves a physician's rule over the sick man. Add to this that, wrongly, in Calvin's communion service, the Papists, that is, idolaters, are excommunicated, while men who are good and holy, such as the Independents, are kept from communion with the Protestants, though not piously enough, merely because they hold their own separate assemblies.

units.la: Quod spectat utilitates & commoda quæ redundare debent in orbem Christianum, ex ruina potestatis Ecclesiasticæ non solùm in animosChristianorum, imprimis Nationis Sacræ & Magistratuum, sed & in totam οἰκουμένην affirmare audeo pertinaci & obstinata, sed sanctaaffirmatione, non majores utilitates àChristo nato,ex re quaquam malâ repudiatâ, aut re bonâ arrepta, dari, præter cognitionem Christi redemtoris,quàm quæ exurgit ex ruina potestatis Ecclesiasticæ.
units.tr: As for the advantages and benefits which ought to flow to the Christian world from the overthrow of ecclesiastical power, I dare to affirm, with a stubborn and obstinate but holy assertion, not only for the souls of Christians, especially of the Holy Nation and the magistrates, but for the whole οἰκουμένη, that no greater benefits have been given by Christ the Redeemer since his birth, from any bad thing rejected or any good thing seized, than the knowledge of Christ the Redeemer which arises from the overthrow of ecclesiastical power.

units.la: 1. Nam primò, ablata potestate Ecclesiastica, nulla supererit Papæ potestas, præterquam Imperii terreni ædificati in Reges & Nationes, & in Imperio alieno: Non ferent semel exoluti hacce impostura, aut æmulum aut consortem imperii, sed statim jubebunt procul res suas sibi habere: quo exule, concidet, tum Papa, tum totum systema Romanense Ecclesiæ, Religionis, & Hierarchiæ, & unâ Romanensis infallibilitas fabula erit canora illorum auribus, cujus potestatem non reformidant.
units.tr: 1. For first, once ecclesiastical power is taken away, no power of the Pope will remain except that of an earthly empire built upon kings and nations, and upon another's empire. Once freed from this imposture, they will not tolerate a rival or partner in rule, but will at once order him to keep his affairs to himself. With him driven out, both the Pope and the whole system of the Roman Church, its religion and hierarchy, will collapse, and along with it the Roman infallibility will be a pleasant tale to their ears, whose power they no longer dread.

units.la: 2. Secundò ablata potestate Ecclesiastica, liquidò constabit quæ sit vera potestas clavium, & quæ sit potestas ligandi & solvendi per quam in regno J. Christi mediatorio homines transferuntur à regno satanæ ad regnum Dei, à tenebris ad lucem, solvuntur homines vinculis peccati, ut donentur libertate filiorum Dei. Eadem ablatâ statuetur modus potestatis qui debetur ministris Evangelicis, & difflabitur in auras fulmen Excommunicationis, aut non amplius lædet quam bulla ex aqua saponis.
units.tr: 2. Secondly, once ecclesiastical power is taken away, it will be made clear what the true power of the keys is, and what the power of binding and loosing is, by which in the mediatorial kingdom of Christ men are transferred from the kingdom of Satan to the kingdom of God, from darkness to light, and men are loosed from the chains of sin so that they may be given the liberty of the sons of God. With that removed, the manner of power due to the evangelical ministers will be established, and the thunderbolt of excommunication will be blown away into the air, or will hurt no more than a soap bubble.

units.la: 3. Et, cum varii sensus sint Protestantium, & scindantur in partes circa naturam & modum regiminis quem unaquæque Ecclesia sibi adoptat jure Divino & ex institutione J. Christi & Apostolorum, concident omnes illæ lites ad casum potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, tanquam examina apum, ad exigui pulveris jactum, Nam ubique arreptâ illâ sententiâ, J. Christum certam regiminis formam non constituisse, sed permisisse vindicibus ordinis humani statuere de disciplina Ecclesiastica, quæ congruat rationi temporum & hominum, tum sub diverso regimine posse constare fidem illibatam, & charitatem non lacessitam, sed immotam, nulla aut minor erit controversia, circa externa, illa, nec Episcopatus, nec Presbyteratus hinc & inde trahetur ad jus Divinum, ut solemne est.
units.tr: 3. And since the Protestants hold various opinions and are divided over the nature and manner of government which each Church adopts for itself by divine right and by the institution of Christ and the apostles, all those quarrels will collapse with the case of ecclesiastical power, like a swarm of bees at the throwing of a little dust. For once that opinion is seized everywhere, that Christ did not establish a fixed form of government but permitted those who claim the rights of human order to decide on church discipline in a way that suits the circumstances of the times and of men, and that under different forms of government the faith can remain unimpaired and charity unassailed but unshaken, there will be little or no controversy about those external matters, and neither episcopacy nor presbyterate will be dragged here and there to divine right, as is customary.

units.la: 4. Et revera Palmaria erit illa utilitas, valere justa potestate Ecclesiastica, quod post ejus ruinam, nulla amplius erit Lis de Episcopatu, deque illa αὐθεντία Episcopi in Presbyteros, an sit juris humani, an verò Divini; Nam si humani, tum illa praelatio non erit à Christo, sed à Magistratu; ipse Episcopus quâ Episcopus, non reputabitur minister Christi sed Regis, per cujus delegationem Episcopus habet imperium in Presbyteros. At si Divini, illa praelatio erit tantum in volentes: nec in regno Christi mediatorio, Episcopus plus habebit potestatis in Presbyterum, quam Presbyter in Episcopum.
units.tr: 4. And indeed this will be a striking advantage: that with the proper power of the Church gone, after its ruin there will be no further dispute about episcopacy, or about that authority αὐθεντία of the bishop over the presbyters, whether it is of human or of divine right. For if it is of human right, then that prelacy is not from Christ but from the magistrate; the bishop himself, as bishop, will not be regarded as a minister of Christ but of the king, through whose delegation the bishop has authority over the presbyters. But if it is of divine right, that prelacy will extend only to those who are willing; and in the mediatorial kingdom of Christ a bishop will have no more power over a presbyter than a presbyter has over a bishop.

units.la: 5. Jam Episcopatu diruto per ruinam potestatis Ecclesiasticae, eadem ruinâ æternetur Episcopatus Papae, Nam si Episcopo particularis Ecclesiae denegatur praelatio in Presbyteros & populum istius Ecclesiae jure Divino, multò magis denegabitur Episcopo illi, seu Papæ qui se venditat Episcopum universalis Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 5. Now, with episcopacy overthrown by the ruin of ecclesiastical power, the same ruin will also destroy the episcopacy of the Pope. For if by divine right prelacy over the presbyters and people of a particular Church is denied to its bishop, much more will it be denied to that bishop, or Pope, who puffs himself up as bishop of the universal Church.

units.la: Par utilitas ex ruina potestatis Ecclesiasticæ accedet, controversiis enodandis, circa electionem, & ordinationem pastorum, nec electio pertinebit ad Episcopum, nec ad synodum, sed ad unamquamque Ecclesiam particularem, nec ordinatio erit actus aut collatio potestatis quam revera non habet ordinans,sed testificatio vocationis Divinæ, & oratio ad Deum, ut benedicat electioni Pastoris factæ ab Ecclesia, in qua electione non opus est potestate Ecclesiastica, sed eâ quæ est de jure naturali divino communi omni Societati.
units.tr: An equal advantage will follow from the ruin of ecclesiastical power in settling controversies about the election and ordination of ministers: the election will belong neither to the bishop nor to the synod, but to each particular congregation; and ordination will be neither an act nor a conferring of power which the ordainer in truth does not have, but a testimony to the divine calling, and a prayer to God that he bless the choice of the minister made by the Church. In that election no ecclesiastical power is needed, but only that which belongs by divine natural law to every society.

units.la: 7. Pariter post amotam potestatem Ecclesiasticam, depositio non erit potestatis illius productio, sed mera declaratio & testificatio, quod Ecclesia nolit ulterius uti ministerio hujus aut illius, Nam injusta est illa occupatio, tyrannidi propior & consimilis fulmini excommunicationis, per quam ut excommunicationis vis se in totum orbem diffundit, ita vis depositionis & exauthorationis per quam depulsus à privata Ecclesia, extorris est Ecclesiæ Catholicæ.
units.tr: 7. Likewise, once ecclesiastical power has been removed, deposition will not be an exercise of that power but a mere declaration and testimony that the Church no longer wishes to use the ministry of this or that man. For that seizure is unjust, closer to tyranny and similar to the thunderbolt of excommunication; just as the force of excommunication spreads through the whole world, so the force of deposition and dismissal, by which one driven from a particular Church is an exile from the Catholic Church.

units.la: 8. Nec finis utilitatum, nam per ruinam potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, statuetur certus modus potestatis qui debetur potestatibus secularibus circa sacra. Ecclesia, quatenus est cœtus Christianorum & fidelium, non habebit caput præter J. Christum, nec alium tenentem locum Christi in terris præter ministrum Evangelicum: at quatenus Ecclesia èst corpus politicum, non aliud agnoscet caput præter summum Magistratum, aut ubi res Ecclesiæ susque deque habet, non aliud præter vindices confœderatæ disciplinæ.
units.tr: 8. Nor is this the end of the advantages: for through the ruin of ecclesiastical power a certain measure of the power due to secular authorities in sacred matters will be established. The Church, insofar as it is an assembly of Christians and of the faithful, will have no head but Christ, and no one holding the place of Christ on earth except the evangelical minister; but insofar as the Church is a political body, it will acknowledge no head but the supreme magistrate, or, where the affairs of the Church are held at nothing, no one but the defenders of the confederated discipline.

units.la: 9. Nec minori negotio disputatio de Judice controversiarum enodabitur, non comparente potestate Ecclesiastica, ad cujus clavum volunt sedere Papam, & ad eum referri de omnibus controversiis: nam intra regnum Christi mediatorium, solus erit judex Christus loquens in sacro Codice: at in eodem regno Pastores Ecclesiarum, & doctores erunt judices, judicio functionis & peritiæ, cui sic unusquisque de plebe Christiana debet reverentiam obsequii, ut non mancipet suum judicium cæca mente, ut dictatoris edictis, sed ipse proprii judicii examine, accedente lumine, tum suo, tum ex Divina revelatione, Divinam veritatem ab humana dignoscat, dein arripiat & sequatur quod sibi videtur bonum & æquum. At in regno Christi naturali, potestate illa Ecclesiastica, civilis consorte aut Domina, semel e medio sublata, solus erit magistratus summus judex, cujus imperio, voluntatis arbitrio,& acutiori gladio, constat vis & ratio legum, cùm bonarum,tum malarum:& itidem constabit Papæ in hoc regno naturali intra sui imperii pomeria, tam Christi Vicario, quam Sultano intra sui imperii fines.
units.tr: 9. Nor with less effort will the dispute about the judge of controversies be settled, once ecclesiastical power, to whose helm they want the Pope to sit and to which all controversies are to be referred, no longer appears. For within the mediatorial kingdom of Christ, the only judge will be Christ speaking in the sacred Code; but in the same kingdom the ministers and teachers of the Churches will be judges, by the judgment of office and skill, to whom every man of the Christian people should show such reverence of obedience that he does not surrender his judgment to them with a blind mind, as to the edicts of a dictator, but by the examination of his own judgment, with light coming both from himself and from divine revelation, he distinguishes divine truth from human, and then seizes and follows what seems to him good and right. But in the natural kingdom of Christ, once that ecclesiastical power, the companion or mistress of civil power, has been removed from the midst, the supreme magistrate alone will be judge; by his command, the arbitrium of his will and his sharper sword, the force and reason of laws, both good and bad, will stand; and likewise the Pope will stand in this natural kingdom, within the boundaries of his empire, as much the vicar of Christ as the Sultan is within the limits of his own empire.

units.la: 10. Ipsaque authoritas Ecclesiæ Romanæ, & Papæ tantopere decantata ab Arnaldo Sorbonista, patietur lumbifragium per ruinam potestatis Ecclesiasticæ: nam tum demum erit authoritas externa, politica, civilis, robore, pompâ, purpurâ potens & fulgens, sibi habens obnoxios Dominos, in quo, quod dives est, & magnificum, ut loquitur Tacitus, habetur pro bono, justo justo & sancto. Nam eadem loquitur Papa Symmachus dist. 40. Quis sanctum dubitet quem apex tantæ majestatis attollit?
units.tr: 10. The very authority of the Roman Church and of the Pope, so much sung by Arnaud the Sorbonist, will suffer a broken back through the ruin of ecclesiastical power. For then at last it will be an external, political, civil authority, powerful and gleaming with strength, pomp and purple, having lords subject to it; in which, as Tacitus says, what is rich and magnificent is held to be good, just and holy. For Pope Symmachus says the same thing in dist. 40: Who would doubt that he is holy whom the summit of such majesty raises up?

units.la: II. Nec leve commodum ex ruina potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, & Catholicæ & nullis certis limitibus conclusæ, quod non ulterius de natura Schismatis & Unionis Ecclesiarum, alternis judiciis hærebunt doctores & sapientes mundi, nam cum Romanenses & Protestantes juxta, nobis statuant potestatem Ecclesiasticam se diffundentem in totum terrarum orbem, ut qui pulsus ab Ecclesia privata vivat extorris ex Ecclesia Catholica: cum id, inquam, statuant, in posterum per ruinam potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, constabit dari jure divino duo genera Ecclesiarum in terris, unum quod est tot hominum quot in mundo dant nomen J. Christo. Secundum tot hominum quot in unum locum conveniunt ad audiendum verbum, & participanda Sacramenta. Cæteras acceptiones & genera Ecclesiarum, ut sunt Romanensis, Nationalis, Provincialis, nomine tenus esse Ecclesias. Unde constabit Schisma non esse se abscindere ab ejusmodi Ecclesiis, quæ non sunt divinæ institutionis. Quid? quod potestate illa chimerica non amplius comparente, nec colligante Ecclesias mundi, aut Nationis, aut Provinciæ, non erit schisma, cum Ecclesia privata, mutuo consensu membrorum, in duas abit Ecclesias. Sed nec esset schisma se abscindere ab Ecclesia Catholica, sed Apostasia: neque etiam ubi conformitas lege patria imperatur, schisma est privatos cœtus agitare, sed rebellio.
units.tr: II. Nor is there a small advantage in the ruin of ecclesiastical power, both Catholic and confined by no certain limits: that the teachers and wise men of the world will no longer cling, in turn, to judgments about the nature of schism and the union of Churches. For since the Romanists and the Protestants alike hold that ecclesiastical power extends over the whole world, so that one driven out of a private Church lives as an exile from the Catholic Church, when they assert this, I say, then after the ruin of ecclesiastical power it will be clear that by divine right there are two kinds of Churches on earth: one, which consists of all the men who in the world give their name to Jesus Christ; the other, of as many men as come together into one place to hear the Word and to partake of the sacraments. The other senses and kinds of Churches, such as the Roman, the National, the Provincial, are Churches only in name. Hence it will be clear that schism is not to separate oneself from such Churches as are not of divine institution. And what more? Since that chimerical power no longer appears, nor gathers together the Churches of the world, or of a nation, or of a province, there will be no schism when a private Church, by mutual consent of its members, becomes two Churches. But it would not even be schism to separate oneself from the Catholic Church; it would be apostasy. Nor, where conformity to the law of the fatherland is commanded, is it schism for private assemblies to meet; it is rebellion.

units.la: Nec de postremis erit illa utilitas, quam nunc in ultimum locum rejicio, nempe quod per ruinam potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, sacra Scriptura liberabitur monstris interpretationum quibus illuditur sacris Codicibus, dum illos imponunt equuleo, ut inde extorqueant suam potestatem Ecclesiasticam, & Excommunicationem, ut sunt ejusmodi loca. Dic Ecclesiæ, Dabo tibi claves. Sit tibi velut Ethnicus, Quodcunque ligaveritis. Tollite improbum è medio vestri. Utinam exscinderentur qui vos turbant. Hæreticum post unam aut alteram admonitionem rejice. Si quis non obedit nostro Sermoni, notate eum per Epistolam. Margaritas vestras ne abjicite ad pedes porcorum. Unde tanquam oleum ex pumice exprimitur potestas Ecclesiastica, pari futilitate quâ Pontificii in duobus gladiis à Petro indicatis Christo, duas jurisdictiones invenerunt, alteram Ecclesiasticam, alteram Civilem. Pari strophâ & sagacitate qua iidem Pontificii, sicubi in Scriptura fit mentio fossæ, lacunæ, carceris, ignis, lebetis, ibi Purgatorium expiscantur.
units.tr: Nor will the following, which I now put last, be the least of the benefits: with the ruin of ecclesiastical power, Holy Scripture will be freed from the monstrous interpretations by which the sacred books are mocked, as men stretch them on the rack to wring out of them their ecclesiastical power and excommunication. Passages of this kind include: Tell it to the Church; I will give you the keys; let him be to you as a heathen; whatever you bind on earth; put away the wicked person from among you; I wish they who trouble you were cut off; reject a heretic after one or two warnings; if anyone does not obey our word, note him by letter; do not cast your pearls before swine. From these texts ecclesiastical power is squeezed out as oil from a pumice stone. With the same futility by which the Papists found two jurisdictions, one ecclesiastical and one civil, in the two swords which Peter showed to Christ, they fish out Purgatory wherever Scripture mentions a ditch, a pit, a prison, a fire, or a cauldron, with the same twisting and cleverness.

units.la: Porrò inde futilitas & vanitas excommunicationis probantur, quod cùm Protestantes omnia sua dogmata in quibus abeunt à Pontificiis, firmis & inconcussis non solum argumentis & rationibus, sed & Scripturæ sacræ locis stabiliant, attamen in materia de Excommunicatione & potestate Ecclesiastica, quam unà cùm Pontificiis arripiunt, desipiant perinde ac hi plusquam infantes, dum iisdem ad hanc & illam astruendam, hoc est perinde vanis & absurdis rationibus & sacræ Scripturæ locis tortis, utuntur. Quin affirmare ausim argumenta & loca è ScripScriptura petita à Romanensibus ad tuendam suam excommunicationem, absurditate longè esse infra illa quæ adducuntur à Protestantium Doctoribus ad fulciendum suam excommunicationem, nam rationi magis congruit, ut tam Rex quam Subditus, seu Minister seu alius, subjectus-sit excommunicationi & depositioni à regno aut ab officio secundum Pontificios, quam solummodo excommunicationi, ut volunt Protestantes, si quidem verba J. Christi. Quicquid ligaveritis, &c. nec causam nec personam eximant.
units.tr: Further, the futility and vanity of excommunication are shown by this: although the Protestants establish all their doctrines in which they differ from the Papists by firm and unshaken arguments and reasons, and by passages of Holy Scripture, yet in the matter of excommunication and ecclesiastical power, which they seize together with the Papists, they dote as much as those who are more than infants, using for its support, just as the Papists do, vain and absurd reasons and passages of Scripture twisted out of shape. Indeed I would venture to affirm that the arguments and texts of Scripture which the Romanists bring to defend their excommunication are far below the absurdity of those which the teachers of the Protestants bring to prop up their own excommunication. For it is more consistent with reason that, according to the Papists, both king and subject, whether minister or other, should be subject to excommunication and to deposition from kingdom or office, than only to excommunication, as the Protestants want, if indeed the words of Christ, whatever you bind, etc., exempt neither the cause nor the person.

units.la: Cumulum addidit persuasioni meæ de futilitate, cum potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, tum excommunicationis, hæc reputatio, quod cum essem in Hollandia, observaverim modum & temperamen- tum potestati illi assignatum fuisse, pro modo stationis quam aut in Ecclesia, aut in Repub. viri sustinebant, hoc est pro sua cuique utilitate, quasi canones Theologici debuissent accommodari ad rationes humanas: namque Walleus, Rivius, Apollonius, Triglandus, & Symmystæ, qui erant pars consistorii, aut synedrii, acerrimi erant defendefensores potestatis Ecclesiasticae & <bl>ἀυτονομίας</bl> retinendae, nec obnoxiae reddendis rationibus magistratui. At vicissim Vedelius, Maresius, Maccovius, Polyander, & Rivetus; de potestate Ecclesiastica sentiebant & scribebant, ut de Potestate subdita Magistratui, ut est Paterna, Maritalis, Herilis, quod plus in Aula & Academia versarentur quam in Synedrio.
units.tr: What added the final weight to my conviction of the futility both of ecclesiastical power and of excommunication was this consideration: when I was in Holland, I observed that the measure and limit of that power were assigned according to the position which men held either in the Church or in the Commonwealth, that is, according to each man's own advantage, as though theological canons had to be adjusted to human interests. For Walaeus, Rivetus, Apollonius, Triglandius and their associates, who were members of the consistory or synod, were the fiercest defenders of ecclesiastical power and of keeping its autonomy [ἀυτονομία], and were unwilling to render an account of it to the magistrate. On the other hand, Vedelius, Maresius, Maccovius, Polyander and Rivetus thought and wrote about ecclesiastical power as they would about a power subject to the magistrate, as paternal, marital or domestic power is subject to the head of the household, because they spent more time at court and in the university than in the synod.

units.la: Caeterum leve esset si duntaxat vana & futilis esset potestas Ecclesiastica, nisi pernicie penè adaequaret, peccatum Adami, imo nisi exitialior esset ipso Papa, veluti, per quod unumquodque est tale, illud magis est tale. Estque Potestas Ecclesiastica quae intulit Papam, gravius malum ipso Papa. Namque cum posset Papa tolli e medio, sine ruina potestatis Ecclesiasticae; nequidem cogitari potest, ut ruina potestatis Ecclesiasticae, non inferat ruinam Papae. Haec arbor radicitus evulsa, nunquam pullulabit aut edet nobis Papam. At intacta radice, non diu erit priusquam inde Papa erumpat.
units.tr: Moreover, it would be a small matter if ecclesiastical power were merely empty and futile, were it not almost equal to the destructiveness of the sin of Adam, indeed were it not even more deadly than the Pope himself. For, as a thing is what it is through what it has, that which brought in the Pope is a greater evil than the Pope himself. For although the Pope could be removed without the ruin of ecclesiastical power, it cannot even be imagined that the ruin of ecclesiastical power would not bring about the ruin of the Pope. Once this tree is torn up by the roots, it will never sprout again or bear us a Pope; but while its root is left untouched, it will not be long before a Pope springs up from it.

units.la: Vix audeo attingere longe perniciosissima mala quae in orbem intulit sententia de Potestate Ecclesiastica retinenda in Ecclesia seorsim à Potestate Magistratûs ; quod causa fuerit non solùm Arminianismi, Socinianismi, imo Atheismi ; qui in orbem nostrum hocce seculo & superiori exundarunt, atque potissimum corruperunt viros Principes de Laica natione, & de Magistratura ; sed & collisionis bonorum virorum inter se Lutheranorum, Calvinianorum, Presbyterianorum, Congregationalium.
units.tr: I scarcely dare touch upon the far more pernicious evils which the opinion of retaining ecclesiastical power in the Church, separate from the power of the magistrate, has brought upon the world. It has been the cause not only of Arminianism and Socinianism, and indeed of atheism, which have overflowed our world in this century and the last, and have chiefly corrupted the princes, the lay nobility and the magistracy, but also of the clashing of good men among themselves: Lutherans, Calvinists, Presbyterians and Congregationalists.

units.la: Namque inde ansa est arrepta à Socinianis, & Arminianis sana sententibus circa potestatem Magistratûs in sacris, obsirmari in dogmatibus suæ fidei, & reputare, Calvinianos & cæteros vindices potestatis Ecclesiasticæ tam graviter errare in sua fide quam cespitant in retinenda hacce sua potestate Ecclesiastica & in exucndo Magistratu summo imperio ordinandi res Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: For from this opportunity was seized by the Socinians and Arminians, who hold sound opinions about the power of the magistrate in sacred matters, to harden themselves in the doctrines of their faith, and to reckon that the Calvinists and the other champions of ecclesiastical power err as gravely in their faith as they stumble in retaining this ecclesiastical power of theirs and in stripping the supreme magistrate of the authority to order the affairs of the Church.

units.la: At gregi illuminatorum & viris Principibus, imo de Magistratura, & illorum qui occulto Livore præ se contemnunt gentem sacram & togatam, pronus est lapsus ad sequius sentiendum dum de Christiana religione, deque probationibus quibus sancti viri illam astruunt, quasi tam futilibus argumentis & rationibus illam fulcirent, quibus solent potestatem Ecclesiasticam sibi retinere.
units.tr: But the party of the enlightened, and princes, and indeed the magistracy, and those who with hidden envy despise the holy and gowned class, are prone to slip into the worse view when they consider the Christian religion and the proofs by which holy men establish it, as though these were propped up by the same flimsy arguments and reasons with which they are accustomed to keep ecclesiastical power for themselves.

units.la: Sane Arminianismus nunquam caput extulisset in Provinciis Belgii foederatis; si Arminius tam foede erraviffet in sententia sua de summarum Potestatum imperio circa sacra, quam in illis quinque capitibus quae ibi secerunt tot collisionum causa: nam tanto se ferociorem & obstinatiorem in recto, ut loquebatur, venditabat in materia de Praedestinatione & gratia, & argumentis potiorem illis quae à Junio & Collegis afferebantur, quanto rationibus & Scriptura hosce superabat in controversia de Potestate Magistratus circa sacra.
units.tr: Certainly Arminianism would never have raised its head in the United Provinces of the Netherlands, if Arminius had erred as shamefully in his opinion about the authority of the supreme powers in sacred matters as he did in those five articles which caused so many quarrels there. For he boasted himself the fiercer and more obstinate in what he called the correct view on predestination and grace, and he was more powerful in arguments than those which Junius and his colleagues brought forward, to the same degree that he was overcoming these men by reason and Scripture in the controversy about the power of the magistrate in sacred matters.

units.la: Quocirca videas in Hollandia, Zelandia, & aliis Belgii Provinciis cum Arminianismo enatam, auctam & longius provectam controversiam de potestate Ecclesiastica, tanto aestu animorum & tanto numero Scriptitantium, ut plura plaustra onerari possent Librorum & Libellorum, hinc à Marefio, illinc à Voetio & eorum æqualibus & Symmystis editorum ; viris ex utraque parte in errore, unis potestatem Ecclesiasticam ad cælos tollentibus, alteris potestati chimericæ modum statuentibus: nemine extante qui, quod ego facio, istius potestatis usum damnaret & è medio in totum tolleret ; quæ sane via fuisset expeditissima componendi controversiam.
units.tr: Accordingly, you may see in Holland, Zeeland and the other provinces of the Netherlands that the controversy about ecclesiastical power, which arose with Arminianism and was increased and carried further, has been conducted with such heat of spirit and by so many writers that several wagonloads of books and pamphlets could be filled, published on one side by Maresius and on the other by Voetius and his peers and associates. Men on both sides are in error: some raise ecclesiastical power to the heavens, others fix limits to that imaginary power. No one has appeared who, as I do, would condemn the use of that power and remove it from the midst altogether; this would surely have been the quickest way of settling the controversy.

units.la: Est quoque illud gravissimum malum, quod, cum Potestas illa Ecclesiastica suâ natura introduxerit, ut dixi, Papam ; saltem tribunal Ecclesiasticum nationale: longè consultius & rationi magis consentaneum videatur, vulgo Christianorum, se subjicere, & mancipare suum intellectum, tribunali infallibili: quale Romanenses volunt suum esse ; quam tribunali errori obnoxio, quale est quod Protestantes erigunt inter se.
units.tr: There is also this most serious evil: since that ecclesiastical power, by its very nature, has brought in the Pope, or at least a national ecclesiastical tribunal, it seems far more prudent and more consistent with reason for the common run of Christians to submit themselves and surrender their own judgment to an infallible tribunal, such as the Romanists claim theirs to be, than to a tribunal liable to error, such as the Protestants set up among themselves.

units.la: Jam tui judicii facio, mi Domine, an tot commoda quibus obviam itur Atheismo, Socinianismo, & Arminianismo, & Medicina adhibetur factionibus inter Christianos concurrere
units.tr: Now, my lord, I leave it to your judgment whether so many benefits, by which atheism, Socinianism and Arminianism are opposed and a remedy is applied to factions among Christians, could be obtained

units.la: possint per ruinam singularis alicujus dogmatis Romanenfis, uti Purgatorii Sacrificii Miffatici, Transubstantiationis, quot ex ruina potestatis Ecclefiasticæ emergunt. Ut reticeam per ejus excidium, consultius, prudentius & sapientius caveri paci, & integritati Ecclesiarum reformatarum, & tum demum in solido stabiliri & statuminari illarum disciplinam.
units.tr: through the ruin of some single Romanist doctrine, such as Purgatory, the Sacrifice of the Mass, or Transubstantiation, as many would emerge from the ruin of ecclesiastical power. To pass over its destruction: it is more advisable, more prudent and wiser to guard the peace and integrity of the Reformed Churches, and only then to establish and secure their discipline on a firm foundation.

units.la: Sed ecce, dum finem huic Epistolæ imponere consilium est, datur nova occasio (licet materia sit eadem) producendi sermonem, qui mihi sufficitur ab Epistola Clarissimi Claudii, quæ nunc in manus traditur, & in qua (pace tanti viri dixerim) mihi affingit quæ nunquam sensi nec scripsi, ut meritò commotior debeat esse, in sua sensa, non mea. Nam me odiosè exagitat, quasi potestatem verbi, & illam quæ est clavium atque ligandi & solvendi abjudicarem à verbi Dei ministris, magistratui vero adjudicarem: tum partes regendi Ecclesiam particularem, & de disciplina statuendi, in eundem conferrem, à ministris depellerem: Cum è contrario plus hac in re tribuam Dei verbi ministris quam de more in usu habetur, & credam solos Pastores, esse Ecclesiæ Christi in regno mediatorio rectores, nec quenquam de Laicis velim allectum in societatem sacræ aut functionis aut authoritatis, imo nec appositum ad clavum regiminis Ecclesiastici, Nam tam de jure Divino, Pastor Evangelicus, sub Christo, est solus in regno Christi mediatorio rector & Episcopus, quam ad solum Patrem familias pertinet regere familiam, & continere in officio uxorem, liberos & servos, quamvis ratione non plane eadem, ut nunc subjiciam, sic enim statuo.
units.tr: But see, while I am about to put an end to this letter, a new occasion arises (though the subject is the same) for taking up a discussion, which is supplied to me by the letter of the most distinguished Claude, which has now been handed to me. In it (with respect to so great a man I may say this) he attributes to me things I never felt or wrote, so that I ought rightly to be more disturbed by his feelings than by mine. For he harshly assails me, as if I denied the power of the Word, and that power of the keys of binding and loosing, to the ministers of the Word, and assigned it to the magistrate; and as if I transferred to the magistrate the part of governing the particular Church and of making decisions about discipline, and removed it from the ministers. On the contrary, in this matter I grant more to the ministers of God's Word than is customary, and I believe that the pastors alone are the rulers of the Church of Christ in his mediatorial kingdom, nor would I wish any of the laity to be admitted into the fellowship of the sacred office or authority, nor even to be set at the helm of ecclesiastical government. For by divine right the evangelical pastor, under Christ, is alone the ruler and bishop in the mediatorial kingdom of Christ, just as it belongs to the father of the family alone to govern the household and to keep the wife, children and servants in their duty, although not in quite the same way, as I shall now set out, for thus I hold.

units.la: I. J. Christum habere duo regna, unum mediatorium, in corda, in volentes, aut quos à volentibus præstiterit volentes per potestatem verbi & administrationem sacramentorum, cujus decreta, leges & canones, neminem cogunt nolentem, sed trahunt volentem & cujus subditi sunt populus spontaneus: Alterum naturale & externum, cujus decreta, canones, leges, non sunt validæ quia sunt bonæ, veræ, & sanctæ, sed quia latæ sunt à D potestate armata, cujus modus imperii, justitiæ, aut obsequii, est in sola voluntate jubentis, & imperantis.
units.tr: I hold that Christ has two kingdoms: one mediatorial, in the heart, over those who are willing, or whom he has made willing through the power of the Word and the administration of the sacraments. Its decrees, laws and canons compel no one against his will, but draw the willing, and its subjects are a spontaneous people. The other is natural and external, whose decrees, canons and laws are valid not because they are good, true and holy, but because they are issued by a power armed with the sword, and whose mode of rule, of justice or of obedience rests on the sole will of the one who commands and governs.

units.la: 2. In hocce regno Naturæ, Ecclesiam visibilem seu nationalem, seu particularem, non disserè à Republica, eique præesse Pastores, non quatenus sunt verbi Dei ministri, sed viri præditi consilio, & prudentia, & peritiores cæteris in jure Divino, atque ordinare & componere negotia, & res suas, ad rationem & modum quo præsecti Collegiorum, Academiarum, Civilium Societatum regunt suos coetus, & quo Sacerdotes & Principes & Judices populi, uno consilio, & uno consessu suam synagogam regebant, absque ulla diserepantia aut causarum aut hominum, ut alii ad classem Ecclesiasticam, alii ad civilem pertinerent.
units.tr: In this kingdom of nature, the visible or national or particular Church is not clearly distinct from the commonwealth, and ministers preside over it not as ministers of the Word of God, but as men endowed with counsel and prudence, and more skilled than others in divine law, to order and arrange affairs and business. They do so in the manner and mode in which the heads of colleges, academies and civil societies govern their bodies, and in which the priests, princes and judges of the people once governed their synagogue by one counsel and one assembly, with no distinction either of causes or of persons, some belonging to the ecclesiastical order and others to the civil.

units.la: 3. Et quemadmodum non alii in Collegio Medicorum, Mercatorum fabrorum, præter selectos Medicos, Mercatores, & fabros, præficiuntur, sic de jure naturali Divino, ut in regno Christi naturali, magis rationi, & juri Divino consentaneum esse, ut verbi Dei minister, sit rector Ecclesiæ particularis, quam quivis de plebe Laicæ.
units.tr: And just as no one is set over a college of physicians, or of merchants, or of craftsmen, except the chosen physicians, merchants and craftsmen, so by natural and divine right, in the natural kingdom of Christ, it is more in accordance with reason and divine law that a minister of the Word of God should be the ruler of a particular Church than any man from the laity.

units.la: Verùm, itidem in hoc regno Naturali, quemadmodum potestas Archiatrorum, Architectorûm, & Archifabrorum, qui seorsim suæ societati præsunt, subsunt potestati seculari, sic potestas Pastorum, licet statueretur juris Divini, subordinata est potestati civili; Dixi, licet statueretur juris Divini, nam etiam potestas paterna & Maritalis, licet juris Divini, nec derivata à Magistratu, ei nihilominus subdita est.
units.tr: Yet, likewise, in this natural kingdom, just as the authority of the chief physicians, chief architects and chief craftsmen, who preside separately over their own societies, is subject to the secular power, so the authority of the ministers, even if it were established by divine right, is subordinate to the civil power. I say "even if it were established by divine right," for the paternal and marital authority, although of divine right and not derived from the magistrate, is nevertheless subject to him.

units.la: 5. Cæterum, licet solis verbi Dei ministris, in regno Christi mediatorio, incumbat sub Christo Præfectura, & cura animarum & corporum in ordine ad promovendum regnum Christi, & salutem animarum, nec debeant quemquam sibi adjungere in societatem operis sacri, attamen poterunt in regno Christi naturali sibi assumere consortes regiminis de primoribus nationis laicæ, ita tamen ut Pastores temperent quantum fieri poterit, regimen naturale, ad modum regiminis mediatorii, in quo nemo in cœtum recipitur aut ab eo pellitur invitus, ut nec ordinatur.
units.tr: Moreover, although in the mediatorial kingdom of Christ the oversight under Christ, and the care of souls and bodies with a view to advancing the kingdom of Christ and the salvation of souls, belong to the ministers of the Word alone, and they ought not to associate anyone with themselves in the fellowship of the sacred work, nevertheless in the natural kingdom of Christ they may take to themselves partners in government from among the leading men of the lay nation. Yet the ministers should temper the natural government, as far as possible, to the pattern of the mediatorial government, in which no one is received into the body, or expelled from it, against his will, nor is he ordained so.

units.la: 6. Potestatem illam duplicem pastorum, alteram in regno Christi mediatorio, alteram in naturali, & ejus actus, se exercere in omni synedrio, consistorio, synodo, seu nationali, seu provinciali: Nam exempli gratia Pastor Evangelicus, allectus in synodum, authoritate functionis sacrae, & propter peritia in jure Divino, sententiam profert quam putat veram justam & sanctam, & congruentem cum jure Divino, & quam ponamus reipsa talem esse qualem ipse mente concepit, & ore protulit, licet experiatur adversa plurium judicia & suffragia. At in regno Christi naturali, minister Evangelicus non decernit in synodo, nec legem condit aut sancit, quae norma sit credendorum & agendorum, nec concedit in sententiam aut excommunicationis aut depositionis cujusquam, ut minister Evangelicus, sed quatenus stat à partibus illorum qui vincunt caeteros numero suffragiorum, aut vincuntur.
units.tr: That twofold power of ministers, one in the mediatorial kingdom of Christ and the other in the natural, and their acts, are exercised in every synedrion, consistory and synod, whether national or provincial. For example, a gospel minister admitted to a synod, by the authority of his sacred office and because of his skill in divine law, pronounces a judgment which he believes to be true, just and holy, and in agreement with divine law. Let us suppose that it is in fact such as he conceived it in his mind and uttered with his mouth, even though he meets the contrary opinions and votes of many. But in the natural kingdom of Christ, a gospel minister does not decide in a synod, nor enact or sanction a law which becomes the rule of what is to be believed and done, nor does he concur in a sentence of excommunication or deposition against anyone, as a gospel minister; rather he stands with those who win the other side by the number of votes, or is defeated.

units.la: Sic in Synedrio tredecim virorum, omnes ex aequo de jure Divino, de aequo & bono respondent, & sententiam dicunt ut in regno Christi mediatorio, & quâ ministri Evangelici: At quod septem de illis xiii. concedunt in sententiam quæ Titum, aut Mævium excommunicant, & quod 7. portior sit numerus quam 6. is actus non pertinet ad actus Pastorum, in regno Christi mediatorio, sed in regno Christi naturali. Quod numerus major vincit minorem, & dat vim & robur legi aut Canoni, id non fit per potestatem Ecclesiasticam aut Spiritualem, sed communem omni societati. Nam par ratio Collegii Medicorum constantis puta Lx. Capitibus, ut est Londinense, nemo non negaverit singulos respondere de re Medica ut Medicos, sed nemo dixerit xxxv. de illo choro, ut potiores numero fixisse legem Candidatis Medicinæ, per potestatem Medicam. Hæc sunt cognitionis adeo obviæ & expositæ, ut non queam satis mirari, quî possit tantus vir, ut Claudius, iisdem præjudiciis abripi & excæcari quibus Romanenses tuentur sua deliria. Tum quî possit fieri, ut in tam candidum pectus, cadat consilium affingendi mihi dogmata à quibus absum quam maximè.
units.tr: So in a Sanhedrin of thirteen men, all alike respond on divine law and on what is fair and good, and give their judgment as in the mediatorial kingdom of Christ, and as gospel ministers. But that seven of those thirteen agree on a sentence which excommunicates Titius or Maevius, and that seven is a greater number than six, is not an act belonging to the acts of ministers in the mediatorial kingdom of Christ, but to the natural kingdom of Christ. That a larger number overcomes a smaller, and gives force and strength to a law or canon, is not done by ecclesiastical or spiritual power, but by a power common to every society. For suppose a college of physicians consisting, say, of sixty members, as the London one does: no one would deny that each of them answers on medical matters as a physician, but no one would say that thirty-five of that company, as the more numerous party, have fixed a law for candidates in medicine by medical power. These things are so obvious and so plain that I cannot sufficiently wonder how so great a man as Claudius could be carried off and blinded by the same prejudices by which the Romanists defend their follies. And how can it be that the plan of attributing to me doctrines from which I am as far as possible could fall into so candid a breast?

units.la: Verùm ad Epimetrum subjiciam tibi, Viro clarissimo, authoritatem trium Episcoporum Anglorum, eadem mecum sentientium, in spem futurum ut summus vir Claudius, æquius in posterum de me sentiat, errante non sine exemplo & authoritate magnorum authorum.
units.tr: But, to the Epimetrum, I shall set before you, most distinguished sir, the authority of three English bishops who think as I do, in the hope that the most eminent Claudius will in future judge me more fairly, since an error is not without example and the authority of great authors.

units.la: Primus est Author tractatus cui titulus est, Episcopalis hæreditas, p. 22. Dogma est Pontificium, Regimen Ecclesiasticum est distinctum à politico, quod Bellarminus tuetur tanquam rem concessam & admissam ab utraque parte, eo solùm consilio, ut Papalem Hierarchiam supra Reges & principes efferat, & clerum eximat à seculari potestate. Calvinus idem affirmat, instit. libr. 4. cap. 11. 8. 1. &c. Sed pace eorum dixerim crassùm hunc errorem esse existimo. Licet id dogmatis sit vulgare Idolum quod quisque animo sibi figuravit, non aliam ob rationem, quàm quia in regno nostro, & forsan in plerisque aliis regnis, divisæ sunt curiæ juridicæ civiles ab Ecclesiasticis, quem credo quidem non fuisse antiquum morem.
units.tr: The first is the author of the treatise entitled Episcopal Inheritance, p. 22: The Papal doctrine is that ecclesiastical government is distinct from the political, which Bellarmine defends as a thing conceded and admitted by both parties, with the sole aim of raising the Papal hierarchy above kings and princes, and of exempting the clergy from secular power. Calvin affirms the same, Institutes book 4, chapter 11, section 8 and following: But with due respect to them, I judge this to be a gross error. Although this is a common idol of doctrine which each man has fashioned in his own mind, for no other reason than that in our kingdom, and perhaps in most other kingdoms, the civil courts of justice have been separated from the ecclesiastical; which, I believe, was not the ancient custom.

units.la: Mox exemplo Ecclesiæ Judaicæ, & authoritate Bertrami, & Sigonii, docet, jurisdictionem Ecclesiæ non differre quicquam à jurisdictione civili, & implet plures paginas ut probet duas jurisdictiones collaterales esse insociabiles.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, by the example of the Jewish Church and the authority of Bertram and Sigonius, he teaches that the jurisdiction of the Church differs in no way from civil jurisdiction, and he fills several pages to prove that two parallel jurisdictions cannot be joined.

units.la: Episcopus Bilsonus, tract. de Subjectione Christiana pag. 358. Episcopi & Pastores habent quoque seorsim regimen distinctum à potestate temporali, & statu. Sed id regiminis administratur per persuasionem & consilium, non autem per terrorem & compulsionem, nec cujusquam corpus aut bona attingit, & pag. 525. Habent quoque Pastores suam correptionem privatorum, imo Principum, sed illa correptio, non excedit illam quæ fit per prædicationem verbi, & administrationem Sacramentorum:
units.tr: Bishop Bilson, in his treatise on Christian Subjection, p. 358: Bishops and ministers also have a government distinct from temporal power and the state. But this government is administered by persuasion and counsel, not by terror and compulsion, and it does not touch anyone's body or goods, and p. 525: Ministers also have their own correction of private persons, indeed even of princes; but that correction does not go beyond what is done by the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments.

units.la: Mox allegat Hilarium, & Chrysostomum, affirmantes Pastoris potestatem in illos se exercere qui ultro se submittunt jugo Christi. Episcopus Lancelotus Andræas concinit Bilsono, Tortura torti. Pag. 383: Ubi ait Christianum subjectum esse Pastori suo ad modum quo æger paret imperiis. riis Medici, aut Rex suo Equisoni.
units.tr: He then cites Hilary and Chrysostom, who affirm that the power of the minister is exercised over those who willingly submit themselves to the yoke of Christ. Bishop Lancelot Andrewes agrees with Bilson in Tortura Torti, p. 383, where he says that a Christian is subject to his minister in the way that a sick man obeys the commands of his physician, or a king obeys his groom.

units.la: Possem insuper allegare Bullingerum, Musculum, Martyrem, Gualterum, Seldenum, Lightfoot, Stillingfleet, pluresque alios de utroque ordine, pariter explodentes potestatem Ecclesiasticam. Sane velim dignum esse qui accenserer doctis & piis illis viris, de quibus loquitur Calvinus, Epistola ad Tigurinos, anno 1553. De Excommunicatione, non omnes hodie idem sentiunt, nec me latet pios & doctos esse homines quibus sub Christianis Principibus non videtur esse necessaria excommunicatio. Sed væ mihi, quod fuit dogma virorum piorum, ut fuerunt Bullingerus, Musculus, Martyr, &c. teste Calvino, dogma est impium & abnorme in ore meo, si creditur reverendo Claudio. Sic fides est verbis Plinii junioris Epist. 24. lib. 6. Quàm multum interest quid à quoque fiat, eadem enim facta claritate aut obscuritate facientium, aut tolluntur altissimè, aut humillimè deprimuntur.
units.tr: I could moreover cite Bullinger, Musculus, Martyr, Walter, Selden, Lightfoot, Stillingfleet, and many others of both orders, who likewise reject ecclesiastical power. Indeed I would be glad to be counted among those learned and pious men of whom Calvin speaks in his letter to the Tigurines, in the year 1553: Concerning excommunication, not all hold the same view today, nor am I unaware that there are pious and learned men who do not think excommunication necessary under Christian princes. But woe is me! What was the doctrine of pious men such as Bullinger, Musculus, Martyr and others, according to Calvin, is an impious and monstrous doctrine in my mouth, if Claudius the reverend is to be believed. So the saying of Pliny the Younger is true, Letter 24, book 6: How much it matters what is done by whom!
