For the same deeds, according to the brightness or obscurity of those who do them, are either raised to the highest or sunk to the lowest.

units.la: Sane reverendus Claudius insigne est mihi exemplum, quantum dogmata à consuetudine, educatione, longo usu obfirmata, inter æquales & gentiles, nec tamen in ulla ratione aut Scriptura, imo ne in authoritate humana fundata, possint ad excæcandum judicium virorum altioris intellectûs, judicii subacti, eruditionis recondite, ut est Claudius, ut nequeant cernere verum, etiam in materia obviæ & expositæ cognitionis, ut est detectio chimericæ istius potestatis Ecclesiasticæ seorsim assumptæ à ministris Evangelicis, & mediæ inter potestatem verbi, & potestatem Magistratûs, quæ quidem potestas media tam est magnum deliramentum, quam scientia media, hâc & illa juxta repudiatâ à tribus illis Episcopis modò memoratis. Mediam certè potestatem repudiavit synodus Parisiensis VI. cujus verba Cedro digna sunt. Intra Ecclesiam potestates necessariæ non essent, nisi quod non prævalet sacerdos efficere per doctrinæ sermonem, hoc impleat potestas per disciplinæ terrorem. Repudiant celebriores Romanenses, Petrus de Marca, Antonius de Dominis, Richerius Sorbonista, Pater Paulus, author historiæ Concilii Tridentini, imo & ipsi Papæ, Nicolaus I. &
units.tr: Certainly the reverend Claude is a striking example to me of how far opinions fixed by custom, upbringing and long use among peers and fellow-countrymen, and founded on no reasoning, on no Scripture, not even on human authority, can blind the judgment of men of deeper intellect, trained judgment and recondite learning, such as Claude is, so that they cannot see the truth even in a matter of plain and obvious knowledge. An example is the exposure of that chimerical ecclesiastical power, claimed apart by Evangelical ministers and placed midway between the power of the Word and the power of the magistrate. This middle power is as great a delusion as "middle knowledge" (scientia media), which, together with it, was rejected by the three bishops just mentioned. The Synod of Paris VI certainly rejected a middle power, and its words are worthy of cedar: Within the Church there would be no need for powers, unless the priest could not prevail by the sermon of doctrine, and that power were to accomplish it by the terror of discipline. It is also rejected by the more notable Romanists: Peter de Marca, Antonio de Dominis, Richer the Sorbonnist, Father Paul, author of the history of the Council of Trent, and even the popes themselves, Nicholas I and Adrian VI, and the canon law, Distinction on repentance, canon Verbum, where a twofold power is laid down, one of the Word and one of the magistrate.

units.la: & Adrianus VI. jusque canonicum distinct. de poenitentia, Canon. Verbum. Ubi duplex potestas statuitur, altera verbi,. altera Magistratūs. Repudiatur & illa potestas media, à reverendo parente meo,necnon à.Chamiero, Cameronē, Tileno, Riveto, Amyraldo, quorum loca attuli Epist. 46. in choro illarum quæ præfixa sunt Jugulo causæ. Parens meus Epistolā ad Subrandum Lubertum, ait jurisdictionem esse nomine tenus jurisdictionem, quæ non habet cogendi & puniendi potestatem, & cujus viri qui ad clavum sedent, non habent jurisdictionem, nec forum, nec apparitionem nec exsecutionem, ut loquitur Cujacius titul. de audientiā, & quæ abnormis est à Jurisdictione Regis in subditos; judicis,in actorem & reum, patris in liberos, Mariti in uxorem, Domini in servos, eóque magis abnormis, quod cum aliæ jurisdictiones pluribus viis & modis puniant reos; istius chimericæ jurisdictioni vindices, non nisi una correptione, quæ est excommunicatio, puniant.
units.tr: That middle power is also rejected by my reverend father, and by Chamier, Cameron, Tilenus, Rivet and Amyraut, whose passages I cited in letter 46, in the company of those prefixed to Jugulum causae. My father, in his letter to Suibertus Lubertus, says that jurisdiction is jurisdiction in name only, one which lacks the power of compelling and punishing, and that those who sit at the helm have no jurisdiction, no forum, no apparitor and no execution, as Cujas says in title on the hearing. It is also abnormal compared with the jurisdiction of a king over subjects, of a judge over plaintiff and defendant, of a father over children, of a husband over wife, of a master over servants, and all the more so because, while other jurisdictions punish offenders in many ways, the defenders of this chimerical jurisdiction punish only by a single rebuke, which is excommunication.

units.la: At cumulus absurditatum est pari vocabulo Ecclesiasticæ insignire illam jurisdictionem quâ viri ipsi qui eam sustinent, dicuntur Ecclesiastici. Sanè si viris ab officio competit denominatio Architectorum, Fabrorum, Medicorum, non inde pari Congruentia infertur, in eos viros ubi jus dicunt in sua societate, cadere jurisdictionem Architectonicam, Fabrilem & Medicam.
units.tr: But the height of absurdity is to label with the same word "ecclesiastical" that jurisdiction by which the men who exercise it are called ecclesiastics. Certainly, if the names architects, smiths and physicians belong to men from their trade, it does not follow with equal fitness that architectural, smithy or medical jurisdiction falls upon those men when they administer justice in their society.

units.la: Porro occasionem introducendi hancce mediam potestatem, tria potissimum dederunt. 1. Quod Ecclesia Christiana sub Ethnicis Imperatoribus, non potuerit suis rebus superesse nisi assumptâ disciplinâ, confœderata, quæ suppleret partes Magistratus, cujus erat in Ecclesia Judaica, disciplinam constituere & imperare, & cujus est in Christiana, ut loquitur Bullingerus Epistola ad Dathenum, idem præstare. Jam versa Imperii facie sub Christianis principibus, plures Episcopi in fraudem Dominorum suorum, crediderunt potestatem illam de disciplina statuendi ad se pertinere, & voluerunt insigniri vocabulis Ecclesiasticæ & Spiritualis.
units.tr: Moreover, three chief things gave occasion for introducing this middle power. (1) The Christian Church under pagan emperors could not survive in its affairs except by assuming a confederate discipline, which would take the place of the magistrate. In the Jewish Church it was the magistrate's office to establish and command discipline, and in the Christian Church, as Bullinger says in his letter to Dathenus, it is the same office. But when the face of the empire changed under Christian princes, many bishops, to the detriment of their lords, believed that the power of establishing discipline belonged to them, and they wished to be called by the names "ecclesiastical" and "spiritual."

units.la: 2. Radices altiores fixit in animis hominum, potestas illa media, inter potestatem verbi, & potestatem magistratus tempore Constantini magni, ex occasione tribunaliumEpiscopalium seu Ecclesiasticorum, ab illo Imperatore constitutorum: quam potestatem demandatam diplomate imperatorio Episcopis, mox habere & retinere voluerunt jure Divino & proprio, & pro potestate sua ligandi & solvendi, & virtute clavium traditarum à Christo solis ministris Verbi & Pastoribus Ecclesiarum.
units.tr: (2) That middle power, between the power of the Word and the power of the magistrate, took deeper root in men's minds in the time of Constantine the Great, from the occasion of the episcopal or ecclesiastical tribunals set up by that emperor. Once this power was committed to the bishops by an imperial charter, they soon wished to hold and keep it by divine and their own right, and as the power of binding and loosing, and by virtue of the keys delivered by Christ to the ministers of the Word and pastors of the churches alone.

units.la: 3. Altius adhuc roborata est illa opinio (nec mirum si usque adeo altas radices agit in mente Clarißimi Pastoris Parisiensis) de potestate media seu Ecclesiastica in reformatione à Papismo superiori sæculo facta, ut plurimum sub Pontificiis Dominis, quibus par & eadem necessitas incubuit Pastoribus, & Ecclesiis, atque incumbebat sub Ethnicis Imperatoribus, tribus primis centuriis res Ecclesiæ ordinare per disciplinam confœderatam, cujus usu vel praxis prono lapsu facilè concessit in eandem opinionem quæ Episcopos primævæ Ecclesiæ tenuit & habuit, nempe hanc disciplinam non retineri aut jure arbitrario, aut tempori, loco, & Dominorum conditioni accommodatam, sed perpetuo & sibi debito, pro potestate illa media seu Ecclesiastica collata à J. Christo in Apostolos & ejus successores, viros de clero. Porro excommunicationem non esse legem Magistratus quae fertur aut versatur in foro civili, sed in Ecclesiastico, de qua cognoscere & pronunciare ad solos Pastores & tribunal seu judicium Ecclesiasticum pertineat. Nam hocce judicium seu tribunal sancivit & edixit Calvinus, & quasi de tripode pronunciavit imo imperavit ut ipse refert Epistolâ Scripta anno 1541. Volui (inquit) ut æquum est spiritualem potestatem, à Civili distingui. Sic in usum rediit excommunicatio. Ubi per spiritualem potestatem, non intelligit potestatem verbi, de quâ Rom. 1. 16. &
units.tr: (3) That opinion has been strengthened even more deeply (and it is no wonder if it has struck such deep roots in the mind of the most distinguished Parisian pastor) concerning the middle or ecclesiastical power, in the reformation from Papism made in the last century, mostly under Papist lords. On the pastors and churches there lay the same necessity that lay on the churches under pagan emperors, who in the first three centuries had to order church affairs through a confederate discipline. The practice, or the use, of this easily slid by a downward course into the same opinion that the bishops of the primitive Church held and possessed: namely, that this discipline is kept not by arbitrary right, nor adapted to time, place and the condition of the lords, but is perpetual and owed to them by that middle or ecclesiastical power which Jesus Christ conferred on the apostles and their successors, men of the clergy. Further, excommunication is not a law of the magistrate which is proposed and operates in the civil forum, but belongs to the ecclesiastical forum, of which knowledge and pronouncement pertain to the pastors alone and to the ecclesiastical tribunal or court. For this court or tribunal was established and decreed by Calvin, and he pronounced and even commanded it, as if from a tripod, as he himself reports in a letter written in 1541: I wished, as is right, that spiritual power be distinguished from civil. Thus excommunication came back into use. Here by spiritual power he does not mean the power of the Word, of which Rom. 1. 16 and

units.la: 2 Cor. 10. 5. Col. 11. 13. quae transfert à regno satanæ ad Deum, & in corda agit, sed potestatem illam mediam quæ est leges ferendi, ordinandi, deponendi, & excommunicandi.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 10. 5 and Col. 11. 13 speak, which transfers from the kingdom of Satan to God and works in the hearts of men, but that middle power which consists in enacting laws, ordaining, deposing and excommunicating.

units.la: 4. Potest addi quarta causa, quamobrem ministri Evangelici sibi imperium ædificaverunt seorsim, & quod medium esset inter imperium verbi, & imperium Magistratus, atque hæc fuit. Quod cum de jure naturæ Divino, imo & præcepto diserto, ministri æquales, si non potiores habeant partes cum Principibus populi in regimine reipublicæ, quæ ex Dei instituto unum est corpus cum Ecclesia, nec nisi per summam injuriam (ut factum est in reformatione superiori sæculo) depelli possunt à Magiftratura, & exui sua libertate Civica, non mirum si gens illa sacra, in ultionem & vindicatam sibi seperatim sumpserit imperium, cujus legibus & censuris ipsi Magistratus subjicerentur, ut sic alterius in alterum esset imperium.
units.tr: (4) A fourth cause may be added, why Evangelical ministers built for themselves a separate empire, one midway between the empire of the Word and the empire of the magistrate. It was this: since by the natural law of God, and even by express precept, the ministers, if not superior, at least equal, have a share with the princes of the people in the government of the commonwealth, which by God's appointment is one body with the Church, and since they can be removed from the magistracy and stripped of their civic liberty only by the greatest injury (as happened in the reformation of the last century), it is no wonder that that holy people, in revenge and to vindicate itself, took to itself a separate empire, by whose laws and censures the magistrates themselves would be subject, so that the one empire would be over the other.

units.la: Modus Epistolæ non fert, ut plura attexam, imprimis ut refellam illud commentum, quod excommunicatio non sit lex aut censura, à Magistratu lata & sancita, sed à viro Ecclesiastico, cujus cognitio, non versetur in foro civili, sed in Ecclesiastico: nam præterquam quod forum Ecclesiasticum (nisi intelligatur de foro conscientiæ)
units.tr: The manner of a letter does not allow me to add more, especially to refute that fiction, that excommunication is not a law or censure enacted and sanctioned by the magistrate, but by an ecclesiastical man, whose cognizance is exercised not in the civil forum but in the ecclesiastical one. For apart from the fact that the ecclesiastical forum (unless it is understood as the forum of conscience)

units.la: fit inane nomen sine re, & Chimera in vacuo pendula, si excommunicatio tam esset de lege divina naturali, quam sunt novem præcepta Decalogi, aut tam esset de jure positivo, quam est observatio diei Sabbathi, attamen nulla inde major accresceret ministro Evangelico potestas arcendi à sacris, adulterum, furem, & diem septimum temerantem, quam eosdem morte plectendi.
units.tr: is an empty name without a thing, a chimera hanging in a void: even if excommunication were as much of divine natural law as the nine precepts of the Decalogue, or as much of positive law as the observance of the Sabbath day, still no greater power would accrue to the Evangelical minister to keep away from the sacred things an adulterer, a thief and one who profanes the seventh day, than to put those same men to death.

units.la: Jam cum altum sit silentium, non solum in Decalogo, sed & in reliquo sacro codice, aut quod detur ejusmodi ens, (nisi sit ens rationis) in natura aut Scriptura, quæ excommunicatio indigitatur, aut quod ad solum virum Ecclesiasticum, eo fulmine excommunicationis amburere impium, pertineat, non video quo tibicine clarissimus Claudius aut suam excommunicationem, aut potestatem excommunicandi supportabit.
units.tr: Now since there is deep silence, not only in the Decalogue but in the rest of the sacred code, either about any such entity in nature or Scripture (unless it is a being of reason) designated by the name excommunication, or about its belonging to the ecclesiastical man alone to strike the impious with that thunderbolt of excommunication, I do not see by what prop the most distinguished Claude will support either his excommunication or the power of excommunicating.

units.la: Sanè Doctor Stillingfleet, tractatu de excommunicatione pagina 30. dicit, Vis & Virtus excommunicationis in foro humano, à civili potestate emanat, neque datur proprium effectum illius, quod non fluat à sanctione Magistratûs.
units.tr: Indeed, Doctor Stillingfleet, in his treatise on excommunication, page 30, says: The force and virtue of excommunication in the human forum proceeds from the civil power, nor is there any proper effect of it that does not flow from the sanction of the magistrate.

units.la: Atque hoc argumento Achillæo, quo potestas Ecclesiastica æternitur, & à fundamentis evertitur, memini me aliquando os occulisse accerrimi vindicis potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, & ad silentium æternum redigisse.
units.tr: With this Achillean argument, by which ecclesiastical power is undermined and overthrown from its foundations, I remember once silencing the mouth of a most fierce defender of ecclesiastical power and reducing him to eternal silence.

units.la: Sed, quod horrendum putat reverendus Claudius, per meas hypotheses, promiscuè pios cum impiis miscéri, nec censet horrendum illud pejus morte & angue malum, aliter evitari posse, quam per ferulam excommunicatoriam, per quam hi ab illis arceantur; conficiam statim meas hypotheses nihil ejusmodi horrendi præ se ferre, nec per illam ferulam excommunicatoriam medelam afferri malo, quod animo sibi figuravit Clarissimus vir. Nam quid opus est virgâ & Censurâ Divinâ fundatâ in potestate ligandi & solvendi, & quæ se per illam potestatem exerat; quandoquidem de jure Divino naturali, & communi omni societati & familiæ, penes sit Ecclesiam particularem, vel à suo coetu vel à sua communione quemlibet removere? Nam id esset lenti unguentum affundere, fluctus excitare in simpulo, ac miracula & Divinam potestatem in auxilium accersere, ad movendum paleam suo loco. Imo quid opus est Acheronta movere, & Diabolum ex inferis evocare ad perficiendum tantum molimen? Ne dicam incoeptum impium esse, Diabolo tradere quem duntaxat velis foras exire.
units.tr: But what the reverend Claudius thinks horrible, namely that on my hypotheses the pious are mixed indiscriminately with the impious, and that this horrible evil, worse than death and the serpent, cannot be avoided except by the excommunicatory rod, by which the one sort is kept away from the other, I shall at once show to be unfounded. My hypotheses carry no such horror, and no remedy is supplied by that excommunicatory rod for the evil which the most distinguished man has pictured in his mind. For what need is there of a rod, and of a divine censure founded on the power of binding and loosing, and exercising itself through that power, since by natural divine right, common to every society and family, it lies with a particular church to remove anyone from its assembly or its communion? To do so by such means would be like pouring ointment on a sluggish man, stirring up a storm in a ladle, and summoning miracles and divine power to move a straw from its place. Indeed, what need is there to stir up Acheron and call the Devil up from the depths to accomplish so great an effort? Not to mention that it is an impious undertaking to hand over to the Devil someone whom you merely wish to see go out.

units.la: Sed, non visum est commodum Pastoribus pro sua cuique utilitate & pro suo amore Imperii retinendi, id jus excommunicandi haberi per potestatem, quæ foret illis communis, vel cum aliis societatibus, vel cum aliis hominibus, sed potius imitari Romanenses Præsules, qui ut sibi authoritatem non vulgarem crearent, sibi solis reservaverunt potestatem ordinandi & confirmandi, ne si cum pluribus communicaretur, vilesceret. Qui affectant authoritatem & imperium in alios, non debent, ut ait Tacitus, promiscuis honoribus affici.
units.tr: But it has not seemed convenient to the ministers, each for his own advantage and from love of retaining dominion, that this right of excommunication should be held through a power shared with other societies or other men. They have preferred to imitate the Roman prelates, who, to create for themselves no ordinary authority, reserved to themselves alone the power of ordaining and confirming, lest, if it were shared with many, it would become cheap. "Those who aim at authority and dominion over others ought not," as Tacitus says, "to be honoured with common honours."

units.la: Sed nec licentia promiscua, ut pii cum impiis communicent, debet horroris quicquam incutere Celeberrimo Claudio, quasi inde piis assricaretur impiorum impietas, & impiorum deterior fieret conditio, & certior aut exitialior damnatio, quam gravare iniquum putat: sed hoc & illud incommodum plane nullum est, & falsitate laborat. Certè venerandus Beza (alioquin acerrimus assertor & vindex potestatis Ecclesiasticae & Excommunicationis) risit hunc scrupulum Pharisaeorum, qui impares in mensura pietatis, prae se contemnunt, aut procul abjiciunt, ut pestifera contagione tactos propter suam impietatem, an potius amore imperii: & existimavit pios, nulla labe affici si cum impiis communicant. Verba ejus sunt, Epistolâ secundâ ad Thomam Tilium. Ut recte accedam ad coenam, non est scrutandum mihi quâ quisque conscientiâ ad eam mecum accedat, sed de mea ipsius conscientia laborandum est. Itaque & cum adulteris, & cum homicidis, etiam sceleratissimis quibusvis, modo nulla mea culpâ tales sint ad coenam casus & sceleris puris accessero. Nihil illorum impuritas mihi nocuerit. Et quod de moribus, etiam de doctrina dico, &c.
units.tr: But neither should the promiscuous liberty by which the pious communicate with the impious cause the most celebrated Claudius any horror, as if the impiety of the impious would thereby rub off on the pious, and the condition of the impious would be made worse, or their condemnation more certain or more deadly, which he thinks an unjust burden. This inconvenience, like the other, is plainly non-existent and rests on falsehood. Certainly the venerable Beza (otherwise a most fierce champion and defender of ecclesiastical power and excommunication) laughed at this Pharisaical scruple, by which men who are unequal in the measure of piety despise others or cast them far away, as if they were touched by a pestilential contagion because of another's impiety, or rather from love of dominion. He judged that the pious suffer no stain if they communicate with the impious. His words, in his second letter to Thomas Tilius, are: To approach the Supper properly, I need not investigate with what conscience each person comes to it with me, but must labour over my own conscience. So, even if they are adulterers, murderers, or wicked men of any kind, provided that such a case of wickedness and sin does not come about through any fault of mine, I shall approach pure. Their impurity will do me no harm. And what I say of morals, I say also of doctrine, etc.

units.la: Haec loquitur Beza post Augustinum Epistola 48. ad Vincentium: Manifestum est non contaminari justos, alienis peccatis, quandocunque cum eis sacramenta communicant. Plus est millies periculi assidere semel in mensa ordinaria socio tibi aut hæreses, aut malos mores instillanti, ad contrahendam horum aut illorum porriginem, quam si centies assideas illi in mensa sacra. Usque adeo sit ex musca facere Elephantem, gravare invidiâ & horrendo crimine, quod facit Clarissimus Claudius, communionem pii viri cum impio : necnon illos qui putant posse tolerari absque profanatione sacrorum, aut offensione & læsione bonorum virorum, tum posse removeri impium à sacra cœna, absque illo apparatu clavium, & potestatis ligandi, & solvendi.
units.tr: Beza says this after Augustine, in Letter 48 to Vincent: It is manifest that the just are not defiled by the sins of others whenever they share the sacraments with them. It is a thousand times more dangerous to sit once at an ordinary table beside a companion who instils heresies or bad morals, and so catch the contagion of this or that, than to sit beside him a hundred times at the holy table. So far is it from the truth to make an elephant out of a fly, and to burden with odium and a horrible crime what the most distinguished Claudius does, namely the communion of a pious man with an impious one. The same goes for those who think that the impious can be tolerated without profaning the sacred things or offending and injuring good men, and yet that the impious can be removed from the holy supper only with that apparatus of keys and the power of binding and loosing.

units.la: Nec potest esse deterior conditio aut certior damnatio aut Judæ, aut perditi hominis (sive communicet, sive non communicet cum piis) in propriam perniciem & ad inferos ruentis, à quibus potius forsan spes sit, fore ut gradum revocet per pœnitentiam, communicando cum piis, quam si in totum à cœna abstinet.
units.tr: Nor can the condition be worse, nor the condemnation more certain, for Judas or for any lost man (whether he communicates with the pious or not), who rushes to his own destruction and to hell. From such a man there is perhaps more hope that, by repentance and by communicating with the pious, he may retrace his step, than if he abstains from the Supper altogether.

units.la: In summa, tantum abest ut excommunicatio sit divinæ institutionis, & res bona, ut sit non solum absurda & inficeta, sed & perniciosa & exitialis censura, & quæ licet sit brutum fulmen, peperit Papæ imperium in Reges & Nationes, quæque nec scfamâ, nec melle, nec quoquam fuco commodæ interpretationis,potest Protestantibus, sine peccato commendari. Similis est ferculo ex cucumeribus, quod nulla arte culinaria, non sale, non aceto, non pipere, non maceratione diuturniori, non horsum sursum jactatione, aut versatione, unquam efficies ut sanitati conducat.
units.tr: In sum, excommunication is so far from being of divine institution and a good thing that it is not only absurd and insipid but also a pernicious and deadly censure. Though it is an empty thunderbolt, it has brought forth the papal empire over kings and nations. It cannot be commended to Protestants without sin by any sweetening of interpretation, not by honey, must, or any other coloring. It is like a dish of cucumbers, which no culinary art, neither salt, nor vinegar, nor pepper, nor longer soaking, nor tossing up and down or turning over, will ever make wholesome.

units.la: Claudam Epistolam verbis longè Doctissimi & Clarissimi viri Domini Eliæ Merlati, Santonis ad me scriptam ante sesqui annum.
units.tr: I shall close the letter with the words of the most learned and distinguished man, Lord Elias Merlat of Saintes, which he wrote to me a year and a half ago.

units.la: 'Omnino ergo certum est illud quod 'tu, vir eruditissime, & passim in tuo 'Jugulo causæ inculcas, & capite xx. 'disputas accuratè, Ecclesiasticis scilicet 'hominibus, officium incumbere persuadendi, jurisdictionem verò quâ 'cogant & submittant nolentes, nullam lam ipsis quâ Pastores sunt competere: sed vel ab ipso politico magistratu in eos derivari, vel ex ædificatione Imperii in Imperio, uti loqui amas, quam subsistendi necessitas, extorqueat, ubi contingit Magistratum politicum Religioni non favere, quod in Gallia nostra locum habet.
units.tr: "It is therefore altogether certain what you, most learned man, press throughout your Jugulo and dispute carefully in chapter 20: that the duty of persuading falls on churchmen, but the jurisdiction by which they compel and subdue the unwilling belongs to them in no way as ministers. It is rather derived to them from the political magistrate himself, or is wrested from them by the necessity of subsisting, through the building of an empire within an empire, as you like to call it, which happens when the political magistrate does not favour religion, as is the case in our France."

units.la: De eo sane viro cum cogito, pono inter mea felicitatis argumenta, & delinimenta curarum, ærumnarumque abfterfiones; eoque nomine gratias ago Deo, & in sinu gaudeo, quod tantum virum habeam sententiæ meæ in summa rei suffragantem, & patrocinantem, & quem merito opponam toti agmini hominum, seu charissimorum capitum, qui me affinitate & cognatione attinent, seu aliorum pietate & eruditione conspicuorum, in quibus pono celeberrimum Claudium, qui nostra damnant, & sequius de me sentiunt.
units.tr: When I think of that man indeed, I count him among the grounds of my happiness, the solace of my cares and the wiping away of my troubles. For this I give thanks to God and rejoice inwardly that I have so great a man supporting my opinion in the main matter and defending it, one whom I may rightly set against the whole crowd of men, whether among my dearest kinsmen by marriage and blood, or among others distinguished for piety and learning, in which company I count the most celebrated Claudius, who condemn our views and think less well of me.

units.la: Sed cumulus gaudii accederet si paria facientem Muffardum cum illis viris, ad meam sententiam perducerem: quod tamen me effecturum non desperro. In qua fiducia positus speque suturum ut dubium & amicè reluctantem, hæc Epistola pervincat; hortor & obtestor, ut spatio hocce vitæ meæ decurso, & me qui sum Septuagenario major, amoto, eandem veritatem aripias, promoveas, deffendas, & ad plures diffundas, monendo, hortando, suadendo, dein persuadendo ; excommunicationem esse terriculamentum avium, & everriculum fraudum Romanensium. Potestatem verò Ecclesiasticam, esse humanum figmentum, atque, (ut loquitur gravissimus author Anglus,quem modò tibi allegavi) Idolum quod Protestantes & Romanenses juxta colunt. Et quo stat stabitque Papa, & unà totus Romanensis apparatus. Et quo acrior sis ἐργα̈ διωκτής, prudenti via & consilio pertentandi sunt prius animi virorum de tuo grege, qui huic Idolo litaverunt, eique sunt mordicus addicti, quàm debellandi.
units.tr: But a crown of joy would be added if I could bring Muffard, who does the same, over to my opinion along with those men, and I do not despair of achieving this. Trusting in that hope, and hoping that this letter will win over a friend who is reluctant and doubtful, I urge and beseech you, while the span of my life that remains (I being past seventy) is run out, to take up this same truth, promote it, defend it and spread it to more people, by admonishing, exhorting, persuading, and then convincing them that excommunication is a scarecrow for birds and a sieve for the frauds of the Romanists, and that ecclesiastical power is a human fiction and, as the most serious English author, whom I have just cited to you, says, an idol which Protestants and Romanists alike worship. By this the Pope stands and will stand, and with him the whole Roman apparatus. And that you may be a more zealous driver of the work [ἐργα̈ διωκτής], the minds of the men of your flock who have sacrificed to this idol and cling to it stubbornly must first be tested by a prudent way and plan, before they are overcome.

units.la: Ante omnia, author sum tibi, Primirofio, cærerisque symmystis, ut diebus sacræ cœnæ celebrandæ destinatis, cùm prælegitur sermo prævius Synaxi, illam pericopen transiliatis in qua, In nomine & authoritate Domini nostri Jesu Christi, anathemate feritis, non solum homines de grege (si qui sunt) vitæ impiæ, & ad omnia vitia projectæ, sed & insuper, idolatras, hoc est Pontificios, item Congregationales nostros seu Independentes, qui coetus seorsim agitant, bonos certè viros, & quos iniquum, imo impium esset satanæ tradere per excommunicationem vestram.
units.tr: Above all, I advise you, Primirosius, and the other fellow symmystae, that on the days appointed for celebrating the Lord's Supper, when the preliminary sermon before the Synaxis is read aloud, you skip that passage in which, in the name and authority of our Lord Jesus Christ, you pronounce anathema not only on the people of the flock (if there are any) of impious life and abandoned to every vice, but moreover on idolaters, that is the Papists, and likewise on our Congregationalists or Independents, who hold their assemblies apart. These are certainly good men, and it would be unjust, indeed impious, to hand them over to Satan by your excommunication.

units.la: Hæc si, Muffarde, vir eruditissime, & maxima authoritate pollens apud bonos viros, pectoris tui candore & pietate, feceris, haud dubium tuo exemplo, crescet audacia reverendo tuo collegæ Primirosio, tum summo viro Claudio, necnon cæteris symmystis, Langlæo, Dallæo, Allixio, & Menardo, Pastoribus Ecclesiæ Parisiensis, viris longè Clarissimis, idem præstandi: à quibus exemplum capiet tota gens sacra in Gallia, quæ Reformationi nomen dedit. In quo omine desino.
units.tr: If, Mussard, most learned man and a man of great authority among good men, you do this with the candour and piety of your heart, then without doubt, by your example, the boldness of your reverend colleague Primerose will grow, as well as that of the most eminent Claude, and of the other fellow-ministers, Langlois, Daillé, Allix and Ménard, ministers of the Church of Paris, men far more distinguished, to do the same; and the whole sacred nation in France, which gave its name to the Reformation, will take example from them. With this omen I end.

units.la: [decorative typographic ornament band]
units.tr: [decorative typographic ornament band]

units.la: Celeberrimo Theologo D. Johanni Claudio, Pastori Ecclesiæ Parisiensis, S D.
units.tr: To the most celebrated theologian, Mr. John Claude, Minister of the Church of Paris, greetings.

units.la: Subiit me sæpè admiratio, Vir Reverende, quod de septuaginta viris, quibus nostram novam Rationem per Epistolas præfixas nostro Jugulo Causæ dicavi, & de quingentis viris doctis, qui illam Rationem ad examen suum revocaverunt, solus extitisti (nisi clarissimus vir Petrus du Bosc paria tecum faciat) qui illam, aut non probaret, aut non pronunciaret, post semel intellectam & arreptam à viris qui præsunt ordini, tum sacro, tum civili, hasce, sed longè magnas utilitates, inde in orbem Christianum redundaturas.
units.tr: It has often occurred to me, Reverend Sir, that of the seventy men to whom I dedicated our new Rationale, by way of prefatory letters, in my The Throat of the Cause, and of the five hundred learned men who submitted that Rationale to their examination, you alone (unless the most distinguished Pierre du Bosc is your equal in this) have neither approved it nor pronounced it sound, once it had been understood and embraced by the men who preside over both the sacred and the civil order, though it promises very great benefits, which would flow from it into the Christian world.

units.la: I. Primò per eam brevissimâ viâ debellari Papam & totum systema Romanense; deinde ad omnes controversias dirimendas, quæ non sunt de fide circa Primatum in Ecclesia, Papæ ἀναμαχητισίαν, Potestatem Pastorum, Synodorum naturam & authoritatem Ecclesiæ, Judicem controversiarum, item circa naturam schismatis & disciplinam Ecclesiasticam, sternere compendiosissimum iter.
units.tr: I. First, by it the Pope and the whole Roman system could be overthrown by the shortest route; and then it would clear a very direct path to settling all controversies that are not matters of faith: concerning the primacy in the Church, the Pope's infallibility, the power of ministers, the nature of synods and the authority of the Church, the judge of controversies, and likewise the nature of schism and church discipline.

units.la: Secundò per novam nostram rationem semel intellectam, probatam & arreptam, disciplinam Ecclesiarum reformatarum à Papismo, longè firmioribus fundamentis & columnis fulciri, quam hactenus experimento comprobatum fuit.
units.tr: Secondly, once our new Rationale has been understood, tested and embraced, the discipline of the Reformed Churches, which is separated from Popery, would be supported on far firmer foundations and pillars than experience has so far proved.

units.la: Tertiò, per illam rationem nostram semel probatam & ad praxim revocatam, plus dignitatis & authoritatis, ut par est, viris de sacro ordine accrescere.
units.tr: Thirdly, once this Rationale of ours has been tested and put into practice, the men of the sacred order would, as is fitting, gain more dignity and authority.

units.la: Quartò, Sed, quæ meretur agmen cæterarum utilitatum ducere, quæ exurgit ex nostra sententia, ubique à bonis & doctis recepta, illa est, expeditissimæ rationis, in Europa quidem, Pontificios cum Protestantibus, Lutheranos cum Calvinistis: At in Anglia Episcopales cum abeuntibus ab Ecclesia Anglicana, ut loquuntur, Presbyterianos cum Congregationalibus, quos vulgus Independentes vocat, conciliandi. Nam cum Presbyteriani & Congregationales, in fide sint concordes, at in disciplinæ modo immensum quantum à se invicem abeant, per nostram sententiam semel imbibitam ab utraque parte, detumescent partium odia; exulabunt apud eos lites, circa certam aliquam disciplinæ normam de jure Divino habendam; atque fidei & charitatis uno vinculo coalescent. Sed & penè solus existitisti, qui per rationem nostram non flecteretur in assensum sequentium corollariorum.
units.tr: Fourthly, but this is the benefit which deserves to lead the rest, and which follows from our opinion, accepted everywhere by good and learned men: it would bring about a most expeditious reconciliation: in Europe, between the Papists and the Protestants, the Lutherans and the Calvinists; and in England, between the Episcopalians and those who have, as they say, left the Anglican Church, the Presbyterians and the Congregationalists, whom the common people call Independents. For although Presbyterians and Congregationalists agree in faith, they differ hugely from one another in the mode of discipline. Once our opinion has been absorbed by both sides, the hatred between the parties would subside; quarrels among them over some particular norm of discipline held to be of divine right would disappear, and they would be joined together by the one bond of faith and charity. Yet you have almost alone been unmoved by our Rationale to assent to the following corollaries.

units.la: 1. Nempe Potestatem, perperam dictam, Ecclesiasticam & Spiritualem & ejus sobolem Excommunicationem, esse humana figmenta, & per hanc & illam, ortum, auctum, & progressum mysterium iniquitatis accepisse.
units.tr: 1. Namely, that the so-called Ecclesiastical and Spiritual power, and its offspring, excommunication, are human inventions, and that through these the mystery of iniquity arose, grew and advanced.

units.la: 2. Potestatem illam Ecclesiasticam, cujuscunque fuerit aut possit statui esse utilitatis, fuisse per plura secula post Apostolos Equum ephipiatum, sollicité adornatum & curatum,in spem,ut aliquando Seffòrem Papam admitteret: qui incidens huic Bucephalo, sibi imperium majus & potentius imperio Alexandri pararet.
units.tr: 2. That this ecclesiastical power, whatever usefulness it may be thought to have or to be able to have, was for many centuries after the Apostles a horse saddled and carefully equipped, in the hope that it would one day admit a Pope as its rider, who, mounting this Bucephalus, would acquire for himself an empire greater and more powerful than that of Alexander.

units.la: 2. προσκσίαν, seu prælationem Epifcopalem, quocunque demum confilio introductam & quocunque jure fundatam, seu Divino, seu Humano, fuisse subicem fuppedaneum, seu ftrepam per quam Papa in dorsum istius equi evaderet.
units.tr: 3. That episcopal precedence [προσκσίαν], or prelation, introduced by whatever counsel and founded on whatever right, whether divine or human, was the footstool or stirrup by which the Pope would climb onto the back of this horse.

units.la: 4. Larvâ detractâ Potestatis Ecclefiafticæ seu Spiritualis, per quam Papa probat & acceptum reddit suum imperium,, reipfa terrenum, Regibus & Populis, statim concidere hocce imperium & suâ ruinâ involvere totum Romanenfe Systema, Papæ, & Religionis: quibus major authoritas accedit abillo fuco potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, quam ab ejus divitiis, robore & pompâ.
units.tr: 4. With the mask of ecclesiastical or spiritual power removed, by which the Pope proves and makes acceptable his empire, which is in fact earthly, this empire would at once collapse before kings and peoples and bring down the whole Roman system with its ruin, both the Papacy and the religion; and greater authority attaches to that pretence of ecclesiastical power than to its wealth, strength and pomp.

units.la: Sed, quod Tu, vir Magne, judicii acerrimi & subacti non credis, aut non admittis hasce utilitates, in causa est quod nostra nequidem obiter & furtivis oculis legeris, sed Te adduci, aut potius excæcari passus fueris præjudiciis charissimorum capitum, quæ me proximâ cognatione contingunt; cætera virorum meritissimorum & eruditione præstantium, ut pariter atque illi (quod semper in more habuerunt) damnares hosce fœtus nec visos, nec lectos, ut eversores omnis ordinis & juris, cum humani tum maximè divini: Nam te virum niveum & pectore candidum, æquiorem censeo, quam ut eo nomine amandes, quod illi secerunt Anticyras, aut constringendum putes vinculis Hipocratis. Quocirca, oro Te, obtestor, vir Magne, ut me ex relatu aliorum, nec probes nec damnes: sed tantillum otii surripias & subducas de studiis tuis: quodque non ultra quadrantem horæ distinebit, quod des conspectui hujus synopseos; in qua, quasi in brevi tabella exhibeo complexum tum Parænefeos nostræ; tum alterius operis nostri cui titulus est, Jugulum Causæ, quem expendas, concoquas, judices, an detur aliqua causa, ob quam à Te aut à quoquam viro repudietur & damnetur. Si primo intuitu & in præsens non arridet; non despero futurum, ubi ad plures abivero, quod brevi fiet; ut non displiceat Tibi, quod prius damnaveras.
units.tr: But the reason why you, Great Sir, of most keen and trained judgment, do not believe or admit these benefits is that you have not even read our work in passing or with a sidelong glance; you have allowed yourself to be led, or rather blinded, by the prejudices of my dearest colleagues, who are closely related to me, and by those of other most worthy men distinguished for learning, so that, like them (as they have always been accustomed to do), you condemn these offspring, neither seen nor read, as destroyers of all order and law, both human and especially divine. For I think you a man of pure and candid heart, too fair to hate someone for what those men have done, or to think he should be bound with the chains of Hippocrates. Therefore, I beg and entreat you, Great Sir, not to approve or condemn me on the report of others. Rather, steal and withdraw a little leisure from your studies; and since it will take no more than a quarter of an hour, give a look at this synopsis, in which I present, as in a small table, the whole of both our Exhortation and our other work entitled The Throat of the Cause. Weigh it, digest it, and judge whether there is any reason why it should be rejected and condemned by you or by any man. If it does not please you at first sight and for the present, I do not despair that, once I have come to more men, which will soon happen, it will not displease you that you had first condemned it.

units.la: I. Cum Dominus Jesus habeat in terris duo regna seu imperia, unum naturale, alterum Mediatorium: quorum alterum est in altero, ut loquitur Optatus Milevitanus; cum ait Ecclesiam esse in republica, statuendum esse, cujusque reipublicæ, imo Ecclesiæ, quatenus est intra regnum Christi naturale, caput esse Regem seu Magistratum, qui cum summo imperio præest humano ordini, cum in Ecclesia, tum in Republica; At in regno Christi mediatorio, Regem Ecclesiæ & caput neminem esse præter Christum; nec alium aut alios vices tenentes Christi præter Ministros Evangelicos; nec alios, qui non sunt de hoc sacro ordine vocatos, nec vocandos in consortium potestatis & operis, quod geminum & idem est, quod Dominus Jesus & Apostoli, si rebus humanis interessent assumerent in regimine Ecclesiæ. Quod quidem id foret conciliare Deo populum & ex infenso præstare spontaneum, cum per prædicationem Evangelii, administra-tionem tionem Sacramentorum : intellectum cognitione illustrare, voluntatem flectere ad pœnitentiam, ad timorem Dei & charitatem proximi ; dein declarare jus Dei, quid concordet cum jure Divino, quid ab eo discordet in doctrina & moribus.
units.tr: I. Since the Lord Jesus has on earth two kingdoms or empires, one natural and the other mediatorial, of which the one is within the other, as Optatus of Milevis says when he states that the Church is within the commonwealth; it must be held that in every commonwealth, and indeed in the Church insofar as it lies within the natural kingdom of Christ, the head is the King or Magistrate, who with supreme power presides over human society, both in the Church and in the commonwealth. But in the mediatorial kingdom of Christ there is no King or head of the Church except Christ, and no one else who holds the place of Christ except the evangelical ministers; nor are others to be admitted or called into the fellowship of power and work, which is twofold and yet one, that the Lord Jesus and the Apostles, if they took part in human affairs, would assume in the government of the Church. This would indeed be to reconcile the people to God and to make them willing instead of hostile, through the preaching of the Gospel and the administration of the sacraments: to enlighten the understanding by knowledge, to bend the will to repentance, to the fear of God and the love of neighbour; and then to declare the right of God, what agrees with divine right and what departs from it in doctrine and morals.

units.la: 2. Ad hanc potestatem in regno Christi Mediatorio pertinere claves regni cælorum & potestatem ligandi & solvendi, seu remittendi & retinendi peccata ; tum munus Episcopi, Pastoris, Oeconomi & Dispensatoris Divinorum oraculorum, quo homines transferuntur à regno satanæ, tum naturæ, quod habet Christus in terris, ad regnum ejusdem Mediatorium & à tenebris ad lucem.
units.tr: 2. That to this power in the mediatorial kingdom of Christ belong the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of binding and loosing, that is, of remitting and retaining sins; also the office of bishop, pastor, steward and dispenser of the divine oracles, by which men are transferred from the kingdom of Satan, and the nature that Christ has on earth, to his mediatorial kingdom and from darkness to light.

units.la: 3. Huic imperio Mediatorio, Potestati, & regno Christi, par esse omnis conditionis homines, Reges, Principes mundi, qui accenseri volunt Christianis & fidelibus se subjicere, atque morigeros præstare, hortationibus, præceptis, imo imperiis Pastorum suorum.
units.tr: 3. That to this mediatorial empire, power and kingdom of Christ, men of every condition, kings and princes of the world, who wish to be counted as Christians and faithful, owe submission and obedience to the exhortations, precepts, and indeed commands of their pastors.

units.la: 4. At in altero Christi imperio & regno quod est naturale, cum Ecclcsia visibilis, non differat à Republica; una ubique sit norma agendorum & morum, quæ imperetur, scilicet decalogus: una regula credendorum, quæ tamen commendetur, non obtrudatur invitis, ut est symbolum Apostolorum: Cumque hujus & illius idem sit finis, cum subordinatus, tum ultimus; nempe pax in terris, in conscientiis, salus animarum & gloria Dei; planè statuendum esse æquo jure, (si non potiori) Ministris Evangelicis deberi imperium, si non summum, saltem subalternum, juxta atque Magistratibus & Principibus populi in regimine seu Ecclesiæ, seu Reipublicæ; atque per injustam occupationem arceri viros Ecclesiasticos à Potestate seculari, si non jus dicendi, saltem leges ferendi, seu in Ecclesia, seu in Republica.
units.tr: 4. But in the other empire and kingdom of Christ, which is natural, where the visible Church does not differ from the commonwealth, there is everywhere one rule of conduct and morals, which is enjoined, namely the Decalogue; and one rule of belief, which is commended but not forced on the unwilling, such as the Apostles' Creed. Since the end of both is the same, both subordinate and ultimate, namely peace on earth, peace in consciences, the salvation of souls and the glory of God, it must clearly be held that by equal right (if not a higher one) authority is due to evangelical ministers, if not supreme, at least subordinate, just as to the magistrates and princes of the people in the government either of the Church or of the commonwealth; and that by unjust usurpation ecclesiastical men are kept from secular power, if not from the right of judging, at least from the right of making laws, whether in the Church or in the commonwealth.

units.la: 5. Sed quia tempora non sunt jugiter usque adeo felicia, cujusmodi erant sub Davide, Josia, Constantino Magno, Theodosiis, ut Ecclesia & Respublica, in unum corpus coalescant & uno consilio regantur, uni imperio subsint: necessitatem incubuisse Christianis coetus seorsim agitare, reluctantibus, aut non attendentibus Potestatibus secularibus ; tum constituere disciplinam communi consensu per confœderationem, quæ locum habet Magistratus : eosdem actus potestatis producendo & exerendo,quos extra illam confœderationem, Magistratus amicus,& cui cordi sunt res Christianorum produceret in Ecclesia : ut si exauctoratio, Excommunicatio & reliquæ censuræ,quæ dicuntur Ecclesiasticæ sunt infligendæ, infligendæ sint ab illis vindicibus disciplinæ confœderatæ : quæ reipsa magistratura est, quæ semper viguit vigetque in Ecclesia visibili, seu nationali, seu particulari, ut loquitur synodus Parisiensis sexta ; ut jam ad illos vindices confœderatæ disciplinæ ; inter quos priores semper sunt partes virorum ordinis sacri, pertineat de omni causa & lite, quæ versantur in foro civili cognoscere & decernere : quæ reputatio, ( ut id obiter moneam ) destruit divisionem tribunalium jurisdictionum , Causarum & Rerum in duas classes, alteram Ecclesiasticam, alteram civilem.
units.tr: 5. But because times are not always so happy as they were under David, Josiah, Constantine the Great and the Theodosiuses, when Church and commonwealth grew together into one body, were governed by one counsel and lay under one authority, it became necessary for Christians to hold their assemblies apart when the secular powers resisted or paid no heed. Then, by common consent and through a confederation, they set up a discipline which takes the place of the magistrate. They performed and exercised the same acts of power that a friendly magistrate, one who had the welfare of Christians at heart, would perform in the Church outside that confederation. So if deposition, excommunication and the other censures called ecclesiastical are to be inflicted, they are to be inflicted by those avengers of the confederated discipline. This is in fact a magistracy, which has always flourished and still flourishes in the visible Church, whether national or particular, as the Sixth Synod of Paris puts it. To these avengers of the confederated discipline, among whom the men of the sacred order always have the first place, belongs the right to take cognizance of and decide every cause and suit that arises in the civil forum. This reckoning (let me note it in passing) destroys the division of jurisdictional tribunals, and of causes and matters, into two classes, one ecclesiastical and the other civil.

units.la: 6. Omnem potestatem quæ non est potestas illa verbi (de qua Rom. 1. 16.
units.tr: 6. Every power that is not that power of the Word (of which Rom. 1. 16.

units.la: 2 Cor. 10. v. 5. Col. 1. 13. Acts 26. 18. Phil. 2. 12,13. & cap. 3- v. 21.) per Ministerium Evangelicum, agens in corda hominum & in volentes, monendo, hortando, suadendo, perfuadendo, nec exercetur intra Ecclesiam per modum correptionis seu coactionis per delegationem Magistratus: nec aflumitur per disciplinam confœderatam : sed dicitur Ecclesiastica & Spiritualis, nomine tenus & per maximam ἀκυρολογίαν sic appellari ; tum abhorrere à sacra Scriptura, nec non à ratione, & à praxi Ecclesiæ Judaicæ ; atque insuper esse iniquam vendicationem & injustam occupationem juris alieni : imprimis fi habetur & retinetur per potestatem ligandi & solvendi, & vi clavium regni Cœlorum.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 10. v. 5. Col. 1. 13. Acts 26. 18. Phil. 2. 12, 13. and ch. 3. v. 21.), exercised by the evangelical ministry, acting on the hearts of men and on those who are willing, by admonishing, exhorting, urging and persuading, and which is not exercised within the Church by way of correction or coercion through delegation from the magistrate, nor is assumed through a confederated discipline, is nonetheless called ecclesiastical and spiritual. It is so called in name only, by a very great catachresis [ἀκυρολογίαν]. Moreover, it departs from holy Scripture, and likewise from reason and from the practice of the Jewish Church. Furthermore, it is an unjust claim and an unlawful seizure of another's right, especially if it is held and maintained by the power of binding and loosing and by the force of the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: 7. Eóque exitialiorem & perniciofiorem esse illam Potestatem Ecclefiasticam, quod fit everriculum, omnium fraudum, impofturarum & tyrannidum Papalium ; atque Episcopatum introduxisse, à quo præftructim ventum est ad Papatum.
units.tr: 7. That ecclesiastical power is all the more deadly and pernicious because it is a sweep-net for all the frauds, impostures and tyrannies of the Papists, and because it introduced the episcopate, from which the way was chiefly paved to the Papacy.

units.la: Habes, Vir Magne, cum in hacce Epistola, tum in illa quam scribo ad Reverendum Muffardum, & quam ad Te scriptam perinde atque ad illum velim putes. Habes, inquam, breviarum sententiae nostrae, a qua visus es hactenus plane alienus: dubium an incuria ad nostra respiciendi, atque indiligentia istius veritatis cognoscendae: an quia instillatum tibi est, prava & detestanda, ut loquitur de nostris Scriptis Sorbonista Arnaldus, edocere; a quibus merito vir pius abhorreat. fateor nostra non esse digna tuis oculis, Teque excusatius errare, si non das aliquam moram cognitioni sententiae, quam audis passim sugillari & profcindi, non solum a Pontificiis, sed & a Protestantibus, qui sunt eruditione conspicui ac doctrina & vita sanctissimi; sed ut lego in Tacito, quandoque profuisse Reo odium & invidiam accusatorum, ut judex ad miserationem & ad disjudicandum integris animis & audiendum defensionem Rei commoveretur: Ego me Tibi sisto fiduciae plenus futurum, ut Te Judice, si causa cado, saltem inauditus & indefensus non peream: quin Te ad meas partes adducam, aut saltem constringam rationibus sic cogentibus, ut Te impetus capiat perrumpendi omnia obstacula praejudiciorum, quae mancipio & nexu praeclarissima quaeque ingenia, ut est Tuum in vinculis tenent ; ut de Te usurpentur & in Te comprobentur verba Christi. Cognoscses veritatem, & illa veritas Te in libertatem asseret. Vix manum de tabula substraxeram, & tibi dicere, vale, apud me constitueram, cum per lectionem libri Episcopi Condonensis, & responsionis institutae ab Illustri adversario, Marco Antonio Bastidio mihi suggeritur, nova occasio, licet nova non sit materia, Te ulterius lacessendi; exponendo Tibi liberè sensa mea de hujus & illius Scriptione circa id de quo modò, mihi fuit sermo Tecum. Porro, cum hujus & illius Gallica mente etiamnum inerrent mea ; non potui temperare mihi, quominus quae hic subjicio sint perinde Gallica.
units.tr: You have here, great sir, both in this letter and in the one I am writing to the Reverend Muffardus, which you may think is written to you just as much as to him, a summary of our view, from which you have so far seemed altogether far removed. I do not know whether it is through neglect of our writings and carelessness in learning this truth, or because you have been drilled, as the Sorbonist Arnauld says of our writings, in things perverse and detestable, from which a godly man should shrink. I confess our writings are not worthy of your eyes, and you err the more excusably if you give no time to learning a view which you hear everywhere disparaged and torn down, not only by the Papists but also by Protestants who are eminent in learning and most holy in doctrine and life. But as I read in Tacitus, the hatred and ill will of the accusers have sometimes helped the accused, so that the judge is moved to pity, and to judge with an unbiased mind and to hear the defence of the accused. I present myself to you full of confidence that, with you as judge, if my cause falls, I shall at least not perish unheard and undefended. Indeed I shall bring you over to my side, or at least bind you with arguments so compelling that the impulse seizes you to break through all the obstacles of prejudice which hold the most excellent minds in bondage and chains, as yours is. Then the words of Christ will be fulfilled in you: You will know the truth, and that truth will set you free. I had hardly drawn my hand from the page and had resolved to say to you, farewell, when, through the reading of the book of the Bishop of Condom and of the reply undertaken by the illustrious adversary, Marc-Antoine de la Bastide, a new occasion was suggested to me of challenging you further, though the subject matter is not new. I shall set out to you freely my views on this writing and that one concerning the matter we discussed a little while ago. Moreover, since my thoughts on this writing and that one still wander in French, I could not refrain from setting down here in French what I now add.

units.la: VOus avez leu, la respónse de Monsieur de la Bastide, à Monsieur de Condom; Et vous l'avez leuë assurément, avec exactitude; puisque vous luy avez donné vostre approbation. Dites-moy Monsieur, avec vôtre candeur ordinaire, si vous n'avez pas remarqué, que cette response, qui est fort scavante & digne de son auteur, dans tout le reste de l'ouvrage, paroit extrémement foible, dans l'endroit, où Mr. de Condom nous attaque, sur le pouvoir que nos Synodes s'attribuent; qui est au fonds le mesme, que celuy que le Pape & ses Conciles s'arrogent : quoy que Monsieur de la Bastide dise, qu'il y a de la difference, comme du plus au moins, je ne vois point du tout cette difference. Car les Conciles Latins ne font tout au plus que de fraper d'anathéme les contredisans. Le supplice que nos Synodes ordonnent contre ceux qui refuseront de se soûmettre à leurs décisions, est, ce me semble, la mesme chose; quoy qu'ils se servent d'autres termes, ascavoir, retrancher de l'Eglise. Il n'y a point de plus grande peine que celle-là. C'est disposer à son plaisir du Paradis & de l'enfer. C'est beaucoup pire que de livrer au bras séculier, & de mettre les corps entre les mains du bourreau, comme a fait le Concile de Constance. Car retrancher de l'Eglise, c'est livrer au diable, & envoier en corps & en ame les personnes en enfer.
units.tr: You have read Monsieur de la Bastide's reply to Monsieur de Condom, and you have certainly read it with care, since you have given it your approval. Tell me, Monsieur, with your customary candour, whether you have not noticed that this reply, which is very learned and worthy of its author, appears extremely weak in the passage where Monsieur de Condom attacks us over the power that our Synods claim for themselves, a power which is at bottom the same as that which the Pope and his Councils arrogate. Although Monsieur de la Bastide says there is a difference, as of more and less, I see no difference at all. For the Latin Councils do no more, at most, than strike their contradictors with anathema. The punishment that our Synods ordain against those who refuse to submit to their decisions is, it seems to me, the same thing, although they use other terms, namely, to cut off from the Church. There is no greater penalty than this. It is to dispose of Paradise and hell at one's pleasure. It is far worse than handing over to the secular arm and putting bodies into the hands of the executioner, as the Council of Constance did. For to cut off from the Church is to deliver to the devil and to send persons, body and soul, into hell.

units.la: Que répond à cela Monsieur de la Bastide. Il dit deux choses : l'une, que le Pape & les Conciles se croient estre infaillibles, & l'autre qu'ils obligent les fidéles à recevoir leurs décisions aveuglément, & sans les examiner: que nos synodes ne font, ni l'un ni l'autre. Cela ne résoud pas la difficulté. Au contraire, puisque l'Eglise Romaine s'attribue l'infaillibilité, elle a raison sur cette supposition, de condamner ceux, qui ne recevront pas aveuglément ses décisions. Mais pour nous qui croyons que nos synodes sont sujets à l'erreur; de quel droit pouvons-nous prétendre que l'on leur doit une obéissance si absolue, que ceux qui y manqueront doivent estre retranchez de l'Eglise: c'est ce que l'on fait, comme Mr. de Condom le prouve fortement par les Articles de la discipline des Eglises reformées de France, & par les actes des synodes Nationaux, que l'on peut lire dans son écrit. C'est ce que Mr. de Condom presse, & à quoy son illustre adversaire ne satisfait pas; car au lieu que le premier insiste, sur ce que, puisque nous avouöus que le tribunal de nos synodes peut errer, nous avons tort d'obliger avec tant de rigueur les fidéles à s'y soumettre. Mr. de la Bastide se sauve en disant que le Pape & les Conciles, ont tort de se croire infaillibles, & qu'il y a de la différence d'eux d'avec nous, comme duplus au moins: mais à quoy sert cette distinction, qui n'est que dans les mots, puisque la chose est la mesme au fonds, & qu'on punit de part & d'autre les contredisans par les mesmes peines, qui sont l'anathéme & le retranchement de l'Eglise.
units.tr: What does Monsieur de la Bastide answer to this? He says two things: first, that the Pope and the Councils believe themselves infallible; second, that they oblige the faithful to receive their decisions blindly and without examination. Our synods do neither the one nor the other. That does not resolve the difficulty. On the contrary, since the Roman Church claims infallibility, it is right on that supposition to condemn those who will not receive its decisions blindly. But as for us, who believe that our synods are subject to error, by what right can we claim that they are owed such absolute obedience that those who fail in it must be cut off from the Church? Yet that is what is done, as Monsieur de Condom strongly proves from the Articles of the discipline of the Reformed Churches of France, and from the acts of the National Synods, which can be read in his writing. This is what Monsieur de Condom presses, and what his illustrious adversary does not satisfy. For the former insists that, since we admit that the tribunal of our synods can err, we are wrong to bind the faithful so rigorously to submit to it. Monsieur de la Bastide escapes by saying that the Pope and the Councils are wrong to believe themselves infallible, and that there is a difference between them and us, as of more and less. But what use is this distinction, which lies only in words, since the thing is the same at bottom, and on both sides contradictors are punished with the same penalties, namely anathema and cutting off from the Church?

units.la: La seconde réponse de Mr. de la Bastide
units.tr: The second answer of Mr. de la Bastide

units.la: Bastide ne me paroît pas plus solide, quand il dit que Rome veut que l'on recoive aveuglément & sans examen les ordonnances de ses Papes & de ses Conciles ; au lieu que nos synodes laissent aux fidèles la liberté d'examiner ce qui leur est proposé de leur part : Car à quoy peut servir cette liberté d'examiner : puisque s'il arrivoit à quelqu'un d'avancer un sentiment, qu'il jugeast-estre plus conforme à la parole de Dieu, il seroit aussi-tost retranché de l'Eglise, comme un libertin, ou comme un profane. L'Eglise Romaine n'a-t-elle pas plus de raison de vouloir que ses devots recoivent à yeux clos les decrets de ses Papes ; & de ses Conciles, puisqu'elle les croit infaillibles, que nous qui faisons semblant de permettre au peuple la liberté d'examiner les choses, & qui ne voulons pas qu'il ait celle de rejetter ce qu'il ne trouve pas conforme à la parole de Dieu. A quoy servira tout cet examen, toute cette recherche, & toute la peine qu'on se fera donnée puis qu' après tout il faut obéir & recevoir comme une vérité ce-la mesme que l'on croira estre une erreur. C'est obliger le monde à trahir les lumiéres de sa consciẹnce, & à estre Hypocrite, & à se jetter les yeux ouverts dans une erreur reconnue Mais je m'exprimeray mieux en employant les beaus termes de Mr. de la Bastide. C'est contraindre & non pas persuader; C'est employer la violence contre l'intention de Dieu, au lieu de l'Esprit de douceur & de charité; C'est entrainer les Chrestiens par un esprit de servitude, tres-indigne de la liberté des enfans de Dieu, & les obliger sous le beau prétexte de déférer à ses conducteurs, à faire une société de corps d'intérests & de grimaces, & non pas une véritable communion d'Esprit & de sentiment. Réponse à Mr. de Condom, pag. 384.
units.tr: Bastide does not seem to me any more solid when he says that Rome requires people to receive the ordinances of its Popes and Councils blindly and without examination, whereas our synods leave the faithful free to examine what is proposed to them on our side. For what use is this liberty of examination? If anyone put forward an opinion that he judged more conformable to the Word of God, he would at once be cut off from the Church as a libertine or a profane person. Does the Roman Church have more reason to want its devotees to receive the decrees of its Popes and Councils with eyes shut, since it believes them infallible, than we do, who pretend to allow the people liberty to examine things but do not allow them the liberty to reject what they do not find conformable to the Word of God? What use will all this examination, all this inquiry and all the trouble taken be, since in the end one must obey and receive as truth the very thing one believes to be an error? It is to oblige the world to betray the lights of its conscience, to become a hypocrite, and to throw itself with open eyes into an error it recognises. But I will express myself better by using the fine words of Mr. de la Bastide: It is to compel and not to persuade; it is to employ violence against the intention of God, instead of the spirit of gentleness and charity; it is to draw Christians along by a spirit of servitude, very unworthy of the liberty of the children of God, and to oblige them, under the fine pretext of deferring to their leaders, to form a society of bodies, interests and grimaces, and not a true communion of spirit and sentiment. Reply to Mr. de Condom, p. 384.

units.la: Je m'estonne comment cét excellent Esprit, ne s'est pas apperçeu que l'on peut retorquer contre l'authorité que nos synodes usurpent, tout ce qu'il allégue contre celle des Conciles de Rome; car si ceux-là doivent estre retranchez de l'Eglise, qui ne se soûmettront pas aux synodes, encore qu'ils tomberoient dans l'erreur, il ne sera pas permis de s'y opposer, Le mal sera sans remède ; l'erreur passera en force de Loy, authentique & irrévocable. Elle se rendra plus générale, plus durable & par conséquent plus difficile à refermer : quoy que les conducteurs soient aveugles, il ne sera pas permis aux particuliers, à qui Dieu a donné plus de force, plus de lumière, & plus de courage de prendre le party de la vérité. ( Rep. à Mr. de Condom, p. 405.)
units.tr: I am astonished that this excellent mind has not noticed that everything he alleges against the authority of the Councils of Rome can be turned back against the authority that our synods usurp. For if those who will not submit to the synods must be cut off from the Church, even when they fall into error, it will not be permitted to oppose them. The evil will be without remedy; the error will pass into the force of law, authentic and irrevocable. It will become more general, more lasting, and therefore more difficult to check: although the leaders are blind, it will not be permitted to individuals, to whom God has given more strength, more light and more courage, to take the side of the truth. (Reply to Mr. de Condom, p. 405.)

units.la: St. Athanase aura eu tort de s'opposer à l'impiété de l'Arrianisme ; nos reformateurs sur tout, seront fort criminels, & ce sera avec justice, qu'on a fulminé contr' eux des anathemes, puis qu'ils ont osé ouvrir la bouche contre tant de Conciles, qui avoient établi les points qu'ils ont combatus ; & une personne comme moy, qui n'en a point d'autre qui la seconde, sera dans l'erreur pour publier ce tombeau de la Puissance Ecclésiastique & son Excommunication, que nos Eglises reçoivent pour une institution de J. C. & pour s'opposer (comme fesoit le seul Athanase à l'Arrianisme) à un sentiment autant généralement reçeu qu'estoit l'Arrianisme.
units.tr: St. Athanasius was wrong to oppose the impiety of Arianism; our reformers above all will be very guilty, and it will be with justice that anathemas have been thundered against them, since they dared to open their mouths against so many Councils, which had established the points they have fought against; and a person like me, who has no one else to support him, will be in error for publishing this tomb of Ecclesiastical Power and its excommunication, which our churches accept as an institution of Jesus Christ, and for opposing (as Athanasius alone did against Arianism) an opinion as generally received as Arianism was.

units.la: Il ne sert de rien, de dire que St. Athanase & nos Reformateurs se sont opposez au mensonge, & que par consequent on les a anathématizez mal à propos : car les Conciles prétendent n'avoir rien ordonné, qui ne soit conforme à la parole de Dieu, dont ils ont allégué les passages, Nos synodes prétendent la mesme chose. Mais qui oséra soûtenir, qu'ils ne puissent jamais établir aucune erreur ; ce seroit les canoniser, & les rendre infaillibles ; ce que nous n'avons pas creu jusqu'à présent. Et l'expérience fait assez voir le contraire. Car quand il n'y auroit que le pouvoir qu'ils se donnent d'obliger à croire leurs décisions, & à y souscrire, comme des véritez incontestables, sous peine d'estre retranchez de l'Eglise, comme des impies, c'est une procédeure que je ne crois pas Chrestienne.
units.tr: It is no use to say that St. Athanasius and our Reformers opposed a lie, and that consequently they were anathematised wrongly. For the Councils claim to have ordained nothing that is not conformable to the Word of God, and they have cited its passages; our synods claim the same. But who would dare to maintain that they can never establish any error? That would be to canonise them and make them infallible, which we have not believed until now, and experience shows the contrary well enough. For even if there were only the power they give themselves to oblige people to believe their decisions and to subscribe to them as incontestable truths, under pain of being cut off from the Church as impious persons, this is a procedure I do not believe to be Christian.

units.la: Je pourrois mettre en mesme rang l'excommunication, qui est une invention des Payens, établie par le Pape parmi les Chrestiens, qui est pourtant au gré de vos Synodes ; que si quelqu'un y alloit soûtenir, que ce n'est qu'une fourberie, comme j'en suis persuadé, on la mettroit d'abord en usage contre luy, comme l'on fit contre le Médecin de la Rochelle l'an 1577 (en plein Synode, où Théodore de Béze présidoit) pour ne l'avoir pas creüe; Mais c'est un expouventail de chenevière, qui ne fait du mal qu'à ceux qui en ont peur, non plus que les foudres du Vatican.
units.tr: I could put in the same rank excommunication, which is an invention of the Pagans, established by the Pope among Christians, and which nonetheless is to the liking of your synods; if anyone were to maintain, as I am persuaded, that it is nothing but a trick, he would at once be made to feel it, as was done to the physician of La Rochelle in 1577 (in full synod, where Théodore de Bèze presided), for not having believed it. But it is a scarecrow of hemp, which harms only those who are afraid of it, no more than the thunderbolts of the Vatican do.

units.la: Vous scavez Monsieur; & vous n'approuvez pas la maniére dont ceux de Genéve & de Suisse se sont avisez depuis peu de traitter ceux qui n'ont pas assez de foy pour croire l'imputation du péché d'Adam antécédente de la corruption: vous scavez qu'ils ont érigé en Articles de foy l'imputation de la justice active de J. C. la damnation des hommes par le défaut d'un Rédempteur, & parce que Dieu ne veut pas qu'ils soient sauvez, ni qu'ils se repentent; l'impuissance Physique d'obéir aux commandemens de Dieu, l'antiquité & la divinité des points du texte Hebreu & divers autres points peu importans au salut, & dont ils imposent aux Ministres la souscription, sous peine à ceux qui refusent d'estre réjettez comme indignes du Ministére: combien y en a t-il qui signent ces nouveaux formulaires contre leur conscience, & qui se pleignent secretment, (car ce seroit un crime digne de déposition de parler haut) que nos assemblées Ecclésiastiques usurpent un empire sur les ames; que l'on fait passer des traditions humaines pour des véritez Divines: que les pasteurs qui ont acquis quelque crédit, veulent faire recevoir leurs sentiments particuliers pour des articles de foy,& qu'enfin les Reformez agissent, avec cette mesme tyrannie, qui a tant fait crier nos Peres, & qui les a obligez à se séparer d'avec l'Eglise Romaine.
units.tr: You know, Sir, and you do not approve of the way those of Geneva and Switzerland have lately taken to treat those who do not have enough faith to believe the imputation of Adam's sin as antecedent to corruption. You know that they have made into articles of faith the imputation of the active justice of Jesus Christ; the damnation of men through the lack of a Redeemer; and, because God does not want them to be saved nor to repent, the physical inability to obey the commandments of God; the antiquity and divinity of the points of the Hebrew text; and various other points of little importance to salvation, to which they require ministers to subscribe, on pain of being rejected as unworthy of the ministry if they refuse. How many there are who sign these new formularies against their conscience, and who complain in secret (for it would be a crime deserving deposition to speak out loudly) that our ecclesiastical assemblies usurp an empire over souls; that human traditions are passed off as divine truths; that the ministers who have acquired some credit want their particular opinions received as articles of faith; and that, in short, the Reformed act with the same tyranny that made our fathers cry out so much and obliged them to separate from the Roman Church.

units.la: Voila les beaux effets de la Puissance Ecclésiastique : est-ce-là une conduite Chrestienne? Et les Apostres nous ont-ils enseigné de prendre ainsi à la gorge nos freres, pour leur faire embrasser aveuglément nos sentimens. Supposé mesme que ce fussent des véritez, puisqu'elles ne sont pas des véritez nécessaires pour le salut : Ne faudroitil pas supporter les foibles avec un esprit. de charité ? D'où vient que les hommes sujeEts à l'erreur demandent plus de soûmissiõn que les Apostres qui estoient infaillibles ? Ne void-on pas clairement que tous les desordres qui troublent nos Eglises, & qui les perdront si Dieu n'y remédie, viennent de cette source mal-heureuse de la Puissance Ecclésiastique qui ne peut pas subsister qu'elle ne produise des violences semblables à celles qu'on a veües dans la communion de l'Antechrist. On appelle cette Puissance-là spirituele; & on a raison à un égard, ascavoir parce qu'elle exerce sa juridiction sur les ames & sur les consciences, qui est entreprendre sur les droits de Dieu, & ravir aux Chrestiens le plus beau fleuron de leur couronne: Car l'avantage que nous avons d'estre faits Rois par J. C. consiste en ce que nous ne dépendons point d'aucune créature, pour ce qui regarde l'homme intérieur, & que nostre conscience ne reconnoit d'autre supérieur que Dieu seul, selon l'ordre de l'Apostre, 1 Cor. 7. Vous avez esté rachêtez par prix ; ne devenez pas les Esclaves des hommes.
units.tr: Here are the fine effects of ecclesiastical power! Is this Christian conduct? Did the Apostles teach us to seize our brothers by the throat, in order to make them embrace our opinions blindly? Suppose, moreover, that these were truths, since they are not necessary truths for salvation: ought we not to bear with the weak in a spirit of charity? Why is it that men subject to error demand more submission than the Apostles, who were infallible? Is it not clear that all the disorders that trouble our churches, and that will ruin them unless God intervenes, come from this unhappy source of ecclesiastical power, which cannot exist without producing violences like those seen in the communion of Antichrist? This power is called spiritual, and rightly so in one respect, namely because it exercises its jurisdiction over souls and consciences. That is to usurp the rights of God and to rob Christians of the finest jewel in their crown. For the advantage we have in being made kings by Jesus Christ consists in this: that we depend on no creature in what concerns the inner man, and that our conscience acknowledges no superior but God alone, according to the Apostle's order, 1 Cor. 7. You were bought with a price; do not become the slaves of men.

units.la: Vouz
units.tr: You

units.la: Vouz direz sans doute que depuis plus d'un siécle, le gouvernement des Eglises de France, n'a apporté aucun trouble, ni à l'Eglise, ni à l'Estat; qui est une preuve que noftre Difcipline, n'eft pas appuyée fur des fondemens fi dangereux que je viens de les remarquer : Je repons à cela que les productions naturelles & ordinaires de la Puiffance Ecclésiastique, n'ont pas paru parmi vous, premiérement à caufe de la contradiction, & du grand pouvoir de nos adverfaires qui a tenu cette beste farouche de Puiffance Ecclésiastique comme enchainée, & qui nous a rendus plus reiglez & moins hardis à bastir fur nos prétensions. En second lieu, parce qu'encore que vous fondiez voftre difcipline fur la prétendue puiffance Spirituele, & fur un droit Divin ; ce n'eft pourtant au fonds que l'érection d'un pouvoir civil authorifé ou délégué par le fouverain, de qui vous dépendez ou ce n'eft tout au plus que l'établiffement d'une authorité prife par un commun confentement, & que l'on appelle difcipline confédérée, qui tient lieu de Magiftrat, & à laaquelle tous vos peuples acquiefcent parce qu'elle eft necessaire dans la condition où vous eftes. Tout le mal qu'il y a, c'eft que vous la retenez, Je ne diray pas par des fourbes & par des mensonges, mais par des fraudes pieuses, y employant les peines Ecclésiastiques, qui sont de pures imaginations, & qui sont destituées de la parole de Dieu, & que vous tâchez en vain d'accréditer par le pouvoir de lier, & de délier,& par le maniement que vous vous attribuez des clefs du Royaume des cieux; car vous faittes entendre à nos peuples ce qui n'est pas, asc. que par lier il faut entendre excommunier & que délier vaut autant que lever l'excommunication ou absoudre, & que par l'excommunication une personne est livrée un Diable. Car J'ay fait voir dans ma Parénèse, à quoy on n'a point répondu, que les Protestans & les Papistes s'accordent mutuellement pour se créer un empire sur les peuples, & combien les uns & les autres se trompent dans l'exposition qu'ils donnent à tous les passages, sur lesquels ils appuyent leur authorité, fur tout dans l'explication de ces paroles de J. C. di-la l'Eglise qui pourroient autant souffrir celle que ceux de Rome luy donnent, c'est à dire di le au Pape ou à l'assemblée des Prélats, que celle de nos Ministres qui veulent que par l'Eglise & on entende un consistoire de Pasteurs & d'Anciens.
units.tr: No doubt you will say that for more than a century the government of the churches of France has caused no disturbance either to the Church or to the State, which is proof that our discipline is not founded on such dangerous foundations as I have just pointed out. I answer that the natural and ordinary products of ecclesiastical power have not appeared among you, first, because of the opposition and great power of our adversaries, which has kept this savage beast of ecclesiastical power as it were chained, and which has made us more restrained and less bold in building upon our pretensions.
