units.la: Cependant, Monsieur, que les hommes fassent de moy tel jugement qu'il leur plaira, je ne m'offencerai pas plus de leurs injures, que St. Paul decelles de Festus, lors qu'il l'accusoit d'estre hors du sens, quand il luy proposoit les mysteres de Christianisme. Si c'est une follie, je croi que c'est une des follies de la predication.
units.tr: Yet, Monsieur, whatever judgement men may pass on me, I shall be no more offended by their insults than St. Paul was by those of Festus, when Festus accused him of being out of his mind because he set before him the mysteries of Christianity. If it is folly, I believe it is one of the follies of preaching.

units.la: Avant que de finir cét entretien, Monsieur, je ne puis pas m'empêcher de remarquer l'étrange persuasion, dont la plus part de nos gens sont prévenus, de s'imaginer que la Reformation à laquelle Calvin a tant contribué ait esté portée par luy au dernier degré de perfection, non seulement pour la doctrine, mais pour le Gouvernement, de sorte que ce soit comme un attentat impie. d'y rien ajouter, & d'en rien didiminuer. Ne voit-on pas tout au contraire que Dieu a difpensé à ses serviteurs ses lumiéres par divers degrez. Au commancement Luther ne fist qu'entrevoir, comme au travers d'une nuée, qu'il y avoit quelques erreurs dans la communion du Pape. Il estoit comme cét homme, dont il est parlé dans l'Evangile, qui au commancement que nostre Seigneur luy eut rendu la vuë, ne voyoit les hommes que comme des arbres. Il acquit peu à peu de grandes connoissances ; mais encore voit-on qu'il y a du défant dans sa Reformation, & qu'il y a des erreurs dans la communion qui se glorifie de son nom. Est-ce une chose impossible que Calvin n'ait pas tout découvert ? estoit-il infaillible ? Il semble à nos gens qu'il ait eu le mesme privilege que Moyse, & que Dieu l'a élevé sur la sainte montagne, où il luy fait voir le modéle d'une Reformation si parfaite, qu'il n'y faut rien faire que suivant ses ordres : On a comme canonisé parmi nous sa Liturgie & son Catéchisme ; non seulement pour le sens, mais jusqu'au moindre de ses vieux mots. Pour moy je le regarde comme un excellent serviteur de Dieu. Je l'égale aux S. Hiéromes, aux S. Augustins, & à tout ce qu'il y a eu de plus excellens Docteurs dans l'Eglise de puis les Apôtres, mais je ne le considére pas comme un Apôtre, ou comme la reigle infallible de ma foy : je me tiens à la mesme reigle, dont il s'est servi luymesme, qui est la parole de Dieu. L'Eglise dans ce monde peut-elle estre sans tache & sans ride ? St. Paul ne nous apprend-il pas que nous ne voyons encore qu'en partie, &c. ? N'est-il pas pû rester quelque paille parmi un grand amas de bon grain, & quelque peu de crasse parmi une grosse masse de bon or ? Faut-il tellement captiver son Esprit, & ses lumiéres à celles du siécle passé, que nous n'ayons pas aujourd'huy la mesme liberté, dont nos prédecesseurs se sont servi d'examiner toutes choses, pour ne retenir que ce qui est bon ? & Dieu aura-t-il tellement épuisé, dans ce temps-là, où il ne donnoit que les dons ordinaires de son Esprit non plus qu'à present, qu'il ne luy en reste plus à dispenser à l'avenir ?
units.tr: Before ending this conversation, Monsieur, I cannot refrain from remarking on the strange conviction by which most of our people are held, that the Reformation to which Calvin contributed so much was carried by him to the last degree of perfection, not only in doctrine but in government, so that to add anything to it, or to take anything from it, is regarded as an impious attempt. Do we not see, on the contrary, that God has dispensed his light to his servants by different degrees? At the beginning Luther only glimpsed, as though through a cloud, that there were some errors in the communion of the Pope. He was like the man spoken of in the Gospel, who, when our Lord had first given him his sight, saw men only as trees. He gradually acquired great knowledge; yet we still see that there is a defect in his Reformation, and that there are errors in the communion which glories in his name. Is it an impossible thing that Calvin did not discover everything? Was he infallible? Our people seem to think he had the same privilege as Moses, and that God raised him up on the holy mountain, where he showed him the pattern of a Reformation so perfect that nothing must be done except in obedience to his orders. Among us his Liturgy and his Catechism have been, as it were, canonised, not only in their sense but down to the smallest of their old words. For my part, I regard him as an excellent servant of God. I put him on a level with St. Jerome, St. Augustine, and all the most excellent teachers in the Church since the Apostles; but I do not consider him an Apostle, or the infallible rule of my faith. I hold to the same rule that he himself used, which is the Word of God. Can the Church in this world be without spot or wrinkle? Does not St. Paul teach us that we see only in part, and so on? Can there not have remained some chaff amid a great heap of good grain, and some dross amid a large mass of good gold? Must we so bind our minds and our lights to those of the past century that we do not today have the same freedom our predecessors used to examine all things, in order to hold fast what is good? And will God have so exhausted himself in that time, when he gave only the ordinary gifts of his Spirit, no more than he gives now, that he has nothing left to bestow in the future?

units.la: Ce sont des maximes bien dangereuses que celles-là. C'est par-là que l'erreur s'est établie dans l'Eglise Rom. On a eu une si grande opinion de ses premiers Docteurs, qu'on a reçeu tout ce qu'ils ont écrit comme des oracles. Sur cette préocupation, on a tout reçeu à yeux clos & sans examiner. Pour peu qu'ils soyent sortis du bon chemin ils ont fait faire de grands égaremens à ceux qui les ont suivis, & leurs petites erreurs ont esté le fondement à de tresgrandes, & en-fin ou en est venu au comble. Si nous persévérons dans nos maximes,il est à craindre que la mesme chose ne nous arrive. On en voit desia des preuves, qui ne sont que trop évidentes dans les démarches que la Puissance Ecclésiastique a fait faire à nos freres de Suisse & de Genéve. Ils ont selon leur prétendu pouvoir d'imposer au peuple, & aux Ministres à croire ce qui plaiît aux plus accréditez d'entreux, érigé diverses doctrines en articles de foy, que le plus grand nombre des Théologiens Orthodoxes condamnent d'erreur. Sur cette paille qu'il a plu à la puissance Ecclésiastique de poser au rang des fondemens inébranables de la foy, l'esprit de mensonge, ne manquera pas de bastir des erreurs, que nous ne pouvons pas prévoir, mais qui feront gémir la postérité. Si je demeurois dans le silence en prévoyant tous ces grands maux, je croirois trahir la cause de Dieu. C'estce qui ne fait employer le peu de force qui me reste pour réveiller les gens de bien, & pour les obliger à se défaire d'un préjugé, dont on voit de si mauvaises suites, & dont on a sujet d'en craindre de beaucoup plus grandes. Je m'y sens d'autant plus obligé que je voi que personne n'ose parler, de peur de s'attirer sur les bras les amis & les ennemis. Combien en connoi-je qui sont persuadez aussi bien que moi de la vérité de mes hypothéses, qui n'oseroient les soûtenir, de peur de perdre la réputation qu'ils ont aquise dans le monde. Ils craignent d'estre traitez d'extravagans. Mais s'il y a icy de la folie, que les personnes desinteressées jugent de quel costé elle est : Ou de la part de ceux qui renoncent volontairement à la liberté de la conscience que J. C. nous a aquise pour se soûmettre au joug des hommes, & de leurs décisions; ou du costé de ceux qui embrafferont mes sentimens, & qui comme moy ne reconnoitront qu'un seul législateur, assavoir celuy qui peut sauver & détruire. Je préfère ma folie à leur prétendue sagesse.
units.tr: Those are very dangerous maxims. It is by this route that error established itself in the Roman Church. People held such a high opinion of its first teachers that they received everything they wrote as oracles. Under this prejudice they accepted everything with their eyes shut and without examination. However slightly those teachers strayed from the right path, they led their followers into great errors, their small mistakes became the foundation of much greater ones, and at last the matter reached its height. If we persist in our maxims, the same thing is to be feared for us. We already see proofs of it, all too evident, in the steps the ecclesiastical power has made our brethren in Switzerland and Geneva take. By its supposed authority to impose on the people and on the ministers the belief that pleases the most influential among them, it has raised various doctrines to articles of faith, which the greater part of orthodox theologians condemn as erroneous. On this straw, which the ecclesiastical power has been pleased to lay down as one of the immovable foundations of faith, the spirit of falsehood will not fail to build errors that we cannot foresee, but which will make posterity groan. If I remained silent while foreseeing all these great evils, I would believe I was betraying the cause of God. This is why I am spending what little strength remains to me to rouse good people and to induce them to rid themselves of a prejudice whose consequences are so bad, and from which we have reason to fear much worse. I feel all the more obliged to do so because I see that no one dares to speak, for fear of drawing both friends and enemies upon themselves. How many do I know who are as convinced as I am of the truth of my hypotheses, yet who would not dare to defend them, for fear of losing the reputation they have acquired in the world! They fear being treated as eccentrics. But if there is folly here, let disinterested people judge on which side it lies: whether with those who voluntarily give up the liberty of conscience that Christ has won for us, in order to submit to the yoke of men and their decisions; or with those who will embrace my views and, like me, will acknowledge only one lawgiver, namely he who can save and destroy. I prefer my folly to their supposed wisdom.

units.la: Je vous souhaitte Monsieur, toute prospérité d'aussi bon cœur que suis,
units.tr: I wish you, Sir, all prosperity, with as good a heart as I am

units.tr: Your most humble and most obedient servant

units.la: Pupugit animum Celeberrimi Johannis Claudii (Vir Clarissime) quod postremis meis ad Eum literis excidit, nec excidisse poenitet, quasi per linguae, aut potius calami intemperantiam, dixerim quod nunc dictum nolim, optandum esse, ut pericope illa In nomine & authoritate Domini nostri Jesu Christi excommunico omnes idololatras, haereticos &c. eraderetur ex Exegesi paraenetica quae pronunciatur à Sacrorum Antistite itite ante Synaxin ; tum affirmaverim si sacrum nomen Jesu Christi mittendum est in compendium, per solam literam quæ est caput cujusque vocabuli, tum nominis, tum cognominis ut est J. C. par esse intelligi,non Jesum Christum, sed Joh. Calvinum, cujus authoritate & in cujus nomine fulmine excommunicationis percuti & amburi reos criminum, quæ ibi longo ordine recensentur, tam certus sum, quam scio me per Dei gratiam etiamnum vivere, nec hac in re quicquam temerè à me dictum esse, quod non fit rationi & veritati consonum, & quod me sententiam mutare cogat. Jam fi propter hoc pronunciatum mihi lis intenditur à summo viro, nolim stare ejus decretorio judicio, nec cujufquam sacri ordinis, imo ne Augustinorum, Ambrosiorum & Hieronymorum, fi rebus humanis hodie interessent, quos ipse Augustinus recusavit, ut minus idoneos & competentes, ut loquuntur, Judices, quam viros qui sunt de natione laica, ut foret Medicus, Mathematicus, Rhetor, Grammaticus, hisce, in re quæ est communis utilitatis, minus præpeditis studio partium,quam viris Ecclesiasticis: quibus solenne est stare pro sua Helena, seu potestate Ecclesiastica, hoc est imperio, cujus amor, ut ait Tacitus, tunica est, quæ primò induitur & ultimò exuitur. Nam si in Claudium omnes dotes Augustinorum, Hieronymorum, Chrysostomorum & Basiliorum concurrerent foedere facto: à quibus tamen non longè abest vir Præstantissimus, malleem in re de qua certamen est inter nos, stare tuo judicio quam illius. Usque adeo verum sit optimos quosque viros aliquâ sua cuique utilitate à vero abduci, in re sua & propria. Certè Augustinus, tantò æquior fuit in Episcopatum, quod ipse esset Episcopus: altrinsecus Hieronymus, tantò iniquior fuit in Episcopatum, quod in ordine Presbyteratûs consisteret. Quocirca, si mihi dispiciendus est Judex: non alium volo in tota Gallia præter Te, Excellentissime Vir, quem figo & destino meum arbitrum, ad quem provoco. Non sub hac ratione, quod Tibi sit multus in Bibliothecis locus, & quòd sis vir ingenii acerrimi, judicii sub-
units.tr: It has troubled my mind, most distinguished sir, that in my last letter to the most celebrated John Claude a remark slipped out, and I am not sorry that it did. Through the intemperance of my tongue, or rather of my pen, I wrote something I would now prefer not to have said: that it is to be wished that the passage In the name and authority of our Lord Jesus Christ I excommunicate all idolaters, heretics, etc. were erased from the paraenetic exhortation that the minister of the sacred rites pronounces before the Synaxis. I then affirmed that if the sacred name of Jesus Christ is to be abbreviated to the single letter that begins each word, both name and surname, as J. C., it should be understood to mean not Jesus Christ but John Calvin. In his authority and name, the offenders of the crimes listed there at length are struck and burned by the thunderbolt of excommunication. I am as certain of this as I am that by God's grace I am still alive, and nothing I said in this matter was rashly said. It is not consonant with reason and truth, and nothing compels me to change my opinion. Now, if on account of this statement a lawsuit is brought against me by that most distinguished man, I would not willingly abide by his decisive judgment, nor that of any sacred order. Nor would I accept that of the Augustines, Ambroses and Jeromes, even if they were alive in human affairs today; Augustine himself rejected them as less suitable and competent judges, as they say, than laymen such as a physician, a mathematician, a rhetorician or a grammarian. In a matter of common utility, these men are less hampered by partisan zeal than churchmen, to whom it is customary to stand up for their own Helen, that is, ecclesiastical power, that is, rule, whose love, as Tacitus says, is a tunic which is put on first and taken off last. For if all the gifts of Augustines, Jeromes, Chrysostoms and Basils were joined together by a pact in Claude, from whom the most distinguished man is not far removed, I would rather in a matter in dispute between us stand by your judgment than by his. So true is it that even the best men are drawn away from the truth by some advantage of their own, in matters that concern themselves personally. Certainly Augustine was all the fairer toward the episcopate because he was himself a bishop; Jerome, on the other hand, was all the more unfair toward it because it stood above the order of presbyter. Wherefore, if I must have a judge examined, I want no one in all of France but you, most excellent sir. I fix and appoint you as my arbiter and appeal to you. I do not do so on the ground that you have much room in libraries, or that you are a man of keenest wit, most refined judgment and most recondite learning, of eloquence and style that rises with natural beauty, or because you have what is the chief thing of piety: you fear and love God and revere his ministers. Rather, it is because you are a physician. That is, you stand among those men who are least of all clouded and blinded by prejudices, and least carried away from the good, the fair and the true. But I ask for you and want you as judge, and also as my advocate and pleader before the most distinguished Claude, one who will make him more favourable to me, and also before others whom nature has formed of finer clay than the common run of talented and learned men. Such men are led not by reason but by custom, by the example and upbringing of many, arranging their affairs like those who float on rivers. They do not swim but are carried, so it is no wonder if they applaud our opinion before they understand it, or before they have heard anything of it except through a fog. But I do not doubt that the weight of the reasons, which I set out more fully to the reverend Pierre Mussard and also in the letter to the most learned Senator of Geneva, Jean Dupan, will please the former all the more, if they please you.

Sed, nec Te solùm posco & volo judicem, sed & pararium & advocatum apud Clarissimum Claudium, commodiorem præstando illum mihi, ut & apud alios, quos natura tuo luto hoc est meliori formavit, quam vulgus ingeniorum & doctorum: qui, cum non ratione, sed consuetudine, plurium exemplo & educatione, ducantur, sua disponentes ad modum eorum, qui fluminibus innatant, non eant, sed ferantur; non mirum si noltram sententiam, prius explaudant quam intelligant; vel priusquam de ea quicquam, nisi per nebulam audiverint. units.tr: of most refined judgment, of most recondite learning; of eloquence and style that rises with natural beauty; and, which is the chief thing of piety, who fears and loves God and reveres his ministers. But you are a physician, that is, you stand in that station of men who are least of all clouded and blinded by prejudices, and least carried away from the good, the fair and the true. But I ask for you and want you not only as judge but also as my advocate and pleader before the most distinguished Claude, offering him to me in a more favourable light, and also before others whom nature has formed of finer clay than the common run of talented and learned men. Such men are led not by reason but by custom, by the example of many and their upbringing, arranging their affairs like those who float on rivers, who do not swim but are carried. It is no wonder if they applaud our opinion before they understand it, or before they have heard anything about it except through a fog.

units.la: ET te quoque, Vir Clarissime, pono inter illos, qui licet forsan non usque quaque in nostram sententiam de Potestate Ecclesiastica pedibus euntes, illam tamen in summa rei, nec improbant, nec damnant. Sed imprimis refero Te in numerum virorum, non vulgaris, sed altioris intellectûs, quam fert captus seculi nostri, qui se non mancipant tyrannidi consuetudinis & opinionum, eo quod sint à pluribus receptæ; cujus rei, mihi luculentum testimonium est, quod cum ante decennium parares editioni luculentum opus, in quo hæcce tria maximè elucebant, eruditio, judicium, oratio: attamen præjudicia tuorum symmystarum obstiterunt, quominus lucem aspiceret; nam eadem præjudicia Te abdunt in Galliæ angulum, in quo prætulisti libertatem prophetandi, & tua sensa tibi habendi, sed cum paucis & intimis communicandi, publicæ stationi & professioni in Theatro Galliæ, in quo os tuum obturatum fuisset. Te etiam liberum esse ab eo morbo præjudiciorum, fidem fecisti, in tuo opere, in quo, cum Te non lateret Parænesim meam passim proscindi & dilacerari, ut fœtum infelicem, & qui futurus esset exitialis toti Ecclesiæ, & cujus parens constringendus esset vinculis Hipocratis, ut pote delirus & sanæ mentis deliquia patiens; Tu vir candide, longè aliis oculis, alio judicio opus meum æstimavisti & introspexisti, & de eo pronunciavisti, non gratiæ causâ, cum tibi plane ignotus essem, cum in tuo opere, tum maximè tuis ad me literis, quibus aurum non est mihi pretiosius. Profecto, si agmen ducis eorum, qui præjudiciis homi-num, num, cæterà virorum, ingenio eruditione & pietate præstantium, penè opprimuntur, proximus ego sum Tibi, in quem (licet imbellem & molliorem infimâ auriculâ, sed solâ bonâ causâ & conscientiâ sustentatum) tempestas illa præjudiciorum, detonuit ad terram afflixit, & penè procuìcavit. Fuit tempus cum cognati, affines, uxor, soror, liberi; nepotes duo, alter Petrus Molinæus, alter Petrus Jurieu: Tum maxima Presbyterianorum cohors, Gallorum, Anglorum, Scotorum, Germanorum, Hollandorum, horum imprimis, me, aut damnarent, aut differrent ut eversorem omnis juris Divini & humani ordinis, vocarent flagrum Ecclesiæ: hortarentur, ut miserer hujusce animulæ, quam ibam perditum, quandiu persistabam obstinatè in incoepto regnum Christi evertendi per ruinam Potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, & Excommunicationis. Venerandus Langlæus Rotomagensis, volebat caput meum in crusibulo fundi, ut inde defæcatius prodiret. Summus vir Samuel Bochartus me relegabat ad gentiles & agnatos, aut mitte-bat bat Anticyras, ut inde esu Hellebori redirem mente, fanior. Clarissimus Durellus, mihi affinitate junctus edicebat per literas fratri meo Petro Molinæo Canonico Cantuariensi, quem Parentis loco habeo & colo, nec ingenium Scriptioni, nec dictis rationem mihi superesse.
units.tr: You too, most distinguished sir, I count among those who, though perhaps not in every respect following our opinion on ecclesiastical power, nevertheless in the main neither disapprove of it nor condemn it. Above all, I number you among men of no ordinary understanding, a higher understanding than the intellect of our age usually bears, who do not enslave themselves to the tyranny of custom and opinion merely because many have accepted them. Of this I have a clear proof: when, a decade ago, you were preparing an excellent work for publication, in which three qualities especially shone forth, learning, judgement and eloquence, the prejudices of your fellow-sympathisers nevertheless stood in the way and kept it from seeing the light. The same prejudices drove you into a corner of France, where you preferred the freedom of prophesying and of holding your own views, communicating them only to a few intimates, rather than a public post and a professorship in the theatre of France, where your mouth would have been stopped. You also showed, in your work, that you are free of that disease of prejudice. You were not unaware that my Parænesis was everywhere torn to pieces and mangled as an unhappy offspring, deadly to the whole Church, whose parent ought to be bound with Hippocrates' chains as a madman, subject to lapses of sound mind. Yet you, candid sir, judged and examined my work with quite different eyes and a different judgement, and pronounced on it, not out of favour, since I was wholly unknown to you, both in your work and especially in your letters to me, to which gold is no more precious. Indeed, if you lead the column of those who are almost crushed by the prejudices of men, while the other men eminent in genius, learning and piety are crushed too, then I am the one closest to you. On me, though feeble and softer than the lowest ear, sustained only by a good cause and a clear conscience, that tempest of prejudice thundered, struck me to the ground and almost prostrated me. There was a time when my relatives, kinsmen, wife, sister, children and two grandsons, one Pierre Molinæus and the other Pierre Jurieu, and then the greatest host of Presbyterians, French, English, Scots, Germans and Dutch, above all these, either condemned me or, deferring, called me the flagrum Ecclesiæ (scourge of the Church), the subverter of all divine and human order. They urged that I pity this little soul which I was ruining, as long as I obstinately persisted in my undertaking to overthrow the kingdom of Christ by destroying ecclesiastical power and excommunication. The venerable Langlæus of Rouen wanted my head melted down in a crucible so that it might come out purer. The eminent Samuel Bochart sent me back to the heathens and my kinsfolk, or sent me to Anticyra, so that after a dose of hellebore I might return to my senses, saner. The most distinguished Durell, joined to me by marriage, wrote to my brother Pierre Molinæus, canon of Canterbury, whom I regard and honour in the place of a father, that I had neither the talent for writing nor reason left.

units.la: Sed nullibi locorum implacabilior iracundia, & minus exorabilis, quam in Hollandia & Zelandia, & cæteris Provinciis fœderatis; nec uspiam major terror subortus, quasi Annibal esset ad portas, & quasi potestati illi Chimericæ, per quam ejus vindices penè seculum integrum subliniverunt ora fatuorum, & submiserunt stupidorum & bardorum colla suo jugo, specie jugi Christi, paratum & in procinctu esset excidium. Narravit mihi aliquando, vir illustris Johannes Borelius legatus apud Serenissimum Regem, odio usque Vatiniano mihi infensos esse, ut si impune & clam liceret, me in frusta & minutim considerent, & in profluentem projicerent, ne ulla mei memoria superesset.
units.tr: But nowhere is anger more implacable or less placable than in Holland and Zealand and the other United Provinces. Nowhere has greater terror arisen, as if Hannibal were at the gates, and as if, for the sake of that chimerical power, by which its champions have for nearly a whole century smeared the faces of fools and bowed the necks of the stupid and the barbarous beneath their yoke, under the appearance of the yoke of Christ, ruin were at hand and ready. The illustrious John Borel, envoy to the Most Serene King, once told me that they were so hostile to me, with a hatred worthy of Vatinius, that if they could do so with impunity and in secret, they would cut me into pieces and bit by bit throw me into a running stream, so that no memory of me would remain.

units.la: Paulo æquiora, sed tamen aspera exexpertus sum in Anglia per præjudicia bonorum virorum. In memoriam revoco, cùm vix bene prodiisset nostra Parænefis, & cum Oxonio Londinum excurrissem, mihi pet viam factum obviam Presbyterianorum primipilum, Lazarum Seaman, virum doctum & pietate conspicuum, nunc inter beatos, & me sic adortum fuisse, animo plane commotiori; Itane per tuum Parænesim pedibus conculcavisti regimen Christi, quod est Presbyterianum. Memini etiam cùm in istius urbis illustri Academia, essem Professor Historiarum, & rogarer quodam die, ut adessem conviva amico ibidem Professori, in prandio, ad quod plures invitati essent, Professores, doctores & reverendi viri de sacro ordine, noluisse unum de istis (nomen erat Edmundus Calamy) turbæ convivarum interesse, cui immixtus esset vir adeo nefarius, ut erat author Paranæseos imperii in imperio: qua in re voluit imitari Johannem Apostolum, qui noluit ingredi balneum, in quod recens intraverat Cerinthus perditus hereticus.
units.tr: I have experienced somewhat milder, yet still harsh, treatment in England at the hands of good men's prejudices. I recall that when our Parænesis had scarcely been published, and I had hurried from Oxford to London, the leader of the Presbyterians, Lazarus Seaman, a learned man distinguished for piety, now among the blessed, met me on the way and addressed me with a mind plainly rather agitated: So through your Parænesis you have trampled underfoot the government of Christ, which is Presbyterian. I also remember that when I was Professor of History in the famous Academy of that city, and one day I was asked to attend, as a guest, a dinner given by a friend who was also a professor there, at which several guests were invited, professors, doctors and reverend men of the sacred order, one of them (his name was Edmund Calamy) refused to join the company of diners, because a man so wicked as the author of the Paranæseos imperii in imperio was mingling with them. In this he wished to imitate the Apostle John, who refused to enter the bath into which the recently arrived heretic Cerinthus had entered.

units.la: Sed per Dei gratiam, idem mihi, quod Jobo evenit, ut itidem illi turbæ adversariorum meorum, quod amicis Jobi: quorum utrobique, horum de Jobo, illorum de me, cum perversissimum & iniquissimum esset judicium, attamen, par æquitas & bonitas est causæ meæ, quæ fuit Jobi: vicissim par sanctitas vitæ reperitur in Jobi amicis, aut potius adversariis, atque in meis; ut jam par sit spes suturum, ut mei adversarii per agnitionem erroris & iniqui de me judicii perinde resipiscant, atque Eliphæ & cæteris sodalibus accidit, ut resipiscerent. Et revera mollito lapsu temporis animo, non solum idem Calamy, sed & itidem Lazarus Seaman, fuerunt æquiores in me, junxerunt que mecum dextras, & unà plures de eodem ordine, Angli & Scoti, aut in meam sententiam concesserunt; aut saltem deposuerunt suum rigorem, & horrorem odiumque in me & sententiam meam de Potestate Ecclesiastica: accedente ad mitigandos eorum animos, hoc commodo, quod meus Patronus bonæ fidei aliquando discordes, postmodum vinculo culo communis utilitatis devinciret & sociaret; quam illi & ego juxta fovebamus. Denique mihi usu venit, circa sententiam meam, tantopere & tam odiose, imo cum horrore acceptam, uno tempore à Gallis, Anglis & Scotis, Germanis, Hollandis; alio vero & posteriori, aut probatam & retentam, aut commodiori interpretatione lenitam, quod legitur in apologo Leonis & Vulpis: quæ cum ad primum conspectum leonis propemodum animam reliquisset; rursus visum, minus timuit, tandem tertio conspectu, non adire modo sed compellare coram & prope familiariter ausa est.
units.tr: But by the grace of God, what happened to Job has also happened to me: my adversaries have been like Job's friends. On both sides, theirs judged Job and theirs judged me, the judgement was most perverse and most unjust. Yet my cause has an equal fairness and goodness as Job's did, and in turn an equal holiness of life is found in my adversaries as in Job's friends, or rather his adversaries, and in mine. So there is now equal hope that my adversaries will, through the acknowledgement of their error and of their unjust judgement of me, repent just as Eliphaz and the other companions did. And indeed, as time softened their minds, not only Calamy but also Lazarus Seaman became fairer towards me, and they joined hands with me; and along with them many others of that same order, English and Scots, either came over to my opinion or at least laid aside their rigour, their horror and their hatred of me and of my view on ecclesiastical power. What helped to soften their minds was this advantage: my Patronus bonæ fidei bound and joined together those once at odds by the common bond of mutual advantage, which both they and I equally cherished. In the end it came about that my opinion, received at first so bitterly and so hatefully, even with horror, by the French, English, Scots, Germans and Dutch at one time, was at another and later time either approved and retained, or softened by a more favourable interpretation. This is what is read in the fable of the Lion and the Fox: when at the first sight of the lion she had almost given up the ghost, then, seeing him again, she feared less; and at last, at the third sight, she dared not merely to approach but to address him face to face, almost familiarly.

units.la: Hæcce in sinum tuum depono familiarius, vir Amicissime, ut lugeam Tecum miseram sortem judicii humani, mancipati tyrannidi præjudiciorum, consuetudinis, educationis, tum suæ cuique utilitatis, & rationum mundanarum: quandoque animi obfirmati, non discedendi ab errore, etiam in pectoris recessu agnito: ne qua inde labes inconstantiæ affricaretur honori, si semel prolata, aut scripto to aut ore retractarentur; ut jam non mirum si Papismus aut Turcismus regnet in mundo: Si deliria transubstantiationis & purgatorii arripiuntur ab ingeniis altioris intellectûs in Ecclesia Romana. Si in reformata maxi-mi quique viri, imo qui cum summo ingenio, summa eruditione junxerunt pietatem defæcatissimam; quales hodie sunt Johannes Claudius & Petrus Jurieu; (quales fuit Samuel Bochartus) perseverant in sententia tam futili, quam est Alcoranus, retinenda; ut est sententia de potestate Ecclesiastica seu media potestate, quæ nec est potestas verbi, nec potestas Magistratus aut confœderatæ disciplinæ.
units.tr: I lay these things more familiarly in your bosom, most friendly sir, so that I may lament with you the wretched lot of human judgement, enslaved to the tyranny of prejudice, custom, upbringing, each man's own advantage and worldly considerations; and sometimes the mind, hardened, will not depart from error even when it recognises it in the recesses of its heart, lest any stain of inconstancy should attach itself to its honour, if once put forward and then retracted, whether in writing or by word of mouth. So it is no wonder that Popery or Turkery reigns in the world, if the delusions of transubstantiation and purgatory are seized upon by intellects of higher understanding in the Roman Church, and if in the Reformed Church the greatest men, indeed those who joined the highest genius and the highest learning to the purest piety, such as John Claude and Pierre Jurieu today (as Samuel Bochart was), persist in retaining an opinion as frivolous as the Alcoran, namely the opinion about ecclesiastical power, or the middle power, which is neither the power of the Word, nor the power of the magistrate, nor of the confederated discipline.

units.la: Hæc etiam quæ attuli de præjudiciis sanctorum virorum, Te obfirmare debent pertinaciâ, in ea sententia; quod nec sint legitima, nec in quaquam ratione aut Scriptura fundata: si imprimis reputas, quod illorum præjudicia & forboniftæ Arnaldi, sint planè gemina: quodque non minus judicio nostrorum quam Arnaldi ratio proposita in jugulo causæ, sit incœptum detestandum & abominandum; qua in re fi æquiparo judicium nostrorum ad judicium Arnaldi, hujus mihi videtur magis æquum & magis rationi consonum, Nam cum nostra sententia de potestate Ecclesiastica & de excommunicatione, merito detestanda sit judicio Arnaldi, insistendo illius hypothesibus, eò quod unâ sundâ & uno silicis jactu aut ictu, ad terram det Papam, & unà totum Romanense systema sternat & funditus diruat : statuendum est quod pietas & ratio fugerent quemquam nostrorum, qui affirmaret nostram sententiam de potestate Ecclesiastica, ideo esse detestandam, quod per eam idem excidium paretur Papæ, quod Arnaldus, aut auguratur aut reformidat.
units.tr: These things I have adduced about the prejudices of holy men ought to confirm you in your view that those prejudices are neither legitimate nor founded on any reason or Scripture. Consider especially that their prejudices and those of the Forbonist Arnauld are plainly twins, and that the argument set forth in jugulo causæ is no less a detestable and abominable undertaking in the judgment of our people than in Arnauld's. In this matter, if I compare the judgment of our people with Arnauld's, his seems to me the fairer and more consonant with reason. For our view of ecclesiastical power and excommunication deserves to be detested in the way Arnauld's judgment would have it, if one follows his hypotheses: with one sling and one stone he brings the Pope to the ground and utterly overthrows the whole Roman system. Yet it must be held that piety and reason would shun any of ours who affirmed that our view of ecclesiastical power is therefore to be detested, because through it the same ruin would be prepared for the Pope that Arnauld either foresees or dreads.

units.la: Absit ut intactam relinquas veram, imo unicam rationem, qualem trado debellandi Papam, veritus ne unâ ruinâ involvat Papam & potestatem Ecclesiasticam. Profecto cum ruina Papæ debeat excipere ruinam potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, & per excidium hujus & illius, Christo regnum suum constare, & salus hominum promoveri, quisquis nollet jactura, Potestatis Ecclesiasticæ fialticæ, & per excidium hujus & illius regnum Christi afferere, haud abfimilis effet illi, qui mallet chariffimam uxorem fubmerfam, quam violatam comam, fi per capillorum ἱμάτιον arreptam undis eriperetur.
units.tr: Far be it from you to leave untouched the true and indeed the only way of combating the Pope, for fear that one collapse should bring down the Pope and ecclesiastical power together. Since the fall of the Pope ought to bring with it the fall of ecclesiastical power, and since Christ's kingdom stands and men's salvation is advanced through the overthrow of the one and the other, whoever was unwilling to lose ecclesiastical power, in order to assert Christ's kingdom through the destruction of this and that, would be no unlike one who preferred his dearest wife to drown rather than have her hair violated, if she were seized by the mantle [ἱμάτιον] of her hair and snatched from the waves.

units.la: Cette consideration, Mr, fait que je ne fcaurois approuver la conduite des noftres, qui au lieu d'attaquer Rome par cét endroit, que je vous ay marqué, où la moindre bleffure feroit un coup mortel,ils enterprenent de luy ofter la vie en refutant ses erreurs en détail. Mais ceux-là de nos Théologiens font bien pis, qui adoucissent ces erreurs, & qui donnent à Rome un visage moins affreus, que plusieurs deses propres docteurs, & dont Monsieur Arnaud & Monsieur de Condom leur scavent bon gré: car cét adoucissement n'est pas pardonable à un Docteur Protestant, quoy qu'il le soit à Monsieur de Condom, & bien éloigné d'un Docteur Puritain en Angleterre qui a nouvellement publié un Livre qui a pour titre, le renversement de la Doctrine, & de la morale de J. C. par les Papistes, & qui peut servir d'antidote à celuy de Monsieur Arnauld: car quel visage agréable peut-on donner à la Doctrine de la Transubstantiation, du Purgatoire, du retranchement de la Coupe, & des Indulgences, sur tout à cét attachement au Pape, auquel les plus éclairez de Rome, mesme ceux qui ne sont pas Ecclésiastiques, comme Monsieur Silhon & Monsieur Pascal, font plus raisonnablement consister toute la Religion Chrestienne, qu'à la créance de toutes les autres Doctrines de Rome ensemble, ou de quelques-unes en particulier, quoy que ces éclairez ne pouvoient ignorer que le corps de Rome, & sur tout son visage, qui paroist au dehors, ne fust fort malade, & plein de fistules & de chancres. Il semble que ceux des nostres que sont pour cét adoucissement, ayent pris à tâche de nous marquer les espaces sains de ce visage de Rome, où la peau n'est pas encore entamée. Pour moi si j'avois entrepris de refuter le livre de Monsieur de Condom, J'eusse fait voir que Rome n'est qu'un composé de mensonges, de fourberies, de tromperies, & d'impostures, dont la principale est la Puissance Ecclésiastique, parce que c'est le fondement sur lequel Rome, son Pape, son Eglise, sa religion & son infaillibilité font bastis, & c'est-là la tâche d'un quart d'heure, ou d'un quart de feuille.
units.tr: This consideration, sir, means I cannot approve the conduct of our people, who, instead of attacking Rome at the point I have marked out, where the slightest wound would be a mortal blow, undertake to take away its life by refuting its errors one by one. But some of our theologians are far worse, who soften these errors and give Rome a less frightful face than several of its own doctors do, and for this Monsieur Arnauld and Monsieur de Condom are grateful to them. Such softening is not pardonable in a Protestant doctor, though it is to Monsieur de Condom, and it is far removed from a Puritan doctor in England who has recently published a book entitled the subversion of the doctrine and morality of J. C. by the Papists, which can serve as an antidote to that of Monsieur Arnauld. For what agreeable face can be given to the doctrine of transubstantiation, purgatory, the withholding of the cup and indulgences, above all to that attachment to the Pope on which the most enlightened men of Rome, even those who are not ecclesiastics, such as Monsieur Silhon and Monsieur Pascal, more reasonably make the whole Christian religion consist, rather than in belief in all the other doctrines of Rome together, or in some of them in particular? Yet these enlightened men could not be unaware that the body of Rome, and above all its outward face, was very sick and full of fistulas and cankers. It seems that those among ours who favour this softening have taken it upon themselves to point out to us the healthy spots on Rome's face, where the skin is not yet broken. As for me, if I had undertaken to refute the book of Monsieur de Condom, I would have shown that Rome is nothing but a compound of lies, knaveries, deceptions and impostures, the chief of which is ecclesiastical power, because it is the foundation on which Rome, its Pope, its Church, its religion and its infallibility are built. That task would take a quarter of an hour, or a quarter of a sheet.

units.la: De la manière que Monsieur l'Evesque se prend pour donner de la couleur, & des apparences de bonté & de vérité à la religion de Rome, il en eust pû faire autant aux plus grandes impostures du Monde: Il eust pû aussi facilement donner de l'agreément à la religion de Mahomet; en supprimant toutes les abominations, & toutes les rêveries de l'Alcoran; comme il fait celles de sa religion.
units.tr: The way in which Monsieur the Bishop sets about giving colour and an appearance of goodness and truth to the religion of Rome, he could have done the same for the greatest impostures in the world. He could just as easily have given charm to the religion of Mahomet, by suppressing all the abominations and all the fancies of the Koran, as he does for his own religion.

units.la: Car les personnes de Mahomet, & du Pape, ne se doivent rien l'une à l'autre en impostures, fraudes, & tyrannies : l'imposture & l'usurpation n'estant pas moindre en l'un de se qualifier, Vicaire de J. C. le Souverain Pontife, la lumière du monde, le gouverneur en chef de l'Eglise Catholique, comme faisoit Martin V. ; qu'en Mahomet de se dire, le troisiéme Prophéte qui devoit venir au monde après Moyse & J. Christ. Il n'y a rien de plus vray que l'éloge, & le characètere, que deux célébres écrivains, l'un Protestant, l'autre de la religion de Rome, ont donnez au Pape, à son Eglise, & à sa religion : voicy celuy du Protestant, qui est Stillingflit, dans un deses Sermons prefché devant le Roy, La primauté que l'Eglise Romaine s'est attribuée, n'est qu'une pure usurpation, qui doit son origine à l'ambition, & son progrez à des tromperies, & à des imposturés, & qui ne se conserve, & ne se maintient que par des tyrannies, & par des cruautez.
units.tr: For Mahomet and the Pope owe each other nothing in imposture, fraud and tyranny. The imposture and usurpation are no less in one who calls himself Vicar of J. C., the Sovereign Pontiff, the light of the world, the chief governor of the Catholic Church, as Martin V did, than in Mahomet, who called himself the third Prophet who was to come into the world after Moses and Jesus Christ. Nothing is truer than the eulogy and character that two famous writers, one a Protestant and the other of the Roman religion, have given of the Pope, his Church and his religion. Here is the Protestant's, Stillingfleet's, from one of his sermons preached before the King: The primacy which the Church of Rome has attributed to itself is nothing but pure usurpation, which owes its origin to ambition, its progress to deceptions and impostures, and which is preserved and maintained only by tyranny and cruelties.

units.la: L'autre qui est Catholique Romain, & autheur de la Politique de France n'a pas meilleure opinion du Pape & de sa Religion, chap. 4.
units.tr: The other, who is a Roman Catholic and the author of the Politique de France, has no better opinion of the Pope and his religion, ch. 4.

units.la: Les Maximes de Rome sont abusives : elles sont purement politiques. Le Pape a formé une monarchie étrangère dans le sein de la France, le nom de religion est un faux prétexte que prend la cour de Rome pour augmenter sa puissance temporelle, & avoir des Créatures.
units.tr: The maxims of Rome are abusive; they are purely political. The Pope has formed a foreign monarchy in the heart of France; the name of religion is a false pretext that the court of Rome takes in order to increase its temporal power and have creatures.

units.la: Ce Marquis qui est l'Autheur de cette politique, ne s'est pas particulièrement expliqué dans ce chapitre, des maximes de Rome : mais il a voulu sans doute entendre ces six, qui sont les fondemens de sa Religion, & les gonds sur lesquels le Pape, ses Doctrines, son Eglise, sa hiérarchie & son infaillibilité, roulent.
units.tr: This Marquis, who is the author of this politics, did not explain himself particularly in this chapter about the maxims of Rome, but he undoubtedly meant those six, which are the foundations of his religion and the hinges on which the Pope, his doctrines, his Church, his hierarchy and his infallibility turn.

units.la: 1 Maxime.
units.tr: 1 Maxim.

units.la: Que le siége de Rome, quelque infame qu'il ait toujours esté, & qu'il soit par ses Simonies, par ses sacrilèges, & par ses prattiques infames ; est pourtant le fondement de la Religion Chrestienne, & qu'il n'y a point de salut pour ceux qui l'abandonnent, qui renoncent à toute communion avec le Pape, & qui ne le reconnoissent pas pour le gouverneur en chef de l'Eglise Catholique.
units.tr: That the see of Rome, however infamous it has always been, and however much it is steeped in simony, sacrilege and infamous practices, is nonetheless the foundation of the Christian religion, and that there is no salvation for those who abandon it, who renounce all communion with the Pope, and who do not acknowledge him as the supreme governor of the Catholic Church.

units.la: 2 Maxime.
units.tr: 2 Maxim.

units.la: Que la teste de l'Eglise Catholique qui est le Pape, peut estre destituée de toute vertu intellectuelle & morale, estre athée, estre remplie de toute l'impiété imaginable, sans communiquer ces maladies-là à aucun des membres de l'Eglise, & sans les infecter.
units.tr: That the head of the Catholic Church, namely the Pope, may be destitute of every intellectual and moral virtue, may be an atheist, may be filled with every conceivable impiety, without passing these diseases on to any member of the Church or infecting them.

units.la: 3 Maxime.
units.tr: 3 Maxim.

units.la: Que la vie abominable & detestable de la plupart des Papes, est compatible & sociable avec leur saintete, leur infaillibilité; & avec celle de l'Eglise Romaine.
units.tr: That the abominable and detestable life of most of the Popes is compatible and consistent with their holiness and infallibility, and with that of the Roman Church.

units.la: 4 Maxime.
units.tr: 4 Maxim.

units.la: Quoy que les élections des Papes se soyent toujours faites par corruption, par fraudes & par monopoles, & bien souvent par meurtres, & que durant 150 ans, comme nous disent Baronius & Genebrard, des gens intrus, des monstres & des Apostats, & les meurtriers de leurs predecesseurs se soyent emparez du Papat; & que les meilleurs d'entr' eux, comme nous dit l'Evesque Godeau, du Pape Vigile, ayent esté des fourbes & des scélérats; ou comme Guichardin le dit des Papes de tous les siécles, aprés Grégoire I. Qu'ils ont esté bons lors qu'ils n'ont pas excédé la méchanceté des autres hommes : Néanmoins le St. Esprit n'a pas laissé d'assister à ces élections, & y a tellement opéré, que la succession des Papes a toujours esté légitime, & n'a jamais esté rompue, ni interrompue.
units.tr: Although the elections of the Popes have always been carried out by corruption, fraud and monopoly, and very often by murder, and although, as Baronius and Genebrard tell us, for 150 years intruders, monsters and apostates, and the murderers of their predecessors, seized the Papacy; and although the best of them, as Bishop Godeau says of Pope Vigilius, were deceivers and scoundrels; or as Guicciardini says of the Popes of all centuries after Gregory I, they were good only when they did not exceed the wickedness of other men: nevertheless the Holy Spirit has not ceased to assist at these elections, and has so worked in them that the succession of the Popes has always been lawful and has never been broken or interrupted.

units.la: 5 Maxime.
units.tr: 5 Maxim.

units.la: Qu'encore que l'Eglise Romaine ait esté souvent divisée, & déchirée en sectes: qu'elle ait esté travaillée de plus de 25 schismes; que les Papes ayent esté des boutefeux, & les incendiaires de la terre, comme nous dit le Président Fauchet, & cent autres historiens; qu'ils ayent rempli le monde de sang, de guerres & de factions, mesme en matière de foy entre les Docteurs de Rome; que les animositez entr'eux ayent esté mortelles, ou plutost immortelles; néanmoins l'union & la concorde en la foy, & entre les membres qui composent l'Eglise Romaine, ont toujours esté admirables &
units.tr: That although the Roman Church has often been divided and torn apart into sects; although it has been afflicted by more than 25 schisms; although the Popes have been firebrands and incendiaries of the earth, as President Fauchet and a hundred other historians tell us; although they have filled the world with blood, wars and factions, even in matters of faith among the teachers of Rome; although the enmities among them have been deadly, or rather immortal; nevertheless the union and concord in the faith, and among the members who make up the Roman Church, have always been admirable

units.la: & glorieufes ; & Rome a toûjours confervé une Sainte uniformité. Et que mefme cette Eglife en croiffant en a-age, a auffi toûjours augmenté en graces, nommément en infaillibilité, en pureté, en fainteté de doctrine, & de vie & en conformité avec l'eftat de l'Eglife du temps des Apoftres.
units.tr: and glorious; and Rome has always preserved a holy uniformity. Moreover, this Church, as it grows older, has also always increased in grace, particularly in infallibility, purity, and holiness of doctrine and life, and in conformity with the state of the Church in the time of the Apostles.

units.la: Ces cinq Maximes ne font pas conteftées par les docteurs de Rome, comme l'eft la fixiéme, qui en effect eft pourtant celle qui foûtient toutes les précédentes, & tout le fyfteme de Rome, fon Pape, fon Eglife, fa religion & fon infaillibilité, assavoir.
units.tr: These five Maxims are not disputed by the teachers of Rome, but the sixth is, and in fact it is the one that sustains all the preceding ones and the whole system of Rome: its Pope, its Church, its religion and its infallibility, namely:

units.la: 6 Maxime.
units.tr: 6 Maxim.

units.la: Que la religion de Rome, n'eft autre chofe qu'un attachement des Rois & des peuples à l'Empire terrien, que le Pape s'eft bafti dans leur Empire ; & dont il continue la possession sous le déguisement de Puissance Ecclésiastique & Spirituele, & d'Empire de Jésus Christ.
units.tr: That the religion of Rome is nothing other than the attachment of kings and peoples to an earthly empire, which the Pope has built for himself within their realms, and whose possession he continues under the disguise of ecclesiastical and spiritual power, and of an empire of Jesus Christ.

units.la: C'est de cette maniére que j'aurois voulu respondre au livre de Monsieur de Condom. J'aurois expofé ces honteufes Maximes de Rome à la veüe de tout le monde, comme Ezéchias déployia en la prefence de l'Eternel les blasphémes de Rabsaké. J'aurois ofté tout ce fard, dont cét Evefque pare le visage de la grande Paillarde pour luy attirer des amoureux. Je luy aurois arraché ce masque trompeur, dont on l'a déguisé, afin que chacun voyant d'un costé ce monstre à decouvert, & de l'autre considérant la naive beauté de la religion reformée, on puft droitement juger de l'une & de l'autre.
units.tr: This is how I would have wished to answer the book of Monsieur de Condom. I would have set these shameful Maxims of Rome before the eyes of everyone, as Hezekiah spread out the blasphemies of Rabshakeh before the LORD. I would have stripped away all the paint with which this bishop adorns the face of the great harlot in order to attract lovers to her. I would have torn from her that deceitful mask with which she has been disguised, so that everyone, seeing on one side this monster uncovered and, on the other, considering the simple beauty of the Reformed religion, might rightly judge between the two.

units.la: Quoi que vous n'ayez pas besoin demes avertissemens là-dessus. Je ne laisseray pas de prendre la liberté de vous prier de vous arrester sur tout à la consideration de la derniére de ces Maximes, qui est d'une vérité si utile, si aisée à comprendre, si importante & si nécessaire à connoitre, pour le bien, & pour la paix du monde, & pour mettre fin à toutes les controverses, qui s'agitent depuis si long-tems entre les Protestans & les Papistes, que je l'ose mettre au nombre des véritez les plus utiles, qui ayent jamais esté publiées, excepté celle qui nous a révélé la venue du Rédempteur au monde pour sauver les pécheurs.
units.tr: Although you have no need of my warnings on this, I will not refrain from taking the liberty of asking you to dwell above all on the consideration of the last of these Maxims. It is a truth so useful, so easy to understand, so important and so necessary to know, for the good and peace of the world, and for ending all the controversies that have been stirred up for so long between the Protestants and the Papists, that I dare to place it among the most useful truths ever published, except the one which revealed to us the coming of the Redeemer into the world to save sinners.

units.la: Je l'a croy si nécessaire qu'il seroit à désirer qu'elle fust affichée à toutes les portes, non seulement du Vatican, mais à celle des Palais des Rois & des Princes, à celles des Maisons de Villes, à tous les coins des rues, à tous les carrefours des grandes Villes, & à toutes les croix des grands chemins : & qu' elle fust imprimée au frontispice de tous les livres de controverse entre Rome & nous : sur tout quelle fust mise à la teste de l'Exposition de la foy Catholique de Monsieur de Condom, pour servir de clef, & d'éclaircissement à son adoucissement de la foy de Rome. Ce qui m'a fait craindre que nos Docteurs ne rejettent ma sixiéme Maxime, quelque vraye qu' elle soit, & quelque intérêt qu'ils ayent à la recevoir, C'est l'aversion pour la main, qui la leur presente, & parce que j'y fai entrer la puissance Ecclésiastique, pour la conservation de laquelle ils ont tant de passion. Mais puis que la vérité est comme un cube, là Monsieur, puisque vous avez sans doute approuvé m'a sixiéme Maxime ; Jugeant qu'elle estoit capable de mettre fin à toutes nos controverses. Pour moy je la tiens si importante, que je ne croirois pas avoir employé m'a vie inutilement, quand je l'aurois donnée toute entiére, à en faire connoitre la vérité & l'utilité. Je croirois avoir travaillé avantageusement à mon salut & à celuy de mes freres. Et je suis assuré qu'en détruisant la puissance Ecclésiastique, J'aurois consumé par le feu de la raison, & de la parole de Dieu la plus méchante paille, que les mauvais ouvriers ayent édifiée sur le bon fondement. Je prie le Seigneur qu'il vous conserve long-tems pour l'édification de son Eglise, dont par sa grace vous estes l'un des plus experts, & des plus sincéres. Archietectes. Croyez que je suis,
units.tr: I consider it so necessary that it would be desirable for it to be posted at every door, not only of the Vatican, but also of the palaces of kings and princes, of the town houses, at every street corner, at every crossroads of the great cities, and at every cross on the highways; and that it be printed on the title page of every book of controversy between Rome and us; above all, that it be placed at the head of Monsieur de Condom's Exposition of the Catholic Faith, to serve as the key and clarification of his softening of the faith of Rome. What makes me fear is that our teachers will reject my sixth Maxim, however true it is and however much interest they have in accepting it, out of aversion to the hand that offers it to them, and because I bring into it the ecclesiastical power, for the preservation of which they feel such passion. But since truth is like a cube, which stands firm on whichever side it falls, and since, sir, you have doubtless approved my sixth Maxim, judging that it is capable of ending all our controversies, I for my part hold it to be so important that I would not think I had spent my life in vain, even if I had devoted all of it to making its truth and usefulness known. I would believe I had worked profitably for my own salvation and that of my brethren. And I am assured that by destroying ecclesiastical power I would have consumed, by the fire of reason and of the word of God, the worst straw that bad workmen have built upon the good foundation. I pray the Lord that he preserve you for many years for the edification of his Church, of which, by his grace, you are one of the most expert and most sincere architects. Believe that I am,

units.la: Monsieur,
units.tr: Sir,

units.la: Vostre très-humble & très-obéissant Serviteur
units.tr: Your very humble and very obedient servant,

units.la: Louïs du Moulin.
units.tr: Louis du Moulin.

units.la: A Monsieur Allix.
units.tr: To Monsieur Allix.

units.la: Monsieur,
units.tr: Sir,

units.la: JE croy vous avoir envoyé un imprimé, où je découvre, que les préjugez ont tant prévalu contre l'une des plus belles, & des plus utiles véritez sur les personnes qui me font les plus chéres, que de les porter à s'y opposer avec emportement, & avec violence. Mais que Dieu qui luy euft pû donner cours en un instant, tant elle est claire & démonstrable; Si des personnes telles que vous, ou Monsieur Claude l'euffent avancée, s'est servi d'un foible instrument comme moy pour la découvrir, & a voulu que les Esprits y fussent préparez, non per saltum, sed per gradus, & qu'ils euffent du tems à la goufter, & à la digérer avant que de se déterminer en sa faveur. C'est ce que Monsieur Vauquelin me prédit il y a vingt ans devoir arriver en ces mots tandem tua bona causa triumphabit. Et c'est ce que j'éprouve depuis la publication de ma parénése, Il y a vingt ans, & celle de mon Jugulum Causæ, il y a cinq ans : car depuis ce tems-là j'ay gaigne peu à peu, & un par un les Esprits les plus obstinez, & remplis de préjugez contre mes hypothéses, & j'ay tiré d'eux cette confession ingénue.
units.tr: I believe I have sent you a printed piece in which I observe that prejudice has so far prevailed against one of the most beautiful and useful truths, concerning the persons who are dearest to me, that it drives them to oppose it with passion and violence. Yet God, who could have given it currency in an instant, since it is so clear and demonstrable, has chosen to use a weak instrument such as myself to uncover it, if persons such as yourself or Monsieur Claude had put it forward. He has willed that minds should be prepared for it non per saltum, sed per gradus, and that they should have time to taste and digest it before making up their minds in its favour. This is what Monsieur Vauquelin predicted to me twenty years ago, in these words: tandem tua bona causa triumphabit. This is what I have experienced since the publication of my Parænèse twenty years ago, and of my Jugulum Causæ five years ago. For since then I have gained, little by little and one by one, the most obstinate minds, full of prejudice against my hypotheses, and have drawn from them this frank confession:

units.la: 1. Que la Puissance Ecclésiastique est l'échelle par laquelle l'homme de péché, le fils de perdition, est monté au faiste, où nous le voyons aujourd'huy.
units.tr: 1. That ecclesiastical power is the ladder by which the man of sin, the son of perdition, has climbed to the height where we see him today.

units.la: 2. Qu'avant que le Pape ait pû parvenir au haut de cette échelle & paroitre à la teste de cette puissance Ecclésiastique, & en estre reconnu la source & l'origine; ce qui est arrivé 850 après St. Paul, au tems des décrétales, cette puissance sans Pape avoit basti son Empire sur les Puissances séculiéres, & en avoit continué la possession, par fourbes, tromperies, & tyrannies.
units.tr: 2. That before the Pope could reach the top of this ladder and stand at the head of this ecclesiastical power, and be recognised as its source and origin (which happened 850 years after St Paul, at the time of the Decretals), this power, still without a Pope, had built its empire upon the secular powers and kept possession of them through fraud, deceit and tyranny.

units.la: 3. Que c'eft en defabufant, non feulement les puiffances féculiéres, mais généralement tous les éclairez de l'une & de l'autre religion de l'illufion & de l'impofture de la Puiffance Ecclefiaftique, & de fon Excommunication, que le Pape doit eftre ruiné & déthrôné, & avec luy tout le fyftéme de Rome, fon Eglife, fa religion & fa hiérarchie.
units.tr: 3. That it is by undeceiving not only the secular powers but generally all the enlightened men of either religion, about the illusion and imposture of ecclesiastical power and its excommunication, that the Pope must be ruined and dethroned, and with him the whole system of Rome: its Church, its religion and its hierarchy.

units.la: 4. Que c'eft une peine perdue que d'attaquer Rome ailleurs, & par la refutation en détail de fes erreurs, & de penfer qu'on peut défaire le Pape fans fe défaire de la Puiffance Ecclefiaftique.
units.tr: 4. That it is wasted labour to attack Rome elsewhere, by refuting its errors one by one, and to think that one can undo the Pope without undoing ecclesiastical power.

units.la: 5. Que quand mefme on fuppoferoit que la ruine de cette illufion ne ruineroit pas l'Eglife Romaine & fon Pape: cependant les hypothéfes qui fe deffont de cette puiffance chimérique, pofent la difcipline des Eglifes Chreftiennes, fur leurs vrais, folides & naturels fondemens.
units.tr: 5. That even if one supposed that the ruin of this illusion would not ruin the Roman Church and its Pope, nevertheless the hypotheses which dismantle this chimerical power place the discipline of the Christian churches on their true, solid and natural foundations.

units.la: 6. De plus, que ces hypothéfes fournif-fent l'abrégé des controverfes, & une voye, courte & aifée & incontestable pour la décifion de plufieurs controverses, comme de celle que nous avons touchant la primauté du Pape en l'Eglise; le Souverain juge des controverses, l'infaillibilité, le pouvoir des Synodes & des Pasteurs: sur tout touchant le droit Divin ou humain de l'Episcopat: sur l'estendue du pouvoir des Rois & des Magistrats en matière de gouvernement de l'Eglise, & sur la facilité ou difficulté des voyes proposées pour la réunion des Eglises qui sont de divers sentimens; sur tout pour celle de la religion de Rome, avec celle des Protestans.
units.tr: 6. Moreover, these hypotheses provide a summary of the controversies, and a short, easy and indisputable way of deciding many of them: such as the one we have concerning the primacy of the Pope in the Church; the sovereign judge of controversies; infallibility; the power of synods and of ministers; above all, concerning the divine or human right of episcopacy; concerning the extent of the power of kings and magistrates in the government of the Church; concerning the ease or difficulty of the methods proposed for reuniting churches that hold different opinions; and above all, for reuniting the religion of Rome with that of the Protestants.

units.la: 7. Mais la principale utilité de la vérification des hypothéses qui ruinent la puissance Ecclésiastique, c'est qu'elle découvre la vraye nature du mystère d'iniquité, dont parle St. Paul, & qu'elle fait voir que l'Empire que le Pape s'est basti, sur les Rois & sur les Nations de la terre, est un vray Empire terrien, Que c'est dans la possession de cét Empire que consiste l'iniquité, mais que le mystère est dans le déguisement de ces mots, de Spirituel, & Ecclésiastique.
units.tr: 7. But the chief use of verifying the hypotheses which ruin ecclesiastical power is that it discloses the true nature of the mystery of iniquity of which St Paul speaks, and shows that the empire the Pope has built for himself over the kings and nations of the earth is a true earthly empire. The iniquity lies in the possession of this empire, but the mystery lies in the disguise of the words Spiritual and Ecclesiastical.

units.la: Ce sont-là, Monsieur, des véritez & & des utilitez, qui ont esté reconnues par cinq cents personnes doctes & esclairées de toutes les nations de l'Europe, qui ont leu, ou qui ont ouy parler de ma Parænèse, ou de mon Jugulum Causæ ; non seulement d'entre les Calvinistes, mais aussi d'entre les Luthériens, & mesme aussi d'entre les Papistes. J'ay bien fait d'avantage, car j'ay planté la foy de mes hypothéses dans Genéve, qui est une entreprife presque semblable à celle que fit St. Paul dans Corinthe, en convertissant ceux qui à cause de leur vie infame n'avoient aucune disposition à recevoir la foy Chrestienne : car j'ay détrompé dans cette ville, qui a esté la forge de cette Puissance, & la source, d'où elle s'est épandue dans l'Europe parmi les Protestans. J'y ay détrompé, dit-je, ceux des sçavàns & des éclairez qui estoient les plus obstinez contre moy, & qui avoient de plus forts attachements à cette Idole, comme Monsieur Turretin m'en a assuré par des Lettres que je conserve. Je pensois que d'abord que ma Parénése, & mon Jugulum Causæ y parurent, qu'on les traitteroit de livres abominables & détestables, comme a fait le Sorbonifte Arnaud, ou que j'y trouverois un foulévement pareil, à celuy qu'on a fait depuis contre les sentimens de Mr. de la Place, & de Mr. Amyrant. Mais Mr. Turretin m'ecrivit que si j'y avois des adversaires, il y en avoit d'autres plusieurs, que soutenoient & approuvoient mes hypothéses. Et c'est ce que je n'ay pas éprouvé en Hollande, où l'emportement des avocats de cette Diane a esté si grand contre moy, qu'ils se sont opposez avec chaleur, à ma réception de Professeur à Leyden, mais j'ay la consolation de sçavoir, que mes sentimens y sont approuvez généralement, par toutes les personnes désintéressées : c'est à dire par tous ceux qui ne sont pas du sacré ordre, par les Magistrats, & par les testes illustres qu'on envoye en Ambassade, & à qui on donne les plus importans emplois de l'Estat. J'espere Monsieur, que vous-vous rengerez dans ce bon party, où je ne me suis engagé parmi les contradictions de tout le monde, par un pur Zele au bien de l'Eglise, &
units.tr: These, Monsieur, are truths and advantages which have been recognised by five hundred learned and enlightened persons from all the nations of Europe who have read my Parænèse or my Jugulum Causæ, or who have heard them discussed. This is so not only among the Calvinists but also among the Lutherans, and even among the Papists. I have done even more, for I have planted the faith of my hypotheses in Geneva, an enterprise almost like that which St Paul undertook in Corinth, converting people who, because of their infamous lives, had no disposition to receive the Christian faith. For I have undeceived, in that city which was the forge of this power and the source from which it spread through Europe among the Protestants, those learned and enlightened men who were most obstinate against me and had the strongest attachments to this idol, as Monsieur Turretin assured me in letters which I keep. I had thought that as soon as my Parænèse and my Jugulum Causæ appeared there, they would be treated as abominable and detestable books, as the Sorbonist Arnauld did; or that I would meet an uproar like the one raised since against the opinions of Monsieur de la Place and Monsieur Amyraut. But Monsieur Turretin wrote to me that if I had adversaries, there were also many others who upheld and approved my hypotheses. This is not what I experienced in Holland, where the zeal of the advocates of this Diana against me was so great that they opposed my appointment as professor at Leiden with heat. Yet I have the consolation of knowing that my opinions are generally approved there by all disinterested persons: that is, by all who are not of the sacred order, by the magistrates, and by the illustrious men who are sent on embassies and given the most important offices of state. I hope, Monsieur, that you will range yourself on this good side, to which I have committed myself, amid the contradictions of the whole world, out of pure zeal for the good of the Church, and

units.la: {u} par un pur zele & à la destruction de l'Antechrist.
units.tr: {u} out of pure zeal, and for the destruction of the Antichrist.

units.la: Vous ne ferez pas fâché, Monsieur, de voir l'extraict d'une Lettre que Mr. Muffard écrivoit derniérement à Mr. Tronchin sur ces matiéres. Elle m'est heureusement tombée entre les mains. Je l'ay leüe avec un grand plaisir, parce qu'il me rend justice, & qu'il y a si naivement compris mes sentimens, que je ne les puis pas si bien exprimer moy mesme. Je luy ay cette obligation qu'encore qu'il ne se déclare pas estre du nombre de mes partisans : il parle pourtant avec fincérité ; bien loin de me déguiser sous un masque horrible, comme font plusieurs pour me rendre odieux. Il se pleindra que je luy fais une supercherie de l'imprimer malgré qu'il en ait : mais la vérité m'est plus precieuse que la complaisance pour mes amis. Je suis,
units.tr: You will not be displeased, Monsieur, to see an extract of a letter which Monsieur Muffard lately wrote to Monsieur Tronchin on these matters. It has happily fallen into my hands. I read it with great pleasure, because it does me justice and comprehends my sentiments so frankly that I could not express them better myself. I owe him this debt: although he does not declare himself one of my partisans, he nonetheless speaks with sincerity, far from disguising me behind a hideous mask, as many do to make me odious. He will complain that I play him a trick by printing it against his wishes, but truth is more precious to me than complaisance towards my friends. I am,

units.la: Monsieur,
units.tr: Monsieur,

units.la: Vostre tres-humble & tres-obéissant Serviteur
units.tr: Your most humble and most obedient servant,

units.la: Louis du Moulin.
units.tr: Louis du Moulin.

units.la: Fragment d'une Lettre de Monsieur Muffard, Mini- stre de l'Eglise Francoise, à Londres, à Monsieur Tronchin, Pasteur & Pro- fesseur en Théologie à Genéve.
units.tr: Fragment of a Letter from Monsieur Muffard, Minister of the French Church in London, to Monsieur Tronchin, Pastor and Professor of Theology at Geneva.

units.la: VOicy, Monsieur, quels sont les sentimens du Dr. Loüis du Moulin, sur le pouvoir des Conducteurs de l'Eglise, autant que je l'ay pû receuillir par les entretiens que j'ay eus avec luy, par la lecture de son traitté intitulé Parænesis ad-ædificatores imperii in imperio. Son but est d'y prouver que la Puissance Ecclésiastique, & l'Excommunication sont des inventions humaines, Il dit que c'eft en cela que confifte le Mystère d'iniquité, dont St. Paul parle: que l'Iniquité est dans la puissance que les Ecclésiastiques se sont arrogée sur les Rois, & sur Magistrats; & le Mystère, en ce qu'ils la voilent du nom de Spirituelle, ou d'Ecclésiastique. Il s'écrie ô tempora ô mores, sur ce que les Reformez, dit-il, pour conserver à leurs consistoires, & à leurs synodes une vaine ombre d'authorité qu'il ne leur contesteroit pas pour la conservation de l'ordre, s'ils ne la vouloient pas couvrir du nom de J. C. prestent sans y penser l'épaule à la subsistance des injustes usurpations du Pape, auquel seul il en veut.
units.tr: Here, Sir, are the sentiments of Dr Louis du Moulin on the power of the leaders of the Church, as far as I could gather them from the conversations I have had with him and from reading his treatise entitled Parænesis ad-ædificatores imperii in imperio. His aim there is to prove that ecclesiastical power and excommunication are human inventions. He says that this is what constitutes the mystery of iniquity of which St Paul speaks: the iniquity lies in the power that the churchmen have arrogated to themselves over kings and magistrates, and the mystery lies in their concealing it under the name of spiritual or ecclesiastical. He cries O the times, O the manners! because the Reformed, he says, in order to preserve for their consistories and synods a vain shadow of authority, which he would not dispute for the sake of good order if they did not wish to cover it with the name of Jesus Christ, unthinkingly lend their shoulder to the maintenance of the unjust usurpations of the Pope, against whom alone he directs his attack.

units.la: Il dit que supposé une Puissance Ecclésiastique émanée de Jésus-Christ, & l'Excommunication, le pouvoir du Pape sera légitime, & qu'il n'y a point de Curè qui ne devienne Pape, quand il luy plaira, puis qu'il aura le pouvoir de tout lier & de délier sans aucune réserve, soit qu'il le face avec justice, ou sans raison; veu que la validité des loix ne consiste pas dans la bonté des loix qu'elles ordonnent, mais dans la volonté de celuy qui a le pouvoir deles établir: ce qu'il prouve par ces mots qu'il m'a fait lire dans une oraison de Monsieur du Moulin son Pere, de Laudibus Theologiæ.
units.tr: He says that, supposing an ecclesiastical power to have come from Jesus Christ, along with excommunication, the power of the Pope will be legitimate, and that there is no parish priest who may not become Pope whenever he likes, since he will have the power to bind and loose everything without any reservation, whether he does so justly or without reason; for the validity of laws does not consist in the goodness of the laws they enact, but in the will of the one who has the power to establish them. He proves this by the words that he showed me in an oration of Monsieur du Moulin his father, On the Praises of Theology.

units.la: Profectò toto cælo errat qui vim legum civilium in hoc positam esse censet quod justæ sint, Lex enim pollet authoritate non quia justa est, sed quia Lex est, & regula ab eo sancita qui habet authoritatem. Il dit qu'il faut nécessairement que le Pape tombe si vous luy ostez cette authorité qu'il appelle spirituelle, quoy que celle du Turc ne soit pas plus temporelle, & qu'il croit tenir de J. Christ en vertu des paroles, Quicquid ligaveris, laquelle il soûtient par l'Excommunication qui a fait trembler durant tant de siecles, les peuples & les Rois. Il souhaiteroit que Calvin, pour qui d'ailleurs il témoigne une profonde vénération, ne se fust pas si fort empressé à établir sa Discipline; ou que du moins il ne l'eust pas nommée le joug de J. Christ. Car encore que Monsieur du Moulin reconnoisse que l'on peut bien admettre ses reiglemens & d'autres semblables, comme ceux des Eglifes de France, pour maintenir l'ordre, il n'eftime pas pourtant que les fondemens fur lefquels il l'appuie foyent légitimes, parce qu'il dit que ce font les mefmes, que ceux fur lefquels le Pape a infenfiblement fondé fon Empire. Il dit que Calvin, aliquid humani paffus eft nec fibi conftat, lors qu' après avoir qualifié fa difcipline le joug de J. Christ, & un joug qui ne peut eftre réjetté que par des libertins & par des profanes : il avoüe ailleurs que le sentiment de plusieurs personnes pieufes & doctes eft, que l'Excommunication n'eft pas néceffaire là où il y a des Princes Chreftiens. C'eft ce qu'il dit dans fa Lettre aux Miniftres de Zurich, De excommunicatione non omnes idem fentiunt, nec me latet, pios & doctos, effe viros, quibus fub Christianis Principibus non videtur necessaria Excommunicatio, Il s'eftonne que plusieurs de fes plus proches parens, s'échauffent comme ils font contre luy, Que quelques-uns l'ayent appelé le fleau de l'Eglife : Qu'on le veuille faire paffer pour un fanatique, pour un vifionnaire, & pour un efprit déreiglé, comme Monfieur fieur Bochart qui l'appeloit, Caput tribus Anticyris vix Janabile, & que cependant on révére la mémoire de Zwingle, de Muscule, de Bullinger, de Gualter, d'Erafte & de plusieurs autres excellens hommes du siécle passé, qui sont célébres entre les reformateurs, quoy qu'ils ayent esté de son sentiment, Il croit que les maximes de ces derniers sur la conduite de l'Eglise auroient prévalu parmi tous les Reformez, si le grand crédit de Calvin & de Béze qui le suivit, n'eust préoccupé les Esprits. Il accorde que là où le Magistrat n'est pas Chrestien, ou lors qu'il ne fait pas son devoir pour réprimer les vicieux, chaque assemblée peut, per confœderatam Disciplinam, & mutuum pacium sibi ipsi potestatem quandam Magistratûs assumere, ἀτάκτως, in ordinem cogere: impios, infidos à se arcere, & res suas sibi habere jubere, aliisque suæ conservationi conducentibus prospicere, & que c'est l'ordre que St. Paul veut que les Corinthiens establissent parmi eux, 1 Cor. 6. Mais il veut que tout cela se fasse par un droit naturel, & non pas par une authorité émaémanée de J. Christ, du nom duquel il se plaint qu'on abuse quand on dit dans la Liturgie, Au nom & en l'authorité de J. Christ j'excommunie, &c. Il accuse encore nos Eglises d'une trop grande rigueur, en ce que lors qu'un Consistoire a exclus une personne de sa communion, on veut que cét Arrest ait lieu dans toutes les autres assemblées de Chrestiens qui sont dans le monde ; & en ce que l'on fixe un certain temps pendant lequel ceux qui sont frappez de la censure, se doivent abstenir de la communion, lequel temps ils ne doivent point anticiper, quelque desir qu'ils ayent de recevoir les gages de leur réconciliation avec Dieu, & quelques preuves qu'ils puissent donner de leur repentance. Car, dit-il, puis qu'il paroit par ces témoignages extérieurs, qu'ils ont fait leur paix avec Dieu, pourquoy l'Eglise refuse-t-elle de les admettre à la sienne ? Jésus-Christ n'a jamais réjetté aucun pécheur repentant en quelque temps qu'il soit venu à luy. Pourquoy serons-nous plus sévéres que luy : & puis que Dieu peut appeller à la repentance les pécheurs à chaque moment, & que ces momens-là sont par devers luy. Pourquoy veut-on borner le toutPuissant, & empescher, entant que l'on peut, l'effect de sa miséricorde, en renvoyant à un certain espace de temps pour se réconcilier avec luy, ceux à qui Dieu luy-mesme ne prescrit point de temps, & qu'il peut visiter en sa grace à chaque moment du jour ?
units.tr: It is utterly mistaken, by heaven, to think that the force of civil laws consists in their being just; for a law holds authority not because it is just, but because it is law, and a rule sanctioned by one who has authority. He says that the Pope must necessarily fall if you take away from him that authority which he calls spiritual, though the authority of the Turk is no more temporal, and which he believes he holds from Jesus Christ by virtue of the words Whatever you bind; and this he upholds by excommunication, which has made peoples and kings tremble through so many centuries. He wishes that Calvin, for whom he otherwise shows deep veneration, had not been so eager to establish his Discipline, or at least had not called it the yoke of Jesus Christ. For although Monsieur du Moulin acknowledges that one may well admit his regulations, and others like them, such as those of the churches of France, to maintain order, he does not think the foundations on which Calvin rests them are legitimate, because, he says, they are the very same foundations on which the Pope gradually built his empire. He says that Calvin has suffered something human and is not consistent with himself, since, after calling his discipline the yoke of Jesus Christ, a yoke that only libertines and profane people can reject, he admits elsewhere that the opinion of many pious and learned persons is that excommunication is not necessary where there are Christian princes.
