This is what he says in his letter to the ministers of Zurich: On excommunication not all think alike, nor am I unaware that there are pious and learned men who do not think excommunication necessary under Christian princes. He is astonished that several of his closest relatives grow as heated against him as they do, that some have called him the scourge of the Church, that he is to be passed off as a fanatic, a visionary and an unbalanced mind, like Monsieur Bochart, who called him a head that three Anticyras could scarcely cure; and yet the memory of Zwingli, Musculus, Bullinger, Gualter, Erastus and many other excellent men of the last century, who are famous among the reformers, is revered, although they shared his opinion. He believes that the maxims of these latter on the conduct of the Church would have prevailed among all the Reformed, had not the great influence of Calvin and of Beza, who followed him, preoccupied minds. He concedes that where the magistrate is not Christian, or where he does not do his duty in restraining the wicked, each assembly may, through a confederated discipline and by mutual pact, assume to itself a certain power of the magistrate, [ἀτάκτως] bring into order by compulsion, keep away the impious and the faithless, bid them keep their own goods, and provide for other things conducive to its preservation; and that this is the order which St Paul wishes the Corinthians to establish among themselves (1 Cor. 6). But he wants all this to be done by natural right, and not by an authority derived from Jesus Christ, in whose name he complains that abuse is made when the Liturgy says, In the name and by the authority of Jesus Christ I excommunicate, etc. He further accuses our churches of excessive rigour, in that when a consistory has excluded a person from its communion, that sentence is expected to hold in all the other assemblies of Christians in the world; and in that a certain period is fixed during which those struck by the censure must abstain from communion, a period they must not anticipate, however much they desire to receive the pledges of their reconciliation with God, and whatever proofs of their repentance they can give. For, he says, since it appears from these outward testimonies that they have made their peace with God, why does the Church refuse to admit them to its own? Jesus Christ has never rejected any repentant sinner, at whatever time he came to him. Why should we be stricter than he? And since God can call sinners to repentance at every moment, and those moments are in his hands, why would one limit the Almighty and hinder, as far as one can, the effect of his mercy, by postponing to a certain space of time the reconciliation with him of those to whom God himself prescribes no time, and whom he can visit with his grace at every moment of the day?

units.la: Il dit que comme les societez, ou les divers corps, par exemple, celuy des Médecins d'une ville, celuy des Marchands, & des Artisans necessaires à la societé, doivent avoir un ordre entr'eux pour leur conservation, qui soit authorisé par le Magistrat, & qu'ils ont le pouvoir de faire des reglements pour ce dessein ; il en est de mesme des societez, qui s'assemblent pour les choses de la Religion. Il est vray que pour ces dernieres, il distingue entre les assemblées qui se font pour ouir la parole de Dieu, pour l'invocation de son nom, pour la célébration des Sacrements, & pour les autres exercices de la piété : & celles des Pasteurs & des Deleguez du peuple pour la conduite de la police Ecclésiastique : Car il dit que les premières ne dépendent pas des Magistrats, & que quand ils les deffendroient, il fraudroit dire comme les Apostres, Il est juste d'obéir à Dieu plustost qu'aux hommes ; mais pour les autres qui ne regardent que le dehors, il croit bien que l'on y peut former des résolutions selon l'occurrence des temps & des affaires, mais il n'estime pas qu'on y ait le pouvoir de faire des loix qui contraignent les hommes ; si ce n'est que le Magistrat authorise ces sortes de reiglemens, comme le Roy de France fait les décisions synodales. Il se met icy de belle humeur, & dit, qu'il est aussi ridicule de parler d'une puissance Ecclésiastique, que si on vouloit ériger une puissance Médicinale, Chirurgique, Charpentiére, Cordonniére, &c. qui fust absolue en son genre & indépendante de celle du Magistrat.
units.tr: He says that just as societies or corporate bodies, for example the physicians of a town, the merchants, and the craftsmen necessary to society, must have an order among themselves for their preservation, authorised by the magistrate, and have the power to make regulations for this purpose, so it is with societies that gather for matters of religion. He does distinguish between these, however: assemblies held to hear the word of God, to invoke his name, to celebrate the sacraments, and for the other exercises of piety are one kind, while the meetings of the ministers and the deputies of the people for the conduct of ecclesiastical discipline are another. The former, he says, do not depend on the magistrates, and even if the magistrates forbade them, one would have to say, as the Apostles did, "We must obey God rather than men." As for the others, which concern only externals, he thinks that resolutions may indeed be taken there according to the circumstances of the times and affairs, but he does not believe that they have the power to make laws binding on men, unless the magistrate authorises such regulations, as the King of France does with the decisions of synods. Here he becomes merry and says that it is as ridiculous to speak of an ecclesiastical power as it would be to set up a medical, surgical, carpentry, or shoemaking power, etc., absolute in its own kind and independent of the magistrate's.

units.la: Il soûtient que le Magistrat seul doit avoir l'inspection sur les meurs, infliger les peines aux mal-vivans, selon l'exigence des cas : que luy seul a le droit d'establir des loix, & d'avoir l'oeil fur la conduite de toutes les sociétez, de quelque nature qu'elles soyent, & par conséquent sur celle de l'Eglise qui au fonds compose l'Estat dans les lieux où tout le peuple est Chrestien, puisque le Christianisme n'empesche pas que nous ne soyons hommes.
units.tr: He maintains that the magistrate alone should have oversight of morals and inflict punishments on evildoers as the cases require; that he alone has the right to establish laws and to keep watch over the conduct of all societies, of whatever kind they may be, and therefore over that of the Church, which in fact makes up the state wherever the whole people is Christian, since Christianity does not prevent us from being men.

units.la: Quant aux Ministres, il dit qu'il leur accorde tout ce que J. Christ & ses Apostres s'attribueroient,s'ils estoient sur la terre, assavoir les voyes de l'endoctrinement, de la persuasion, des remontrances, des promesses, & des menaces, par lesquelles ils ouvrent le ciel aux croyans, & le ferment aux impénitens. Ceux qui les escoutent ils escoutent J. Christ luy-mesme, & ceux qui les rejettent, ils le rejettent.
units.tr: As for the ministers, he says he grants them everything that Jesus Christ and his Apostles would claim for themselves if they were on earth: namely, the means of teaching, persuasion, admonition, promises, and threats, by which they open heaven to believers and shut it against the impenitent. Those who listen to them listen to Jesus Christ himself, and those who reject them reject him.

units.la: Il veut que l'on confidére les reiglements des Consistoires & des Synodes, les décifions des Ministres sur les points de doctrine, les Confessions de Foy, les Catéchismes, &c. comme des Responsa sapientum, aufquelles il faut déférer, comme l'on fait aux décifions des experts qui parlent de leur art, mais non pas comme à des loix qui obligent la conscience, laquelle ne releve que de Dieu seul. Il me disoit l'autre jour qu'il ne sçauroit digérer cette clause que les Consistoires de France mettent dans leurs Lettres d'envoy aux Synodes Provinciaux & Nationaux, Nous promettons devant Dieu de nous soûmettre à tout ce qui sera décidé par vous, estans persuadez que le St. Esprit présidera au milieu de vous, &c. Vous savez de qu'elle manière Monsieur de Condom presse cette soûmission. Il prétend que le Pape & les Conciles n'en demandent pas d'avantage.
units.tr: He wishes that the regulations of consistories and synods, the decisions of ministers on points of doctrine, the confessions of faith, the catechisms, etc., be regarded as responsa sapientum, which must be deferred to as one defers to the judgements of experts who speak of their art, but not as laws that bind the conscience, which answers to God alone. The other day he told me that he could not stomach the clause that the consistories of France put in their letters sending delegates to the provincial and national synods: We promise before God to submit ourselves to all that shall be decided by you, being persuaded that the Holy Spirit will preside in the midst of you, etc. You know how Monsieur de Condom presses this submission. He claims that the Pope and the councils ask for no more than this.

units.la: Monsieur du Moulin distingue entre trois sortes de Jugemens, l'un de discernement naturel; l'autre de sçavoir & d'expérience, le troisiéme d'authorité coactive. Il attribue le premier à tous les hommes de sens, le second aux Docteurs, aux Professeurs & aux Ministres; le troisiême au Magistrat seul. Car il dit, qu'il n'y a que deux voyes pour porter les hommes à leur devoir, le Conseil, & le Commandement. La premiére voye s'exerce en esclairant l'esprit, en instruisant, en exhortant, en persuadant, en representant les malheurs, où tombent les rebelles & les avantages de ceux qui se portent au bien; C'est ce que Monsieur du Moulin attribue aux Ministres; La seconde est, en commandant avec authorité, & en contraignant les rebelles par les chatimens; C'est ce, qu'il n'attribue qu'au Magistrat seul; ou à des hommes extraordinaires, comme estoient les Apostres, qui avoyent le don des miracles, qu'il appelle virgam Apostolicam; laquelle estoit nécessaire dans un temps extraordinaire, où il s'agissoit d'establir une nouvelle Religion, à laquelle les Magistrats estoient contraires: & qu'alors avoit lieu cette maxime du droit, ubi deficit lex sibi quisque seu coetus, seu homo, lex esto.
units.tr: Monsieur du Moulin distinguishes three kinds of judgement: one of natural discernment, another of learning and experience, and a third of coercive authority. He attributes the first to all sensible men, the second to teachers, professors, and ministers, and the third to the magistrate alone. For he says there are only two ways of bringing men to their duty: counsel and command. The first way works by enlightening the mind, by instructing, exhorting, and persuading, and by setting before people the misfortunes that befall rebels and the advantages of those who turn to what is good. This is what Monsieur du Moulin assigns to the ministers. The second way is to command with authority and to restrain rebels by punishments; this he assigns to the magistrate alone, or to extraordinary men such as the Apostles were, who had the gift of miracles, which he calls the apostolic rod. That rod was necessary in an extraordinary time, when a new religion had to be established against the wishes of the magistrates, and then the maxim of the law held: where the law fails, let each man, or assembly, or person be the law.

units.la: Mais afin que nous ne nous plaignions pas, comme s'il vouloit par quelque malignité secrette contre nostre Ordre, nous oster, ce qui nous appartient; il dit qu'on fait tort aux Ministres, de ne les admettre pas aux charges de la Magistrature, à laquelle ils ont droit, puis qu'ils sont Citoyens, Peres, Maris, Maitres, & de plus, personnes sonnes pour l'ordinaire plus esclairées que le Commun : Puis donc, dit-il, qu'ils jouissent de leurs biens, & de tous les privilèges des autres hommes dans la societé, puis qu'ils supportent les charges de l'Estat, & qu'ils ont le mesme intéreft à sa conservation, que le reste des habitans ; pourquoy fait-on ce tort à leur ordre de l'exclure de la Judicature ? Il tire de-là cette conjecture, que comme au commencement de la Reformation, les Pasteurs se virent privez de ce droit, pour se consoler de l'injure qu'on leur faisoit, ils s'avisèrent de s'ériger une Jurisdiction à part, collatérale à celle du Magistrat, & indépendante de lui à l'imitation de celle de Prélats de l'Eglise Romaine ; Que pour authoriser ce nouveau Sénat, ils ont retenu le nom de Puissance Spirituelle, quoy que le plus souvent il ne s'y traitte que de choses temporelles. Pour moy je suis persuadé, que nos Reformateurs cherchoient uniquement la gloire de Dieu, & la conservation de l'Ordre.
units.tr: But so that we do not complain, as if he wished, out of some secret malice against our order, to take away what belongs to us, he says that ministers are wronged when they are not admitted to the offices of the magistracy, to which they have a right, since they are citizens, fathers, husbands, and masters, and moreover, as a rule, people more enlightened than the common sort. Since, then, he says, they enjoy their goods and all the privileges of other men in society, since they bear the burdens of the state and have the same interest in its preservation as the rest of the inhabitants, why is their order wronged in being excluded from the judiciary? From this he draws the conjecture that, at the beginning of the Reformation, when the pastors saw themselves deprived of this right, they consoled themselves for the injury done to them by setting up for themselves a separate jurisdiction, alongside that of the magistrate and independent of him, in imitation of the prelates of the Roman Church. To lend authority to this new senate, he says, they have kept the name of spiritual power, although for the most part only temporal matters are dealt with there. For my part I am persuaded that our Reformers sought solely the glory of God and the preservation of order.

units.la: Il croit que les Magistrats seuls doivent prendre la connoissance de toutes sortes de matières de quelque nature qu'elles soyent. Il dit pour preuve de cela, que la Magistrature n'est pas un employ profane qui ne se doive mesler que de décider le Meum & le Tuum, & les contestations de Finibus. Que ceux qui l'exercent sont des personnes sacrées, & les Images vivantes de Dieu, qu'il a establies en son nom pour estre Custodes utriusque tabulæ, & que les assemblées Ecclésiastiques ne peuvent traitter d'aucun sujet qui ne se rapporte à l'une, ou à l'autre table de la Loy: de sorte que s'ils le font, ils entreprennent sur la charge du Magistrat.
units.tr: He holds that the magistrates alone should take cognisance of all sorts of matters, of whatever nature they may be. In proof of this he says that the magistracy is not a profane calling, to be concerned only with deciding mine and thine and disputes over boundaries. Those who exercise it are sacred persons, the living images of God, whom he has established in his name to be guardians of both tables, and ecclesiastical assemblies cannot treat of any subject that does not relate to one table or the other of the Law. So if they do so, they encroach upon the office of the magistrate.

units.la: Il fait l'histoire de la Puissance Ecclésiastique, & il en rapporte l'origine au temps de Constantin, Il dit que ce premier Monarque Chrestien estant parvenu à l'Empire, laissa dans les Cours de Justice, les mesmes Juges qui y avoyent esté establis par ses prédécesseurs : mais que comme ces Juges estoient presque tous payens, & que les Chrestiens se plaignoient de leurs injustices, cela obligea Constantin à donner aux Evesques le pouvoir de décider les différents qui arrivoient entre les Chreftiens de leurs Diocéfes, Que par la fuite du temps, lors que le Paganifme fuft entiérement aboli, les Evefques demeurérent prefque les feuls juges ; car tout s'addreffoit à eux : Mais qu'au lieu de fe fouvenir que leur pouvoir venoit de l'Empéreur, ils fe le voulurent conferver comme un droit que J. Chrift leur avoit déféré, & que pour cét effet ils cherchérent tout ce qu'ils jugérent propre dans le Nouveau Teftament pour maintenir leur poffeffion ; Qu'ils mirent en ufage le Quicquid ligaveris, &c. le Dabo tibi claves, le, Dic Ecclefiæ, &c. & que pour fe rendre formidables, ils mirent en ufage l'Excommunication. Monfieur du Moulin explique ces paffages au fens qu'Erafte les a entendus.
units.tr: He gives the history of ecclesiastical power and traces its origin to the time of Constantine. He says that this first Christian monarch, having come to the Empire, left in the courts of justice the same judges who had been established there by his predecessors; but since these judges were almost all pagans, and the Christians complained of their injustices, this obliged Constantine to give the bishops the power to decide the disputes that arose between Christians within their dioceses. In the course of time, when paganism was entirely abolished, the bishops remained almost the only judges, for everything was referred to them. But instead of remembering that their power came from the Emperor, they wished to keep it as a right that Jesus Christ had conferred upon them, and to this end they searched the New Testament for everything they judged suitable to maintain their possession. They put to use the Quodcumque ligaveris, etc., the Dabo tibi claves, the Dic Ecclesiae, etc., and to make themselves formidable they employed excommunication. Monsieur du Moulin explains these passages in the sense in which Erastus understood them.

units.la: Il nie avec luy que l'Excommunication fe puiffe trouver dans les livres de Moyfe, ou dans ceux des Prophétes, il foûtient au contraire que les pécheurs eftoient obligez foûs la Loy de faire offrir des facrifices pour leurs péchez & d'y affifter ; Il dit que les foüillures cérémonielles excluoient bien du Tabernacle, mais non pas les momorales ; que les Pharisiens-mesmes ne faisoient pas scrupule d'entrer dans le temple avec les peágers & les gens de mauvaise vie ; & qu'encore que les Juifs regardassent J. Christ & ses Apostres, comme des personnes abominables, ils ne les excluoient pourtant pas du temple, & ne leur empeschoient pas de manger l'Agneau de Pasque. Enfin il allégue dans sa Parénèse divers passages pour prouver que l'Excommunication est de l'invention des Payens, & entre autres celuy de Césa r, là où il parle des coûtumes des Anciens Gaulois, de leur Police, de leur Religion, & de leurs conducteurs.
units.tr: With him he denies that excommunication can be found in the books of Moses or in those of the Prophets. On the contrary, he maintains that under the Law sinners were obliged to have sacrifices offered for their sins and to be present at them. He says that ceremonial defilements did indeed exclude from the Tabernacle, but not moral ones; that the Pharisees themselves had no scruple about entering the temple with the tax collectors and people of bad life; and that although the Jews regarded Jesus Christ and his Apostles as abominable persons, they nevertheless did not exclude them from the temple, nor prevent them from eating the Passover lamb. Finally, in his Paraenesis he adduces various passages to prove that excommunication is an invention of the pagans, and among others that of Caesar, where he speaks of the customs of the ancient Gauls, their polity, their religion, and their leaders.

units.la: Le premier ordre, (dit cét auteur) qui est celuy des Druïdes, a l'intendance du culte des Dieux, & de la Religion. Lors que quelqu'un ne veut pas acquiescer à leurs jugemens, ils luy interdisent la communion de leurs mystères. Ceux qui sont frappez de cette foudre, passent pour scélérats & pour impies, chacun fuit leur rencontre & leur entretien ; s'ils ont quelque affaire, où ne leur fait point de justice : Ils ne sont point admis aux charges, ni aux dignitez, & meurent sans bonneur[?], & sans crédit, &c.
units.tr: The first order, (says this author), which is that of the Druids, has charge of the worship of the gods and of religion. When someone is unwilling to accept their judgements, they forbid him the communion of their mysteries. Those who are struck by this thunderbolt are regarded as criminals and impious; everyone avoids their company and their conversation; if they have any business, no justice is done them; they are not admitted to offices or dignities, and they die without honour and without credit, etc.

units.la: [ornament band, not printed text]
units.tr: [ornament band, not printed text]

units.la: A Monsieur Allix.
units.tr: To Monsieur Allix.

units.la: Monsieur,
units.tr: Sir,

units.la: JE n'ay rien à ajoûter à la Lettre de. Monsieur Muffard, sinon les prières que je vous fais, de juger s'il y a quelque chose dans mes sentimens de la maniére que vous les y voyez expliquez, qui soit dangereux, qui répugne au Christianisme, & qui ne soit conforme à la nature du Ministére de l'Evangile, qui ne se déploye pas par une puissance extérieure, comme est celle des Magistrats, quæ imperat, vetat, cogit, punit: comme nous dit Justinien; Mais par cette Puissance à salut, dont parle St. Paul, Rom. 1. v. 16. qui éclaire qui anime, qui persuade, qui sanctifie, & en un mot qui manie les Esprits par les anses de la raison, & par la voye de l'intelligence. C'est là le grand dessein de l'Evangile. C'est-là la conduite de J. C. agissant comme médiateur. Il établit son Empire sur les cœurs, & non pas sur les corps, ni sur les biens : quoy que comme vray Dieu, il soit le souverain maistre de toutes choses. C'est ce que J'ay eu dessein de faire connoitre en décriant la Puissance Ecclésiastique, dont la ruine rétablit J. C. sur son thrône, & fait comprendre aux Ministres le vray usage de leurs fonctions sacrées, sous l'Empire de leur Maistre. Ceux qui ont publié les pensées de Monsieur Pascal après sa mort, se sont avisez d'y en fourrer une qui est extrémement hors d'oeuvre, & qui combat tout le dessein du livre. Ils luy font établir un Empire de J. C. semblable à celuy des Rois de la terre où il a mis le Pape pour son Lieutenant. Cette pensée est si impertinente, & si contraire aux vrais sentimens de Monsieur Pascal, qu'il eust mieux valu que ces corrupteurs de livres eussent condamné à un silence éternel les ououvrages de ce grand homme, que de luy attribuer des pensées, directement oppofées aux autres qui sont si belles. Pour découvrir la fraude grossiere de ces gens-là, il n'y a qu'à écouter le véritable Monsieur Pafchal. Il a pensé & s'eft exprimé sur ce sujet d'une maniere entierement conforme à mes hypotheses, comme on le peut cognoitre par ces paroles. Il eust esté inutile (dit-il) à Archiméde de faire le Prince, dans ses livres de géometrie, quoy qu'il le fust, c'est ce qu'a fait J. C. il venoit pour gaigner un peuple, par la grandeur & par la vérité de ses doctrines, & de leur bonté : non pour dominer en Roy sur eux. J'amais homme n'eust tant d'eclat, dans un estat d'humilité & d'ignominie. Cette pensée est si éloignée des prétentions der hiérarchiques, qu'elle bannit entierement le Pape, & sa chimérique puissance. J'allégue les sentimens de ce célebre Catholique Romain, pour émouvoir s'il est possible mes freres à jalousie. C'est une chose bien étrange qu'il se trouve dans le party des ennemis, des gens qui reconnoissent, & qui découvrent les fraudes & les usurpations de leur Dieu en terre, & que parmi nous, où il est décrié comme ille mérite, on appuye son thrône, & qu'on pose les mesmes fondemens qui l'y ont élevé. Dieu veuille guérir les Esprits de leurs faus préjugez & inspirer à chacun de nous le dessein de chercher plûtost sa gloire, que la gloire des hommes. Je le prie qu'il vous conserve long-tems à son Eglise. Je suis,
units.tr: I have nothing to add to the letter of Monsieur Muffard, except the request that you judge whether there is anything in my sentiments, as you see them explained here, that is dangerous, repugnant to Christianity, or not in keeping with the nature of the ministry of the Gospel. That ministry does not operate by an external power, such as that of the magistrates, quæ imperat, vetat, cogit, punit, as Justinian tells us, but by that power unto salvation of which St. Paul speaks (Rom. 1. v. 16), which enlightens, animates, persuades and sanctifies, and in a word handles minds by the handles of reason and by the way of understanding. That is the great design of the Gospel. That is the conduct of J.C. acting as mediator. He establishes his empire over hearts, not over bodies or goods, although as true God he is the sovereign master of all things. This is what I have aimed to make known in decrying the ecclesiastical power. Its overthrow restores J.C. to his throne and teaches the ministers the true use of their sacred functions under the empire of their Master. Those who published the thoughts of Monsieur Pascal after his death thought fit to insert one that is extremely out of place and that undermines the whole design of the book. They make him establish an empire of J.C. like that of the kings of the earth, and in it he has put the Pope as his lieutenant. This thought is so foolish, and so contrary to Monsieur Pascal's true sentiments, that it would have been better for these corrupters of books to condemn the works of this great man to eternal silence than to attribute to him thoughts directly opposed to the others, which are so fine. To expose the coarse fraud of these people, one need only listen to the true Monsieur Pascal. He thought and expressed himself on this subject in a manner entirely in keeping with my hypotheses, as can be seen from these words: It would have been useless (he says) for Archimedes to play the prince in his books of geometry, although he was one. This is what J.C. did. He came to win a people through the greatness and truth of his doctrines and their goodness, not to rule over them as a king. Never did a man have such brilliance in a state of humility and ignominy. This thought is so far from the pretensions of the hierarchs that it entirely banishes the Pope and his chimerical power. I allege the sentiments of this celebrated Roman Catholic in order to stir, if possible, my brethren to jealousy. It is a very strange thing that there are people on the side of the enemies who acknowledge and expose the frauds and usurpations of their God on earth, while among us, where he is decried as he deserves, men support his throne and lay the same foundations that raised it there. May God heal minds of their false prejudices and inspire each of us to seek his glory rather than the glory of men. I pray that he preserve you long to his Church. I am,

units.la: Monsieur,
units.tr: Sir,

units.la: Vostre tres-humble & tres-obéissant Serviteur
units.tr: Your most humble and most obedient servant,

units.la: Loüis du Moulin.
units.tr: Loüis du Moulin.

units.la: Clarissimo & Reverendo Viro D. Carolo Rupiforti F. V. D. Verbi Dei Mini- stro, Olim in Insulis Americæ: Nunc verò Ecclesiæ Gallo-Belgicæ quæ Ro- terodami colligitur, Pastori, S.
units.tr: To the most distinguished and reverend man, Mr. Carolus Rupiforte, faithful Minister of the Word of God, formerly in the islands of America, and now pastor of the Gallo-Belgic church gathered at Rotterdam: greetings.

units.la: NOlim, in limine, Vir, multis nominibus mihi observandé quemquam, Te arcessere crimine æquioris animi & Pietatis in sententiam meam de Potestate Ecclesiastica, quia hæc Epistola appareret in tuo nomine: Nam id à me fieri, Te non opinante, imo haud dubium reluctante confiteor Tibi: ut jam istius culpæ ( fi tamen foret culpa ) non magis debeas esse Reus;quam aut Celeberrimus Claudius aut reverendus Muffardus ; Nam uterque itidem nolens, volens, à me compellatur: ac proinde geminum & par tuum & illorum crimen fit: Claudium enim nemo ambigit longissimè à meis sensibus abire, in re, de qua idem forsan inter Te, & me est certamen. Sed in quo perinde atque apud Claudium & Muffardum constitutum est cœptis instare, quoad vos ex æquo ad meas partes perduxerim: capta occasione istius Syllogcs Te referendi in numerum illorum, quos observo, & colo, & quibus nostra probari impensé, cupio, Teque rogandi, ut nolis oculos avertere, à lectione cum Epistolarum in unum fasciculum collectarum, tum imprimis hujusce, sed velis quod ab alio non possem, aut sperare aut impetrare, propter argumenti seu dignitatem, seu veritatem indulgere amori nostro otium ( quod beneficium interpretabor ) legendi quicquid nunc cartis illino: nam quid Epistola lecta nocebit ?
units.tr: I was not willing, sir, to summon you, on many grounds that I hold in regard, into the charge of a fairer mind and piety regarding my opinion on ecclesiastical power, because this letter appears under your name. I confess to you that I did this without your knowledge, and indeed against your unmistakable reluctance. So you need not be held guilty of this fault, if it is a fault, any more than the most famous Claudius or the reverend Muffardus. Both of them, whether they wished it or not, are likewise addressed by me, so that the fault is double, shared by you and by them. No one doubts that Claudius is very far from my views on the matter in which there is perhaps the same dispute between you and me. But just as I have resolved to press on with Claudius and Muffardus, so I have brought you to my side on equal terms. Seizing the opportunity, I wish to count you among those whom I respect and cherish, and by whom I eagerly wish our views to be approved. I ask you not to turn your eyes away from reading this collection of letters gathered into one bundle, and especially this one. Grant me, since I cannot hope for or obtain this from anyone else, the leisure to read whatever I now put on paper, because of the dignity or the truth of the subject. I will take this as a kindness. For what harm can a letter do when it is read?

units.la: Cum vir apprimè doctus perlegisset meum Epistolarum fasciculum, ibi maximè substitit, in Epistola ad reverendum Muffardum, ubi inter alia quæ probant futilitatem potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, dico nihil magis debere firmare virum cordatum in sententia de vanitate Potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, quam hæc reputatio, quod Pastores in Hollandia & cæteris fœderati Belgii provinciis, de ea semper statuissent secundum stationem, quam sustinent, vel in Ecclesia, vel in Republica; nihil que magis in me culpavit quam quod id affirmo, non corroboraverim exemplis, nec plura attulerim quæ arguant istius potestatis futilitatem, quocirca, ut benè monenti obtemperem, mantissæ loco subjeci apud Te quæ in mentem venerunt in hanc rem.
units.tr: When a very learned man had read through my bundle of letters, he stopped most of all at the letter to the reverend Muffardus. There, among other arguments that prove the futility of ecclesiastical power, I said that nothing should confirm a sensible man in the opinion of the vanity of ecclesiastical power more than this consideration: that the ministers in Holland and the other provinces of the Belgic confederacy have always judged the matter according to the station they hold, either in the Church or in the Commonwealth. He blamed me most of all for affirming this without supporting it with examples, and for not bringing forward more arguments showing the futility of that power. Therefore, to comply with his kindly admonition, I have added as an appendix to you what came to mind on this subject.

units.la: Cum ergo priusquam Calvinus pedem fixisset Genevæ, Farellus & Viretus jecissent fundamenta reformationis à Papismo; non venit in mentem viris sanctis, quemadmodum non venerat apud Helvetios, de ordine sacro viris, constituere potestatem Ecclesiasticam & Synedrium, cui soli viri Ecclesiastici clesiastici præessent, seorsim & à latere Jurisdictionis civilis. Is ergo captâ, ut credibile est occasione, quod Magistratus nullos viros de grege Pastorum reformatorum admitteret in Senatum urbis, in locum aut Episcopi Genevensis aut cleri Romanensis ex eo pulsi, quod quidem factum per summam injuriam à Magistratu: incoeptum audax, ne dicam temerarium agressus est Calvinus propria authoritate, ut loquitur in quadam Epistola, ut erigeret tribunal & judicium Ecclesiasticum plane distinctum & independens à Civili: ut licet quidam de Senatu admitterentur in Synedrium Pastorum, ab eo tamen provocatio non fieret ad Judicium civile. Sed duo essent in una urbe tribunalia collateralia, alterum civile, cujus jurisdictioni subessent homines sub ratione civium & incolarum urbis; alterum Ecclesiasticum, cui submitterentur omnes, ipsi que viri de Magistratura sub ratione Christianorum, qui reformatæ religioni nomen dederunt. Atque ad hunc typum, (quem à Papa) licet optima mente, sed luctuoso Ecclesiæ consilio arreptum ; ad hunc, inquam typum, & schema duplicis regiminis, Ecclesiastici & civilis, suum quoque fumplerunt & exscripserunt, omnes ubique reformati, pari injuriâ, & fraude & iniqua occupatione juris pertinentis ad Magistratum, quâ ipse Magistratus, in prima reformatione exuerat viros de clero suâ civicâ libertate, & suo jure civili: unde enata materia litium, dissidiorum & collifionum perpetuarum inter Judicia Ecclefiaftica, & civilia, non solùm quandiu vixit Calvinus, sed & deinceps Genevæ & alibi ; imo ubique locorum in orbe reformato, qui suam disciplinam à Calvino acceperat : minus tamen in Anglia, quam aut in Scotia, aut in Hollandia, eò quod duo tribunalia, unum ex æquo in terris agnofcerent caput, nempe Regem : non sic in Scotia, ubi Presbyteriani nunquam passi sunt, uni capiti in terris fe subjicere præter quam Christo, unde factum fuerit ut major semper ibi effet tribunalium & jurisdictionum conflictus, quam alibi locorum, ubi reformatio obtinuit.
units.tr: So, before Calvin fixed his foot at Geneva, Farel and Viret had laid the foundations of the reformation from Popery. It did not occur to those holy men, just as it had not occurred to those in Helvetia, to establish a sacred order of men with ecclesiastical power and a court, over which the ecclesiastical men alone would preside, separately and alongside civil jurisdiction. Calvin, seizing the occasion, as is credible, because the magistrate would admit no men from the flock of reformed ministers into the Senate of the city, and because the bishop of Geneva and the Roman clergy had been driven out of it (an act done with the greatest injustice by the magistrate), undertook, on his own authority, as he himself says in a certain letter, a bold, not to say rash, enterprise: to erect a tribunal and an ecclesiastical judgment, entirely distinct from and independent of the civil one. Thus, although some members of the Senate were admitted into the synod of ministers, appeal would not be made from it to the civil court. Instead there would be two collateral tribunals in one city: one civil, to whose jurisdiction would be subject the men considered as citizens and inhabitants of the city; the other ecclesiastical, to which all would be submitted, including the magistrates themselves, considered as Christians who had given their name to the reformed religion. To this pattern, which was taken from the Pope (though with the best intention, yet to the sorrow of the Church), to this pattern, I say, and this scheme of a double government, ecclesiastical and civil, all the reformed everywhere likewise adopted and copied it, with the same injustice, fraud and unjust seizure of the right that belonged to the magistrate. In the first reformation the magistrate himself had stripped the clergy of their civic liberty and their civil right. From this arose the matter of perpetual lawsuits, disputes and collisions between the ecclesiastical and civil courts, not only as long as Calvin lived, but afterwards at Geneva and elsewhere, indeed in every place in the reformed world that had received its discipline from Calvin. Yet this was less so in England than in Scotland or in Holland, because in England the two tribunals acknowledged one head on earth, namely the King. It was not so in Scotland, where the Presbyterians never allowed themselves to submit to any earthly head except Christ. Hence it came about that there was always a greater conflict of tribunals and jurisdictions there than in other places where the reformation took hold.

units.la: Sed nec tantum magnus fuit conflictus in uno territorio, inter duo tribunalia, altero ad se trahente alterius causas: Sed & inter sacri ordinis viros de tribunali Ecclesiastico: nonnullis de hoc tribunali, agnoscentibus iniquitatem & impium incœptum cuiusquam Tribunalis Ecclesiastici, saltem in eo, quod ab illo non daretur provocatio ad civile, aliis independentiam, ut ita loquar tribunalium & judiciorum Ecclesiasticorum à civilibus jure Divino afferentibus; qua in re semper fuerunt, potissimum in Hollandia, & cæteris Belgii Provinciis, varii sensus, ut obiter tetigi Epistolâ ad reverendum Muffardum: his & illis pro latione, quam in republica, aut in Ecclesia sustinebant, vel subjicientibus tribunalia Ecclesiastica civilibus, ut fecerunt Maresius, Vedelius, Maccovius, Polyander, Rivetus, quod essent Academici ac proinde minores partes haberent in Synedriis, vel è contra Magistratum plane arcentibus à cognitione & revisione judiciorum Ecclesiasticorum, in quibus fuerunt Walæus, Apollonius, Triglandius ejusmodi, quod effent de Synedrio, & in eo haberent jus suffragii, adeoque acerrimi vindices Potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, & in ea sententia se in synodo aut syncdrio considentes nullo jure obnoxios esse reddendis rationibus Magistratui. Non erit alienum hos & illos audire loquentes.
units.tr: Nor was the conflict great only within one territory, between two tribunals, one drawing the causes of the other to itself. There was also conflict among men of the sacred order who sat on the ecclesiastical tribunal. Some of them acknowledged the iniquity and impious undertaking of any ecclesiastical tribunal, at least in that it allowed no appeal to the civil court. Others asserted, by divine right, the independence, as I may call it, of ecclesiastical tribunals and judgments from civil ones. On this matter there have always been, especially in Holland and the other provinces of Belgium, various opinions, as I touched on briefly in my letter to the reverend Muffardus. These men and those held views according to the position they held in the commonwealth or in the Church. Some made ecclesiastical tribunals subject to civil ones, as Maresius, Vedelius, Maccovius, Polyander and Rivetus did, because they were academics and therefore had a lesser part in the synods. Others, on the contrary, kept the magistrate entirely away from the cognizance and review of ecclesiastical judgments. Among these were Walaeus, Apollonius and Triglandius, because they belonged to the synod and had the right of vote there. Thus they were the most fierce defenders of ecclesiastical power, and, sitting in synod or consistory, held that they were under no legal obligation to give an account to the magistrate. It will not be out of place to hear these men and those speaking.

units.la: Agmen de illis qui synedria & synodos, Magistratus subjiciunt judicio, ducat Marefius. Is loco 16 loc. com. sic decurtat authoritatem synodorum & canonum, ut dicat pastores in synodo non esse judices, sed referre doctores prudentes & peritos, non alia præditos authoritate in populum fidelem, quam Medicos in ægros, quorum canones, non obligant, nisi quatenus concordare videntur cum sacro codice.
units.tr: The line of those who subject synods and assemblies to the judgment of the magistrate is led by Maresius. In his 16 loc. com. he so cuts down the authority of synods and canons that he says ministers in synod are not judges, but are teachers who are prudent and skilled, endowed with no more authority over the faithful people than physicians have over the sick. Their canons do not bind, except insofar as they appear to agree with the sacred code.

units.la: Rivetus in Decalogum, Ministri quatenus Ministri, sunt summi Magistratus subditi; cur autem à subditis & eorum judicio, non liceat provocare ad summum Magistratum? Et cur supremo Magistratui judicia subditorum non liceat recognoscere: si bona, rata habere, si mala abolere?
units.tr: Rivetus, on the Decalogue: Ministers, insofar as they are ministers, are subjects of the supreme magistrate. Why then should it not be lawful to appeal from subjects and their judgment to the supreme magistrate? And why should it not be lawful for the supreme magistrate to review the judgments of subjects, to approve them if good and to abolish them if bad?

units.la: Polyander Synopf. defp. 50. Magistratus penes quem est summi imperii potestas; disciplinam illam, aut præsens approbare, aut absens examinare potest: & si quid in ea desideratur à pastoribus exigere, ut illud ex verbo Dei, & ejus analogia addatur & emendetur.
units.tr: Polyander, Synopsis, disputation 50: The magistrate, in whom the power of supreme authority lies, can either approve that discipline when it is present, or examine it when it is absent. And if anything is lacking in it, he can require the ministers to add and correct it from the Word of God and its analogy.

units.la: Maccovius cum esset Polonus & professor Theologiæ Franekeræ, nec ullas partes haberet jurisdictionis in synedriis pastorum, tantò defæcatiori judicio & abducto à præjudiciis pronunciabat de jurisdictione aut Pastorum aut Magistratûs circa sacra. Cumque suo tempore colliderentur inter se pastores, & cum Magistratu, circa modum potestatis assignandum aut huic, aut illis, hancce invenit viam concordiæ Scripto publici juris facto & in tres propositiones digesto, quod in omnes partes, loca, urbes & Ecclesias fœderati Belgii transmissum fuit, & maximè probatum à viris pacis amantibus senatoriæ gravitatis, Professoribusque & doctoribus Academiarum; sed quod à vindicibus potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, ut eit gens sacra, lacerabatur & differebatur, ut carmen exitiale & veneficum vel ut sica jugulum potestatis Ecclesiasticæ petens & transfodiens, à nonnullis vocaretur mors, & funus Potestatis Ecclesiasticæ. Et cujus author merito diceretur flagrum Ecclesiæ. Summus vir Bochartus Epistolâ ad Morlæum ait per sarcasmum illis propositionibus Maccovianis inditum nomen libellorum. Ejusmodi autem sunt.
units.tr: Maccovius, though he was a Pole and professor of theology at Franeker, held no part of jurisdiction in the synods of ministers. With a far clearer judgment, free from prejudices, he pronounced on the jurisdiction of ministers or magistrates in sacred matters. In his time the ministers collided among themselves and with the magistrate over how power should be assigned to one or the other. He found a way of concord, a writing made public and digested into three propositions. It was sent to all parts, places, cities and churches of the Belgic confederacy, and was greatly approved by men of peace of senatorial gravity, and by professors and teachers of the academies. But it was torn apart and deferred by the champions of ecclesiastical power, who were a sacred people. Some called it death and the funeral of ecclesiastical power, like a deadly charm, or like a dagger seeking out and piercing the throat of ecclesiastical power. And its author was rightly called the scourge of the Church. The very distinguished man Bochart, in his letter to Morlaeus, says that by way of sarcasm the name of "libels" was given to those Maccovian propositions. They are as follows.

units.la: 1. Officium & partes Magistratûs sunt curare & providere, ut verbum Dei sancte & pure prædicetur, & rite sacramenta & disciplina Ecclesiastica administrentur: tum inquirere in doctrinam, vitam, mores pastorum, an bene aut male, diligenter, an perfunctorie officio defungantur suisque partibus, ut cunctantes, aut in officio cessantes puniant.
units.tr: 1. The office and duties of the magistrate are to take care and see that the word of God is preached purely and holily, and that the sacraments and church discipline are properly administered; and also to inquire into the teaching, life and conduct of the ministers, whether they discharge their office and their duties well or badly, diligently or carelessly, and to punish those who are slack or neglect their office.

units.la: 2. Quandoquidem decisiones, definitiones, sententiæ, imo canones, decreta, censuræ latæ à synodis, synedriis, pastoribus, nullam vim legis habeant, nec quemquam obligent illis parendi citra sanctionem Magistratûs, inde conficitur summum judicium imperii circa sacra, non pertinere ad pastores, nec ad synedria & synodos, sed ad Magistratum atque in ejusmodi censuris, canonibus decretis ferendis & imperandis, summum & ultimum judicium summamque authoritatem pertinere ad Magistratum, non vero ad Synodos aut Pastores.
units.tr: 2. Since the decisions, definitions, judgements, indeed the canons, decrees and censures issued by synods, synedria and ministers have no force of law and bind no one to obey them without the sanction of the magistrate, it follows that the supreme judgement of the commonwealth concerning sacred matters does not belong to the ministers, nor to the synedria and synods, but to the magistrate; and that in enacting and imposing such censures, canons and decrees, the supreme and final judgement and highest authority belong to the magistrate, and not to the synods or the ministers.

units.la: 3. Cum ergo canones, decreta, censurae latae à pastoribus, definitiones & constitutiones nullam vim legis habeant, quae parendi illis cuiquam necessitatem imponant, citra sanctionem, voluntatem & approbationem Magistratus, plane conficitur eum teneri & obligari, vel illas constitutiones & definitiones pastorales aut synodales caeco judicio approbare & ratas habere citra examen proprii judicii suggerentis, quod concordent cum sacra scriptura, aut ab ea discordent: quodque plus minusve cedant in bonum Ecclesiae: vel illas constitutiones Ecclesiasticas in totum, saltem de illis tantum suo assensu ratum habere, quantum post examen debitum proprii judicii, ipsi videbitur bonum, justum & aequum. Hic, inquit Maccovius, constrictos teneo vindices potestatis Ecclesiasticae & compello ad assentiendum uni de duobus hisce: nempe ut reputent Magistratum, vel summum judicem & arbitrum circa sacra, Ecclesiasticarum definitionum & censurarum, vel lictorem & miniftratorem Pastorum, Synodorum & Synedriorum, quorum imperia non interpretari, sed exsequi caeco judicio debeat.
units.tr: 3. Therefore, since canons, decrees and censures issued by ministers, and their definitions and constitutions, have no force of law imposing on anyone the necessity of obeying them without the sanction, will and approval of the magistrate, it plainly follows that he is bound either to approve those pastoral or synodal constitutions and definitions with blind judgement and to ratify them without examining them by his own judgement, to see whether they agree with Holy Scripture or disagree with it, and whether they tend more or less to the good of the Church; or else to ratify those ecclesiastical constitutions wholly, or at least to give his assent only to such part of them as, after due examination by his own judgement, seems to him good, just and fair. "Here," says Maccovius, "I hold the defenders of ecclesiastical power bound and compel them to assent to one of these two alternatives: namely, either that they regard the magistrate as the supreme judge and arbiter in sacred matters of ecclesiastical definitions and censures, or else as the lictor and servant of the ministers, synods and synedria, whose commands he must not interpret but carry out with blind judgement."

units.la: Huic sententiae Maccovii, qua nihil verius, nihil defaecatiori, & fubactiori judicio prolatum, astipulantur multi in Anglia de sacro ordine, imo Episcopi, nulli quod sciam in Gallia inter reformatos sacri ordinis viros, nisi quos pervicit mea Parænefis aut meum Jugulum Causæ. In Anglia ergo sunt Davenantius, Bilfonus, Lancelotus Andreas Episcopi, tum Hookerus & author doctissimæ differtationis, cui titulus est Episcopalis hæreditas, omnes ex æquo assensuri Maccovianis libellis.
units.tr: To this opinion of Maccovius, than which nothing truer, nothing more refined and more thoroughly considered has been put forward, many in England who belong to the sacred order agree, indeed bishops; but among the reformed men of the sacred order in France, so far as I know, none, except those whom my Paraenesis or my Jugulum Causae has persuaded. In England, then, Davenant, Bilson, and the bishops Lancelot Andrewes, as well as Hooker and the author of the very learned dissertation entitled Episcopal Inheritance, will all agree equally with Maccovius' little books.

units.la: Hujus quem ex Anglis ultimo loco nominavi, attuli verba in Epistola ad Muffardum, quibus affirmat dogma esse Pontificium asserere Potestatem Ecclesiasticam distinctam esse à civili. Et revera è Papæ officina, & è visceribus iniquitatis prodiit distinctio illa
units.tr: I quoted the words of the last-named of these Englishmen in my letter to Muffardus, in which he affirms that it is a Papist dogma to assert that ecclesiastical power is distinct from civil power. And indeed that distinction between ecclesiastical and civil power, and along with it that national ecclesiastical tribunal (or the Pope's), came forth from the workshop of the Pope and from the bowels of iniquity.

units.la: R potestatis in Ecclesiasticam & civilem, & unà tribunal illud Ecclesiasticum nationale; seu Papæ; tremendum quidem quia armatum ἀναμαρτησία, sed non usque adeo cum ratione pugnans, ut quis mancipet suum intellectum judicio infallibili, atque quod habetur inter Protestantes, tanto magis absurdum & inficetum quam Romanense quod exigat obsequium judicio erròri obnoxio.
units.tr: It is a tremendous thing, indeed, because it is armed with infallibility [ἀναμαρτησία], yet it is not so much at odds with reason that anyone should surrender his understanding to an infallible judgement; and what obtains among Protestants is all the more absurd and ridiculous than the Roman system, which demands obedience to a judgement liable to error.

units.la: Venio ad Theologos in contrarias oras delatos, non solùm in sœderatis provinciis, sed & in Gallia, vix in Anglia, nisi inter Presbyterianos: at magno numero in Scotia.
units.tr: I come to the theologians who have been carried to the opposite shore, not only in the United Provinces but also in France; scarcely in England, except among the Presbyterians; but in great numbers in Scotland.

units.la: Prodeat primus Antonius Walæus, Professor Leydensis* Synops. Purioris Theologiæ disp. 48. Thes. 19. qui erit instar omnium quos longo ordine recensere possem, Negamus Spiritualem Potestatem, aut ejus praxin à Magistratus suprema authoritate pendere, sicut quidam recentiores contendunt: cum à solo Christo pendeat, & ab ipso sit immediatè concessa Ecclesiæ; ac proinde, nec per appellationem, aut provocationem proprie dictam, potestas hæc ad Magistratus, aut Principum tribunal deferri potest ; cum ejus exsecutio penes ipsos non fit.
units.tr: Let Antonius Walaeus, professor at Leiden, come forward first, in his Synopsis of Purer Theology, disputation 48, thesis 19, who will serve as an example for all whom I could list in a long series: We deny that spiritual power, or its exercise, depends on the supreme authority of the magistrate, as some more recent writers contend; since it depends on Christ alone and was granted immediately by him to the Church; and therefore this power cannot be carried by appeal, or properly speaking by provocation, to the magistrate's or the princes' tribunal, since its execution does not lie with them.

units.la: Paria loquuntur Galli reformati de sacro ordine : nec mirum, ut pote assueti ; suas res sibi seorsim habere, absque provocatione à Synedriis & Synodis ad confessus Politicos, contra quod usurpatur inter Romanenses in Gallia in qua solenne est provocare à curiis Episcopalibus ad curias civiles per appellationes ad abusum, ut loquuntur : qua in re Pontificii Senatores & Judices in Gallia longè rectius sentiunt de potestate Ecclesiastica, quam reformati Pastores: hi enim credunt, etiam sub Magistratu reformato, appellare ad Magistratum de sententia Synodorum, id esse transfire à regno Christi ad regnum Mundi, Altrinsecus illi quatenus subjiciunt potestatem Ecclesiasticam civili, illam penè pro nihilo habent.
units.tr: The reformed Frenchmen speak in the same way about the sacred order, and this is no surprise, since they are accustomed to keep their own affairs apart, without appeal from the synedria and synods to the political courts. The opposite is practised among the Romanists in France, where it is customary to appeal from the episcopal courts to the civil courts by appeals for abuse, as they call them. In this matter the Papist senators and judges in France think far more rightly about ecclesiastical power than the reformed ministers do. For the latter believe that, even under a reformed magistrate, to appeal to the magistrate from the sentence of the synods is to pass from the kingdom of Christ to the kingdom of the world. The former, on the other hand, since they subject ecclesiastical power to the civil, almost count it as nothing.

units.la: Verba sunt synodi Lugdunensis reformatarum Ecclesiarum articulo 28. De politia civili constituere Magistratus est, cui omnes parere tenentur, sed de rebus Ecclesiasticis pastorum est & Synodorum. Nam hæc vox est omnium penè reformatorum de clero: & quam concepit vir reverendus frater meus Cyrus Molinæus, Dissertatione de Potestate Ecclesiastica sectione 4. 8. 12. Deus commisit regimen Ecclesiæ Pastoribus, ut reipublicæ, Magistratibus & Regibus, ac proinde pastorum est dispone‑re de muneribus reipublicæ. Ibidem unicum medium hasce duas jurisdictiones conciliandi, & integritatem unius sine alterius dispendio tuendi, est illas totas & illibatas in eodem statu: quo Deus eas instituit relinquere. Magistratui politico rerum civilium, Pastoribus Ecclesiasticarum cognitionem & judicium permittere.
units.tr: These are the words of the Synod of Lyon of the reformed Churches, article 28: To establish civil polity belongs to the magistrates, to whom all are bound to submit; but in ecclesiastical matters it belongs to the ministers and synods. For this is almost the common language of all the reformed concerning the clergy, and it is the form my reverend brother Cyrus Molinaeus conceived, in his dissertation on ecclesiastical power, section 4, 8, 12: God committed the government of the Church to ministers, as the government of the commonwealth to magistrates and kings; and therefore it belongs to ministers to dispose of the offices of the commonwealth. In the same place: The only means of reconciling these two jurisdictions, and of preserving the integrity of each without loss to the other, is to leave them both whole and unimpaired in the state in which God established them: to let the political magistrate have the cognizance and judgement of civil affairs, and the ministers that of ecclesiastical affairs.

units.la: Eadem loquuntur purioris reformationis vindices in Scotia, qui sibi tantum authoritatis vendicant, ut velint penes se esse rescindere & refigere statuta, & constitutiones civiles, sine ulla intercessione, aut provocatione ad judicem civilem: verba sunt prolata & lata in conventu Edimburgensi anno 1570.
units.tr: The defenders of the purer reformation in Scotland speak in the same way; they claim for themselves so much authority that they wish to be able to annul and make new statutes and civil constitutions on their own, without any intervention or appeal to a civil judge. These words were uttered and passed at the Edinburgh assembly in the year 1570.

units.la: Nuperus liber cui nomen, Nephtali Jehovah Scama affirmat Ecclesiam donatam natam natam à Deo potestate completa, cognoscendi de negotiis Ecclesiasticis, statuendi, decernendi absque appellatione ad Magistratum.
units.tr: A recent book, entitled Nephtali Jehovah Scama, affirms that the Church has been given by God, from birth, complete power to examine ecclesiastical matters, to legislate and to decree, without appeal to the magistrate.

units.la: Sed si quicquam astruit futilitatem potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, illud sanè est, quod ejus vindices mille modos, mille distinctiones, mille divisiones cudant quibus se tueantur, adversus eversores istius potestatis Chimericæ; aiunt dari potestatem Ecclesiasticam, persectam, imperfectam; proprie dictam, improprie dictam, internam, externam, intrinsecam, extrinsecam, declarativam, coactivam, privativam, cumulativam, imperativam, executivam, constitutivam, auxiliarem, destructivam, elicitivam, directivam, authoritativam, objectivam, formalem ratione objecti, & formalem ratione modi illam exercendi. Rogatus Gillespy Scotus, quænam esset potestas Magistratus circa sacra, & de ea re aliquid statueret, Respondit Conferre Magistratum potestatem suam ad promovendum Christi regnum, non perfectè, sed imperfectè. Pro tanto, non omni modo, sed more suo; non intrinsecè, sed extrinsecè; secè, non primariò, sed secundariò; non directè sed per consequentiam: non sub formalitate scandali, sed sub formalitate criminis.
units.tr: But if anything proves the emptiness of ecclesiastical power, it is surely this: that its defenders coin a thousand modes, a thousand distinctions, a thousand divisions with which to protect themselves against the subverters of that chimerical power. They say that there is ecclesiastical power perfect and imperfect; properly so called and improperly so called; internal, external, intrinsic, extrinsic, declarative, coercive, privative, cumulative, imperative, executive, constitutive, auxiliary, destructive, elicitive, directive, authoritative, objective, formal in respect of its object, and formal in respect of the mode of exercising it. When the Scot Gillespie was asked what the power of the magistrate in sacred matters was, and was pressed to state something about it, he replied: the magistrate contributes his power to advancing Christ's kingdom, not perfectly but imperfectly; so far, not in every way but in his own way; not intrinsically but extrinsically; secondarily, not primarily; not directly but by consequence; not under the formality of scandal but under the formality of crime.

units.la: Non alio, inquam, evidentiori argumento fatilitas, fraus & mendacium potestatis Ecclesiasticæ demonstrantur, quam quod ad eam fustinendam tot tibicines, aut potius tot festucas distinctionum, & divisionum, sed revera evasionum adhibeant, muribus similes, qui in intricatis locis, inter scamna & scabella fallunt prensantem, sed in aperto facilè comprehenduntur, aut vulpibus, quæ foveas variis foraminibus pervias fodiunt, ut sint tot effugia. Nam id in more habent Jesuitæ cum suarum Puparum venerationem probant populis adversus Scripturæ & rationis lumina, solentque ad hunc modum confugere ad anchoram effugiorum, ut eludant Protestantium argumenta. Dicunt dari adorationem latriæ, duliæ, hyperduliæ, directam, indirectam, reductivam, analogicam, absolutam, secundum quid: quocirca tam aptè potestas Ecclesiastica, mysterium indigitatur quàm congruè Athenæus vocavit, illa murium foramina quo se proripiunt, mysteria.
units.tr: I say that by no other more evident argument are the flimsiness, the fraud and the falsehood of ecclesiastical power shown than by the fact that to sustain it they bring in so many flute-players, or rather so many straws of distinctions and divisions, which are in truth mere evasions: like mice, which in tangled places escape the one who grasps at them among the stools and footstools, but are easily caught in the open; or like foxes, which dig holes with many openings so that they have many means of escape. For this is the habit of the Jesuits when they commend the veneration of their idols to the people against the light of Scripture and reason, and they are accustomed to take refuge in this way at the anchor of evasions, so as to elude the arguments of the Protestants. They say there is a worship of latria, of dulia, of hyperdulia; direct, indirect, reductive, analogical, absolute, relative. Therefore, as aptly as Athenaeus called those mouse-holes into which they dart away "mysteries," so ecclesiastical power is designated a "mystery" with equal fitness.

units.la: Nec imbellis est machina, per quam verberatur, imo diruitur Potestas Ecclesiastica, quod ejus vindices nondum diserte & explicitè definiverint. 1. Quid sit potestas Ecclesiastica? 2. Quid differat, cum à potestate verbi agentis in corda per ministerium Evangelicum, tum ab illa potestate, quæ præest humano ordini, seu externis &ἀδιαφόροις ordinandis. 3. Quid sit Excommunicatio? 4. An eadem sit atque traditio satanæ. 5. An qui in Ecclesia privata præsunt humano ordini debent esse iidem homines, an verò alii ab illis qui vacant verbo & orationi. 6. Quis modus potestatis tribuendus est illis qui præsunt humano ordini, in Ecclesia particulari, tum in nationali. 7. Quis modus potestatis tribuendus est Synodis nationalibus. 8. An jure divino detur Ecclesia nationalis. 9. An jure divino ponendum est tribunal Ecclesiasticum, seu concilium nationale distinctum à politico confessu nationali, quorum illud tam ordinet cum summo imperio res Ecclesiasticas, quam hic res civiles & politicas, & in quibus non detur provocatio ab uno ad alterum. 10. An qui præsunt humano ordini non sunt perinde custodes Evangelii, atque utriusque tabulæ Decalogi. Sanè via est plana & expeditissima eversoribus potestatis Ecclesiasticæ; at impeditissima & senticcetis aspera ejusdem assertoribus ad enodendas hasce quæstiones, ut nequeat ab his via complanari, nisi per stratum tessulatum potestate elicitiva, cumulativa, destructiva &c. Nam nec ipsi mystæ sibi constant.: diversis diversa, imo uno homine diversa sentientibus, & orsa à se detexente. Exemplo mihi sint Angli Presbyteriani in sua confessione fidei cap. 1. artic. 6, & capite 30. primo loco dicunt in Ecclesia duas potestates se exerere: unam verbi, per quam homines perducuntur ad fidem, & inde ad salutem; alteram quæ communis est omnibus societatibus, per quam de circumstantiis & externis circa cultum & regimen Ecclesiæ statuitur: at posteriori loco dant nobis potestatem mediam, & volunt regimen Ecclesiasticum circa illa externa distinctum esse à civili seu politico.
units.tr: Nor is the machine by which the Ecclesiastical Power is battered, indeed overthrown, a feeble one, because its defenders have not yet clearly and explicitly defined: (1) what the Ecclesiastical Power is; (2) how it differs, on the one hand, from the power of the Word working in hearts through the Evangelical ministry, and, on the other, from that power which presides over human order, that is, over external indifferent things [ἀδιαφόροις] that are to be ordered; (3) what excommunication is; (4) whether it is the same as delivering someone over to Satan; (5) whether those who preside over human order in the Church must be the same men, or rather other men than those who devote themselves to the Word and prayer; (6) what measure of power is to be granted to those who preside over human order, both in the particular Church and in the national Church; (7) what measure of power is to be granted to national synods; (8) whether a national Church is given by divine right; (9) whether an ecclesiastical tribunal, or a national council distinct from the political national assembly, must be established by divine right, one which would govern ecclesiastical affairs with supreme authority just as the civil assembly governs civil and political affairs, and from which there is no appeal from one to the other; (10) whether those who preside over human order are not equally guardians of the Gospel and of both tables of the Decalogue. Certainly the road is smooth and very easy for the overthrowers of the Ecclesiastical Power, but for its champions it is most obstructed and rough with thorns in working through these questions, so that the way cannot be levelled by them except over a mosaic pavement of an elicitive, cumulative, destructive power, and so on. For the initiates themselves do not agree with one another: they hold different views, indeed one and the same man holds different views, and he unravels what he himself has begun. Let the English Presbyterians serve as an example to me, in their Confession of Faith, chapter 1, article 6, and chapter 30. In the first place they say that two powers operate in the Church: one of the Word, by which men are brought to faith and from there to salvation; the other, which is common to all societies, by which decisions are made about the circumstances and externals of worship and the government of the Church. But in the second place they give us a middle power, and they wish the ecclesiastical government in respect of those external matters to be distinct from the civil or political government.

units.la: Atque hactenus, vir Clarissime, conficitur quam inficeta sit potestas Ecclesiastica, quæ instar cinguli ex corio ductili, elongatur & coarctatur, assumitur & deponitur, pro sua cuiquc utilitate & prout conducit : quæque ad rationes humanas, non Divinas accomodatur, & cui nulla accedit authoritas, præterquam ab injusta occupatione juris alieni, per mendacia, fraudes & imposturas, non quidem virorum sanctorum, qui eam arripuerunt cæco judicio, & quia sic mos est; sed quorumdam malè animatorum qui cæteros in fraudem illiciunt, specie pacis, pietatis & juris Divini. Cæterum pietate & reverentiâ viri impedior, quominus veteranum illum bellorum Domini Militem Gisbertum, Voetium eruditione & ætate venerandum, qui in me nuper acrius invectus est, ascribam numero illorum, qui potestate suâ Ecclesiastica fucum faciunt, sed eorum, qui præjudiciis excæcati nequeunt se expedire laqueis, nec liberare tyrannidè præjudiciorum & erroris altè imbibiti, sed qui speciè veritatis, & propter antiquitatem suam imponit. Vale.
units.tr: Thus far, most distinguished sir, it is established how flimsy the Ecclesiastical Power is: like a belt of pliable leather, it is lengthened and shortened, taken up and laid down, according to each man's advantage and as it suits him. It is adapted to human reasons, not divine ones, and no authority attaches to it except that which comes from an unjust seizure of another's right, through lies, frauds and impostures. These are not the doing of holy men, who have seized it by blind judgement and because that is the custom, but of certain ill-disposed men who draw the rest into deceit under the pretext of peace, piety and divine right. Yet out of piety and reverence for him I am prevented from counting among those who play the trickster with their ecclesiastical power that veteran soldier of the Lord's wars, Gisbertus Voetius, venerable for his learning and age, who lately attacked me more sharply. Rather I count him among those who, blinded by prejudices, cannot extricate themselves from the snares, nor free themselves from the tyranny of prejudices and error deeply soaked in; who are imposed upon by the appearance of truth and by their own antiquity. Farewell.

units.la: JE n'eu pas si toft achevé mes Lettres, que je me mis à remuer un amas de vieux imprimez, entre lesquels je jettay la veüe sur dés ordonnances de Guillaume Prince d'Orange publiées en Flaman en l'An 1583. & traduites en François par Daniel de Niele, Ministre de la Parole de Dieu, Pasteur de l'Eglise Françoise de Middlebourgh : En l'An 1599. ces ordonnances, qui sont de deux feüilles, font voir clairement que l'establissement de la Reformation dans les Provinces, detachées de l'Empire de Philippe Second, n'a pas commencé par la construction d'une collateralité de Jurisdictions & de Tribunaus, de la maniere que Calvin l'establit dans Geneve, & qu'encore qu'on embrassast la Reformation, quant à la Doctrine, on ne receut pas pourtant la puissance Ecclesiastique.
units.tr: I had not yet quite finished my letters when I began to rummage through a heap of old printed matter, among which my eye fell upon the ordinances of William, Prince of Orange, published in Flemish in the year 1583 and translated into French by Daniel de Niele, minister of the Word of God and pastor of the French Church of Middelburg, in the year 1599. These ordinances, which are two sheets long, clearly show that the establishment of the Reformation in the Provinces detached from the Empire of Philip II did not begin with the construction of a collateral system of jurisdictions and tribunals, in the manner in which Calvin established it at Geneva. Even though they embraced the Reformation as to doctrine, they did not receive the ecclesiastical power.

units.la: La matiere de ces ordonnances estoit touchant les Assemblées des Papistes, les Marriages, l'observation du jour du Dimanche, l'interdiction des Livres, des Chansons & des Vers impudiques, les Maisons de débauches; & touchant la regle du Culte, & des mœurs des particuliers. Dans ces Reglements il est parlé d'une maniere bien differente des Ministres, & de leurs Consistoires; & des Estats du Pays: Car le Prince declare, qu'à l'egard de ceux-cy, il ne publie & n'ordonne aucune chose que par leur avis; au lieu qu'il ordonne & commande à ceux-là de prester la main à l'execution de ses ordonnances, comme il feroit à des Officiers de Justice. Et c'eft de cette maniere que ce grand & fage Prince en a agi depuis l'Annêe 1572. jufqu'à 1584. (qui fut le tems de fon Gouvernement) dans toutes les Provinces Confederées; Et c'eft encore de cette maniere, qu'en agirent les Magiltrats Reformez, non feulement à Geneve avant que Calvin y euft une demeure fixe, mais auffi dans les Cantons des Suiffes : Chez qui on ne parla point de puissance Ecclefiastique distincte de la Civile, durant l'espace de vingt ans, comme aussi ces Cantons n'en eurent aucun usage tout le tems de la vie de Calvin, mais seulement lors que sa grande reputation eust gagné sur les esprits des Ecclesiastiques ; & celles-cy sur les esprits des Magistrats, de se conformer à l'institution que Calvin avoit faitte d'abord qu'il arriva à Geneve pour la seconde foix, & d'etablir dans un mesme territoire deux tribunaus independans l'un de l'autre. Les villes imperiales, sur tout Strazbourg, se conformerent à la tablature de Calvin. Le Prince Palatin du Rhin, n'y voulut pas entendre, durant plulieurs années : Eraltus en ayant fait voir la vanité & la nullité.
units.tr: The subject matter of these ordinances concerned the assemblies of the Papists, marriages, the observance of the Lord's Day, the prohibition of books, songs and impure verses, houses of debauchery, and the rule of worship and the morals of individuals. In these regulations the ministers and their consistories are spoken of in a very different way, and so are the States of the country. For the Prince declares that, as regards the latter, he publishes and ordains nothing except with their advice; whereas to the former he orders and commands that they lend a hand in carrying out his ordinances, as he would to officers of justice. This is the way in which this great and wise Prince acted from the year 1572 to 1584 (which was the period of his government) in all the Confederate Provinces. And it is also the way in which the reformed magistrates acted, not only at Geneva before Calvin had a fixed residence there, but also in the cantons of the Swiss, among whom for the space of twenty years nothing was said of an ecclesiastical power distinct from the civil one. Likewise these cantons made no use of it during the whole of Calvin's life, but only when his great reputation had gained ground over the minds of the churchmen, and theirs over the minds of the magistrates, so that they conformed to the institution Calvin had made as soon as he arrived at Geneva for the second time, namely, to set up two tribunals independent of each other in one and the same territory. The imperial cities, above all Strasbourg, conformed to Calvin's ordinance. The Palatine Prince of the Rhine would not listen to it for several years, Erastus having shown its vanity and nullity.

units.la: Mais la mort, du Prince d'Orange qui fuit assassiné l'an 1584. & la grande jeunesse du Prince Maurice son fils & son successeur, donnerent belle prise aux Pasteurs, & aux assemblées Ecclesiastiques des pays bas de se former une Puissance, qui alloit du pair avec celle du Magistrat ; & on ne pust s'ops'opposer à la faction de Barnavel, qui estoit celle d'Arminius, & qui depoüilloit l'Eglife de toute authorité, au reglement des affaires de Religion, pour la faire reposer fur le Magistrat, sans exalter l'authorité des Pasteurs & celle des synodes : dont la jurisdiction Ecclesiastique estoit autant raisonnable, & vraye dans l'estime du Prince d'Orange, & du menu peuple, que les cinq points en debat leur sembloient Orthodoxes : comme d'ailleurs les mesmes ne doutoient point, que ceux qui erroient en matiere de foy, n'errassent aussi dans leur entreprise de bannir du monde la puissance Ecclefiastique, & d'en faire une puissance chimerique. Car c'est pour cette raison, & sur ce pied, que la puissance Ecclesiastique doit autant lever la teste dans les Pays bas, que la puissance du Magistrat dans les choses sacrées, & la doctrine des Arminiens doivent estre humiliées. Comme si la doctrine de Calvin, & la Puissance Ecclesiastique, devoient aller toujours raisonnablement de compagnie, & que l'une ne pouvoit estre bonne & vraye, à moins que l'autre ne le fust. En fin il est evident que cette puissance chimerique n'a esté introduite dans les pays bas, que par l'oppofition de la doctrine de Calvin à celle d'Arminius, & que fi le party de Barnavel n'eust jamais paru, la puiffance des Pasteurs & des Synodes, fust demourée bornée comme elle l'estoit du tems du Prince d'Orange. De forte que voila la Puiffance Ecclesiastique baitie fur de faux prejugez, & fur cette fauffe maxime, que celuy qui est erronné en un point, comme estoit Arminius au regard des cinq points en debat, le doit aussi estre au regard de son autre sentiment, qui depouille les Pasteurs & les Synodes de l'authorité de regler souverainement les affaires de religion pour en revestir le Magistrat.
units.tr: But the death of the Prince of Orange, who was assassinated in the year 1584, and the great youth of Prince Maurice, his son and successor, gave the pastors and the ecclesiastical assemblies of the Low Countries a fine opportunity to form a power that would go on a par with that of the magistrate. And they could not oppose the faction of Barneveldt, which was that of Arminius, and which stripped the Church of all authority in regulating religious affairs in order to rest it upon the magistrate, without exalting the authority of the pastors and of the synods. Their ecclesiastical jurisdiction seemed as reasonable and true in the estimation of the Prince of Orange and of the common people as the five points in dispute seemed to them orthodox. Likewise these same men had no doubt that those who erred in matters of faith were also erring in their enterprise of banishing ecclesiastical power from the world and making it a chimerical power. For it is for this reason, and on this footing, that the ecclesiastical power must lift its head as much in the Low Countries as the power of the magistrate in sacred matters, and that the doctrine of the Arminians must be humbled. As if the doctrine of Calvin and the Ecclesiastical Power were bound always to go reasonably together, and one could not be good and true unless the other were too. In the end it is evident that this chimerical power was introduced into the Low Countries only by the opposition of Calvin's doctrine to that of Arminius, and that if the party of Barneveldt had never appeared, the power of the pastors and synods would have remained limited as it was in the time of the Prince of Orange. So the Ecclesiastical Power is built upon false prejudices and upon this false maxim: that whoever is wrong on one point, as Arminius was with regard to the five points in dispute, must also be wrong with regard to his other opinion, which strips the pastors and synods of the authority to govern religious affairs sovereignly in order to clothe the magistrate with it.

units.la: En Angleterre on retint la doctrine de Calvin, mais on forma la collateralité de juridiétions sur le modele de Rome, excepté qu'on osta de dessus la teste du Pape, la charge de gouverneur en chef de l'Eglife Anglicane, pour la faire reposer sur la teste du Roy ; ce qui estoit en effect reunir cette collateralité de juridictions. Mais cette collateralité fut retenüe en France parmi nos Eglises, non seulement à l'imitation du modele de Calvin ; mais aussi par un pure necessité où on se trouvoit, & qui les empechoit d'evoquer leurs causes aux cours civiles, acause de la contrarieté de religions. Neanmoins les pasteurs tirerent de cette necessité la vertu des clefs, & le pouvoir de lier & de delier, & cette loy perpetuelle, & ce droit pretendu Divin : que les Pasteurs & & les Eglises reccuillies, ou sous un Magistrat contraire à leur religion, ou sous un qui la favorise, devoient se gouverner independemment, ou de l'inspection, ou des commandemens de leur Souverain : car cette necessité dont je parle les a jettez dans ce sentiment, que ce n'est pas le fait, ni le droit des Puissances seculieres, de regler par un jugement souverain, qui est le Judicium Imperii, les matieres de religion dans ses Estats : Mais que ce droit appartient aux Pasteurs & aux Synodes. Et voila la puissance Ecclesiastique de nos Eglises, bastie sur des prejugez aussi faux & auffi mal fondez, que ceux que les Pasteurs & les Synodes en Hollande se sont figurez.
units.tr: In England the doctrine of Calvin was retained, but the collateral jurisdictions were formed on the model of Rome, except that the office of chief governor of the Anglican Church was taken from the Pope's head and placed on the King's head, which in effect reunited this collateral jurisdiction. In France, however, this collateral jurisdiction was retained among our Churches, not only in imitation of Calvin's model but also out of sheer necessity, which prevented them from referring their causes to the civil courts because of the difference of religion. Nevertheless the pastors drew from this necessity the power of the keys, the power to bind and to loose, and this perpetual law and supposed divine right: that the pastors and the gathered churches, whether under a magistrate opposed to their religion or under one who favours it, ought to govern themselves independently, either of his oversight or of his commands. For this necessity I speak of has thrown them into the opinion that it is not the business or the right of secular powers to regulate matters of religion within their states by a sovereign judgment, which is the Judicium Imperii, but that this right belongs to the pastors and the synods. And so the ecclesiastical power of our churches is built on prejudices as false and as ill-founded as those the pastors and synods in Holland have imagined.

units.la: Car c'est là un pur galimatias, & une imagination creuse d'etablir deux juridictions Souveraines collaterales & independantes l'une de l'autre dans un mesme territoire. Musculus s'en moque plaisamment, & dit que c'est s'imaginer un corps à deux testes.
