Et pourtant les Independans disent assez raisonnablement que presupposant plusieurs familles, & plusieurs Eglises particulieres dans un mesme territoire, il n'y a non plus d'incompatibilité entr' elles, ou avec la paix publique, si celles cy se gouvernent chacune à sa fantasie, que si celles là en font autant. Mais que c'est une chose inconcevable, & une extravagance du pays d'Eutopie d'establir dans un mesme Estat une collateralité de gouvernemens nationaus, & de tribunaus souverains.
units.tr: For this is pure nonsense, and an empty fancy, to establish two sovereign jurisdictions, collateral and independent of each other, in one and the same territory. Musculus mocks it pleasantly and says it is to imagine a body with two heads. The Independents therefore say, quite reasonably, that if we presuppose several families and several particular churches in one territory, there is no more incompatibility between them, or with public peace, if these govern each as it pleases, than if those do the same. But to establish in one and the same state a collateral government of national bodies and sovereign tribunals is an inconceivable thing, an extravagance worthy of the land of Utopia.

units.la: Mais je veux icy' toucher au doigt une maladie de tous les siecles, & qui n'est pas guerillable, que dans le ames tout à fait degagées des interests mondains, & depouillées de cette preoccupation, & de cette perfuafion, dont ils font prevenus. Et cette maladie eft d'autant plus incurable, qu'elle eft hereditaire, parce qu'elle a paffé des plus doctes, & des plus eclairez des premiers tems à ceux des derniers, qui ne leur font point inferieurs, ni en fcavoir, ni en belles lumieres. C'eft que ceux qui font dans une erreur de plufieurs fiecles, comme eft la religion de Rome, l'opinion d'une Puiffance Ecclefiaftique diftinête de celle du Magiftrat, & de la puiffance de la parole fur les cœurs, & l'opinion qu'il n'y a point d'Antipodes, croient acaufe de cette longue prefcription eftre dans la poffeffion du bon fens, & de la raifon: au lieu que fi l'opinion touchant ces matieres eftoit de nouvelle date, ils là mettroient comme je fai entre les reveries de l'Alcoran:
units.tr: But I want here to touch with the finger a sickness of all ages, one that cannot be cured in minds wholly freed from worldly interests and stripped of that preoccupation and persuasion with which they are prejudiced. This sickness is all the more incurable because it is hereditary: it has passed from the most learned and enlightened men of earlier times to those of later times, who are in no way inferior to them, either in learning or in brilliance of mind. Those who are in an error of several centuries, such as the religion of Rome, the opinion of an ecclesiastical power distinct from that of the magistrate and from the power of the word over hearts, and the opinion that there are no antipodes, believe, because of this long prescription, that they are in possession of good sense and reason. Yet if the opinion on these matters were of recent date, they would place it, as I know, among the dreams of the Koran.

units.la: Car certes, comme je ne doutepoint qu'un Evefque de Condom, & un Arnauld ne priffent la Tranfubftantiation, le purgatoire, le culte des images, le fervice Divin en la langue que le peuple n'entend pas pour des doétrines & des practiques impies & ridicules, si elles estoient nouvelles; & que d'ailleurs elles ne soient aujourd'huy dans leur estime des doctrines & des prattiques Divines, excellentes & raisonnables, pour cette seule raison qu'elles ont esté receües depuis plusieurs siecles dans l'Eglise Romaine : Je croy que l'on doit faire le mesme jugement de tant de grands hommes du party reformé des deux derniers siecles, entr' autres de Calvin, Beze Monsieur Diodati, Bochart, Amyraut, Daillé, de Langle, Monsieur Claude, Monsieur de Primerose, Monsieur Jurieu (car je ne mets pas de ce nombre Martyr, Bullinger, Muscul-us, Vedelius, Rivet) & assurer qu'ils ont en grande veneration la puissance Ecclesiastique, & son excommunication acause de leur antiquité, & pour avoir commencé des le tems de St. Paul avec le mystere d'iniquité, & que d'ailleurs ils les prendroient pour des illusions, & des impostures si elles estoient encore plus nouvelles qu'aucune des doctrines de Rome.
units.tr: For certainly, just as I do not doubt that a Bishop of Condom and an Arnauld would regard transubstantiation, purgatory, the worship of images, and divine service in a language the people do not understand as impious and ridiculous doctrines and practices if they were new; and that, on the other hand, they now esteem these as divine, excellent and reasonable doctrines and practices for the sole reason that they have been received for several centuries in the Roman Church: so I believe one must make the same judgment of the many great men of the reformed party of the last two centuries, among them Calvin, Beza, Monsieur Diodati, Bochart, Amyraut, Daillé, de Langle, Monsieur Claude, Monsieur de Primerose, and Monsieur Jurieu (for I do not count Martyr, Bullinger, Musculus, Vedelius and Rivet among this number). They hold ecclesiastical power and its excommunication in great veneration because of their antiquity, and because they began from the time of St Paul with the mystery of iniquity; and moreover, they would take them for illusions and impostures if they were even newer than any of the doctrines of Rome.

units.la: Mais la principale chose que j'ay eu en veüe, dans celle que j'ay jettée sur ces ordonnances du Prince d'Orange, c'est qu'elles sont une confirmation bien expresse des propositions de Maccovius sur tout de la troisieme, & font voir clairement.
units.tr: But the principal thing I had in view, in what I have written on these ordinances of the Prince of Orange, is that they are a very express confirmation of the propositions of Maccovius, above all of the third, and make clearly evident:

units.la: 1. Que la Puissance Ecclesiastique des Pasteurs & des Anciens assemblez en consistoires, Colloques & Synodes, est une puissance chimerique, tant pour estre nommée Ecclesiastique, que parce que ce n'est une juridiction que de nom, à moins que leurs declarations ne recoivent leur force & vigueur des ordonnances de la puissance seculiere.
units.tr: (1) That the ecclesiastical power of the pastors and elders assembled in consistories, colloquies and synods is a chimerical power, both because it is called ecclesiastical and because it is a jurisdiction in name only, unless their declarations receive their force and vigour from the ordinances of the secular power.

units.la: 2. Que leurs canons ou reglemens ne sont que de pures & de simples declarations de sentiment, des conseils & des avis, avant qu'ils ayent receu la force, & la sanction de loix & d'ordonnances, par celle du souverain Magistrat.
units.tr: (2) That their canons or regulations are only pure and simple declarations of opinion, counsels and advice, until they have received the force and sanction of laws and ordinances from the sovereign magistrate.

units.la: 3. Que le Souverain, n'est, nine se tient pas obligé de ratifier, bien-moins de suivre leurs jugemens, par un jugemens aveugle, & sans avoir la liberté, ou de les examiner, ou de les changer, ou mesme de n'y avoir aucun egard.
units.tr: (3) That the sovereign is not, and does not hold himself obliged, to ratify, much less to follow, their judgments with blind obedience, and without having the liberty either to examine them, or to change them, or even to pay them no regard at all.

units.la: 4. Que là où il s'agit d'etablir une discipline Ecclesiastique dans une nation entiere, d'en commander la pratique, & apres qu'elle est etablie, de la casser, d'en changer, alterer, ou corriger les inconvenians, les erreurs, & les abus : d'infliger des peines & des censures Ecclesiastiques à ceux qui y contreviennent : le Magistrat n'est, ni ne se tient point obligé de suivre ou mesme de prendre l'avis, ou des Ministres de l'Evangile, ou mesme des Consistoires.
units.tr: (4) That where it is a matter of establishing an ecclesiastical discipline in an entire nation, of commanding its practice, and, once it is established, of annulling it, changing, altering or correcting its inconveniences, errors and abuses, and of inflicting penalties and ecclesiastical censures on those who contravene it, the magistrate is not, and does not hold himself, obliged to follow, or even to take the advice, either of the ministers of the Gospel or even of the consistories.

units.la: 5. Que dans les ordonnances qu'il fait touchant des matieres purement Ecclesiastiques, il ne considere pas les Synodes, ni les consistoires, ni mesme les Ministres & Pasteurs des Eglises, que comme des executeurs de ses commandemens.
units.tr: (5) That in the ordinances he makes concerning purely ecclesiastical matters, he regards the synods, the consistories, or even the ministers and pastors of the churches, only as executors of his commands.

units.la: Ces considerations qui detruisent la Puissance Ecclesiastique, ou du moins qui ranversent un tribunal dans l'Eglise independamment du Magistrat en vertu des clefs mises entre les mains des Ministres de la parole de Dieu, & non entre celles du Magistrat, sont d'une verité si incontestable, que mesme les plus rigides defenseurs de cette puissance Ecclesiastique sont contrains d'en enerver toute la force. C'est ce qui paroît par le discours que Monsieur Jurieu me tint il n'y a pas long tems.
units.tr: These considerations, which destroy ecclesiastical power, or at least overturn a tribunal in the Church independent of the magistrate by virtue of the keys placed in the hands of the ministers of God's Word and not in those of the magistrate, are so incontestably true that even the most rigid defenders of this ecclesiastical power are forced to weaken all its force. This is clear from the discourse that Monsieur Jurieu held with me not long ago.

units.la: Je vous envoye le recueil des actes solennels, qui Je sont faits de ma part en mes inaugurations & promotions. Vous y trouverez entr' autres une dispute de potestate Clavium : la matiere m'en a esté donnée par l'Academie, apparamment afin que je fisse voir, quel estoit mon sentiment, & que je me purgeasse du soupcon, qu'on auroit pû avoir qu'estant vostre neveu, je n'eusse vos opinions. C'est pourquoy je n'ay pas pû m'empecher de me declarer la dessus : Cependant je l'ay fait sobrement, modestement, & mesme en vous suivant, autant qu'il m'a esté possible. Car comme vous je mets le principal usage des clefs, In administratione verbi & sacramentorum, Et je ne m'oppose point à ce qu'on face la Juridiction Ecclesiastique subordonnée à la civile, dans les lieux, où le Magistrat est non seulement Chrestien, mais entierement Orthodoxe. Il n'estoit pas necessaire, qu'il se purgeast envers ceux de son Academie, pour la raison qu'il allegue : car au contraire cette parenté de neveu, frere & coufin, leur devoit eftre un fort prejugé qu'il n'estoit pas de mes sentimens. Au reste Monsieur je vous laisse à faire un commentaire, & des reflexions sur ce discours, où sans doute vous comprendrez qu'il fait les trois quarts du chemin vers mes hypotheses, & vous y remarquerez l'accomplissement de la prediction de vostre bon ami Monsieur de Vauquelin, Tandem tua causa triumphabit.
units.tr: I am sending you the collection of solemn acts that I performed at my inaugurations and promotions. You will find there, among others, a disputation de potestate Clavium: the subject was given to me by the Academy, apparently so that I might show what my opinion was and clear myself of the suspicion that might have arisen, since I am your nephew, that I did not hold your opinions. That is why I could not keep myself from declaring my position on this point. Yet I did so soberly and modestly, and even following you as far as I could. For like you I place the principal use of the keys In administratione verbi & sacramentorum (in the administration of the Word and the sacraments). And I do not object to making ecclesiastical jurisdiction subordinate to the civil in places where the magistrate is not only Christian but entirely orthodox. He did not need to justify himself to those of his Academy on the ground he alleges. On the contrary, this relationship of nephew, brother and cousin ought to have been a strong presumption to them that he did not share my views. Moreover, Sir, I leave it to you to make a commentary and reflections on this discourse, in which, no doubt, you will understand that he goes three quarters of the way towards my hypotheses, and you will notice in it the fulfilment of the prediction of your good friend Monsieur de Vauquelin: At last your cause will triumph.

units.la: Triumphabit sanè ad casum Potestatis Ecclefiasticæ. Nam illa erit nomine tenus potestas, ligandi & solvendi, hoc est excommunicatione innodandi & absolutione enodandi, quæ pro conditione temporum & Magistratuum sub quibus pastores vivunt, naturam mutat : nam potestatis maritalis, Paternæ, par & idem jus est Divinum, ubicunque locorum, & sub quo-
units.tr: Certainly it will triumph, to the ruin of ecclesiastical power. For that will be power only in name, of binding and loosing, that is, of binding by excommunication and loosing by absolution, which, according to the condition of the times and of the magistrates under whom the pastors live, changes its nature. For marital and paternal power have the same and equal divine right wherever they exist and under whichever

units.la: quocunque demum Magistratu seu Christiano, seu Ethnico, seu Pontificio, seu Reformato. At non sic de Potestate Ecclesiastica; cujus censurae sub Magistratu infenso sunt in cælis ratæ, at sub amico & Orthodoxo non ulterius quam quatenus ab eo probantur: sed an mancipatus Satanæ per excommunicationem, potest solvi à Magistratu, à quo abjudicatur potestas ligandi & solvendi.
units.tr: magistrate, whether Christian, pagan, Papist or Reformed. But it is not so with ecclesiastical power: its censures under a hostile magistrate are ratified in heaven, but under a friendly and orthodox one they are valid no further than he approves them. Yet can one who has been delivered to Satan by excommunication be loosed by the magistrate, from whom the power of binding and loosing has been taken away?

units.la: Sed si ratio recte putatur, par validitas censurarum Ecclesiasticarum sub Magistratu, seu infenso & heterodoxo, seu amico & orthodoxo. Utrobique etiam viget vera potestas ligandi & solvendi, nec vultum mutat aut naturam pro ratione Magistratuum locorum & temporum: nam ubi lex & Magistratus deficiunt, eorum locum supplet disciplina confœderata, ut nullus fit locus potestati Ecclesiasticæ, nec opus sit in usu potestatis alicujus retinendæ in Ecclesia & exerendæ, recurrere sub Magistratu infenso ad claves regni cælorum & potestatem ligandi & solvendi, at sub amico, ad civilem: quo nihil absurdius fingi potest. Certè potestas illa, seu clavium, seu ligandi & solvendi, si ad regimen externum extendi debet, quod tamen non credo: non alio modo se exercebat Sedani sub Principe Bullionæo Orthodoxo & amico, atque sub Rege: utrobique vigebat in Ecclefia Sedanensi Magistratura, vel confœderata & assumpta per communem consensum sub Rege, vel delegata à Principe Sedanensi.
units.tr: But if the matter is rightly judged, the validity of ecclesiastical censures is equal under a magistrate who is either hostile and heterodox or friendly and orthodox. In both cases the true power of binding and loosing is in force, nor does it change its face or nature according to the character of magistrates and the circumstances of places and times. For where law and magistrate are lacking, the confederated discipline supplies their place, so that there is no room for ecclesiastical power, and there is no need, in order to retain and exercise some power in the Church, to have recourse under a hostile magistrate to the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of binding and loosing, but under a friendly one to the civil power; nothing more absurd can be imagined. Certainly that power, whether of the keys or of binding and loosing, if it ought to extend to external government (which, however, I do not believe), was not exercised otherwise at Sedan under the orthodox and friendly Prince de Bouillon than under the King. In both cases there was a magistracy in the Church of Sedan, either confederated and assumed by common consent under the King, or delegated by the Prince of Sedan.

units.la: VOus pouvez aussi remarquer, Mr. que ce n'est pas faute d'Esprit ni de scavoir en ce professeur de Sedan, non plus qu'en Mr. de la Bastide dans ses prises avec l'Evêque de Condom, & dans la défense qu'il a entreprife, d'un tribunal Ecclésiastique parmi nos Eglises par un droit Divin, ce n'est pas, dis-je, faute ou d'esprit ou de scavoir, ni en Mr. de la Bastide, ni en Mr. Jurieu, qu'ils se servent des mesmes desfaites, plûtost que de ne rien dire en faveur de leur puissance chimérique, mais c'est un défaut de bonne cause. je rends graces à Dieu que depuis 20 ans, que je traitte de ces matieres, j'ay toujours rendu le mal pour le bien : Je n'ay parlé de ceux qui m'estoient contraires qu'avec tout respect & honneur ; au lieu, que la plûpart d'entr' eux, ou m'ont dit des injures, ou m'ont mis entre les deraisonnables. Je n'use point de deffaites, & je ne mets point en œuvre des illusions de distinctions de puissance élicitive, cumulative, destructive, auxiliaire. Je n'impute à personne des opinions qu'il ne croit pas, de la maniere qu'on m'a toujours traitté, & dont le grand Mr. Claude ne se peut entierement excuser : comme lors qu'il m'accuse de mettre entre les mains du Magistrat, les clefs du royaume des cieux : la verité que je soûttien ressemble à un cube, elle ne peut estre renversée, & on ne peut empêcher qu'elle n'ait une assiette ferme. Mes hypotheses touchant les clefs, la puissance de lier, & de délier, celle des Pasteurs & des Synodes : la nature de l'Eglise, & de l'ordination sont claires, nues; elles n'ont point de détours : Elles sont toujours les mesT mes, & ne changent point selon les tems, les lieus & les Magistrats, sous lesquels les Eglises sont recueillies, & elles attaquent Rome, son Pape, son Eglise & sa Religion, bien autrement vigoureusement, que ne fait la voye que nos docteurs ont prise, depuis 150 ans, le chemin que je prens est incomparablement plus court, & plus efficace, parce que comme je renferme toutes les controverses entre Rome, & nous dans ma sixiéme maxime, que vous pourrez lire dans la Lettre que j'ecris à Monsieur Merlat, & qui n'est que de quattre ou cinq lignes, tout ce que nos docteurs auront à faire à l'avenir sera, non de la refuter, car elle est tres-vraye, mais d'en faire voir, & comprendre la vérité aux Rois, & aux Magistrats; certes si Dieu mettoit au cœur de nos Docteurs d'insister sur cette maxime, Ils verroient bien-toft la fin de l'Eglise Romaine, & conséquemment la fin de toutes nos controverses.
units.tr: You may also notice, Sir, that it is not for lack of wit or learning in this professor of Sedan, any more than in Monsieur de la Bastide in his disputes with the Bishop of Condom and in the defence he has undertaken of an ecclesiastical tribunal among our churches by divine right, that they resort to the same evasions rather than say nothing in favour of their chimerical power. It is, I say, not for lack of wit or learning, either in Monsieur de la Bastide or in Monsieur Jurieu, but a defect of a good cause. I give thanks to God that for twenty years, while I have treated these matters, I have always returned good for evil. I have spoken of those who opposed me only with all respect and honour, whereas most of them have either insulted me or put me among the unreasonable. I use no evasions, and I do not bring into play the illusory distinctions of elicitive, cumulative, destructive and auxiliary power. I impute to no one opinions he does not hold, unlike the way I have always been treated, and which the great Monsieur Claude cannot wholly excuse himself for, as when he accuses me of placing in the hands of the magistrate the keys of the kingdom of heaven. The truth I maintain resembles a cube: it cannot be overturned, and one cannot prevent it from having a firm base. My hypotheses concerning the keys, the power of binding and loosing, that of the pastors and synods, and the nature of the Church and of ordination are clear and bare; they have no detours. They are always the same and do not change according to the times, places and magistrates under whom the churches are gathered, and they attack Rome, its Pope, its Church and its religion far more vigorously than the path our teachers have taken for the last 150 years. The way I take is incomparably shorter and more effective, because, as I comprise all the controversies between Rome and us in my sixth maxim, which you may read in the letter I am writing to Monsieur Merlat and which is only four or five lines long, all our teachers will have to do in future is not to refute it, for it is most true, but to make its truth seen and understood by kings and magistrates. Certainly, if God put it into the hearts of our teachers to insist on this maxim, they would soon see the end of the Roman Church, and consequently the end of all our controversies.

units.la: Aussi ce que j'avance, ou touchant les grandes utilitez, que l'absence de la puissance Ecclésiastique, ou touchant les grands maux que sa presence apporte au monde, n'est pas contestable par ceux qui se sont donnez la liberté du raisonnement: Car ce sont-là des suites naturelles de sa presence, qu'elle a introduit, non seulement le Pape, mais aussi l'infaillibilité, ou un tribunal infaillible, & de plus l'obligation des peuples de s'y soûmettre, ou du moins elle rend l'erreur, & la faute plus pardonnable de se soûmettre à un tribunal infaillible, qu'à celuy qui est faillible. Au lieu que la presence d'une puissance, ou d'un tribunal Ecclésiastique sujet à erreur, de la manière que Mr. de la Bastide en a entrepris la défense, ne condamne pas seulement la soûmission des peuples à un tel tribunal, mais aussi l'authorité qu'il s'attribue de lancer les mesmes anathémes, & censures Ecclésiastiques, que seroit un tribunal infaillible, l'usage d'une puissance Ecclésiastique, dans quelque Eglise que ce soit est pernicieus : mais il est plus raisonnable, & mieux ajusté de la manière que Rome s'y prend, que selon la pratique de nos Eglises.
units.tr: Likewise, what I advance, both concerning the great advantages of the absence of ecclesiastical power and concerning the great evils its presence brings into the world, cannot be contested by those who have granted themselves the liberty of reasoning. For these are natural consequences of its presence: it has introduced not only the Pope but also infallibility, or an infallible tribunal, and moreover the obligation of peoples to submit to it; or at least it makes the error and fault of submitting to an infallible tribunal more pardonable than submitting to one that is fallible. Whereas the presence of an ecclesiastical power or tribunal liable to error, in the way Monsieur de la Bastide has undertaken to defend it, condemns not only the submission of peoples to such a tribunal but also the authority it claims to launch the same anathemas and ecclesiastical censures as an infallible tribunal would. The exercise of ecclesiastical power in any church whatever is pernicious, but it is more reasonable and better adjusted in the manner Rome goes about it than according to the practice of our churches.

units.la: En-fin je me puis glorifier, comme
units.tr: Finally, I may glory, as

units.la: St. Paul dans le 24 des Actes v. 20 & 21, que dans toute ma conduite, je ne puis estre trouvé coupable, de quoy que ce soit : si ce n'est qu'on me veille faire un crime (comme on luy en vouloit faire, un, de la parole qu'il avoit prononcée hautement ; mais qui en effect n'estoit pas un crime) de ce que j'ay dità Mr. Claude, que dans la maniere de célébrer la Sainte Cene le Ministre devroit plutost dire, qu'il excommunie au nom de Jehan Calvin, qu'au nom de Jésus-Christ.
units.tr: St. Paul does in Acts 24, verses 20 and 21, that in my whole conduct I cannot be found guilty of anything at all. The only exception would be if someone chose to make a crime of it, as they wished to make one of the words he had spoken openly, though in fact they were no crime. The charge would be that I told Mr. Claude that, in the manner of celebrating the Holy Supper, the minister ought rather to say that he excommunicates in the name of John Calvin than in the name of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Mais c'est assez de ces matieres que Mr. Jurieu pourra dire, s'il prend la peine de les lire, que je rebats cent & cent foix : quoy que luy, ni autre ne soient pas capables de combattre mes hypothéses une seule fois.
units.tr: But enough on these matters. Mr. Jurieu may say, if he takes the trouble to read them, that I refute him a hundred and a hundred times, though neither he nor anyone else is capable of overturning my hypotheses even once.

units.la: Je prie Dieu, Mr. , qu'il vous donne longue- & heureuse vie, pour l'avancement de sa gloire, & pour la guerison des préjugez de vos Pasteurs. Je suis,
units.tr: I pray God, Sir, that he grant you a long and happy life, for the advancement of his glory and for the healing of the prejudices of your ministers. I am,

units.la: Vostre tres-humble & tres-obeissant Serviteur
units.tr: Your most humble and most obedient servant

units.la: Louïs du Moulin.
units.tr: Louis du Moulin.

units.la: Nobilissimo & Amplissimo Viro, D. Johanni Dupanio Reipublicæ Geneven- sis Primario Exconsuli, S.
units.tr: To the most noble and most distinguished man, Mr. Johann Dupan, former First Syndic of the Republic of Geneva, greetings.

units.la: Quod perè ex ultima Thule prodiens, tot spatia marium & terrarum trajiciam ut ad lacum Lemanum pervenia-m, & Ego, qui sum homo privatæ sortis compellem Virum Principem, publicam stationem sustinentem, & primi ordinis inter Senatores Genevenses, tum florentem fortunâ & magna authoritate pollentem, ne sapientiam tuam, prudentiam & eruditionem in utroque jure, Divino & humano ponam inter illa fortunæ missilia: effecit fama tuæ humanitatis, & obviæ ac expositæ comitatis ex relatu, mihi unicè reverendi Viri Petri Mussardi, Effecit inquam, ut in spem venirem futurum, ut ego, qui ubique in Orbe Christiano, mihi parare conor Patronos, & vindices sententiae meae, & novae Rationis, Te inter illos sistam & habeam meum pariter Patronum & Vindicem.
units.tr: Since I am coming almost from the farthest Thule, crossing so many stretches of sea and land to reach the Lake of Geneva, I, a man of private station, address a man of rank who holds a public office and is among the foremost Senators of Geneva, one who is also prosperous and powerful in great authority. I will not place your wisdom, prudence and learning in both laws, divine and human, among the missiles of fortune. The reputation of your kindness, and of the courtesy you show to all who approach you, reported to me by the Reverend Mr. Pierre Mussard alone, has brought it about, I say, that I have come to hope that I may present you, among those whom I try to secure everywhere in the Christian world as patrons and defenders of my opinion and my new argument, and that I may have you as my patron and defender alike.

units.la: Cum ergo, secundum opus promovendi salutem propriam id maximè incumberet totos hosce viginti annos, debellare Papam, per novam, nec hactenus à quoquam tritam viam & rationem. Imprimis operam dedi per Paraenesim meam editam, cum Oxoniae defungerer publica Professione historiarum, & ab eo tempore per meum Jugulum Causae, ut haecce quatuor subjicerem cognitioni bonorum & doctorum.
units.tr: Therefore, since the work of advancing my own salvation has been my chief concern for these twenty years, namely to overthrow the Pope by a new way and method that no one has yet trodden, I first took pains with my published Paraenesis, when I was discharging the public professorship of history at Oxford. From that time onward, in my Jugulum Causae, I have set these four points before the judgment of the good and learned.

units.la: 1. Potestatem Ecclesiasticam, quam volunt esse mediam inter Potestatem Verbi in corda agentis, & Potestatem Magistratus, esse merum figmentum humanum, tum abhorrere à sacra Scriptura & ratione.
units.tr: 1. The ecclesiastical power, which they hold to be intermediate between the power of the Word acting in the heart and the power of the magistrate, is a mere human fiction, and is also repugnant to Holy Scripture and to reason.

units.la: 2. Per illam Potestatem Ecclesiasticam à Protestantibus & Pontificiis juxta ta retentam, imo mordicus, quasi pro aris & focis defensam, introductam fuisse in Orbem Christianum, imo reformatum, vel Papalem, vel cum Papali paria facientem Potestatem.
units.tr: 2. Through that ecclesiastical power, retained by Protestants and Papists alike, and even defended tooth and nail as if for altars and hearths, the power of the Pope or a power equal to the papal one was introduced into the Christian world, even into the reformed world.

units.la: 3. Non sperandum, imo non expectandum esse, ut per aliam viam & rationem Papa ruat, & una totum Systema Romanense, Ecclesiae, religionis & hierarchiae, eadem ruina cadat, quam per ruinam Potestatis Ecclesiasticae, qua fascinantur hominum mentes, quamque ruinam, nostri Pastores & Doctores, quatenus sunt istius potestatis, non solum dicam chimericae, sed & perniciosissimae retinentissimi, morantur, imo inhibent.
units.tr: 3. It is not to be hoped, nor even expected, that the Pope will fall by another way and method, and that the whole Roman system of church, religion and hierarchy will fall in one collapse, unless it falls by the ruin of that ecclesiastical power by which men's minds are bewitched. Our ministers and teachers, so far as they belong to that power, not only keep this ruin at bay, which I call not merely chimerical but most pernicious, but even actively hinder it.

units.la: 4. Ac proinde Nostros Pastores Theologos, Doctores & Professores jam sesquiseculum, operam & oleum perdidisse & etiamnum hodie perdere in confutandis singulis, & [illegible, ~6 letters] doctrinis fidei, (ut sunt Transubstantiatio, Purgatorium) de quibus lis est inter Protestantes & Pontificios, quarum, nec unius, nec omnium conjunctim, ruina, nec Jugulum Causae petit, nec ejus arcem invadit.
units.tr: 4. Accordingly, our ministers, theologians, teachers and professors have for a century and a half wasted, and even today still waste, their labour and their oil in refuting single doctrines of the faith, such as transubstantiation and purgatory, over which Protestants and Papists dispute. The ruin of none of these, nor of all of them taken together, aims at the Jugulum Causae, nor attacks its citadel. [illegible]

units.la: Cum que non ita pridem prodiisset Expositio Catholicæ Fidei authore Episcopo Condomensi, & paulò post ejus discussio ab Illustri Adversario Marco Antonio Bastidio. Tu commodum Vir Amplissime & Consultissime, ad cujus notitiam & amicitiam fores aperuit, Tuus & idem meus Mussardus, venisti in mentem apud quem sensa mea de hujus & illius Scriptione deponerem; & quæ ad tempus clausa diu tenui alternis sententiis pendulus inter timorem offensionis & studium veritatis patefaciendæ, palam facerem, circa supremam illam authoritatem, quam Condomensis quidem, inter Pontificios, Bastidius verò inter Reformatos, optimo consilio & subacta prudentiâ constitutam fuisse, affirmant in Gallia, distinctam à civili: tum sapienter hîc & illic erecta fuisse tribunalia Ecclesiastica, ut præstructim ascensus fieret ab infimo ad summum perinde Ecclesiasticum; cui æquum sit etiam in negotio Fidei, cujusvis fortis homines, sed Christianos & Confessus Ecclesiasticos inferiores se subjicere & se morigeros præstare, sub pœna sub eundæ Ecclesiasticæ censuræ, ut sunt exauctoratio, suspensio, Excommunicatio & Traditio Satanæ: quæ quidem dum affirmat ille Præsul factitari apud nostros, nihil nobis affingit: quicquid pertendat Bastidius pro sua charitate, quâ flagrat erga sanctissimam hominum Nationem, ut est Reformatorum in Gallia, dum præxim illam Judiciorum & tribunalium per omnia geminam, licet nolens nec opinans, cum Romanensi facit, & aliquo boni, justi & æqui colore inducere conatur.
units.tr: Since not long ago the Exposition of the Catholic Faith by the Bishop of Condom appeared, and shortly afterwards its refutation by the illustrious adversary Marc-Antoine Bastide, you, most distinguished and most learned sir, to whose acquaintance and friendship my friend Mussard, who is also yours, opened the door, came to my mind as the man before whom I might set down my thoughts on this writing and that. I have long kept closed what I now wish to make plain. Wavering between the fear of giving offence and the zeal to bring out the truth, I hold that the supreme authority, which the Bishop of Condom among the Papists, and Bastide among the Reformed, affirm with the best counsel and considered prudence to be established in France, is distinct from the civil power. They also affirm that ecclesiastical tribunals have been wisely erected here and there, so that the ascent may run from the lowest to the highest ecclesiastical court. It is fair, they say, that even in matters of faith, men of any strength, but Christians and inferior ecclesiastical assemblies especially, should submit themselves and show obedience, under penalty of ecclesiastical censures such as deposition, suspension, excommunication and delivery to Satan. Whatever Bastide may maintain out of his charity, which burns towards that most holy nation of men, the Reformed in France, the bishop, in affirming that this practice is carried on among our people, invents nothing against us. Bastide, though unwilling and unaware, makes this practice of judgments and tribunals, in every respect a double of the Roman one, agree with it, and tries to induce it under some colour of the good, the just and the equitable.

units.la: Verùm utrobique errari puto, (ut sufius doceo in prima mea Epistola ad celeberrimum virum Johannem Claudium) & apud Reformatos, & in Romana Ecclesia, circa tribunalium Ecclesiasticorum constitutionem & supremam illam authoritatem Ecclesiasticam, quam Episcopus Condomensis, tum Arnaldus forbonista, ut & nostri Reformati, tantopere venditant; & sic necessariam censent, ut absque illis tribunalibus, ratio constare nequeat aut fidei, aut disciplinæ. Errari inquam, & utrobique, cum apud Ro-ma manenses, tum apud nostros constitui vel Papam, vel Papale tribunal, saltem erigi tribunal Regium, merè politicum & civile, hoc est regnum in regno, censeo; & quod ideo tam nomine tenus dicitur Ecclesiasticum, quam iniquè censuras infligit Ecclesiasticas, quæ sunt alieni fori: qua in re nostri, & Romanenses juxta errant ignoratione, & inscitiâ circa naturam, & definitionem Ecclesiæ, & circa authoritatem datam aut concreditam à Jesu Christo, cum Ecclesiæ, tum Pastoribus Ecclesiæ, ut aliquot corollariis palam faciam.
units.tr: But I think that both sides are in error, as I show more fully in my first letter to the most celebrated Mr. Johann Claude. Both among the Reformed and in the Roman Church, the error concerns the constitution of ecclesiastical tribunals and that supreme ecclesiastical authority which the Bishop of Condom, and Arnauld the Forbonist, and our own Reformed people also so extol, and which they think so necessary that without those tribunals neither faith nor discipline can stand. I say that both sides are in error, and I hold that among the Romanists as well as among ours a Pope or a papal tribunal is set up, or at least a royal tribunal, purely political and civil, that is, a kingdom within a kingdom. It is called ecclesiastical in name only, and it wrongly inflicts ecclesiastical censures, which belong to a foreign jurisdiction. In this matter our people and the Romanists alike go astray through ignorance and lack of skill concerning the nature and definition of the Church, and concerning the authority given or entrusted by Jesus Christ both to the Church and to the ministers of the Church. I shall make this plain in several corollaries.

units.la: I, Unaquaque Ecclesia particularis, est primarium subjectum de jure Divino perpetuo, omnis potestatis & disciplinæ retinendæ in orbe Christiano, ad quam nec ad aliam seu Nationalem, seu Provincialem, tenentur omnes qui dederunt nomen Christo, se aggregare, & ad quam solam pertinet potestas eligendi & ordinandi, & munere suo exuendi suos Pastores; sed suos, non alienos, de disciplina statuendi, decidendi, & componendi lites & controversias subortas intra suos paparietes; assumendi in saum gregem, aut ab eo quos lubet arcendi, sine provocatione ad Synodum quamcumque.
units.tr: I. Every particular church is by perpetual divine right the primary subject of all power and discipline to be maintained in the Christian world. To this church, and not to any other, whether national or provincial, all who have given their name to Christ are bound to join themselves. To it alone belongs the power of choosing and ordaining its ministers, and of stripping them of their office; but its own ministers, not those of others. It has the power to make rules of discipline, to decide and settle the disputes and controversies that arise within its own walls, and to receive into its flock, or to exclude from it, whomever it pleases, without appeal to any synod whatever.

units.la: 2. Cæteras notiones & acceptiones Ecclesiæ, ut Nationalis & Provincialis, cum singulæ Ecclesiæ particulares intra territorium aut regnum aliquod ad mutuam sui conservationem, & ad modum liberarum civitatum in Achaia, in Belgio, & inter Helvetios colliguntur, & in unam regiminis formam concedunt, coeunt, & in unum corpus adunantur, non esse juris Divini, sed humani & arbitrarii, nec pertinere ad formalem rationem Ecclesiæ. Ac proinde iniquè & perperam infligi & decerni censuras Ecclesiasticas à Synodo, seu tribunali, quod nullam habet formalem rationem Ecclesiæ, sed est merè cœtus politicus.
units.tr: 2. The other notions and senses of the Church, such as the national and the provincial, are not of divine right but of human and arbitrary institution, and do not belong to the formal nature of the Church. These arise when the particular churches within some territory or kingdom are gathered for their mutual preservation, after the manner of the free cities in Achaia, in Belgium and among the Swiss. They agree to a single form of government, come together and unite into one body. Accordingly, censures inflicted and decreed by a synod or tribunal that has no formal nature of the Church, but is merely a political assembly, are wrongly and unjustly imposed.

units.la: 3. Ecclesias sic colligatas, conficere unum corpus politicum, cujus rectores non habent rationem Pastorum, sed res suas habent per jurisdictionem ejusdem naturæ cum illa potestate quâ induuntur qui sedent ad clavum Reipublicæ,
units.tr: 3. Churches so bound together form one political body, whose rulers do not have the character of pastors. They hold their authority through a jurisdiction of the same kind as the power of those who sit at the helm of the commonwealth.

units.la: 4. Ejusmodi confœderationem admitti posse citra violationem juris Divini, modo nihil inde decedat de privilegiis & libertatibus Ecclesiarum particularium, nec infringantur jura collata à Christo uni cuique Ecclesiæ particulari, nec fides, nec disciplina invitis obtrudantur.
units.tr: 4. Such a confederation can be admitted without violating divine right, provided that nothing is thereby taken from the privileges and liberties of the particular churches, that the rights conferred by Christ on each particular church are not infringed, and that neither faith nor discipline is forced upon the unwilling.

units.la: 5. Quod quidem fieret, si inter illas Ecclesias uno confœderationis vinculo sic colligatas, tribunal Ecclesiasticum supremum erigeretur, cujus dictatis & legibus, in fidei & disciplinæ negotio, tenerentur parere singuli cætus & homines sub poena excommunicationis, quemadmodum sancit disciplina nostrarum Ecclesiarum, Capit. 5. Artic. 31. titul. de Consistoriis.
units.tr: 5. This would indeed happen if, among those churches thus bound together by the single bond of a confederation, a supreme ecclesiastical tribunal were set up, by whose decrees and laws in matters of faith and discipline individual assemblies and persons would be bound to obey, under penalty of excommunication, as the discipline of our churches enacts in chapter 5, article 31, under the title On Consistories.

units.la: 6. Eoque gravioribus incommodis urgeretur ejusmodi tribunal, si ubi diversitas religionis non obstat, non daretur provocatio ad summum Magistratum, seu ad curias civiles.
units.tr: 6. Such a tribunal would be burdened with still graver inconveniences if, where difference of religion is no obstacle, there were no appeal to the supreme magistrate, or to the civil courts.

units.la: 7. Sed grande crimen foret jurisque alieni vendicatio & occupatio, si in territorio Magistratus, seu amici, seu infensi, distinctum & independens erigeretur ejusmodi tribunal Ecclesiasticam supremum, nationale, virtute clavium & potestatis ligandi & solvendi.
units.tr: 7. But it would be a great crime and an usurping of another's right if such a supreme national ecclesiastical tribunal, distinct and independent, were set up within the territory of the magistrate, whether friendly or hostile, by virtue of the keys and the power of binding and loosing.

units.la: 8. Namque ejusmodi tribunal plane analogum effet Papali, quod Episcopus Romanus sibi struxit in imperio alieno in Reges & Nationes, quodque Episcopus Condomensis graphicè exscribit in sua expositione fidei Catholicæ, sed perinde iniquum inter Reformatos, atque inter Romanenses, nisi quod iniquius videatur se subjicere cæca mente; & absque examine causæ, judicio errori obnoxio, quam illi quod Romanenses ἀνυπεύθυνον censent: minus tamen iniquius, in eo quod Protestantes, non aliud tribunal infallibile admittant præter scripturam sacram.
units.tr: 8. For such a tribunal would be entirely analogous to the papal one, which the Roman Bishop built for himself in the dominions of others, over kings and nations, and which the Bishop of Condom copies out in his exposition of the Catholic faith. Yet it would be just as unjust among the Reformed as among the Romanists, except that it seems more unjust to submit with a blind mind and, without examination of the case, to a judgment liable to error, than what the Romanists judge to be unaccountable [ἀνυπεύθυνον]. It is less unjust, however, in that the Protestants admit no infallible tribunal besides Holy Scripture.

units.la: In eo tamen culpandi quod tribunal erigant perinde Ecclesiasticum ac Romanenfe: quod si non ἀναμαρτήτοι αι, saltem Papam, Papalem tyrannidem in corpora & conscientias, tum inquisitionem Hispanicam & Lernam malorum intulit; imprimis sævitiam in hæreticos, & in sententes non tam prava quam diversa, cujus quidem sævitiæ in puniendis hæreticis, si quæ supersunt vestigia inter Protestantes, id imputari debent suo Ecclesiastico tribunali.
units.tr: Yet they are to be blamed for setting up such an ecclesiastical tribunal, just as the Romanists do. If they are not infallible [ἀναμάρτητοι], at least the Pope has brought papal tyranny upon bodies and consciences, and also the Spanish and Roman inquisition, and very great evils, above all savagery against heretics, and against dissenters not so much perverse as different. If any traces of that savagery in punishing heretics survive among the Protestants, they must be imputed to their own ecclesiastical tribunal.

units.la: §. Porro iniquitas ejusmodi tribunalis Reformatarum Ecclesiarum, in eo stat & consistit, non quod res suas habeant, tractent & dispungant citra appellationem ad curias civiles, quandiu non est sperandum æquum judicium causæ apud infensos judices, & abhorrentes à religione reformata, sed quod fit constans sententia Pastorum reformatorum in Gallia, non convenire cum jure Divino, ut à tribunalibus Ecclesiasticis fiat appellatio ad politica & civilia, seu infensa, seu amica religioni Protestantium, qua in re sententia Pastorum reformatorum in Gallia, magis redolet Papismum quam quod vulgò creditur & factitatur à vindicibus libertatum Gallicanæ Ecclesiæ, licet Pontificiis: ut qui volunt fieri provocationem à curiis Ecclesiasticis, & decretis Papæ, ad tribunalia Regia & Civilia: quod tamen non paterentur Pastores nostri in Gallia, etiam libera facta potestate provocandi ad seculares judices suæ Religioni faventes: nec immerito; nam illa provocatio à Synodis ad curias civiles, quatenus subjicit. Jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam Civili, eatenus dicit illam jurisdictionem nomine tenus esse Ecclesiasticam, cujus supremum tribunal est politicum:
units.tr: §. Moreover, the injustice of this kind of tribunal in the Reformed Churches lies and consists in this: not that they handle, settle and dispose of their own affairs without appeal to the civil courts, since a fair judgment of the case is not to be hoped for before judges who are hostile and abhorrent to the Reformed religion. Rather, it lies in the fact that the settled opinion of the Reformed pastors in France is that it does not agree with divine law that appeals from ecclesiastical tribunals be made to political and civil authorities, whether hostile or friendly to the Protestant religion. In this matter the opinion of the Reformed pastors in France smells more of Popery than is commonly believed and practised by the champions of the liberties of the Gallican Church, although they are Papists: those who wish appeals from ecclesiastical courts and papal decrees to be made to royal and civil tribunals. Yet our pastors in France would not allow this, even if the power of appealing to secular judges favourable to their religion were made free. Nor without reason: for that appeal from synods to civil courts, in so far as it subjects ecclesiastical jurisdiction to civil jurisdiction, to that extent makes that jurisdiction ecclesiastical in name only, when its supreme tribunal is political.

units.la: 10. In eo etiam iniquitas ejusmodi tribunalium se prodit, quod non solum, ut dixi, se tueantur ad eorum constitutionem jure Divino, & potestate ligandi & solvendi, quam Ecclesiasticam & spiritualem aiunt & vocant, & habent seorsim à potestate aut magistratus, aut vindicum disciplinæ confœderatæ, sed & retineant separatim à potestate Verbi, ad quam solam pertinent claves regni Cœlorum & potestas ligandi & solvendi, cum tamen affirment per virtutem & potestatem illam verbi divini quæ transfert à tenebris ad lucem, & à potestate satanæ ad Deum, & peccatores compedibus & vinculis peccati solvit: cum tamen, inquam, affirment per eam immorigeros traditione satanæ, excommunicatione, suspensione, exauthoratione & & expulsione ab omni cætu. Ecclesiastico, plecti, authoritate & jussu illius tribunalis Ecclesiastici.
units.tr: 10. The injustice of such tribunals also betrays itself in this: they claim to be supported, as I have said, by divine law and by the power of binding and loosing, which they call ecclesiastical and spiritual, and they hold it separately from the power of the magistrate or of the confederated champions of discipline. But they also retain it separately from the power of the Word, to which alone belong the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of binding and loosing. Yet they affirm that by that power and virtue of the divine Word which transfers from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, and looses sinners from the fetters and chains of sin, by that same power, I say, they affirm that the disobedient are punished, by delivering them to Satan, by excommunication, suspension, deprivation of office and expulsion from every ecclesiastical assembly, by the authority and command of that ecclesiastical tribunal.

units.la: 11. Inde etiam liquet potestatem illám Ecclesiasticam, esse non solum iniquam, sed & merum figmentum.
units.tr: 11. From this it is also clear that this ecclesiastical power is not only unjust but a mere fiction.

units.la: 1. Quod tantum abest ut Dominus Jesus contulerit potestatem ligandi & solvendi Ecclesiæ, aut Nationali, aut Provinciali, eique commiserit claves regni cælorum, ut nequidem, nec has commiserit, nec illam contulerit in Ecclesiam particularem, nisi nomine Ecclesiæ, soli Pastores intelligantur: nec illi in cœtum allecti cum primoribus Ecclesiæ ad res ordinandas quæ sunt de jure naturali divino, vel de jure societatis, sed cum pro suggestu concionantur & prædicant Evangelium, aut in mensa, divina symbola distribuunt.
units.tr: 1. Far from the Lord Jesus having conferred on the Church, whether national or provincial, the power of binding and loosing, and having committed to it the keys of the kingdom of heaven, not even did he commit these, nor confer that power, upon the particular church, except in the name of the Church, meaning only the ministers. Nor are those who are gathered with the leading men of the Church to settle matters that belong to divine natural law or to the law of society thereby invested with that power. Rather, it belongs to ministers when they preach from the pulpit and proclaim the Gospel, or when they distribute the divine symbols at the table.

units.la: 2. Quod potestas illa verbi, & illæ claves non administrari nec tractari possunt ab ullo cœtu hominum seu Ecclesiastico, seu Civili, aut Provinciali, sed à solis verbi divini ministris, & administris, nec nisi intra parietes Ecclesiæ particularis.
units.tr: 2. That power of the Word and those keys cannot be administered or handled by any assembly of men, whether ecclesiastical, civil or provincial, but only by the ministers and servants of the divine Word, and only within the walls of the particular church.

units.la: 3. Quod abhorret ab omni scriptura sacra, tum ab omni ratione, ut detur in mundo ejusmodi potestas Ecclesiastica; multò magis abhorret, ut potestas ligandi & solvendi, & claves regni Cælorum pertineant ad illam potestatem futilem & Chimericam.
units.tr: 3. It is contrary to all Holy Scripture, and to all reason, that such an ecclesiastical power should exist in the world. Much more contrary is it that the power of binding and loosing and the keys of the kingdom of heaven should pertain to that futile and chimerical power.

units.la: 12. Quocirca prudenter Amyraldus, illam iniquitatem, aut sustulit à tribunalibus Ecclesiasticis, aut mollivit, dum non admittit tribunalia Ecclesiastica exscribi ad formam, typum, & modum supremarum curiarum civilium, quarum modus aut Imperii assumpti, aut obsequii imperati, non pendet à voluntate tribunalium inferiorum & subalternorum. Nam disputatione de authoritate Conciliorum thesi 28 dicit, Institutum illud esse pulcherrimum & salubberrimum, quando Conciliorum decreta subjiciuntur judicio particularium synodorum nationalium, aut particularium Ecclesiarum: extra quod temporamentum, omnis disciplina Ecclesiastica, & ordo degenerant in tyrannidem. Qua in re Independentes Amyraldo concinunt, ut qui non repudiant synodorum usum, nec fe subjicere eorum decretis recusant, dummodò ab illis fiat provocatio ad Ecclesias particulares, juxta temperamentum propositum ab Amyraldo, & quod maximè probat Reverendus Baxterus, & comprobat authoritate summi viri Jacobi Ussherii, ut fusius doceo in meo Patrono bonæ fidei Epistolâ, pag. 75. Profectò non alia gens inter Christianos proprius accedit ad doctrinam, disciplinam & vitam Apostolicam. Credunt enim Independentes, vel si Synodi omnes essent erroris expertes, non aliter debere suos canones concipere quam per modum consilii, ut loquitur prima synodus quæ fuit Apostolorum Act. 15. Si quæ à nobis lata sunt decreta observatis, bene feceritis. Nisi de illis Synodis fiant coetus politici, aut accedat authoritas Magistratûs, extra quam, rectè affirmant Synodorum decreta mere esse consilia, hortationes, & animi declarationes, ut fuit decretum Concilii Carthaginensis anno 402. (Barlaam de Papæ Primatu cap. 24.) Decretum est ut scriberetur sancto Innocentio, circa discordiam inter Ecclesiam Alexandrinam & Romanam, ut inter se pacem colant quam jubet Dominus. Ut jam iniquè nostri congregationales vapulent à Synodo Carentonensi anno 1645. Nec non à magno viro Joanne Dallæo part. 2. pag. 127. libri in Adamum Jesuitam, & in transfugam Cottiby, ut secta inaudita Patribus & toti antiquitati, tum infensa omni bono ordini, & cui si fides esset apud orbis Dominos, Divina humanis, sacra profanis sursum deorsum permistura, & dominationes & Imperia eversura.
units.tr: 12. Wherefore Amyraut wisely either removed that injustice from ecclesiastical tribunals or softened it, since he does not admit that ecclesiastical tribunals should be modelled on the form, type and manner of the supreme civil courts, whose manner, whether of assumed empire or of commanded obedience, does not depend on the will of the inferior and subordinate tribunals. For in his disputation on the authority of councils, thesis 28, he says: That arrangement is most excellent and most salutary when the decrees of councils are subjected to the judgment of particular national synods or particular churches. Outside that moderation, all ecclesiastical discipline and order degenerate into tyranny. In this matter the Independents agree with Amyraut, since they do not reject the use of synods, nor refuse to submit to their decrees, provided that appeal is made from them to the particular churches, according to the moderation proposed by Amyraut. This is what the Reverend Baxter especially approves, and what he confirms by the authority of the great man James Ussher, as I teach more fully in my letter to my patron of good faith, p. 75. Certainly no other people among the Christians comes closer to the Apostolic doctrine, discipline and life. For the Independents believe that, even if all synods were free from error, their canons ought to be framed only by way of counsel, as the first synod of the Apostles, Acts 15, puts it: If you keep the decrees which have been issued by us, you will do well. Unless such synods become political assemblies, or the authority of the magistrate is added, the Independents rightly affirm that the decrees of synods are merely counsels, exhortations and declarations of mind. So it was decreed by the Council of Carthage in the year 402 (Barlaam on the Primacy of the Pope, ch. 24): It was decreed that it be written to Saint Innocent, concerning the discord between the Church of Alexandria and the Roman Church, that they should keep peace between themselves, as the Lord commands. Thus our congregationalists are now unjustly beaten by the Synod of Charenton in the year 1645, and also by the great man John Daillé, part 2, p. 127 of his book against the Jesuit Adam, and against the deserter Cottiby, as a sect unheard of by the Fathers and by all antiquity, and hostile to all good order. If it were trusted among the masters of the world, it would mix divine things with human, sacred with profane, turn everything upside down, and overthrow dominions and empires.

units.la: Sanè Independentes rectissimè omnium Christianorum qui abeunt ab Ecclesia Romana, sentiunt circa naturam Ecclesiæ, potestatis clavium, ordinationis, schismatis, item circa potestatem Ecclesiæ, Pastorum, Synodorum, & de Antichristo, & in hisce proximè accedunt ad <bl>Ἀ</bl>ξας, & sententiam Clarissimorum virorum, Mestrezatii, Riveti, Claudii, Musfardi, Pajoni, Merlati, qui nullam Ecclesiam visibilem de jure Divino admittunt in terris præter particularem, & qualem modo excripsi, nullamque legitimam ordinationem, nisi quæ in Ecclesia particulari, & ab Ecclesia particulari confertur.
units.tr: Certainly the Independents, most rightly of all the Christians who have departed from the Roman Church, think about the nature of the Church, the power of the keys, ordination, schism, and likewise about the power of the Church, the ministers and synods, and about Antichrist. In these matters they come closest to the extremes [ἄκρας], and to the opinion of the most distinguished men, Mestrezat, Rivet, Claude, Musfard, Pajon and Merlat, who admit no visible church by divine law on earth except the particular church, of the kind I have just described, and no legitimate ordination except that which is conferred in and by the particular church.

units.la: Cæterum Episcopus ille maximæ celebritatis, tum inter suos Romanenses, propter suam eruditionem & eloquentiam, tum inter noltros reformatos propter suum eximium candorem, aliud agens nec opinans laudat & probat Independentium formam regiminis, ut pote pariter adversam regimini horum & illorum, quod quidem eatenus facit, quatenus affirmat, eodem & perinde bono consilio, necefsariam, justam, & æquam arreptam fuisse judiciorum formam à Reformatis atque à Romanenlibus. Sed quam perinde bonam æquam & justam judiciorum formam apud hos, atque apud illos constitutam fuisse pronunciat, ego contra pronuncio perinde iniquè habitam & retentam fuisse apud hos atque apud illos, tum in Ecclesiam reformatam per potestatem Ecclesiasticam, introductam fuisse potestatem cum Papali paria facientem: ut jam nulla sit spes futurum ut Ecclesiæ nostræ ad summum apicem, & culmen re-
units.tr: But that bishop of the greatest fame, both among his own Romanists on account of his learning and eloquence, and among us Reformed on account of his remarkable candour, while doing something else and without intending it, praises and approves the form of government of the Independents, as being equally opposed to the government of these and of those. He does this so far as he affirms that, with equal and the same good counsel, a necessary, just and fair form of judgment was adopted by the Reformed and by the Romanists alike. But whereas he declares that a form of judgment equally good, fair and just was established among these as among those, I, on the contrary, declare that it has been equally unjustly held and retained among these as among those. Moreover, in the Reformed Church, through ecclesiastical power introduced, a power has been introduced that is on a par with the papal, so that there is now no hope that our churches will rise to the highest peak and summit of re-

units.la: reformationis assurgant, priusquam propius accedant ad formam regiminis in usu apud congregationales nostros, adeoque quicquid remanet fibrarum de radicibus mysterii iniquitatis extirpent hoc est priusquam, non quidem abusus, sed usus potestatis Ecclesiasticæ in totum è nostris Ecclesiis eliminetur. Per quam potestatem tam scio populos, clerum Romanensem, inprimis mundi dominos qui sunt in communione Romanensi arctè Papæ alligatos esse, quàm scio neminem devinciri Christo quàm fide & charitate.
units.tr: reformation, before they draw nearer to the form of government used among our Congregationalists, and so root out whatever fibres remain from the roots of the mystery of iniquity. That is, before the use, not merely the abuse, of ecclesiastical power is entirely removed from our churches. For I know that through this power the peoples, the Roman clergy, and above all the lords of the world who belong to the Roman communion are closely bound to the Pope, just as I know that no one is bound to Christ except by faith and charity.

units.la: Quocirca tibi, vir consultissime & clarissime, enitendum est, ut tuâ maximè opera, tuo consilio, imo molimine & authoritate, quâ plurimum vales Genevæ, propter tuam insignem in utroque jure divino & humano eruditionem, junctam cum summa probitate, & in Deum pietate, Urbs quæ est fons & origo purioris reformationis, & quæ, proh dolor! parens est potestatis Ecclesiasticæ, unde in totam Galliam, Angliam, Scotiam, Germaniam, Belgium, Helvetiam, Hungariam, Transylvaniam, imo totum orbem
units.tr: Therefore, most learned and distinguished sir, you must strive that, chiefly by your own work, your counsel, indeed your effort and authority, in which you have great weight in Geneva because of your outstanding learning in both divine and human law, joined with the highest integrity and piety towards God, the city which is the source and origin of the purer reformation, and which, alas, is the parent of ecclesiastical power, from which it has overflowed into all of France, England, Scotland, Germany, Belgium, Switzerland, Hungary, Transylvania, indeed the whole reformed world,

units.la: Nothing further printed on the page. bem reformatum exundavit, itidem prima deponat usum istius potestatis non dicam Chimericæ, sed & perniciofæ; à qua urbe & Ecclesia, exemplum capiant cæteræ Ecclesiæ, feque exolvant hacce fraude, & hocce mendacio. Atque ut huic operi alacrius & acrius incumbas, lubet ob oculos tuos ponere naturam mysterii iniquitatis; Et quod plane imbibi, nondum plane è vestra urbe extirpatum esse, & tamdiu ibi moram facturum, quoad inde pellatur Potestas Ecclesiastica, seu tribunal Ecclesiasticum distinctum à civili, quoadque hoc & illud, tum Ecclefia vestra & refpublica in unum corpus coalescant, quod una authoritate uno consilio, & ab iisdem viris, cum sacri, tum civilis ordinis animetur & regatur. Nam illud duplex tribunal quod ad remedium malo fuit adhibitum à Constantino Magno, cum Chriftianifmus effet ædificandus in Paganifmo, & nunc adhibetur inter reformatos sub Rege minus favorabili noftris; plane sub magistratu amico, & reformato ut est Genevenfis, non folum inutile & insuetum effet, sed
units.tr: overflowed, likewise let it first lay down the use of that power, which I will not call chimerical but also pernicious. Let the other churches take an example from that city and church, and free themselves from this fraud and this lie. And so that you may apply yourself to this work more eagerly and keenly, I am pleased to set before your eyes the nature of the mystery of iniquity. What I have thoroughly grasped is that it has not yet been fully uprooted from your city, and will remain there as long as ecclesiastical power, or an ecclesiastical tribunal distinct from the civil, is not driven out of it, and until this and that, both your church and commonwealth, coalesce into one body, animated and governed by one authority, one counsel, and the same men, of both the sacred and the civil order. For that double tribunal which was applied as a remedy to the evil by Constantine the Great, when Christianity was to be built up amid paganism, and which is now applied among the reformed under a king less favourable to ours, would not only be useless and unfamiliar under a friendly and reformed magistrate such as the Genevan, but

units.la: perniciosum & pugnans cum θεokρατία Judaica, in qua unus legislator, unus Judex, una lex obtinuit, certè per hocce duplex tribunal intravit Papa in mundum, & mysterium iniquitatis impletum hoc est incoeptum, auctum & ad summum culmen perductum fuit.
units.tr: pernicious and at odds with the Jewish theocracy [θεοκρατία], in which one lawgiver, one judge and one law prevailed. Certainly it was through this double tribunal that the Pope entered the world, and the mystery of iniquity was begun, increased and brought to its highest pinnacle.

units.la: Cum ergò sanctus Paulus affirmet, & Mysterio & Iniquitate defectionem à veritate, & sanctitate doctrinæ, & vitæ perfici, statuendum est id factum iniquitate seu Imperio Papali, terreno, divitiis, pompâ, & robore magnifico, quod per injustam occupationem, Imperatoribus Occidentis ereptum, sibi Papa struxit in Reges & populos: Mysterio verò, quando Papa illud imperium terrenum incrustavit tectorio vocabulorum Papæ, Episcopi, Sanctitatis, & potestatis Ecclesiasticæ & Spiritualis. Et sub hoc fuco & mangonio hactenus illusit, & insultavit capitibus Regum & Mundi Dynastarum, quamquam non opinantibus, imo hanc injuriam pro beneficio & honore computantibus. Nam eatenus potissimum iniquitas fucata est mysterio quod non
units.tr: Since therefore St Paul affirms that the defection from the truth and from the holiness of doctrine and life will be brought about by the iniquity and by the mystery, we must hold that the iniquity, that is, the earthly Papal empire, with its wealth, pomp and magnificent might, was accomplished by the Pope, who, by unjust seizure, wrested it from the Emperors of the West and built it for himself over kings and peoples. The mystery, however, is when the Pope plastered that earthly empire with the veneer of the words Pope, Bishop, Holiness, and ecclesiastical and spiritual power. Under this disguise and trickery he has hitherto deceived and mocked the heads of kings and the rulers of the world, though they did not perceive it, indeed counted this injury as a benefit and honour. For the iniquity has been chiefly disguised by the mystery in that

units.la: [Small illegible marks at the foot of the page, not text.] non difpalefcat, imo probetur & ametur à terrarum Dominis, qui in Papæ nomen juraverunt, haud absimiles avibus cavea inclusis, quæ ex suis Clathris emissæ, suum ergaftalum aperto aeri & libertati præferunt.
units.tr: [Small illegible marks at the foot of the page, not text.] it is not exposed, indeed is approved and loved by the lords of the lands, who have sworn an oath in the name of the Pope, much like birds shut in a cage, which, let out from their bars, prefer their prison to open air and liberty.

units.la: Cum inquam Sanctus Paulus Iniquitate & Mysterio, defectionem quam ominatur futuram, complexus fuerit, lubet hic tuis oculis subjicere & exponere, & qua ratione & quot modis, Mysterium illud iniquitatis sic potuerit suis incantamentis & illusionibus retinere hactenus triplex genus hominum mancipio, & in servitio Papæ, ut nec suam servitutem sentirent, neque fe in libertatem afferere cuperent: namque triplici nodo, triplex cuneus affigi debuit à mysterii Iniquitatis fabris.
units.tr: Since, I say, St Paul has embraced under Iniquity and Mystery the defection which he foretells as coming, I want to set before your eyes and explain by what reasons and in how many ways that mystery of iniquity has been able, by its enchantments and illusions, to keep a threefold class of men hitherto in bondage and in the service of the Pope, so that they neither feel their servitude nor desire to assert their liberty. For with a threefold knot the mystery's smiths had to fasten a threefold wedge.

units.la: 1. Unus quidem terrarum Monarchis.
units.tr: 1. On the one hand, the monarchs of the lands.

units.la: 2. Alter nationi virorum Ecclesiasticorum.
units.tr: 2. Another, the order of ecclesiastical men.

units.la: 3. Tertius populis & subditis de gente laica, per quos Papa hos & illos adamantinis vinculis sibi astrictos, & devinctos attinet, non vero per amorem rem & reverentiam, aut cultûs Romanensis, aut veritatis & sanctitatis, quam Reges, clerus, & populi credant inesse religioni & doctrinis Romanensibus.
units.tr: 3. The third, the peoples and subjects of the lay class, through whom the Pope keeps these and those bound fast to himself with adamantine chains. This is not through love, respect or reverence for Roman worship, or for the truth and holiness which kings, clergy and peoples believe to inhere in the Roman religion and doctrines.

units.la: 1. Populus retinendus fuit & conciliandus, non ullo emolumento, quod in ipsius rationes redundet, cum contrà à Papa & Clero pecuniis emungatur, sed aut terrore aut amore imperii florentis, pompâ, auro, & Margaritis fulgentis: nam his artibus, hoc fulgore, hacce pompa, sibi devincit Papa turbam pullatam, inertem & ignaram, qualis plerumque est plebs & gens laica, quæ vel omne ignotum habet pro magnifico, vel pene divinum credit quicquid in alto fastigio est positum, ac fortuitis & fortunæ missilibus dives est: at miserum, fatuum, & plumbeum censet Calvinistam, qui per viam factus est obviam, quod repudiat Transubstantiationem, aut Purgatorium, Indulgentiasve Papales, quibus authoritas & gratia conciliatur ab illo Imperio Papali, Majestate, & fulgore coruscante.
units.tr: 1. The people had to be kept and won over, not by any advantage that redounds to their own interests, since on the contrary they are fleeced of their money by the Pope and the clergy, but by either terror or the love of a flourishing empire, shining with pomp, gold and pearls. For by these arts, this glitter and this pomp, the Pope binds to himself the crowd in dark clothing, inert and ignorant, as the common people and the lay folk generally are. They either regard everything unknown as magnificent, or believe almost divine whatever is set on a lofty height and is rich in the chance gifts of fortune. But they think the Calvinist, who happens to come in their way because he rejects transubstantiation, purgatory or papal indulgences, by which authority and grace are obtained from that Papal empire glittering with majesty and splendour, a miserable, foolish and leaden fellow.

units.la: 2. Clerus verò in partem prædatorio se prædicat, suo imperio terreno in quo i(ut gloriantur pueri) suis crepundiis, & rudibus gladiatoriis deauratis) tam jactat suum imperium ἀνυπεύθυνον, & nulli præterquam Deo reddendis rationibus obnoxium, quam Papæ placét suum quoque imperium ἀνυπεύθυνον in eodem territorio, sed Ecclesiasticum & Spirituale: licet larvâ illâ vocabulorum Ecclesiastici & Spiritualis detractâ, plane æquas partes, si non priores in eodem & imperio, & territorio, Papa se probat habere cum ipso Principe, hic verò revera precariò duntaxat regnare. Sæpè miratus sum quod Reges id maximè accurrent ut fit Papa in mundo, atque ei constet sua authoritas, cum si Papæ soluta esset optio, nullus Rex esset in mundo.
units.tr: 2. The clergy, however, lay claim to a share of the plunder: with their earthly empire, in which they (as boys boast) with their rattles and gilded wooden swords, they boast of their empire [ἀνυπεύθυνον, unaccountable], answerable to no one except God for their account. It pleases the Pope to have his own empire [ἀνυπεύθυνον, unaccountable] in the same territory, but ecclesiastical and spiritual. Although that mask of the words ecclesiastical and spiritual has been stripped away, the Pope plainly proves that he has equal, if not prior, shares in the same empire and territory with the Prince himself, whereas the Prince in truth reigns only on sufferance. I have often wondered that kings most of all hasten to make the Pope the one in the world, and to secure his authority for him, since if the choice were left to the Pope, there would be no king in the world.

units.la: Atque per hæc firmiter credo, triplicem illum esse cuneum, qui arctè Reges, clerum, & populos affigit Papæ, ut, quamdiu vel commoda humana collata ad rationes præponderabunt, vel illusiones aut Imperii Papalis fulgore suo oculos fatuorum perstringentis, aut vocabulorum Ecclefiastici & Spiritualis non intelliguntur, non fit sperandum ut etiam illi qui sequius de religione Romana sentiunt in plerisque ejus capitibus, se à Papa divellant, quoad illo errore alte radicato exolvantur mentes, nempe mundum Christianorum regi debere per duplicem potestatem alteram civilem, alteram Ecclesiasticam, cui praesint Christianorum Antistites, ut illi mundi Monarchae. Nam inter reformatos ut plurimum caligant oculi ad ejusmodi illusiones, minus homines de gente laica, minime omnium viri Senatoriae dignitatis, ut est Dupanius: tum abducti suo genere vitae, à sua cuique utilitate, ut sunt Philosophi, Medici, quorum nonnullos videas invicto adversus mundana delinimenta animo, nec hebescentibus oculis mentis ad incantamenta vocabulorum, omnia illa lenocinia, honestâ & Christianâ superbiâ conculcare.
units.tr: And from these things I firmly believe that this is the threefold wedge which binds kings, clergy and peoples tightly to the Pope. So long as human advantages collected for reasons outweigh, or the illusions of the Papal empire, dazzling the eyes of fools with its glitter, or the words ecclesiastical and spiritual are not understood, it is not to be hoped that even those who think otherwise of the Roman religion in most of its heads will separate themselves from the Pope, until their minds are freed from that deeply rooted error, namely that the world of Christians ought to be ruled by a twofold power, one civil and the other ecclesiastical, over which the leaders of the Christians preside, as the monarchs of the world preside over the civil one. For among the reformed, the eyes are for the most part dimmed to such illusions: the men of the lay class least of all, and of all the least the men of senatorial dignity such as Dupanius. Then men are drawn away by their own way of life and by their own advantage, as are philosophers and physicians, some of whom you may see with a spirit unconquered against worldly allurements, and with eyes of the mind not dulled by the enchantments of words, trampling underfoot all those flatteries with an honourable and Christian pride.

units.la: In hoc etiam triplici cuneo, stat formalis ratio Papismi seu Mysterii iniquitatis: nam is non est Papista, qui firmiter credit & admittit Transubstantiationem, sacrificium Missae, Purgatorium, cultum imaginum & sanctorum, & cætera religionis Romanæ deliramenta; sed qui credit, recipit, & retinet in Ecclesia, vel Papam, vel potestatem Papali consimilem, ut est Potestas Ecclesiastica, quæ est purus putus Papismus (etiam ipso Papa non comparente in orbe Christiano, nec alligato ad illam potestatem Ecclesiasticam) & qui obtinuit à tempore sancti Pauli ad enatas Decretales, nec dum evulsus fuit superiori sæculo à viris sanctis Luthero, & Calvino, qui quidem non tam à Papa & Papismo defecerunt, quam à religione Romana, ut qui (saltem Calvinus) in reformatione sua, imitati sunt Tyrios, obsidione cinctos ab Alexandro Magno, cum aurea catena devinxerunt Apollinis simulachrum, ne urbem desereret. Nam Calvinus, amandatâ Papali religione retinuit sibi Potestatem Papalem, & sedulo cavit, ne Genevam desereret. Sanè Patres Tridentini, crediderunt in eo Papismo, seu Potestate Ecclesiastica, consistere formalem rationem Religionis Romanæ, ut is censeri debeat bonus Catholicus, non qui fidem Tridentinam recipit, sed qui imperio Papæ subest. Nam cum in Concilio, nunciatum esset, Henricum VIII. Angliæ Regem defecisse à Religione Romana, & id pernegatum esset à legatis Regis, Patres Tridentini definiverunt illum demum deficere à Religione Romana qui deficit à Papa. Crimen Henrici fuit, quod Papam sibi separatim constitueret in Anglia, valere jussu non cultu Romanensi, sed Episcopi Romani imperio.
units.tr: In this threefold wedge also stands the formal essence of Papism, or of the mystery of iniquity. For he is not a Papist who firmly believes and admits transubstantiation, the sacrifice of the Mass, purgatory, the worship of images and saints, and the other follies of the Roman religion. Rather, he is a Papist who believes, accepts and retains in the Church either the Pope or a power like the Papal one, such as ecclesiastical power, which is sheer Papism (even if the Pope did not appear in the Christian world, nor were bound to that ecclesiastical power). This has held since the time of St Paul to the rise of the Decretals, and was not uprooted until last century by the holy men Luther and Calvin, who indeed defected not so much from the Pope and Papism as from the Roman religion. Like the Tyrians, besieged by Alexander the Great, they (Calvin at least, in his reformation) bound the image of Apollo with a golden chain so that it would not desert the city. For Calvin, having cast off the Papal religion, retained for himself Papal power and carefully took care not to desert Geneva. Certainly the Fathers of Trent believed that the formal essence of the Roman religion consists in that Papism, or ecclesiastical power, so that a man should be judged a good Catholic not because he accepts the Tridentine faith but because he is subject to the empire of the Pope. For when it was announced in the Council that Henry VIII, King of England, had revolted from the Roman religion, and the King's legates denied it, the Fathers of Trent determined that the man revolts from the Roman religion only when he revolts from the Pope. Henry's crime was that he set up the Pope for himself separately in England, renouncing not the Roman worship but the authority of the Bishop of Rome.

units.la: J'Ay encore un mot à vous dire, Monsieur : mais pour vous délasser, quoy que je ne change pas de sujet je changerai de langue. C'est pour appuyer ce que je n'ay fait que toucher en passant, dans mon huitième corollaire, où je vous parle des cruels effets de la Puissance Ecclésiastique. Genéve qui est le lieu, à qui elle doit son établissement dans le party des Protestans, en a veu de terribles effets. Il y a passé cent ans qu'on y a brulé Servet, & il y a passé cent ans qu'on vous le reproche. Pour soûtenir cette cruelle exécution, Monsieur de Béze mit en lumiére un traitté, par-où il prétend de prouver, qu'il faut employer l'épée contre les hérétiques. Cette épée dégaignée si téméPrairement, a coupé la gorge à un million de fidéles. Le massacre de la St. Barthelemi en est une malheureuse production. Béze dit, Il faut égorger les hérétiques : Rome a dit vous estes des hérétiques : Et la conclusion de ces deux prémisses, qui sont aussi fausses l'une que l'autre, a esté suivie de tous les massacres que l'Eglise Romaine exerce de tems en tems contre nous. Il auroit esté à souhaitter qu'une si triste expérience, nous eust rendu sages. Cependant aprés toutes ces horreurs, nos Eglises continuent dans ces furieuses maximes, qui exposent ses enfans à la boucherie. Genéve a nonobstant cela condamné au feu un Ministre nommé Antoine, qui fut brûlé il y a environ 45 ans parce qu'il Judaïzoit. Dans ce Royaume, en l'an 1611. le Roy Jacques s'estant laissé surprendre aux remontrances des hiérarchiques en vertu d'un Statut de COMBURENDIS HÆRETICIS, que l'Angleterre sous la tyrannie Papale avoit publié contre les vrais adorateurs de J. C. consentit à la mort de Bartolomée Légate, & de Edovard Whigtman. Et ils furent tous deux brûlez vifs pour l'Arrianisme dans Londres. Mais ce bon Prince en conçeut une si grande horreur, qu'il en témoigna toute sa vie un extrême déplaisir, & protesta qu'il ne permettroit jamais de semblables cruautez si indignes de la modération Chrestienne.
units.tr: I have one more word for you, Sir. To give you a rest, I will change the language though not the subject. It is to support what I have only touched on in passing in my eighth corollary, where I speak of the cruel effects of ecclesiastical power. Geneva, the place to which the Protestant party owes its establishment, has seen some terrible effects of it. A hundred years ago Servetus was burned there, and for a hundred years that has been thrown in your faces. To defend that cruel execution, Monsieur de Bèze published a treatise in which he claims to prove that the sword must be used against heretics. That sword, drawn so rashly, has cut the throats of a million faithful people. The massacre of St. Bartholomew is one of its unhappy products. Bèze says: heretics must be slaughtered. Rome says: you are heretics. The conclusion drawn from these two premises, which are as false as each other, has been followed by all the massacres that the Roman Church from time to time carries out against us. It would have been desirable for such a sad experience to make us wise. Yet after all these horrors our churches continue in those furious maxims, which expose their children to the butcher's block.
