Nevertheless Geneva condemned to the fire a minister named Antoine, who was burned about forty-five years ago because he judaized. In this kingdom, in the year 1611, King James, having allowed himself to be persuaded by the remonstrances of the hierarchs under a statute concerning the burning of heretics, which England under papal tyranny had published against the true worshippers of Jesus Christ, consented to the death of Bartholomew Legate and Edward Wightman. Both were burned alive in London for Arianism. But this good prince conceived such a great horror of it that he showed extreme displeasure all his life, and protested that he would never permit such cruelties, so unworthy of Christian moderation.

units.la: Je m'assure Monsieur, que pendant que Genéve sera assez heureuse pour vous avoir à son timon, vous ne souffrirez pas non plus de telles violences; Vous qui estes l'un des plus vigoureus obstacles aux efforts que la puissance Ecclésiastique fait dans vostre ville, pour arracher le gouvernail des mains du Magistrat, & pour s'élever sur les ruines de cette légitime authorité: Vous apprendrez à vos Pasteurs à se conduire par l'Esprit de Christ, qui est un Esprit de douceur, de modération & de sens rassis, vous leur apprendrez à gaigner les cœurs par la raison, & par les persuasions, sans entreprendre de vouloir forcer les corps par la violence. *Cela est bon à Mahomet, de planter la foy de son Alcoran à coups d'épée. Jésus-Christ n'établit celle de son Evangile, que par l'évidence de sa vérité. Il faut laisser cette première voye au Pape, qui n'a établi, & maintenu son Empire que par le fer, & par le feu, par les impostures de son Excommunication, & par les fureurs Diaboliques de son infernale Inquisition. Nous n'avons pas ainsi appris J. C. C'est faire tort à sa vérité, de croire qu'elle ait besoin du bras de la chair. Laissons sa croix toute seule, & elle opérera mille-fois plus, qu'en y joignant la violence : cette dernière peut bien forcer la bouche ou la main des personnes timides, pour faire des confessions & des signatures feintes : mais on ne scauroit gaigner ce cœur que Dieu demande, autrement que par la raison. C'est la méthode que J. C. & ses Apostres ont suivie. Leurs plus proches successeurs durans trois cents ans, ont fait de merveilleus progrez. Ils ont répandu l'Evangile presque par tout, mais par quel moien? Est-ce en persécutant ceux qui refusoient de recevoir leur doctrine? Tout au contraire ils estoient exposez eux-mesmes aux persécutions les plus violentes. Ils n'avoient point d'autre feu que celuy de la charité & de l'évidence de leur doctrine, ni d'autres armes que cette épée à deux tranchans, qui atteint jusques au fond de l'ame, dont il est parlé dans l'Epitre aux Hebreux.
units.tr: I am sure, Monsieur, that while Geneva is fortunate enough to have you at her helm, you will not tolerate such violence either. You are one of the most vigorous obstacles to the efforts that ecclesiastical power is making in your city to tear the rudder from the hands of the magistrate and to rise on the ruins of that lawful authority. You will teach your ministers to conduct themselves by the Spirit of Christ, which is a spirit of gentleness, moderation and sober judgement. You will teach them to win hearts by reason and persuasion, without undertaking to force bodies by violence. That may be good for Mahomet, who planted the faith of his Koran by the sword. Jesus Christ established the faith of his Gospel only by the evidence of its truth. That first way must be left to the Pope, who has established and maintained his empire only by iron and fire, by the frauds of his excommunication, and by the diabolical fury of his infernal Inquisition. We have not learned Christ in this way. It does wrong to his truth to believe that it needs the arm of flesh. Let his cross stand alone, and it will accomplish a thousand times more than it does with violence joined to it. Violence may indeed force the mouths or hands of timid people, to make confessions and feigned signatures; but it cannot win the heart that God requires, except by reason. This is the method that Christ and his Apostles followed. Their nearest successors, for three hundred years, made marvellous progress. They spread the Gospel almost everywhere; but by what means? Was it by persecuting those who refused to receive their doctrine? Quite the contrary: they were themselves exposed to the most violent persecutions. They had no other fire than that of charity and the evidence of their doctrine, and no other weapon than that two-edged sword which reaches to the depths of the soul, spoken of in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: On m'opposera peut-estre l'exemples des Apostres-mesmes qui ont frappé d'aveuglement, & de mort ceux qui leur contredisoient, comme St. Paul en usa envers l'enchanteur Elymas, & St. Pierre contre Ananias & Sapphira. Mais je croy que J'auray raison de répondre à ceux, qui veulent couvrir leur cruauté par ces exemples, qu'ils ne savent de quel Esprit ils sont menez, comme nostre Seigneur le répondit à ses disciples, lors qu'ils vouloient faire tomber le feu du ciel sur leurs ennemis, parce qu'Elie en avoit ainsi usé sous la loy. Car premiérement ment les Apostres avoient le discernement des Esprits, ce que nous n'avons pas : Ils savoient distinguer les hypocrites d'avec les gens de bien. Ils connoissoient ceux qui avoient péché contre le St. Esprit, & ceux qui n'estoient pas tombez dans cét état desespéré. Parce qu'ils regardoient les premiers comme des damnez, qui estoient desia entre les mains du diable, & qui estoient déterminez à l'impénitence, ils en faisoient des exemples des jugemens de Dieu, & des tableaux d'épouvantement, qui rendoient la doctrine de l'Evangile plus vénérable.
units.tr: Perhaps it will be objected to me that the Apostles themselves struck with blindness and death those who opposed them, as St. Paul did to the sorcerer Elymas, and St. Peter to Ananias and Sapphira. But I think I shall be right to answer those who want to cover their cruelty by these examples, that they do not know what spirit they are of, as our Lord answered his disciples when they wanted to call down fire from heaven upon their enemies, because Elijah had done so under the law. For, first, the Apostles had the discernment of spirits, which we do not have. They could distinguish hypocrites from good people. They knew those who had sinned against the Holy Spirit, and those who had not fallen into that desperate state. Because they regarded the first as damned, already in the hands of the devil and determined to impenitence, they made of them examples of God's judgements and pictures of terror, which made the doctrine of the Gospel more venerable.

units.la: Mais puis que nous n'avons pas aujourd'huy la mesme connoissance, il ne nous est pas permis d'agir de la mesme manière. Je di encore que dans l'établissement de l'Eglise Chrestienne, la providence divine a permis qu'il y ait eu de ces fortes d'exemples, pour faire connoitre que le Christianisme n'estoit pas une école de libertinage & d'hypocrifie, mais de vérité & de sainteté. Il en est arrivé comme dans tous les Estats du monde, où c'est la coûtume de punir sévérément les premiéres fautes ceux qu'on appelle Hérétiques. Car St. Paul n'a pas puny ceux qui renversoyent la foy de la résurrection des morts ; ni St. Jean, ceux qui de ce temps-là nioyent la divinité du fils de Dieu. St. Paul emploie contre les premiers ces beaux raisonnemens que l'on ne peut lire sans admiration dans sa 1. aux Cor. ch. 15. & St. Jean a écrit contre les autres son Evangile, dont le dessein, selon le sentiment de tous les Peres, est de prouver la divinité du fils de Dieu : Comme ces pechez-là peuvent estre appelez Spirituels, ils doivent estre combattus par les lumières de la raison éclairées decelles de la grace, & les Apostres ont dit à cét egard,Les armes de noftre milice ne sont pas charnelles. Contre qui estce qu'ils ont exercé les châtimens corporels ? ç'a esté contre ceux qui violoyent les préceptes de l'équité ou de l'honnesteté naturelle,contre les hypocrites qui vouloyent imposer aux hommes,& à Dieu-mesme, comme Ananias & Sapphira,comme l'incestueux de Corinthe, & comme ces Epicuriens de la mesme Eglise qui s'enyvroyent honteufeteulement dans le temps mesme qu'ils se prépàroj ent à la communion. Si lors qu'il falloit établir l'Evangile, les Apostres n'ont pas puny de peines corporelles les hérétiques, combien moins lat'on du faire dans les aages suivans ? & sur tout puis que nous n'avons pas une connoissance aussi grande que celle des Apostres pour connoitre asseurément ceux qui sont dans l'erreur. Presque toutes les communions s'accusent les unes les autres d'hérèsie, s'il estoit permis d'exterminer ceux que l'on tient pour tels, les Chrestiens donneroyent un agréable divertissement aux Turcs, en s'egorgeant les uns les autres. Autrefois le grand zele des Papes, qui a tous-jours esté animé parcét Esprit meurtier, faisoit prefcher les croisades contre les Vaudois & les Albigeois. Tous les Rois qui reconnoissoient son Empire, secondoyent de toutes leurs forces la fureur de cét homme de péché: mais à present on s'est un peu modéré; on a de la honte des violences passées; & ces mouvements bouillans, qui ne parlent que de détruire les hérétiques, ne sont plus que dans la cervelle d'une sotte populace : Les personnes sages & bien sensées, mesme dans la communion Romaine, font dans les sentiments d'un Ancien Evesque de nos Gaules, c'est Martin Evesque de Tours, qui eut en horreur la cruauté dont Ithacus & Idacius avoyent usé contre Priscillien, de qui ils solliciterent le supplice : Quelque hérétique qu'il fust & quelque Orthodoxes que fussent ses ennemis, le bon Martin détesta leur conduite : Il creut que s'ils gardoyent la vérité, ils avoyent renoncé à la charité, qui n'est pas moins essentielle au Christianisme, & il se retira de leur communion.
units.tr: But since we do not today have the same knowledge, we are not permitted to act in the same way. I say further that, in the establishment of the Christian Church, divine providence allowed such examples to occur, to make it known that Christianity was not a school of licentiousness and hypocrisy, but of truth and holiness. It happened as in all the states of the world, where it is the custom to punish severely the first offences of those called Heretics. For St. Paul did not punish those who overthrew the faith in the resurrection of the dead; nor did St. John punish those who at that time denied the divinity of the Son of God. St. Paul uses against the former those fine arguments which one cannot read without admiration in his 1 Cor. 15; and St. John wrote against the others his Gospel, whose purpose, according to the judgement of all the Fathers, is to prove the divinity of the Son of God. Since these sins can be called spiritual, they must be combated by the light of reason illuminated by grace, and the Apostles have said in this regard: The weapons of our warfare are not carnal. Against whom did they exercise bodily punishments? It was against those who violated the precepts of equity or natural honesty, against hypocrites who wished to impose on men and even on God, like Ananias and Sapphira, like the incestuous man of Corinth, and like those Epicureans of the same Church who got drunk shamefully at the very time they were preparing for communion. If, when the Gospel had to be established, the Apostles did not punish heretics with bodily penalties, how much less ought we to do so in the ages that followed? Above all, since we do not have a knowledge as great as that of the Apostles to know for certain who are in error. Almost all the communions accuse one another of heresy. If it were permitted to exterminate those held to be such, Christians would give a pleasant entertainment to the Turks by butchering one another. Formerly the great zeal of the Popes, which has always been inspired by that murderous spirit, had crusades preached against the Waldensians and the Albigensians. All the kings who acknowledged his empire supported with all their strength the fury of that man of sin. But now people have moderated themselves somewhat; they are ashamed of past violence; and those fiery movements, which speak only of destroying heretics, survive only in the heads of a foolish populace. Wise and sensible people, even within the Roman communion, hold the views of an ancient bishop of our Gauls, namely Martin, Bishop of Tours, who abhorred the cruelty that Ithacius and Idacius had used against Priscillian, whose execution they sought. However heretical he was, and however orthodox his enemies were, good Martin detested their conduct. He believed that if they kept the truth, they had renounced charity, which is no less essential to Christianity, and he withdrew from their communion.

units.la: Quoy que je parle fort souvent de ces matiéres-là à Mrs les Théologiens, je n'espére pourtant pas, Mr. d'en pouvoir recueillir le mesme fruit que j'en attends de vous; Ils écoutent ou lisent mes raisons, comme un attentat sur leur prétenduë authorité; & si je les faisois mes juges je craindrois qu'ils ne tinssent pas la balance droite, parce qu'ils sont mes parties. Aussi quelque dissentiment qu'il y ait entreux sur les autres articles de la religion Chrestienne enné, quoy que les uns se difent les difciples de Luther, & que les autres fuivent Calvin ; quoy que les uns veulent l'Episcopat, & que les autres foûtiennent avec chaleur qu'il n'y a que le gouvernement Presbytérien qui foit Apostolique ; quoy que les Eglises Reformées ayent le malheur d'estre divisées d'affections, de communion, de créance, & de Discipline, cependant il y en a tres-peu qui ne veuille ériger un tribunal Ecclésiastique distinct du Civil, Sic enim discordes sociantur, & eandem utilitatem fovent, ubi omnium est idem amor imperii ; comme dit Tacite.
units.tr: Although I speak very often on these matters to the gentlemen theologians, I do not hope, Sir, to get from them the same fruit I expect from you. They hear or read my arguments as an attack on their supposed authority, and if I made them my judges I would fear they would not hold the balance straight, since they are my opponents. So, however much disagreement there is among them on the other articles of the Reformed Christian religion, whether some call themselves disciples of Luther while others follow Calvin, whether some want episcopacy while others insist warmly that only Presbyterian government is apostolic, and however unhappy it is that the Reformed Churches are divided in affection, communion, belief and discipline, yet there are very few of them who do not want to set up an ecclesiastical tribunal distinct from the civil one. Sic enim discordes sociantur, & eandem utilitatem fovent, ubi omnium est idem amor imperii, as Tacitus says.

units.la: Mais, Mr., il ne faut pas que le plaisir que j'ay de vous entretenir me rende ennuyeux. Je m'en apperçois peut-estre un peu trop tard, puis que je voy qu'au lieu d'une Lettre, je vous ay fait un petit livre, & je suis d'autant moins excusable qu'il ne faut pas beaucoup de paroles à un juge aussi éclairé que vous ; toutes fois je ne m'adresse pas seulement à vous comme à mon Juge, je cherche en vôtre personne un associé qui se joigne à moy pour donner un dernier coup de massi ë ac l'Evesque de Rome, qui subsistera toujours pendant que Mrs. nos Ministres défendront la puissance Ecclésiastique & l'Excommunication, qui sont les deux piliers qui soûtiennent son injuste Monarchie. Du moins, Mr. je ne croiray pas avoir perdu le peu de temps que j'ay employé à vous faire cette Lettre si elle sert à m'acquérir quelque part à vos bonnes graces, & à vous persuader que je suis avec autant de respect que de sincérité,
units.tr: But, Sir, I must not let my pleasure in conversing with you make me tiresome. I perhaps notice this a little too late, since I see that instead of a letter I have written you a little book, and I am all the less excusable because a judge as enlightened as you needs few words. Yet I do not address you only as my judge; in your person I seek a partner who will join me in dealing a last blow to the Bishop of Rome, who will survive for as long as our ministers defend ecclesiastical power and excommunication, which are the two pillars that support his unjust monarchy. At the least, Sir, I will not think I have wasted the little time I spent writing this letter to you, if it wins me some place in your good graces and persuades you that I am, with as much respect as sincerity,

units.la: Monsieur,
units.tr: Sir,

units.la: Vostre très-humble & très-obéissant Serviteur
units.tr: Your most humble and most obedient servant,

units.la: Loüis du Moulin.
units.tr: Louis du Moulin.

units.la: Nobili & Reverendo Viro D. Davidi Primirosio, Pastori Ecclesiae Gallo- Londinensis, S.
units.tr: To the noble and reverend man, Mr. David Primerose, minister of the French Church in London, greetings.

units.la: SÆpenumerò, vir Reverende, me interpellavisti de schedula viri Clarissimi D.Edoardi Stillingflit (merito suo Celeberrimi propter acre ingenium, eruditionem, cujus est celerior cursus quam ætatis, & luculenta scripta publici juris facta) de Excommunicatione instar mantissæ Irenico suo adjuncta: in quâ, cum iisdem hypothesibus, quibus insisto in Parænesi mea, Jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam profligasset; imo è medio sustulisset, adeoque ejus propaginem Excommunicationem eâdem ruinâ involvisset; nec inter hæc placeret ceret certet Irenicum Viris Principibus de Hierarchia sua, apud quos gratiam & sacerdotia aucupabatur, & quibus imprimis Excommunicatio est fructuosa, commodum existimavit, è visceribus Parentis, seu Jurisdictionis Ecclesiasticæ, fœtum in vitæ & mortis confinio adhuc spirantem extrahere, quem foveret & aleret absque uberibus Matris, in spem ut vitalis foret, assurgeret, & aliquando in pedes insisteret. Sæpenumeró, inquam, submonuisti & edixisti, hactenus à me parata arma, & nomine tenus decretoria esse in Potestatem Ecclesiasticam, quandiu intacta & inviolata remaneret excommunicatio per quaternionem illum cartæ, nec ullo Scripto contrario à me refelli posset, propter argumenta, tuo judicio usque adeo cogentia, quibus Doctor Stillingflit Excommunicationem asserit & astruit, ut ad pallnodiam quemquam qui esset author Paranæseos adigerent, meque imprimis cogerent retractare verba quæ non semel tibi protuli & affirmavi, non sine offensa Celeberrimi Claudii, scilicet, siquidem Excommunicatio non effet institutio Evangelica, sed merum & figmentum humanum & terriculamentum sesquipedalis vocabuli, ut est Transubstantiatio & Batrochomyomachia, par esse ut Antistes qui præest sacris, in synaxi prævia celebrationi Eucharistiæ, non ulterius dicat se excommunicare impios, idololatras, hæreticos authoritate & in nomine Jesu Christi, sed potius, authoritate & in-nomine Johannis Calvini, nisi malit totam pericopen transilire, de Excommunicandis illis, qui longo ordine ibi recensentur, homines vitæ projectæ ad vitia & scelera. Nam insuper optarem ut eraderetur è confessione nostra articulus 33. quo dicitur Excommunicatio res bona, & in Ecclesia retinenda. Certè Presbyteriani Angli, volunt non solum esse bonum & sanctum institutum, sed & ad salutem perinde necessarium, atque verbum & sacramenta, verba sunt in suo Dissensu à fratribus Independentibus pag. 63. Excommunicatio recipi debet ut salvifica animarum institutio facta à Jesu Christo, non minus quam verbum & sacramenta, Anglicè, Excommunication should be embraced as a Soul saving Ordinance of Jesus Christ, as well as the Word and the Sacraments. Adhæc horrui & steterunt comæ, ut qui non dubitem affirmare Excommunicationem non solum esse vanam, futilem & inutilem censuram, sed & perniciosam, & tam absurdè Potestatem quæ eam peperit dici Ecclesiasticam & Spiritualem, quàm illa authoritas quam adhibent medici, fabri, mercatores in ordinandis suæ societatis rebus diceretur Potestas Medica, fabrilis & mercatoria: sed hæc obiter. Decumbit mihi probare quàm innocentes sint tibicines, quàm fluxa argumenta quibus Doctor Stillingfleet suam Excommunicationem succollat: Nam audacter dixerim tam infirmis præsidiis & argumentis defendi Excommunicationem à Clarissimo Anglo, quàm tribunal Ecclesiasticum inter Reformatos conatur astruere vir longè illustris, isque Gallus, Marcus Antonius Bastidius: ita tamen ut nec hic, nec ille laborent defectu aut ingenii, aut eruditionis, quæ utrisque supersunt, imo superfluunt, sed infirmitate causæ.
units.tr: Very often, Reverend Sir, you have pressed me about the little paper of the most distinguished Mr. Edward Stillingfleet, famous for his sharp wit and learning, whose progress has outrun his years, and whose brilliant writings have been published. It concerns the excommunication he appended, as a supplement, to his Irenicum. In it, using the same hypotheses on which I rely in my Parænesis, he had overthrown ecclesiastical jurisdiction, or rather removed it altogether, so that excommunication, its offspring, was buried in the same ruin. Nor, given all this, was it pleasing to the Irenicum (which in its account of hierarchy sought favour and clerical offices from the princes, for whom excommunication is especially profitable). He thought it fitting to draw out of the womb of its parent, that is, ecclesiastical jurisdiction, an offspring still breathing on the border of life and death, which he could cherish and nourish without a mother's breast, hoping that it might survive, rise up, and at last stand on its feet. Often, I say, you have warned me and declared that the arms I have so far prepared are, in name at least, decisive against ecclesiastical power, as long as excommunication, set out in that quire of paper, remains untouched and unviolated, and cannot be refuted by any contrary writing. You say the arguments by which Doctor Stillingfleet asserts and establishes excommunication are so compelling in your judgement that they would force anyone who is the author of the Parænesis to retract, and above all would compel me to take back words I have more than once stated to you and affirmed, not without offence to the most famous Claudius. Namely, that if excommunication is not an evangelical institution, but a mere human invention and a bugbear of a long-winded word, like transubstantiation and the Batrachomyomachia, then it is fitting that the minister who presides over the sacred rites, in the preparatory service before the celebration of the Eucharist, should no longer say that he excommunicates the impious, idolaters and heretics by the authority and in the name of Jesus Christ, but rather by the authority and in the name of John Calvin, unless he prefers to skip the whole passage about those to be excommunicated, which lists in a long sequence there the men of abandoned life, given to vices and crimes. Moreover, I would wish that the thirty-third article of our Confession, which says that excommunication is a good thing and to be retained in the Church, were erased. Certainly the English Presbyterians want excommunication not only to be a good and holy institution, but also as necessary to salvation as the Word and the sacraments. Their words in their Dissent from the Independent brethren, page 63, are: Excommunication should be embraced as a Soul saving Ordinance of Jesus Christ, as well as the Word and the Sacraments. Hearing this, my hair stood on end. I do not hesitate to affirm that excommunication is not only a vain, trifling and useless censure, but also a harmful one, and that it is as absurd to call the power that gave birth to it ecclesiastical and spiritual as it would be to call the authority which doctors, smiths and merchants exercise in arranging the affairs of their guilds a medical, smithy or mercantile power. But these are incidental remarks. It remains for me to show how harmless these pipers are, and how weak the arguments by which Doctor Stillingfleet props up his excommunication. For I will boldly say that excommunication is defended by the most distinguished Englishman with as feeble supports and arguments as those with which the far more illustrious Frenchman, Marc Antoine de Bastide, tries to establish an ecclesiastical tribunal among the Reformed. Yet neither of them labours under a lack of wit or learning, which both possess in abundance, indeed in excess, but under the weakness of their cause.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: 1. Porro noster Anglus unâ chordâ oberrat & perpetuo paralogismo suum opusculum texit, per indiligentiam, ne dicam ignorationem inquirendi in naturam & authoritatis & Ecclesiae. Fingit nobis authoritatem mediam, inter authoritatem persuasionis quae est consilii & declaratio sententiae & animi suggerentis, quid facto cuipiam opus sit, quid justum, quid æquum, quid rebus ipsius conducat, & sit conveniens; & authoritatem jurisdictionis, seu coactionis & Magistraturae, quae sit imperando, vetando, cogendo, puniendo; per quam mediam potestatem, vult unamquamque Ecclesiam particularem Excommunicare impium; cum tamen, non sacra Scriptura, non ars, ingenium, sapientia humana; non: Jurisconsulti, Patres, non Theologi, seu Protestantes, seu Pontificii, non experientia omnium seculorum, non hodierna, possint edere, nisi duas vias, per quas & homo ad aliquid agendum, dicendum, ferendum adducatur, vel qui sunt sub Potestate, cives, liberi, uxores, servi exsequantur, id quod illa potestas jubet, aut fieri cupit. Certè probi authores, seu profani, seu Sacri, Græci, Latini, nullum unquam interposuerunt medium consilio & imperio. Dominus Jesus non alios, in epulis quas celebravit sibi adjunxit convivas præter illos aut quibus persuasit, aut quos compulit intrare. S. Petrus 1 Epist. cap. 5. v. 2. & 3. vult omnia peragi in Ecclesia non imperio, sed exemplo, non cogendo Dominorum modo, sed voluntatem flectendo, ut quis ultro, ex nolente fiat volens. Jus canonicum ubique nobis ponit duos gladios, alterum Spiritūs & Verbi, alterum materiale, quod est Potestatis secularis. Synodus Parisiensis sexta, diserte affirmat intra Ecclesiam duas solummodo authoritates conspici & vigere; alteram per doctrinæ sermonem, alteram per disciplinæ terrorem, hanc ascribit Magistratui & Potestati seculari illam sacerdoti. Rivetus duas hasce vias tradit, tom. I. p. 1371, & 1374. unam hortando, monendo, movendo & permovendo, & fit à Ministro; alteram imperando & cogendo, per Magistratum. Calvinus ipse Excommunicationis acerrimus vindex idem putat. Si quis (inquit in disciplina Genevensi inter epistolas pag. 125.) contumaciter spreto consistorii judicio ad mensam sacram se ingerat, repellatur à ministro: nempe vir magnus existimavit Excommunicationis sententiam, merè consilium esse, aut verba incassum aerem ferientia, ut sunt animi & sententiæ declarationes, nisi accedat coercitio.
units.tr: 1. Further, our Englishman wanders with one string and weaves his little work from a constant paralogism, through carelessness, not to say ignorance, of inquiring into the nature of authority and of the Church. He invents for us an intermediate authority, between the authority of persuasion, which is that of counsel and the declaration of an opinion and mind suggesting what someone needs to do, what is just, what is fair, what is advantageous and fitting for his affairs, and the authority of jurisdiction, or coercion and magistracy, which consists in commanding, forbidding, compelling and punishing. By this intermediate power he wants each particular Church to excommunicate the wicked. Yet neither Holy Scripture, nor art, nor talent, nor human wisdom, nor the jurists, nor the Fathers, nor the theologians, whether Protestant or Papist, nor the experience of all ages, nor that of our own day, can produce anything but two ways by which a man is brought to act, speak or endure something, namely, either those under power, citizens, free men, wives and slaves carry out what that power orders or wishes done. Certainly the good authors, whether secular or sacred, Greek or Latin, never interposed any intermediate means between counsel and command. The Lord Jesus did not admit to the feasts he celebrated any guests other than those whom he had either persuaded or compelled to come in. St Peter, 1 Epistle, chapter 5, verses 2 and 3, wants everything in the Church done not by command but by example, not by lording it over people but by bending their will, so that someone who was unwilling becomes willing of his own accord. Canon law everywhere gives us two swords, one of the Spirit and the Word, the other material, which belongs to secular power. The Sixth Synod of Paris expressly affirms that within the Church only two authorities are seen and operate: one through the speech of doctrine, the other through the terror of discipline; it ascribes the second to the magistrate and secular power, and the first to the priest. Rivet hands down these two ways, vol. I, pp. 1371 and 1374: one by exhorting, admonishing, moving and persuading, which is done by the minister; the other by commanding and compelling, through the magistrate. Calvin himself, the fiercest champion of excommunication, thinks the same. If anyone (he says in the Genevan discipline among his letters, p. 125) stubbornly ignores the judgment of the consistory and thrusts himself into the holy table, let him be repelled by the minister. Clearly that great man thought that the sentence of excommunication was merely counsel, or words beating empty air, like declarations of mind and opinion, unless coercion were added.

units.la: 2. Percurrantur omnes hominum societates, cœtus, synodi, collegia, mirum ni in singulis duæ authoritates sint conspicuæ; una functionis, peritiæ, sententiæ animi & consilii, per quam uni cuique in sua arte perito, multum tribuimus, & viro senatoriæ gravitatis etiam in vultu & verbis fides est & authoritas; altera jurisdictionis, coercitionis, Magistraturæ. Episcopus in Synodo, putà Constantinopolitana, contra Macedonium, sententiam fert pro peritia, & functione sacra in gratiam orthodoxæ fidei exeritque primæ classis authoritatem. Sed se aggregat & concedit in majorem numerum qui vincit Macedonios Episcopos numero tantum triginta quinque, non per primam authoritatis classem sed per secundam, nec in illa Synodo exerit quam vir doctus mediam potestatem fingit.
units.tr: 2. Let us run through all human societies, assemblies, synods and colleges. In each of them, surely, two authorities are visible. One belongs to office, skill, judgement and counsel: by it we give much weight to each person expert in his own art, and a man of senatorial dignity also commands trust and authority in his face and words. The other belongs to jurisdiction, coercion and magistracy. A bishop in a synod, for instance the Constantinopolitan one against Macedonius, pronounces sentence by virtue of his expertise and sacred office, for the sake of orthodox faith, and exercises the authority of the first class. But he joins and yields to the greater number, which defeats the Macedonian bishops, who were only thirty-five. He does this not by the first class of authority but by the second, and in that synod he does not exercise the "middle power" which the learned man imagines.

units.la: 3. Non facit ad rem quod multis verbis conare probare conatur, Ecclesiam realiter distinctam esse à republica, adeoque donatam à Christo authoritate ut res suas seorsim ageret & ordinaret; fideles in suum coetum admitteret, impios & ἀπίστους pelleret. Nam una quidem ratione, (& unà tantum) differt Ecclesia à republica, ut quando tot Christiani conveniunt in unum locum ad audiendum verbum & participanda sacramenta. Sub hacce ratione ipsa respublica & qui ad ejus sedent clavum, concedunt in formam Ecclesiæ & Stationem tenent fidelium ut minimi de plebe Christiana, tenentur juxta se morigeros præstare hortationibus imo imperiis pastorum. Per quam quidem Ecclesiæ acceptionem, verius dicitur & locutione aptiore rempublicam esse in Ecclesia, quam Ecclesiam esse in republica, ut loquitur Optatus Milevitanus. At per alteram rationem, quatenus Episcopi Presbyteri, teri, seniores & primores de plebe Christiana coeunt in consistorium, aut synodum, & conficiunt, ut volunt Ecclesiam representativam; tum ejusmodi Ecclesia non differt a republica, sed induit naturam communem omnibus coetibus, civilibus, politicis, ut sunt hæteriæ fratrum, vicinorum, opificum mercatorum; collegia Medicorum, Philosophorum : confessus senatorum & virorum militarium, in quibus conspicua est duplex authoritas, altera functionis & peritiæ; altera jurisdictionis & Magistraturæ, nec refert utrum nec ne, hæc Ecclesia sit collecta sub Magistratu infenso & heterodoxo, an vero sub amico & orthodoxo & cui res Ecclesiæ sunt cordi; nam utrobique Ecclesia ejusmodi non differt a republica, vigetque in ea Magistratura, seu delegata ab amico Magistratu, seu assumpta per disciplinam confœderatam, ut non opus sit potestatem ligandi & solvendi, nec non claves regni cælorum accersere in auxilium, unius Magistraturæ potius quam alterius. Nec hic se infert viri docti media potestas, ut nec minus se exerit in illa Ecclesia duplex authoritas, at nulla Excommunicandi potestas, nisi sit essectus unius aut alterius authoritatis: hoc est aut primae, aut secundae classis.
units.tr: 3. It is beside the point that he labours with many words to prove that the Church is really distinct from the commonwealth, and so was endowed by Christ with authority to conduct and order its own affairs separately: to admit the faithful into its assembly and to expel the impious and unbelievers [ἀπίστους]. For the Church differs from the commonwealth in one respect only, namely when so many Christians gather in one place to hear the Word and partake of the sacraments. In this respect the commonwealth itself, and those who sit at its helm, yield to the form of the Church and take their place as the humblest of the Christian people, bound to obey the exhortations and even the commands of the ministers. In this sense of the Church, it is more truly and more aptly said that the commonwealth is in the Church than that the Church is in the commonwealth, as Optatus of Milevis puts it. But in the other respect, insofar as bishops, presbyters, elders and leading men of the Christian people meet in a consistory or synod and form what they wish to call a representative Church, such a Church does not differ from the commonwealth. It takes on the common nature of all civil and political assemblies, such as the brotherhoods of kinsmen, neighbours, craftsmen and merchants, the colleges of physicians and philosophers, and the meetings of senators and military men. In all of these a twofold authority is evident: one of office and skill, the other of jurisdiction and magistracy. It makes no difference whether this Church is gathered under a hostile and heterodox magistrate or under a friendly and orthodox one who has the affairs of the Church at heart. In either case such a Church does not differ from the commonwealth, and in it a magistracy flourishes, either delegated by a friendly magistrate or assumed through a confederated discipline. So there is no need to summon the power of binding and loosing, or the keys of the kingdom of heaven, as an aid to one magistracy rather than the other. Nor does the learned man's "middle power" arise here. In that Church the twofold authority exerts itself no less, yet there is no power of excommunication unless it is the effect of one or the other authority, that is, of the first or the second class.

units.la: 4. Sane vir doctus Irenic. pag. 41. nullum relinquit locum potestati mediae per quam impius, aut arceatur sacris, aut coetu moveatur per Excommunicationem; ibi enim distincte edit nobis duas classes authoritatis in Ecclesia, vel intra Ecclesiam.
units.tr: 4. Certainly the learned man, in his Irenicum, p. 41, leaves no room for a middle power by which the impious man is either barred from the sacred things or removed from the assembly by excommunication. For there he plainly sets before us two classes of authority, within the Church or in the Church.

units.la: Distinguere debemus inter potestatem externam seu objectivam circa materiam religionis, & internam & formalem: hanc vocant elicitivam & potestatem ordinis: illam imperativam seu jurisdictionis, quae est potestas Ecclesiastica, ut altera est circa Ecclesiastica: duae illae potestates ponuntur diserte & distincte a Constantino magno apud Eusebium; altera τῆς ἐκκλησίας, altera τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν: interna formalis & elicitiva potestas, quae est ordinis consistit in authoritate & exercitio functionis ministerialis in praedicando & administrandis sacramentis: altera externa objectiva seu imperativa quae est jurisdictionis consistit in provisu, defensione & protectione ac propagatione religionis, prima ad solos ministros pertinet, secunda ad supremum Magistratum: per eam distinctionem intelligere possumus & solvere hancce quaestionem tantopere & tam diu agitatam: circa mutuam subordinationem potestatis civilis & Ecclesiasticae, nam ut ait Petrus Martyr, hae duae potestates sunt quodammodo antisegu& variis modis circa unum versantur: neque enim est Pastorum jus dicere & justitiam administrare, sed jus & justitiam declarare ut rite administretur. Vice versa non debet Magistratus concionari & administrare sacramenta, sed curare debet ut non desint qui illis muneribus defungantur.
units.tr: We must distinguish between external or objective power concerning the matter of religion, and internal and formal power. The latter they call elicitive and the power of order; the former they call imperative or of jurisdiction, which is ecclesiastical power, just as the other is concerned with ecclesiastical matters. These two powers are stated expressly and distinctly by Constantine the Great in Eusebius: one of the Church [τῆς ἐκκλησίας], the other of the churches [τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν]. The internal, formal and elicitive power, which belongs to order, consists in the authority and exercise of the ministerial function in preaching and administering the sacraments. The other, external, objective or imperative power, which belongs to jurisdiction, consists in the provision, defence, protection and propagation of religion. The first pertains to the ministers alone, the second to the supreme magistrate. By this distinction we can understand and resolve the question that has been argued so much and for so long: the mutual subordination of civil and ecclesiastical power. For, as Peter Martyr says, these two powers are in a way correlative and are occupied with one thing in various ways. It is not the right of the ministers to pronounce law and administer justice, but to declare law and justice so that it may be rightly administered. Conversely, the magistrate ought not to preach and administer the sacraments, but ought to see to it that there are not lacking those who discharge those offices.

units.la: 5. Longus hic Sermo, nec decurtatus per ἀπόσπασμα nec aliorsum tractus totam dissertatiunculam Excommunicatoriam viri docti convellit & diruit: imprimis destruit potestate millam mediam, quae nec est potestas verbi nec potestas Magistratus, aut saltem non est potestas quae supplet locum & officium Magistratus: Namque clare diserte & expressim, duas nobis intra Ecclesiam exhibet potestates juxta Synodum Parisiensem sextam, alteram per doctrinæ sermonem, alteram per disciplinæ terrorem; alteram pertinentem ad sacerdotes Dei, ut loquitur synodus, alteram ad Potestates seculares, seu Principes populi. Id quoque est notandum in viri docti sermone, quod censeat potestatem quæ res externas ordinat in Ecclesia, & quæ perperam dicitur Ecclesiastica, pertinere ad Magistratum & si cuiquam duarum harumce potestatum ascribenda sit potestas Excommunicandi, ascribendam esse Magistratui seu potestati, analogæ potestati Magistratus intra Ecclesiam: hic tamen te submonebo obiter virum doctum paulo minus tribuere potestatis Ministris Evangelicis quam tribuo & tribuere soleo & æquum puto: nam præterquam quod integram illis potestatem tribuam, quæ est functionis & ordinis, insuper æquam & eandem quæ est jurisdictionis ascribam illis potestatem, quæ sacerdotibus attributa erat; non quidem quâ sacerdotibus & functione sacra præditis, sed quâ principibus populi. Hic observandum quod vir doctus, seorsim incedat & abeat ab omnibus Protestantibus, imo à suis
units.tr: 5. This long discourse, neither cut short by a fragment nor dragged elsewhere, overthrows and demolishes the learned man's little treatise on excommunication. Above all it destroys the middle power, which is neither the power of the Word nor the power of the magistrate, or at least is not a power that supplies the place and office of the magistrate. For he clearly and expressly sets before us two powers within the Church, following the Sixth Synod of Paris: one through the preaching of doctrine, the other through the terror of discipline; the one pertaining to the priests of God, as the synod says, the other to the secular powers, or princes of the people. This also is to be noted in the learned man's discourse: he thinks that the power which orders external matters in the Church, and which is wrongly called ecclesiastical, belongs to the magistrate; and if the power of excommunication is to be ascribed to either of these two powers, it is to be ascribed to the magistrate, or to a power analogous to the power of the magistrate within the Church. Here, however, I will briefly warn you that the learned man attributes a little less power to the evangelical ministers than I do, and than I am accustomed to, and think fair. For besides granting them the whole power that belongs to function and order, I also ascribe to them, in equal measure, that same power of jurisdiction which was attributed to priests: not indeed as priests endowed with sacred function, but as princes of the people. Here it is to be observed that the learned man goes his own way and departs from all Protestants, even from his own

units.la: Note: the catchword "An-" is the start of the next page, as printed at the foot.
units.tr: Catchword: the word "An-" is the start of the next page, as printed at the foot.

units.la: Anglis, qui volunt orbem Christianum regi per tres Potestates, unam merè spiritualem quæ est verbi in corda hominum ; secundam, quæ dicitur Ecclesiastica, quæ tribuitur viris de sacro ordine in regimine externo Ecclesiæ, tertiam quæ est politica pertinens ad Magistratum. Primam agnoscit vir doctus, sed secundam & tertiam tribuit Magistratui, ut jam nullum locum det protestati suæ mediæ secundum hoc Potestatum diagramma.
units.tr: English, who want the Christian world to be ruled by three powers: one purely spiritual, which is that of the Word in the hearts of men; a second, called ecclesiastical, which is given to men of sacred order in the external governance of the Church; and a third, which is political and belongs to the magistrate. The learned man acknowledges the first, but assigns the second and third to the magistrate, so that according to this diagram of powers he leaves no place at all for his middle power.

units.la: 6. Porro quod Ecclesia (de illa loquor quam representativam vocant) quod consistorium, synodus constans ex Episcopis, Presbyteris, seu Ministris, & ex senioribus differant à republica, id factum est per hominum improbitatem, præsertim per typhum, & ambitionem cleri annitentis sibi imperium struere in imperio alieno, & in capita Regum & Magistratuum ; eaque tela, quæ texi cœpit tempore Pauli à fabris mysterii iniquitatis, contra morem & praxim Ecclesiæ Dei per quatuor millia annorum ante adventum Christi : namq; toto hoc tempore, Ecclesia & Respublica, unum erat corpus, unus erat decalogus, una norma & regula morum, fixa & praescripta sacerdotibus, Principibus populi & ipsi populo. Una erat juridictio, unum tribunal. Ipsi Sacerdotes & Levitæ æquas habebant partes in Magistratura & ex æquo erant custodes utriusque tabulæ: Synagoga erat tam Ecclesia quam coetus juridicus & politicus, in quo homines iidem qui vacabant verbo & orationi, dirimebant lites inter fratres & de omni causa cognoscebant; ut jam si Excommunicatio fuit in usu, quod tamen non credo fuisse liberâ republicâ, tum non magis esset actus Ecclesiæ quam reipublicæ. Illa distinctio Ecclesiæ à republica, & discrepantia legum Ecclesiasticarum à civilibus, Jurisdictionis Ecclesiasticæ à politicis, tribunalis virorum sacri ordinis à tribunali laicæ gentis ædificavit imperium in imperio, & implevit mysterium iniquitatis, sed defuit ars Cuforibus mysterii, per quam peritè esset dicotomia, decalogorum & Evangeliorum atque Jurisdictionum & tribunalium, ut unus esset fixus decalogus, unumque Evangelium viris de sacro ordini, at unus juxta decologus unumque Evangelium laicæ nationi. Illæ fuerunt satanæ & mysterii iniquitatis profunditates & abyssi quos opposuit satan festinanti Evangelio se diffundere in totum orbem, nam sedulò cavit impurus dæmon ne ejusmodi remorà sufflaminerentur tot Ethnicorum religiones, nihil enim magis impedivisset religiones Ethnicorum pervagare gentes & nationes, quam si sacerdotibus & mystis sua jurisdictio separatim suisset attributa distincta à Jurisdictione civili & politica: namque (ut accidit inter Christianos) Jurisdictionum collisio & conflictus potuisset parere odium Paganæ religionis & animum divertendi ad alias religiones; inter quas forsan placuisset fides Christi, licet displicuisset eadem tribunalium & Jurisdictionum distinctio. Certè cum satan tot religiones commendaverit Ethnicis, in nulla tamen excogitavit dividere Jurisdictiones & tribunalia; nec fuit intellecta illa distinctio priusquam una cum mysterio iniquitatis exoriretur Christiana religio. Cum Ethnici haberent suos Pontifices, Sacerdotes, Auspices, Aruspices, Augures, funĉtione distinĉtos à muneribus civilis politiæ, imo haberent suum summum Pontificem qui præsset sacris illis; nulla tamen inter eos suit distinĉtio Jurisdiĉtionum, unius quidem quæ præesset religioni & ceremoniis, alterius quæ reipublicæ.
units.tr: 6. Furthermore, that the Church (I speak of what they call the representative Church), that is, the consistory and the synod made up of bishops, presbyters or ministers, and elders, differs from the commonwealth: this has come about through human wickedness, above all through the pride and ambition of the clergy, who strive to build for themselves a dominion within another's dominion, and over the heads of kings and magistrates. These weapons, which began to be woven in Paul's time by the craftsmen of the mystery of iniquity, are contrary to the custom and practice of God's Church for four thousand years before the coming of Christ. For throughout all that time the Church and the commonwealth were one body, one decalogue, one norm and rule of morals, fixed and prescribed for priests, princes of the people and the people itself. There was one jurisdiction, one tribunal. The priests and Levites themselves had equal parts in the magistracy and were equally guardians of both tables. The synagogue was as much a church as a judicial and political assembly, in which the same men who devoted themselves to the word and prayer settled disputes between brothers and took cognizance of every cause. So if excommunication was in use, which however I do not believe was the case in a free commonwealth, then it was no more an act of the Church than of the commonwealth. That distinction of Church from commonwealth, and the disagreement of ecclesiastical laws from civil laws, of ecclesiastical jurisdiction from political, of the tribunal of men of sacred order from the tribunal of the lay people, built an empire within an empire and fulfilled the mystery of iniquity. But the craftsmen of that mystery lacked the skill by which the dichotomy of decalogues and gospels, and of jurisdictions and tribunals, might be skilfully managed, so that there would be one fixed decalogue and one gospel for men of sacred order, and yet one decalogue and one gospel for the lay nation. These were the depths and abysses of Satan and of the mystery of iniquity, which Satan set against the Gospel hastening to spread through the whole world. For the impure demon took care that the religions of so many Gentiles should not be hindered by such a check, since nothing would have impeded the religions of the Gentiles from spreading among peoples and nations more than if separate jurisdiction had been assigned to priests and initiates, distinct from civil and political jurisdiction. For (as happens among Christians) a collision and conflict of jurisdictions could have bred hatred of the pagan religion and an inclination to turn to other religions, among which perhaps the faith of Christ might have pleased, although the same distinction of tribunals and jurisdictions would have displeased. Certainly, though Satan commended so many religions to the Gentiles, he never devised dividing jurisdictions and tribunals. Nor was that distinction understood before the Christian religion arose together with the mystery of iniquity. Although the Gentiles had their pontiffs, priests, auspices, haruspices and augurs, distinguished in function from the offices of civil polity, and indeed had their supreme pontiff who presided over those rites, yet among them there was no distinction of jurisdictions: one which presided over religion and ceremonies, and another which presided over the commonwealth.

units.la: Innotuit viro emunĉtæ naris & solertiæ sagacissimæ & Imposturarum Romanensium probè gnaro, authori tractatus longè doĉtissimi, cæterum partibus Hierarchiæ Anglicanæ addiĉtissimo & quem quidam volunt fuisse Episcopum; innotuit, inquam illi hæc fraus & impostura distinĉtionis Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ, ut duo in uno territorio erigerentur tribunalia, vultque per eam distinĉtionem Papam introduĉtum fuisse in orbem Christianum, cum dicit libro cui titulus Episcopalis hæreditas, Dogma esse Pontificium afferere quod respublica discrepet ab Ecclesia. Integrum locum habeo in Epistola ad Reverendum Mussardum. Hæc si sunt verissima, perinde nihil erit ad quam, ad hanc vel illam vir doĉtus referat & ascribat potestatem Excommunicandi, cum utrobique non major futura fit discrepantia inter Ecclesiam & Rempublicam Christianam quam inter hominem & animal rationale, adeoque nullum sit medium inter duo quæ unum & idem sunt.
units.tr: A man of keen judgement and sharp skill, well versed in Roman impostures, the author of a very learned treatise but otherwise fully devoted to the party of the English Hierarchy, and whom some believe to have been a bishop, has come to know, I say, this fraud and imposture of distinguishing Church and commonwealth, so that two tribunals are set up in one territory. He holds that the Pope was introduced into the Christian world through this distinction, when he says in the book entitled Episcopal Inheritance: It is a Papist dogma to assert that the commonwealth differs from the Church. I have the full passage in my letter to the Reverend Mussard. If these things are most true, then it will make no difference to which of the two a learned man refers and ascribes the power of excommunicating, since on either view there will be no greater difference between the Church and the Christian commonwealth than between man and rational animal, and so there is no middle ground between two things that are one and the same.

units.la: 8. Addo, siquidem omnes nostræ actiones voluntariæ, cogitata, dicta, facta, artes, sententiæ, negotia publica, privata, tendere & collimare debeant ad spiritualem finem, dicente Paulo, si editis, bibitis & quicquam agitis id fieri debere, habendo pro scopo & ultimo fine gloriam Dei & salutem animarum: tum siquidem unus est decalogus, una morum norma, una scriptura fixa omnibus hominibus cujusque sortis & stationis, par esse ut omnes cœtus hominum, Senatorum, Judicum, Philosophorum, Jurisconsultorum, Medicorum, Mercatorum, Opificum, tot sint Ecclesiæ Christianæ & eorum πολίτευμα, ut loquitur St. Paulus, sit virorum piorum & fidelium; ut jam si Excommunicatio est institutum Christi in Ecclesia usurpanda, utique sit actus cujusvis cœtus aut societatis quæ nomen Ecclesiæ usurpare debet, nec minor sit potestas medicorum excommunicandi, & arcendi quempiam de suo collegio, quam consistorii imo quam Ecclesiæ proprie dictæ, ad quam fideles conveniunt ad audiendum verbum,& participanda sacramenta, certè quam consistorii, quod sanè non est magis Ecclesia Christiana quam conventus Judicum & Senatorum,qui profitentur Christianam religionem, & ad quem non denegatur fieri congruè appellationem, hocce non minus quam illo tractante res quæ pertinent ad regnum cælorum; nec consistorio infligente censuram cuiquam, quâ Jure & merito plecti non possit judicio confessus Senatorum.
units.tr: 8. I add that, since all our voluntary actions, thoughts, words, deeds, arts, opinions, public and private affairs ought to aim at a spiritual end, as Paul says, "whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, it must be done" with the glory of God and the salvation of souls as the goal and final end; then, since there is one decalogue, one standard of morals, and one Scripture fixed for all men of every sort and station, it follows that all the assemblies of men (of senators, judges, philosophers, jurists, physicians, merchants, craftsmen) are as many Christian churches, and their commonwealth [πολίτευμα], as St. Paul calls it, is that of pious and faithful men. So if excommunication is an institution of Christ to be exercised in the Church, then surely it is the act of any assembly or society that ought to claim the name of Church. The power of physicians to excommunicate and exclude someone from their college is no less than that of the consistory, indeed no less than that of the Church properly so called, to which the faithful gather to hear the Word and partake of the sacraments. Certainly it is no less than that of the consistory, which is no more a Christian church than a gathering of judges and senators who profess the Christian religion, and to which it is not wrongly denied that appeal may be made, since it handles matters pertaining to the kingdom of heaven no less than the other does. Nor can the consistory inflict a censure on anyone whom the assembly of senators could not rightly and justly punish.

units.la: §. Et revera nulla est in Scriptura lex lata aut fixa consistorio potius quam Senatorum consessui, ut de disciplina Ecclesiæ aut de dignitate aut de indignitate ejus qui participet sacramenta, cognoscat, judicet & sententiam ferat, eoque minus si Excommunicatio non definitur per Scripturam quod potius debeat esse lex consistorii quam confessus civilis: verba sunt viri docti pag. 12. Irenici, hoc quod
units.tr: §. Indeed, there is no law in Scripture laid down or fixed for the consistory rather than for the assembly of senators, to inquire into, judge and pronounce sentence on church discipline, on the worthiness or unworthiness of one who partakes of the sacraments. Still less is this so if excommunication is not defined by Scripture, so that it ought to be a law of the consistory rather than of the civil assembly. These are the words of the learned man, page 12 of the Irenicum: What I must now

units.la: mihi nunc est illustrandum nullam legem tanquam universalem, fixam & permanentem quemquam Christianum obligare, nisi clarè & disertè pateat rem ita se habere ex instituto & voluntate Christi, ad eam subeundam usque ad finem mundi, hoc cum ita fit poterit homo dubitare usque ad finem mundi, non solùm an detur Excommunicatio, an à confessu virorum sacri ordinis, multò magis an à consistorio, an verò à consessu senatorum Excommunicari possit aut debeat, quandoquidem Scriptura de hoc nihil certi statuat, quin affirmet Calvinus dari pios & doctos viros qui existimant non esse necessariam Excommunicationem ubi Magistratus est Christianus, saltem si datur Excommunicatio satis esse si administretur à Magistratu ut affirmat Bullingerus.
units.tr: make clear is that no law, as universal, fixed and permanent, binds any Christian unless it is clearly and expressly evident that the matter stands so by the institution and will of Christ, to be undertaken until the end of the world. When this is so, a man may doubt until the end of the world not only whether there is excommunication at all, whether it is pronounced by the assembly of men of sacred office, much more whether by the consistory, or by the assembly of senators, and whether it can or should be pronounced by them; since Scripture settles nothing certain on this point. Indeed Calvin affirms that there are pious and learned men who think excommunication unnecessary where the magistrate is Christian, and Bullinger affirms that, if excommunication exists at all, it is sufficient if it is administered by the magistrate.

units.la: Et siquidem Excommunicatio refertur ad externa Ecclesiæ quæ non pertinent ad verbum, & sacramenta, & de illis externis statuere debeat Magistratus, ut docet vir doctus passim in suo Irenico ubi præsertim de re agitur de qua in scriptura nihil est diserè & expressè constitutum, non peccabit homo, si se subjicit legi excommunicatoriæ, ut legi latæ à Magistratu politico.
units.tr: And since excommunication relates to the external affairs of the Church, which do not pertain to the Word and the sacraments, and since the magistrate ought to decide on those external matters, as the learned man teaches throughout his Irenicum, especially where the matter is one on which Scripture has laid down nothing clearly and expressly, a man will not sin if he submits to an excommunicatory law as a law enacted by the civil magistrate.

units.la: 10 Nam si mandatum de excommunicando impio tam esset lex Divina, quam mandatum, non occides, tamen nulla ejus vis foret in foro humano priusquam sanciretur à Magistratu: si sancir debet à Magistratu aut à potestate analoga potestati Magistratus, ergo non est actus potestatis mediæ.
units.tr: 10. For if the command to excommunicate the wicked were as much a divine law as the command "you shall not kill," yet it would have no force in human courts until it was sanctioned by the magistrate. If it must be sanctioned by the magistrate, or by a power analogous to the power of the magistrate, then it is not an act of a middle power.

units.la: 11. Sed subit mirari quod vir doctus ascriptus ordinibus hierarchicorum, ascribat potestatem excommunicandi societati, contra morem & praximusurpatum inEcclesia sua, ubi unus homo seu singularis Episcopus, sola & propria authoritate excommunicat.
units.tr: 11. But it is surprising that the learned man, enrolled among the hierarchical orders, ascribes the power of excommunicating to a society, contrary to the custom and practice prevailing in his own Church, where one man, a single bishop, excommunicates by his sole and personal authority.

units.la: 12. Sed quid opus est Ecclesiæ particulari recurrere ad jus Divinum positivum, ut sibi comparet facultatem arcendi à se noxium aut malum, cum id datum sit omni Eteriæ, familiæ, societati de jure Divino naturali.
units.tr: 12. But there is no need for a particular Church to appeal to positive divine law in order to obtain for itself the power of removing what is harmful or evil to it, since this has been given to every family, household and society by natural divine law.

units.la: 13. Longum esset singula persequi in quibus ipse se non intelligit, & lectorem suum aut fatigat, aut circumscribit, saltem ducit per ambages & laborinthios: quod admittit certam fuisse Ecclesiastici regiminis & disciplinae formam in Ecclesia Judaica, at nullam penitus in Christiana, diruit omnia argumenta in gratiam excommunicationis: Nam apud quos ( qui habebant operosam, expressam disertamque disciplinam) nulla erat mentio Excommunicationis, multò minus statuenda apud eos qui nullam omnino habent disciplinae formam praescriptam. Et si apud Judaeos obtinuit disciplina Ecclesiastica certa & particulatim scripto consignata, absque tamen ulla jurisdictione Magistratus, multò minus censendum est in Ecclesia Christiana dari Jurisdictionem distinctam à civili, cujus nulla extat disciplinae forma & regula: nam congrueret cum ratione, ut certa & exacta disciplinae Ecclesiasticae forma, esset effectus potestatis Ecclesiasticae, cum tamen nulla inter Judaeos extaret potestas Ecclesiastica distincta à civili; at planè incongruum, absurdum & futile est statuere in Ecclesia Christiana potestatem Ecclesiasticam, ex instituto Christi distinctam à potestate Magistratûs, cujus tatamen nullus sit realis effectus, ut est præscriptio certæ & exactæ disciplinæ.
units.tr: 13. It would be long to follow each point, in which he does not understand himself, and which either wearies his reader or confines him, or at least leads him around in circles and labyrinths. He admits that there was a certain form of ecclesiastical government and discipline among the Jewish Church, but none at all in the Christian Church, and he overturns all arguments in favour of excommunication. For among those who had a laborious, explicit and clear discipline, there was no mention of excommunication, much less should it be laid down among those who have no prescribed form of discipline at all. And if among the Jews an ecclesiastical discipline held sway, certain and particularly recorded in writing, yet without any jurisdiction of the magistrate, it is much less to be thought that in the Christian Church there is a jurisdiction distinct from the civil one, of which no form or rule of discipline exists. For it would agree with reason that a certain and exact form of ecclesiastical discipline should be the effect of ecclesiastical power, whereas among the Jews there existed no ecclesiastical power distinct from the civil. But it is plainly incongruous, absurd and frivolous to establish in the Christian Church an ecclesiastical power, distinct from the power of the magistrate by Christ's institution, of which, nevertheless, there is no real effect, such as the prescription of a certain and exact discipline.

units.la: 14 Sed nihil tam evanidam reddit Excommunicationem, quam quod judicio viri docti nullo pede insistat: nam passim in sua schedula ponit formalem rationem excommunicationis in obligatione non externa parendi, sed interna, seu in fide conscientiæ quam sibi facit justam vel injustam esse Excommunicationem, qua assertione totam suæ schedulæ compagem discerpit, & in frusta concidit, quatenus validitas legis aut censuræ non pendet à legislatore, nec à Judice, sed à Reo & Testimonio de se interno: quod tamen testimonium cum sæpe non concordet cum declaratione facta à Pastore aut à Societate, nec id testimonium internum sit ab his notum nullibi comparebit Excommunicatio.
units.tr: 14. But nothing makes excommunication so empty as the fact that, in the judgement of the learned man, it rests on no foundation. For throughout his little pamphlet he places the formal reason of excommunication in an obligation that is not external, to obey, but internal, that is, in the faith of conscience which each man forms as to whether the excommunication is just or unjust. By this assertion he tears apart the whole fabric of his pamphlet and cuts it into pieces, insofar as the validity of a law or a censure depends not on the lawgiver, nor on the judge, but on the accused and on his inward testimony about himself. Yet since that testimony often does not agree with the declaration made by the minister or by the society, and since that inward testimony is not known to them, excommunication will appear nowhere at all.

units.la: 15 Nec minus diruitur per hanc agnitionem pag. 23. Schedulæ suæ, ubi ait sibi non constare an privatio ob crimen sit à communione, an vero à toto cœtu, & an excommunicatus sit exutus omnibus privilegiis, quæ concediuntur à societate, quandoquidem de ea re scriptura nihil certi constituerit. Sane qui hac in re haeret, & est pendulus, poterit totam fidem excommunicationis in dubium revocare, quo, & quo usque tendat & a quibus ferri debeat, an jure societatis communi omnibus societatibus, an vi clavium, & potestatis ligandi & solvendi; denique toto suae dissertatiunculae complexu quae est 30 paginarum, nihil solvit aut exolvit, ut merito quod in me jocatur retorquere queam, quasi meum aegrum privaverim facultate expultrice, conjecerimque in morbum quem vocamus miserere mei: nam contra, expeditissima per meas hypotheses est via ad cognoscendum, quid facto opus sit ad movendum aliquem, aut coetu aut communione, quod fit non recurrendo ad potestatem ligandi & solvendi, non ad internum testimonium quod cujusque conscientia sibi facit, sed ad potestatem Magistratus, quae in quaque Ecclesia particulari viget; ad quam vir doctus in exitu suae dissertatiunculae nolens volens recurrit, cum asseverit totam vim excommunicationis pendere a Magistratu, & ab eo rite &c. & recte fieri provocationem à sententia seu societatis, seu pastorum, haud absimilis Bellarmino, qui postquam diu disputavit de Justificatione, an per opera, an verò per fidem, claudit suam disputationem per illud Tutissimum, in solam Dei misericordiam recumbere.
units.tr: 15. Nor is it less overturned by the admission on page 23 of his pamphlet, where he says that he does not know whether deprivation for a crime means separation from communion or from the whole assembly, and whether the excommunicated person is stripped of all the privileges granted by the society, since Scripture has laid down nothing certain on this matter. Certainly, one who hesitates in this matter and wavers may call the whole faith in excommunication into doubt: to where and how far it extends, and by whom it ought to be pronounced, whether by the common right of all societies or by the power of the keys and of binding and loosing. In short, by the whole compass of his little dissertation, which runs to thirty pages, he loosens and resolves nothing. So I can fairly turn back the jest he makes against me, as if I had deprived my patient of the power of expulsion and thrown him into the disease we call "have mercy on me." For, on the contrary, by my hypotheses the way is most expedite to knowing what must be done to remove someone from an assembly or from communion. This is done not by appeal to the power of binding and loosing, nor to the inward testimony that each man's conscience makes for himself, but to the power of the magistrate, which prevails in each particular Church. To this power the learned man, in the conclusion of his little dissertation, willy-nilly has recourse, since he asserts that the whole force of excommunication depends on the magistrate, and that an appeal from the sentence, whether of the society or of the ministers, is properly and rightly made to him. In this he is not unlike Bellarmine, who, after disputing at length about justification, whether by works or by faith, closes his disputation with the safest course: to rest on the mercy of God alone.

units.la: Dum prelum fervet & laborant operæ typographorum, ad eum locum ubi excommunicationis futilitatem exculpo ex verbis viri docti, quod ejus inanis vis seu effectus sit, nisi accedat sanctio Magistratus, venit in mentem me nihil annotasse ad verba quæ subjungit, inde confici supremum Magistratum non posse comburi fulmine excommunicationis, sed eximi debere è numero eorum qui huic anathemati subjiciuntur, hic rogo cum supremus Magistratus perinde detur Genevæ, & in Hollandia, quam in Anglia, licet verò forsan ducenti aut trecenti; Et cum in Republica, puta Romana fieret provocatio ad populum tanquam ad supremum Magistratum, Rogo, inquam, an omnes Archontes, singuli an conjunctim liberi sunt à censura excommunicationis, eo quod sunt susupremus Magistratus. Et quandoquidem in regno Christi Mediatorio, nullus sit hominum ordo qui non subsit jugo Christi & Pastoris sui hortationibus, imo imperiis, adeoque censuræ, , non video cur qui tenetur esse pius & fidelis sive Rex, sive Imperator, si quid cessat in officio aut Regis aut fidelis, non tenetur subjici Pastoris ferulæ perinde ac minimus de plebe. Et si verba Christi; quicquid ligaveritis, &c. nec personam, nec rem excipiunt, mirum cur Rex se proripiat, ut exlex ex agmine rerum & personanarum: Et cum Rex non sit caput Ecclesiæ, quatenus est cœtus Christianorum & fidelium, non est putandum illum non subjici legibus societatis, eoque minus censendum, si ut vult vir doctus excommunicationis ratio formalis stat in interno sensu obligationis parendi.
units.tr: While the press is busy and the typesetters are at work, I have reached the place where I expose the futility of excommunication, taken from the learned man's words, that its empty force or effect depends on the sanction of the magistrate. It occurred to me that I had said nothing about the words he adds, that from this it follows that the supreme magistrate cannot be struck by the thunderbolt of excommunication but must be exempted from the number of those subject to this anathema. Here I ask: since the supreme magistrate is found just as much at Geneva and in Holland as in England, and perhaps there are two or three hundred of them, and since in a commonwealth, for example the Roman, appeal was made to the people as the supreme magistrate, I ask, I say, whether all the Archons, singly or together, are free from the censure of excommunication because they are the supreme magistrate. And since, in the mediatorial kingdom of Christ, there is no order of men that is not subject to the yoke of Christ and to the exhortations of their Pastor, indeed to his commands and therefore to his censures, I do not see why a king or emperor, who is bound to be pious and faithful, if he fails in his duty as king or as a believer, should not be bound to submit to the rod of the Pastor just as the humblest of the common people. And if the words of Christ, whatever you bind, etc., except neither person nor thing, it is strange that the king should slip away, like one outside the law, from the company of persons and things. And since the king is not the head of the Church, insofar as it is the assembly of Christians and believers, it must not be thought that he is not subject to the laws of the society, and it is still less to be judged so if, as the learned man wishes, the formal reason of excommunication consists in the inward sense of obligation to obey.

units.la: Porro postquam non semel hanc dissertatiunculam objecisti, quasi potestatem Ecclesiasticam, quam, non quatuor dies in fœtore sepulchri, sed viginti annos attineri mihi spondebam, videretur è mortuis excitasse, cujus judicio acerrimo perinde ac Tuo multum tribuebam, coepi apud me cogitare, si Excommunicatio lacertos movet, procul dubio vitae redonatam per miraculum à nemine praeterquam à Te & illo edendum. Sed perlectâ iterum atque iterum viri schedulâ, nihil ex ea exculpere potui quod non altius me firmaret in sententia pristina de futilitate Potestatis Ecclesiasticae. Ducit lectorem per ambages & labyrinthos, & sua sensa abscondit ne intelligantur, sepiae similis, quae succo atro ut est loliginis sic inficit aquam, ut nequeat deprehendi à Piscatore. Profecto de hoc viro pronunciare possum, idem quod de Arnaldo Sorbonilla, qui quandiu manus conseruit cum Jesuitis, adeoq; vindex fuit melioris causae, semper victoriam reportavit, & de adversariis triumphavit: At ubi adortus est Claudium, (sed quem virum!) hoc est ipsam veritatem Evangelicam, semper impar non solum causâ, sed & ingenio & argumentorum pondere recessit, usque adeo ut in lite contra Calvinistas ut vocat, plusquam infans desipere videretur: namin compositione Irenici, author author nobis exhibuit Judicium sub-actum & eruditionem congruentem veritati quam ibi asserit & astruit. At in structura differtatiunculae Excommunicatoriae, videtur oblitus suae, cum mentis, tum eruditionis, atque aliam personam agere, atque sustinuit cum Irenicum composuit: ut in eo dictum Sancti Pauli comprobetur, se nullis viribus pollere, nisi cum defendit veritatem. Quocirca hortor, ut te exolvas amore Ecclesiasticae potestatis, quam vides à praestantissimis ingeniis, ut est viri docti ingenium non aliis armis defendi quam plumbeis, & in nostram accedas sententiam, quae redonat suam cuique authoritatem: persuasionis quidem, & quae transfert à tenebris ad lucem, & à regno, satanae ad Deum verbi Dei Ministris; at Jurisdictionem quae punit vel in corpore, vel in ære, vel in fama, Magistratui, seu intra, seu extra Ecclesiam, ne forsan statuas Deum aliquem (sed qui non fuit Deus Abrahami, Isaaci, & Jacobi, nec Pater Domini nostri Jesu) qui de caelo descendens in montem expressim edicat mortalibus se cum publicavit legem gem de monte Sinai, Mosi, Juridictionem civilem & politicam, Aaroni vero Ecclesiasticam attribuisse: hanc quae Ecclesiasticis rebus & Ecclesiae: Illam quae civilibus & reipublicae, cum summo imperio praeesset, & postmodum sub Evangelio mentem summi legislatoris Christi itidem hanc fuisse, ut ad illum typum pastores Evangelici, & viri de Magistratura Jurisdictiones partirentur. Profecto Deus, seu sub lege, seu sub Evangelio, nullam authoritatem concessit sacrorum rerum administratoribus, praeter illam quae agit in corda, nec milit Ministros ut essent quasi Plenipotentiarii ut loquuntur: nec injunxit populis ut caeco judicio forent audientes dictis Pastorum suorum in omnibus & singulis quae praeciperent vel commendarent, sed semper modo & temperamento coercuit pruritum nationis sacrae assurgendi & excurrendi extra limites suos & transeundi a regno Christi mediatorio ad regnum Christi naturale, quemadmodum conqueruntur Patres in Synodo tertia oecumenica quae fuit Ephesina: nunquam jussit Deus ut particulatim, & & singula quæque imperata à Pastore præstarentur, nec Christus protulit verba ad ministros suos quos legimus dicitos à Virgine Maria Architriclino, facite quodcunque Iesus vobis dicet. Certè si semel in sacro Codice populus præcipitur ut Rectoribus suis obtemperent, vigesies instruitur ne cæcos Duces sequatur; probet spiritus, doctrinas scrutinet; optimam retineat; Caveat à lupis qui gregem absumunt, aut sub tegumento fidelium pastorum ambulant: atque uni animarum Pastori adhæreant Iesu Christo, imo se mancipet: & pro anathemate percussto habeat, etiam Apostolum, si prava docet; Tum ne fidat omnibus Pastoribus quorum nonnulli reipsa satanæ, speciem præbent Angelorum lucè & splendore coruscantium. Quid? quod pro uno loco ubi diserte agitur de Potestate pastorum in regimine externo Ecclesiæ; centum extant qui illam potestatem statuunt esse Spiritualem, quæ agit in corda, pungit & intima viscerum & adyta penetrat, tum illuminat, movet, permovet, suadet, persuadet; denique ad salutem perducit, non armis carnalibus, sed vi flexamina.
units.tr: Furthermore, since you have more than once objected to this little dissertation, as if it had raised up from the dead the ecclesiastical power, which I promised to keep alive not after four days in the stench of the tomb but for twenty years, and since I greatly valued your very keen judgement as well as his, I began to consider whether, if excommunication stirs his muscles, this power, restored to life by a miracle, is undoubtedly to be put forward by no one but you and him. But after reading the man's little pamphlet again and again, I could extract nothing from it that did not confirm me more deeply in my former opinion of the futility of ecclesiastical power. He leads the reader through ambages and labyrinths, and hides his meaning so that it cannot be understood, like the cuttlefish, which clouds the water with its black ink so that it cannot be detected by the fisherman. Certainly I can say of this man what I said of Arnauld of the Sorbonne: as long as he joined battle with the Jesuits, and so was the champion of the better cause, he always carried off the victory and triumphed over his opponents; but when he attacked Claude (and what a man he was!), that is, the very truth of the Gospel, he always withdrew, unequal not only in his cause but also in his wit and the weight of his arguments, to such a degree that in his dispute against the Calvinists, as he calls them, he seemed to talk nonsense more than an infant. For in the composition of the Irenicum the author showed us a judgement chastened and an erudition consistent with the truth that he there asserts and maintains. But in the construction of the excommunicatory dissertation he seems to have forgotten his own mind and learning, and to have played another part from the one he sustained when he composed the Irenicum; so that in him the saying of St. Paul is proved, that he has no power except when he defends the truth. Wherefore I urge you to free yourself from love of ecclesiastical power, which you see is defended by the most distinguished minds only with leaden weapons, since the learned man's talent is not armed with any other, and to come over to our opinion, which restores to each his own authority: to the ministers of the Word, the authority of persuasion, which turns people from darkness to light and from the kingdom of Satan to God; but to the magistrate, whether inside or outside the Church, the jurisdiction that punishes in body, in money, or in reputation. Lest perhaps you should imagine some God (who was not the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, nor the Father of our Lord Jesus), who, descending from heaven onto the mountain, openly declares to mortals that he has published the law from Mount Sinai, and that he gave civil and political jurisdiction to Moses, but ecclesiastical jurisdiction to Aaron: the latter for ecclesiastical matters and the Church, the former for civil matters and the commonwealth, since he presided over the supreme power; and that afterwards, under the Gospel, the mind of the supreme lawgiver Christ was likewise that the Evangelical pastors and the men of the magistracy should divide the jurisdictions after that type. Certainly God, whether under the law or under the Gospel, has granted no authority to the administrators of sacred things except that which works in the heart; nor did he send ministers who would be, as they say, plenipotentiaries; nor did he enjoin on the peoples that with blind judgement they should obey their pastors' words in all and each of the things that they commanded or recommended. He always restrained with measure and moderation the itch of the sacred nation to rise up and rush beyond its own limits and pass from the mediatorial kingdom of Christ to the natural kingdom of Christ, as the Fathers complained in the Third Ecumenical Synod, which was at Ephesus. God never commanded that each and every thing commanded by the pastor should be performed piece by piece, nor did Christ utter to his ministers the words that we read were spoken by the Virgin Mary to the head waiter: do whatever Jesus tells you. Certainly, if in the sacred Code the people is instructed on many occasions to obey its rulers, it is taught twenty times over not to follow blind leaders; to test the spirits and examine the doctrines; to hold fast what is best; to beware of wolves that devour the flock or walk under the cover of faithful pastors; and to cling to the one Pastor of souls, Jesus Christ, indeed to surrender himself to him; and to hold as accursed even an Apostle, if he teaches perverse things; and then not to trust all pastors, some of whom in reality present the appearance of the angels of Satan, flashing with light and splendour. What then?
